applications, where attack patterns are progressively sophisticated, quick, and adaptive [7]. Ensemble and hybrid models
have shown good predictive accuracy in intrusion detection,
but their static structure and offline training limit them. Fixed
combination weights or batch learning make these models less responsive to changing attack patterns or zero-day
threats. Studies have revealed that static ensemble techniques
cannot adapt to time-varying complex environments and lose
prediction power in new scenarios [8]. DRL allows agents
to interact with the environment, learn from delayed feedback, and adjust their policies in real time. Deep Q-Learning
(DQL) integrates numerous decision paths under uncertainty,
surpassing static ensemble models [9]. These qualities make
DRL ideal for hostile cybersecurity because threat surfaces
change quickly. The methodological foundation for adaptive
and autonomous intrusion detection in this study is DRL.
The Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and DQL
models are carefully tested to see how well they work.
The CIC-IDS2017 dataset is used as a standard for intrusion detection [10], [11]. Unlike many prior studies that
focus only on detecting known classes, this work systematically evaluates model performance under both familiar
and unfamiliar threat conditions, thereby highlighting the
generalization power of DRL. The tests evaluate model
effectiveness against both recognized attack types and novel
zero-day attacks. The results show that RF is the most accurate at finding known attack patterns, while DQL is better
at finding unknown attacks, such as zero-day threats and
known attacks. The study also examines the influence of
hyperparameter optimization on the efficacy of DRL-based
IDS. The experimental results show that improving factors
such as the learning rate, exploration strategy, and experience
replay buffer makes the DRL model much more flexible and accurate at detecting things. This multi-perspective
evaluation also contributes a reproducible framework for
assessing DRL-based models under evolving network conditions. Despite this, real-time applications face problems like
long training times and high computing costs that make them
impractical in high-speed network settings.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
• The DRL model employs a reward function that dynamically adjusts to evolving intrusion patterns, improving
its responsiveness to novel threats. Unlike traditional
ML models, DRL supports online learning, allowing
continuous parameter updates as new threats emerge in
real-time network environments.
• DRL
enhances
intrusion
detection
accuracy
and
real-time response capabilities by autonomously learning from network interactions and optimizing security
policies over time. The proposed DQL model achieves
10.7% higher F1-score than DT and 7.5% higher than
RF in zero-day attack detection on the CIC-IDS2017
dataset. This quantifies the model’s superior generalization capacity over widely used ML baselines.
• By systematically evaluating the strengths and limitations of DRL, RF, and DT models in intrusion detection,
this study provides valuable insights into the potential of
reinforcement learning-based security systems for future
autonomous and adaptive cybersecurity applications.
• Unlike most existing DRL-based IDS frameworks, this
study explicitly targets the detection of previously
unknown, zero-day attacks using the CIC-IDS2017
dataset, emphasizing DQL’s generalization capability.

II. RELATED WORK
New research has looked into how well DRL and DQL work
in IDS, focusing on their benefits in constantly changing
cybersecurity environments [5], [12]. Alavizadeh et al. [12]
made a DQL-based intrusion detection system that found
90% of unauthorized intrusions and had a lot fewer false
positives. They developed the model as a framework that
allows for consistent updates, making it effective against
the ongoing evolution of cyber threats. In the same way,
Kim and Park [13] built a hybrid framework that combines
DRL with supervised learning using deep autoencoders and
Q-learning. The goal was to shorten the training time and
make the learning process more stable. Their method focuses
on eliminating manual feature extraction and speeding up
convergence, but it hasn’t been tested on new attack types,
such as zero-day threats. On the other hand, our study uses
only a DQL framework without any supervised aspects,
focusing on the agent’s ability to generalize to new types
of attacks on its own. Our investigations also include a full
comparison with traditional ML models and a sensitivity
study of hyperparameters that affect generalization. Kim and
Park’s study mostly looks at how well convergence and classification function on existing data. Our study, on the other
hand, focuses on adaptive detection in the context of evolving
cyber threat scenarios.
In addition to detection, certain research has incorporated
DRL with adaptive response mechanisms. Reference [14]
presented an off-policy Q-learning methodology to improve
real-time intrusion response, facilitating swifter and more
flexible responses against cyberattacks. Unlike traditional
static response mechanisms, this model constantly changed
protection techniques based on the state of the network.

introduced a multi-agent Deep Q-Network (DQN) model that
uses attention mechanisms to find important threat patterns

III. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
In RL algorithms, the principal aim is to identify the Maximum Value (max-value). This process is undertaken under
deterministic conditions, signifying that the selected action
is performed with absolute certainty [17]. In a chess game,
a piece moves ahead by one square with complete certainty;
it cannot move sideways or backward. Conversely, stochastic
(non-deterministic) actions pertain to scenarios in which an
action lacks a 100% likelihood of occurring as anticipated.
A fundamental idea in RL is action. In the context of the
chess analogy, advancing a piece by one square is regarded
as an action for the agent. In Q-Learning (QL), the term
‘‘set of actions’’ denotes the potential motions an agent may
execute [18]. A chess piece can advance, shift left, or shift
right. The algorithm determines actions based on the probability of their outcomes. Examine a dice roll there exist six
distinct outcomes, each clearly delineated. In Q-Learning,
actions are derived from a discrete set, with each action
yielding a distinct, deterministic result. The objective of QL
is to choose a singular deterministic action from the set and
acquire knowledge during the execution of that action to
determine the maximum value. This allows the agent to optimize the reward and identify the most advantageous route.
For example, if an autonomous vacuum cleaner employs a RL
algorithm with the objective of traversing from one side of the
room to its charging station, it must ascertain the most direct
and efficient route to do this task expeditiously. To accurately
comprehend RL algorithms, it is crucial to possess a thorough understanding of the following fundamental concepts:
(1) Environment, (2) State, (3) Action, (4) Reward, (5) Agent.
The environment refers to the situation in which artificial
intelligence (AI) operates. For an agent (e.g., a robot) utilizing
a RL algorithm, the environment must provide feedback to aid
the agent in achieving its reward. In the QL process, the environment must furnish the agent with observation and reward.
The idea of observation relates to data obtained from the
environment, which may vary across different environments.
In the QL algorithm, an agent occupies a certain state,
which denotes an element within a collection of potential
states. For instance, if the agent (e.g., a robotic vacuum
cleaner) is positioned 2 meters from a door, that represents the
agent’s state. When the agent shifts from one state to another,
an action is executed. As the agent transitions between states,
the environment administers penalties or reward points as
feedback inside the environmental matrix. The feedback system is the environment, which provides rewards or penalties
contingent upon the agent’s activities.

The term ‘‘reinforcement’’ originates from the notion that

We divided the dataset into 80% for training and 20% for

and testing stages accurately reflected the diverse range of
attacks. After feature scaling, we implemented the StandardScaler method, which transformed all features into a
zero-mean, unit-variance scale. DQL, known for their sensitivity to feature scaling, rely heavily on this preprocessing
stage. Standardizing the features improves learning efficiency
and performance, contributing to a more stable model training

We taught different ML models, such as RF and DT,
and DRL models, such as DQL. Then, we compared how
well these models worked to other models. For training, the
DQL model used a deep neural network architecture based
on reinforcement learning. RF and DT, on the other hand,
were made using standard machine-learning techniques. The
hyperparameters for the machine learning models were automatically optimal. The Random Forest model is configured
with 100 decision trees (n_estimators=100) and employs

A three-layer ANN was used to build a DQL model. The

assess every model’s generalization capacity under novel and
surprising conditions. Training the models is based on the
changed dataset; evaluations of accuracy, precision, recall,
and F1-score help to evaluate their classification performance. We want to find out if DQL, a technique based on

On the AWID dataset characterized by extreme imbalance
and a huge sample size, the DQL model demonstrated competitive results, with an accuracy of 0.9400, precision of
0.9484, recall of 0.9400, and an F1-score of 0.9434.
In intrusion detection experiments, this kind of validation
is very important because models need to work well not only
in controlled experiments but also when they have to deal
with new and unbalanced traffic patterns. The results thus
illustrate both the capabilities and constraints of DQL; it
demonstrates considerable accuracy and adaptability in intricate situations, yet its pronounced sensitivity to distributional
shifts, as evidenced in the NSL-KDD dataset, poses a substantial obstacle for practical implementation. Also, it should
be noted that the comparative evaluation reported here was
done on known-attack instances from all three datasets to
ensure that the experimental conditions were the same. This
constraint was imposed because heterogeneous attack taxonomies and attack dynamics (for example, a port scan in
one dataset versus a volumetric DDoS in another) introduce
confounding factors that can substantially alter feature distributions, temporal patterns, and class imbalance, thereby
biasing cross-dataset comparisons.

We investigated two different configurations to see how they
affected the model’s generalizing capability and classification
accuracy in spotting zero-day threats. The first configuration used a high learning rate of 0.99, an epsilon decay
rate of 0.99, a large batch size of 256, a limited experience replay buffer of 1000, and a brief training time of
3 epochs. Under these conditions, the DQL model obtained

patterns. The fast epsilon decay may have made it harder

In the second setup, the learning rate was slowed down

extended training period improved performance and generalization. The findings show that for intrusion detection models
that use DRL, a lower learning rate, more exploration, and a

VI. CONCLUSION
We demonstrate the differences between DRL and standard
ML models in IDS using the CIC-IDS2017 data. It assesses
their efficiency in relation to both known risks and unknown
attacks. RF is the advised tool according to studies showing
clear assault patterns. The tool’s 99.95% accuracy in spotting
known attackers calls for its application. Still, RF discovers
problems with zero-day attacks, which sharply lowers its
recall rate. DQL shows greater generalizing capability with
an F1 score of 90.28% for unidentified threats. This implies
that it finds fresh cyber threats more effectively than models
like RF and DT.
DQL has real-time intrusion detection issues, even with
great autonomy, flexibility, and learning powers. The 3.87-
second longer inference time causes delayed identification of
newly emerging hazards. In high-velocity network situations,
this renders quick response solutions less successful. Its 654-
second prolonged training length also makes it less suited
for fast-changing cybersecurity surroundings. This affects
model updates and responses to new risks but not real-time
detection.
The proposed DQL-based IDS exhibits robust detection
capabilities, especially for zero-day attacks. Nonetheless,
its practical implementation necessitates attention to computational limitations. DQL exhibits greater training and
inference durations than RF and DT, potentially constraining its applicability in latency-sensitive contexts. Recent
advancements, like Double DQN, prioritized experience
replay, and lightweight neural architectures (e.g., TinyML),
present significant opportunities to diminish model complexity and enhance inference speed. Moreover, the modular
integration of the DQL agent into current Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems can facilitate
effortless real-world implementation. These considerations
indicate that, although resource-intensive, DRL models can
be customized for operational settings through architectural
and infrastructural enhancements.
Although DQL shines in finding unknown attack assaults,
RF is the most efficient method for rapidly and financially
recognizing known hazards. When you connect a DRL-based
IDS to a real-time network, the latency of inference goes
down, which makes the model more efficient. By means
of improved DRL models and DQL training optimization,
we can match self-learning with real-time cybersecurity
defense. We looked at both training overhead and inference
feasibility to put the computational efficiency of the models
we looked at into context. RF and DT train and predict faster
since their structures are static and dependent on rules. However, they generally don’t work well with new attack patterns.
DQL, on the other hand, makes training harder because it uses
an iterative learning method and neural networks to approximate functions. However, once trained, DQL can make quick
and reliable inferences with just one forward pass, which
makes it possible to use it in almost real time. This shows a
very important trade-off. DRL-based systems can generalize
better and find zero-day threats, but they require more training
time. Because of this, DQL is still a favorable choice for
adaptive intrusion detection, especially in places where it is
more important to have strong detection than to have to retrain
it often.
In future work, the integration of federated learning could
be explored to enable distributed intrusion detection across
decentralized environments without compromising data privacy. Additionally, hybrid ML-DRL models may offer a
promising balance between interpretability, efficiency, and
adaptive learning in dynamic threat landscapes.

A Human–Machine Joint Learning Framework to
Boost Endogenous BCI Training
Hanwen Wang , Yu Qi , Member, IEEE, Lin Yao, Yueming Wang , Member, IEEE,
Dario Farina , Fellow, IEEE, and Gang Pan , Senior Member, IEEE
Abstract— Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) provide a direct
pathway from the brain to external devices and have demonstrated great potential for assistive and rehabilitation technologies. Endogenous BCIs based on electroencephalogram (EEG)
signals, such as motor imagery (MI) BCIs, can provide some
level of control. However, mastering spontaneous BCI control
requires the users to generate discriminative and stable brain
signal patterns by imagery, which is challenging and is usually
achieved over a very long training time (weeks/months). Here,
we propose a human–machine joint learning framework to boost
the learning process in endogenous BCIs, by guiding the user to
generate brain signals toward an optimal distribution estimated
by the decoder, given the historical brain signals of the user.
To this end, we first model the human–machine joint learning
process in a uniform formulation. Then a human–machine joint
learning framework is proposed: 1) for the human side, we model
the learning process in a sequential trial-and-error scenario and
propose a novel “copy/new” feedback paradigm to help shape the
signal generation of the subject toward the optimal distribution
and 2) for the machine side, we propose a novel adaptive learning
algorithm to learn an optimal signal distribution along with the
subject’s learning process. Specifically, the decoder reweighs the
brain signals generated by the subject to focus more on “good”

Index Terms— Brain–computer interface (BCI), electroencephalogram (EEG), motor imagery (MI), neural decoding.
I. INTRODUCTION
B
RAIN–COMPUTER interfaces (BCIs) act as an intermediary between the brain and external devices, translating
brain signals to control signals [1], [2]. BCIs employing electroencephalogram (EEG) signals have been developed successfully for many applications, including neural rehabilitation,
prosthesis control, and emotion recognition [3], [4], [5], [6],
[7], [8], [9], [10]. Most existing BCI systems can be divided
into endogenous and exogenous BCIs [11], [12]. Exogenous
BCIs such as the P300 and SSVEP systems, rely on brain
signals evoked by external stimuli [13], [14], such as visual
flashes or audio events. Conversely, endogenous BCIs, such
as based on motor imagery (MI), rely on self-regulated brain
signals often induced by users’ covert attention or mental
tasks [15], [16]. Thus, endogenous BCIs can provide more
flexible and natural brain control, resulting in high potential for a wide range of applications [17], [18], [19], [20].
In the remainder of this article, we will only focus on
endogenous BCIs.
Effective BCI control relies on the close collaboration of
the brain (the subject) and the machine (the decoder) [21]. The
user should generate discriminative and sufficient brain signals
as different control commands, while the decoder should identify different brain signal patterns and robustly interpret/map
them into control commands. For endogenous BCIs, the main
challenge lies in the difficulty for the user in generating
effective and stable brain signals. To achieve robust online
control, the BCI user should be able to accurately replicate at
least two discriminative and stable patterns for basic control,
such as going left and right. A typical endogenous BCI is
based on MI, where the user is asked to imagine movements,
for example of the left/right hand. However, generating MI
is challenging for most users, and a typical user usually
requires a long and difficult training process to learn the MI
control. Commonly, training for MI lasts several weeks or even
months [22], [23]. Furthermore, there are at least 15%–30% of
subjects across the population who cannot control BCI systems
through learning, a case called BCI illiteracy [24]. For these
reasons, the facilitation of the learning process in endogenous
BCIs is a very relevant problem.
The learning process in BCIs includes two parts: the learning of the decoder (machine learning), and the learning of the

WANG et al.: HUMAN–MACHINE JOINT LEARNING FRAMEWORK TO BOOST ENDOGENOUS BCI TRAINING

user (human learning). Here, we briefly review the existing
approaches.
1) Machine Learning: Traditional BCI training processes
start with a static subject learning process where the
subject tries to generate brain signals without feedback.
Then a decoder is trained with the initial data to
learn discriminative features from different brain signals
[as shown in Fig. 1(a)]. The discrimination of different
brain signal patterns can be regarded as a typical classification problem. Thus, linear and nonlinear classifiers
have been proposed for the decoding problem. For linear
methods, decoding in MI can be separated into feature
extraction and classification. Common spatial pattern
(CSP) is a widely used linear approach for extracting
discriminative features from different brain signal patterns. Filter bank CSP (FBCSP) [25] extends CSP with
a set of bandpass filters to enhance features, and it
can also be applied in neural networks [26]. However,
traditional CSP is not suitable for multiclass problems.
Joint approximate diagonalization (JAD)-based methods
are used to improve CSP [27]. Moreover, modifications have been made to enhance CSPs to deal with
the nonstationarity in EEG signals. Fuzzy covariance
matrices are deployed in DivCSP-WS to extract steady
features [28]. Channel selection methods could also
improve stability between sessions, improving the classification accuracy [29].
In terms of classification methods, linear discriminant
analysis (LDA) is commonly used for extracted features [30]. To enhance robustness on nonstationary EEG
signals, variations of LDA such as regularized LDA
(rLDA) and Bayesian LDA (BLDA) have been introduced [31], [32], [33]. Support vector machines (SVMs)
with flexible kernel design are with feature extraction
methods in some studies [34], [35]. Recently, deep
learning approaches including long short term memory (LSTM) [36], [37], [38] and convolutional neural
networks (CNNs) [39], [40], [41], [42], [43], such as
EEGnet [44], have demonstrated effectiveness in MI
classification. Combining the feature extraction methods and the deep learning approach, neural structured
learning (NSL) has been proposed to train deep neural
networks with feature inputs and the structured signals,
which enhances the robustness [45].
2) Human Learning: After the initial decoder is trained, the
subject can learn to control the BCI with the feedback
of the decoder, where the design of the feedback plays
an important part [see Fig. 1(b)]. Traditional feedbacks
usually directly reflect the decoding result, using a
moving cursor or a falling ball [46], [47]. To improve
the efficiency of subject learning, new paradigms with
different types of feedback have been introduced. For
example, Hwang et al. [23] proposed an intuitive feedback that uses a surface topography of EEG signal,
where the real-time spectrogram is presented to enhance
the MI [48]. Wang et al. [49] proposed a neurofeedback
training paradigm, in which the performance of MI
was transferred into the distance between a needle and
hands on the screen. Alternatively, auditory feedbacks
of different sounds have been presented to subject
depending on their MI performance [50]. Nevertheless, Shu et al. [51] and Yao et al. [52] proposed tactile
stimulation to help subjects improve the MI activation.
Also, Ono et al. [53] adopted exoskeleton attached to
subjects, making feedbacks more sensible.
3) Coadaptive Learning: The aforementioned approaches
mostly focus on one side of the learning, either the
signal generation by the user or the algorithm training
by the machine. However, coadaptive methods have also
been introduced [54], [55]. Instead of using a fixed
decoder after the initial training process, coadaptive
approaches retrain both the decoder and the subject
iteratively in sequential learning sessions to cope with
each other [54], [56] [see Fig. 1(c)]. To this end, different
decoder recalibration algorithms have been proposed
using machine learning approaches such as LDA [57],
SVM [58], probabilistic graphical models [59] to update
the decoder with newly collected data to cope with
changes in brain signals during the subject learning process. By considering the interaction between the subject
and the decoder, coadaptive approaches demonstrated
superior performance in BCI learning than separate
learning approaches [60], [61]. To provide a mathematical basis of coadaptive learning processes, previous
work has modeled the process with mathematical formulations. For example, in
[62], an encoder–decoder
model was proposed, in which the coadaptation was
described by the optimization of the user’s control.
With the assumption of two linear learning systems,
a theoretical formulation was derived by the stochastic
gradient descent method in [63].
In Fig. 1, we illustrate and compare the aforementioned
learning process in an intuitive way. Suppose there is a global
optimal point for the human–machine BCI learning process.
With the machine learning model alone [see Fig. 1(a)], where
the human model is static, the optimal performance is highly
limited by the boundary of brain signal patterns. With the
human learning model alone [see Fig. 1(b)], where the decoder
is fixed, the subject can learn with the guidance of the
decoder’s feedback. The performance highly relies on the
effectiveness of the decoder. Since the decoder is usually
trained with the initially imperfect brain signals of the subject,
it can be suboptimal and can degrade the human learning
process. The coadaptation model [see Fig. 1(c)] considers both
machine learning and human learning, where the decoder is
iteratively updated along with the human learning process.
Specifically, it contains an iterative process where the machine
and the human learn alternately, which improves the theoretical overall performance. However, it assumes that the subject
can effectively learn at every human learning stage, which can
be difficult, especially at the beginning rounds of the training
process.
This study proposes a novel BCI learning scheme for
efficient and effective BCI training. As shown in Fig. 1(d),
we aim to construct a joint learning model between humans
and machines, where human and machine processes can be
optimized simultaneously. To this end, we propose a novel
human–machine joint learning framework for effective BCI
training. Specifically, we assume the human learning behavior
in sequential training is a trial-and-error process, and let the
decoder determine whether a brain signal is “good” or “poor”
by its discrimination ability according to the distribution of the
feature space. The contribution of this study is summarized in
threefold.
1) We formally formulate the human–machine joint learning model and propose a human–machine joint loss

II. HUMAN–MACHINE JOINT LEARNING FRAMEWORK
We first formulate the BCI learning process in a uniform
model and propose a human–machine joint loss function
for learning. Then we propose the human learning model
and propose a loss function for the human learning process.
We then introduce the machine learning process where the
decoder learns to select optimal brain signals that the subject
generated to guide and cope with the learning process of the
subject. Finally, we propose a novel BCI learning paradigm
and framework for human–machine joint learning.
A. Modeling of the Human–Machine Joint Learning
Considering BCI learning as a human–machine learning
problem, the subject and the decoder share the same goal of
accurate intention decoding from brain signals. To achieve
this goal, the subject tries to generate more discriminative
brain signals, and the decoder optimizes the classifier to best
separate different brain signal patterns. To this end, the human
learning model can be described as

1) “Copy/New” Feedback Strategy: We propose a novel
“copy/new” feedback strategy to indicate whether the
previous brain signal is “good” or “poor.” In our
paradigm, the trials are split into pairs and the instruction
for the next trial depends on the quality of the previous
trial. If the previous trial is of good quality, there
would be a “copy” for the next trial. With the “copy”
feedback, the subject is encouraged to generate brain
signals similar to the previous one, which increases PGG.
Otherwise, there would be a “new” instruction where
the subject is asked to change the way of thinking
and explore better signals, which helps decrease PBB
in Section II-A1.
In other words, the “copy” signals
help subjects to maintain the previous “good” signal,
and the “new” instruction will guide subjects to try other
possibilities. The feedback lets the subject learn in a
trial-and-error process, where the subject learns to shape
the distribution of brain signals to a more discriminative
condition with the guidance of the decoder.

Assuming we have a set of labeled data, we first randomly
split the data into a training set {X, Y} of N samples and a
validation set {X′, Y ′}. At first, 3 × N samples are randomly
selected from the training set. These data are used to train
the initial weighted CSP and weighted SVM. After that, all
data in the training set could get a weight, and the accuracy
of the validation set is calculated. If 3 < 1, which means
not all the training set has been used, more data would be
included in the update of weighted CSP and weighted SVM
according to their weights. The iteration will continue until
all the training set has been included. And the round with the
highest accuracy on the validation set would be selected. The
weight and parameters of weighted CSP and weighted SVM
are the output.
Also, the joint learning method could be employed in other

condition, random selected λ × N samples will be fed to the
neural network for initialization. After that, more and more
samples would be assigned with different weights according
to their loss to update the network by iteration. And the best

III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
A. Experimental Settings
We evaluated the proposed human–machine joint learning
model with online BCI experiments in comparison with coadaptive BCIs without joint learning.
A total of 18 subjects
participated in the BCI experiments (eight females and ten
males, age ranging from 23 to 27). 14 subjects took part in the
experiment with CSP and SVM. And four subjects attended
the experiment of EEGnet. Each participant performed two
experiments: a joint learning experiment and a coadaptive
learning experiment (baseline). To mitigate the effects of
session order, the two experiments were arranged on two
different days, at least two days apart. The order of the
experiments was also randomly selected, where nine subjects
conducted joint learning first the rest performed coadaptive
learning experiments first. After each experiment, a simple
questionnaire was filled out by the subject. The settings of the
experiments were as follows.
1) Joint Learning Experiment: There were a total of five
sessions in the joint learning experiment. The first one
was an initial calibration session without feedback,
which had 60 trials including 30 left and 30 right
trials in random order. After the initial calibration
session, there were four joint learning sessions with
feedback, consisting of 20 trials for each direction,
and each trial was 9-s long. The trials were presented
in Fig. 3 and Section II-B1. For preprocessing, a fourthorder Butterworth Filter was adopted to filter the data
from 8 to 30 Hz. The classifier was updated after every
session. The threshold T of “copy/new” was set to 70%.
3 was set to 0.2 for initialization and 13 was set
to 0.05 for updating the sample reweighting algorithm
for SVM. While for EEGnet, more samples were needed
to initialize the training process, so 3 was set to 0.5.
And 13 was set to 0.1 to reduce training iterations for
saving time.
2) Coadaptive Learning Experiment Without Joint Learning (Baseline): We used the classical coadaptive learning
paradigm as the baseline for comparison. Specifically,
the coadaptive learning method in this article is adopted
from [60], named as RETRAIN, which achieved the best
performance. The same method was also used in [61].
The number of sessions in the coadaptive learning
experiment (control group) was the same as in the joint
learning experiment. After the calibration session, the
trials in the rest training session were provided with
feedback from an
SVM/EEGnet decoder, which was
also updated after every session.
For both the joint learning and the coadaptive learning
experiments, the software system was set up in MATLAB,
with the Psychtoolbox [72]. And the computer was equipped
with an Intel i7-10700k CPU, 64-GB RAM, and an NVIDIA
GeForce RTX 3080 GPU. In CSP feature computing, three
pairs of features were selected for classification. In the SVM
classifier, a linear kernel was adopted. The time for inference
was approximately 0.003 s. And the training of the algorithm
cost 5.55 ± 2.87 s. For EEGnet, we chose adaptive learning
rate optimization algorithm (ADAM) as the optimizer which is
same to [44]. The inference time was approximately 0.004 s,
while the training time was 153 ± 23 s.
The feedback were calculated by the window of 1 s and
updated every frame (1/60 s). α was set to 0.2 for the feedback.
For the offline analysis, we cut the 5-s trial into four trial
slices for 1 s, starting from 0.5 s and ending at 4.5 s after the
instruction.
The EEG signals were recorded using a wireless EEG
system (NSW24, Neuracle) with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
A total of 20 electrodes were placed on FC5, FC3, FC1, FCz,
FC2, FC4, FC6, C5, C3, C1, Cz, C2, C4, C6, CP5, CP3, CP1,
CPz, CP2, CP4, and CP6, according to the standard international 10–20 system. The ground and reference were FPz
and CPz, respectively. The impedances of all electrodes were
below the recommended value (10 k) in the experiments.
B. Comparison of BCI Control Performance
Here, we compared the performance of the joint learning
and the coadaptive learning method both on SVM and EEGnet.
The performance was evaluated by the accuracy of online
BCI control. We chose the highest accuracy among the last
two sessions as the online BCI control accuracy, where the
accuracy of sessions was averaged by the accuracy of all trials
in the sessions.
1) Analysis on SVM With Joint Learning: Fig. 4(a) illustrated the online BCI control accuracy for both joint learning
and coadaptive learning with the 14 subjects. Overall, the BCI
control accuracy of joint learning sessions was significantly
higher than coadaptive learning sessions without joint learning
(paired t-test, p < 0.005). The average accuracies of methods
with joint learning and without joint learning were 74.75%
and 69.06%. For 11 out of 14 subjects, joint learning achieved
a superior BCI control accuracy compared with the baseline
coadaptive experiments. The performance increases were most
obvious with subjects with lower BCI control performance,

In Fig. 4(b), we examined the discrete performance by the
proportion of successful trials. Specifically, we defined a trial
with accuracy above the threshold T (70%) as a successful
trial, which can be used as the discrete control signal. Overall,
the joint learning sessions obtained a higher proportion of
successful trials compared with the baseline. With the joint
learning system, the proportion of successful trials rose sustainingly over the four sessions, indicating the improvement of
the subject’s BCI control ability. Specifically, the proportion
of successful trials increased to 60.0%, 64.2%, 65.5%, and
at the second, third, and fourth, respectively. While without
joint learning, the proportion rose with the first two sessions,
and the increase became trivial afterward. With session 4,
the joint learning system outperformed the coadaptive system
significantly by 9.83% (paired t-test, p < 0.05). We further
compared the trialwise accuracy of BCI control. The trialwise
accuracy was computed by the mean accuracy of online
accuracy during the trials, which was smoothed by the window
of ten points. Fig. 4(c) illustrates the average accuracy of
every trial over all the subjects. For both joint and coadaptive
systems, the initial accuracies were around 60%. With the
learning process, the accuracy of joint learning rose rapidly to
76.58%, while the accuracy of the baseline coadaptive learning
increased slower to 70.79%. The results indicated that the
subject learned more effectively with the joint learning system.

both online and pseudo-online experiments on EEGnet with
the proposed joint learning framework. The results are presented in Fig. 5. Specifically, we conducted pseudo-online

D. Effectiveness of the “Copy/New” Paradigm
In this section, we evaluated the effectiveness of our
“copy/new” paradigm from the aspects of accuracy and weight.
We compared the averaged accuracy before and after a
“copy/new” instruction. Specifically, we labeled the trials with
four groups: 1) the first trial in a “copy” pair (before a
“copy” instruction); 2) the next trial in a “copy” pair (after
a “copy” instruction); 3) the first trial in a “new” pair (before
a “new” instruction); and 4) the next trial in a “new” pair
(after a “new” instruction).
Overall, the “copy” instruction guided the subjects to maintain a good brain signal pattern effectively, while the next
trials after a “new” instruction demonstrated a significant
performance increase. As shown in Fig. 9(a), the first trials
in a “copy” pair demonstrated a high average accuracy of
88%; after the “copy” instruction, the performance of the
next trial slightly decreased while still keeping a high average
accuracy of to 81%. The results suggested that the “copy”
instruction could guide the subject to repeat and keep a good
brain signal pattern. With the “new” instruction, the first trials
were with low accuracies of about 43%. After the “new”
instruction, the average accuracy of the next trial rose to 60%.
The results showed that the subjects tried to generate a new
brain signal pattern different from the previous ones to seek a
better performance, which was in line with expectations.
Furthermore, we analyzed the weights in different types
of trials to show the cooperation between our paradigm and
algorithm. Fig. 9(b) presented the weight in different types of
trials. The weights were calculated by averaging the weights
on trials of the selected type. Overall, although the weights
varied in a big range, the average weight on the next trials was
slightly higher than the weight on the first trials. Specifically,
the mean weight on the first trials was 0.58, and the mean
weight on the next trials was 0.62 (p < 0.05 with one-sided
t-test), which explained the better separability of the next
trials. This indicated that the proposed “copy/new” instructions
worked well with the sample reweighting algorithm, which
also demonstrated the validity of the proposed learning
paradigm.
E. Analysis of the Questionnaires
The results of the questionnaire were presented to analyze
from a subjective point of view. The questionnaire consisted of
six simple questions, measured by scores from one to seven,
which were shown in the Supplementary Material in detail.
The first four questions were about the ability of MI of the
left and right hand, respectively. One pair was answered before
the experiments and the other pair should be scored after
the experiments (How do you think about your MI ability
of left/right hand before/after the experiment? one stands for
very poor, and seven stands for very good). The result was
plotted in Fig. 10(a), where the score change was calculated
by the sum of two questions after the experiments minus the
sum before the experiments. It could be seen from the picture
that red lines often had a higher value than blue lines, which
meant subjects thought that they had better MI ability after
our experiment with joint learning. In detail, the mean value of
score change for the coadaptive paradigm was −0.14, while for
our joint learning paradigm, the mean change was 1.64. This
meant subjects thought the coadaptive training did not have
significant effects, while our proposed joint learning method
had a better training effect. This result was self-reported by
subjects, which might be because the better control accuracy
made subjects feel more confident.
Question 5 was about the degree of interaction, and level of
knowing the feedback (do you think you can understand the
feedback? one stands for no, and seven stands for very good
understanding). The results were in Fig. 10(b). Our proposed
method turned out to be slightly better than the control group,
achieving an average score of around 6.29 (5.5 in the control
group). This might be due to the “copy/new” instructions in
our paradigm, giving subjects a stronger sense of participation.
Also with the instructions, the subject can know about the
separability or quality of generated signals more clearly. This
also helped with the interaction during the experiments.
The last question was about fatigue (how much fatigue do
you feel during the experiment? one stands for none, and seven
stands for too much and intolerable). Fig. 10(c) showed the
averaged score, in which scores of both experiments were
almost the same (3.29 in the control group and 3.35 in our
experiments). So, there was no significant difference between
the efforts in the two experiments. Our experiments just helped
subjects to change or hold their thoughts. This did not increase
the workload of subjects.
IV. DISCUSSION
A. Novelty and Contributions
Spontaneous BCI training is often hindered by the training
burden it poses. Existing coadaptive learning methods, which
adopt an alternate learning process, have shown suboptimal
performance. In such methods, either the decoder or the user
learns at a time [60], [61]. However, human and computer
algorithms are heterogeneous in information representation
and learning mechanisms. Therefore, it is difficult to let
humans and computers learn together in a uniform framework.
In this study, we use brain signal samples generated by
subjects as the intermedia, to enable the joint learning process
between both sides. In the human learning process, the subject
tries to generate “better” brain samples with the guidance of
the computer, which tells the subject what are “good” samples.

At the same time, the computer continuously updates itself
adaptively to the human learning process. Thus, the learning
process of both humans and computers can be optimized
simultaneously.
In this article, we first modeled the aforementioned joint
learning process in a uniform model, with the Markov-based
human learning process and the self-paced learning-based
computer learning process. And then, we implement the framework by proposing a novel copy/new paradigm, to achieve the
joint learning process. Online experiments demonstrated the
effectiveness of the joint learning process.
B. Sensitivity of Parameters
In this section, we conducted experiments to investigate
the sensitivity of the algorithm’s parameters. Specifically,
we focused on two parameters, 3 and 13, which control the
initialization and training pace of the algorithm. To evaluate
their influence, we performed a grid search on the data from
14 subjects. We varied 3 in the range of [0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]
and 13 in the range of [0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20]. The results
are presented in Fig. 11(a). We observed that the accuracy
ranged from 75.81% to 78.11%, with no significant difference
found among the different parameter settings. The highest
accuracy was achieved with 3 = 0.2 and 13 = 0.05, which
is consistent with the parameter settings used in the online
joint learning experiment. Conversely, the lowest accuracy
was obtained with 3 = 0.2 and 13 = 0.20. Moreover,
we found that the accuracy increased with the increment of
13 when 3 = 0.2. This suggests that when the number of
initial samples is relatively small, more rounds are needed to
reduce the effect of random initialization. In contrast, when
more samples are included in the initialization, the results tend
to be more stable.
C. Electrode Selection
Electrode selection is a critical issue for MI performance,
in addition to parameters such as 3 and 13. The primary area
for MI in the brain is the primary motor cortex (M1), which
is located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe [47].
Therefore, electrodes of interest are typically C3 and C4,
which are located over the left and right primary motor cortex,
respectively [73]. In the online experiments, we recorded data
from 20 electrodes, along with CPz as a reference. As shown
in Fig. 11(c), the selected electrode set was centered at
C3 and C4. To investigate the impact of electrode selection
further, we reduced the number of electrodes from the outer
side toward the center. We reduced the original 20 electrodes
(FC5, FC3, FC1, FCz, FC2, FC4, FC6, C5, C3, C1, Cz,
C2, C4, C6, CP5, CP3, CP1, CPz, CP2, CP4, and CP6)
to 14 electrodes (FC3, FC1, FCz, FC2, FC4, C3, C1, Cz,
C2, C4, CP3, CP1, CP2, and CP4), then eight electrodes
(FC3, FCz, FC4, C3, Cz, C4, CP3, and CP4), and finally to
three electrodes (C3, Cz, and C4). The accuracy change is
plotted in Fig. 11(b). As expected, the accuracy decreased
with the reduction of electrodes from 74.75% to 63.97%.
The average accuracy of our proposed methods was always
higher than the method without joint learning. However, the
advantage diminished from 5.69% to 1.64%. This could be
attributed to the decreasing number of electrodes resulting in
less useful information. This result also helps to demonstrate
the effectiveness of our proposed method.

D. Limitations and Future Works
1) Multiclassification Problem: In this article, we proposed
novel a joint learning framework for effective BCI training,
which took an MI system of the binary classification as
an example. With the framework, different base algorithms
could be deployed to deal with the training problem. For the
multiclassification problem, our framework could easily fit to
the problem. Because from the algorithm aspect, the key part is
to evaluate samples according to their loss, to guide the human
learning process. From the aspect of paradigm, the “copy/new”
instructions would remain the same. As a result, the challenge
lies in the base algorithm. In the experiments, we adopted
the CSP SVM and the EEGnet as the base algorithms. For
the EEGnet, it was introduced to deal with all kinds of EEG
problems. So it would be rather convenient to deal with multiclassification problem. For the CSP SVM, it was designed
for the binary classification problem [25]. However, there are
some improvements to enhance CSP for multiclass MI [27].
With these new methods, our proposed framework promises
to achieve good results on multiclassification problems.
2) Markov Process and Endogenous Attention: As discussed in Section II-A1, the Markov process is a widely used
framework for modeling human decision-making processes.
Recently, it has been applied to the study of endogenous
attention, as it can accurately reproduce reaction times in
GO–GO experiments [64]. Moreover, Markov models have
been employed in the field of visual decision-making [65], and
hidden Markov models have been used to reveal endogenous
neural activities that trigger perceptual changes by analyzing dynamic neural patterns [74]. In this article, we model
the learning process, including decision-making about MI
strategies, using a Markov process. In future work, we aim
to expand the model to include EEG patterns and features.
This will provide further insights into human learning and
decision-making processes in MI training.
3) Applications on Various EEG Devices: The emergence
of advanced sensor technology has facilitated the creation
of compact and intelligent wearable electroencephalography
devices tailored for personal use [75]. Devices with novel dry
EEG sensors, which is convenient to wear and remove, have
enhanced the usability of BCI systems [76]. Wireless devices
with dry and noncontact EEG electrode sensor have also been
introduced [77]. These devices are intended for real-life usage
scenarios, which are significantly more complex than controlled laboratory environments. Consequently, ensuring the
stability of BCI systems poses a considerable challenge. Our
proposed human–machine joint learning framework exhibits
vast prospects for application and further work in this field.
V. CONCLUSION
Toward efficient and effective BCI training, the proposed
human–machine joint learning framework enables the simultaneous learning of both the user and the decoder. We model
the human–machine joint learning process in a uniform formulation and propose a novel joint learning framework for
efficient BCI training. Online and psuedo-online experiments
demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed joint learning
framework in rapid BCI learning. The proposed framework
can be extended to MI tasks with more control degrees and
also has the potential to guide the subject to generate new
brain patterns out of the MI manner, to broaden the usability
of BCI systems.

A Hybrid Machine Learning Model for Efficient
XML Parsing
MUHAMMAD ALI
1, MINHAJ AHMAD KHAN
1, AND RAIHAN UR RASOOL
2,∗
1Department of Computer Science, Bahauddin Zakariya University, Multan 60800, Pakistan
2IBM Technologies, Melbourne, VIC 3006, Australia
Corresponding author: Minhaj Ahmad Khan (mik@bzu.edu.pk)
ABSTRACT The Extensible Markup Language (XML) files are extensively used for representing structured
data on the web for file configuration, exchanging data between distinct applications, web development, and
many other applications. Consequently, effective parsing techniques are necessary for XML files to enhance
the performance of applications. The existing parsing techniques have their strengths and weaknesses
affecting the performance of applications. Researchers point out that the selection of an efficient and
appropriate parser is the most challenging issue regarding a particular condition. This paper proposes a
framework XML Parsing Optimization using Hybrid Machine Learning (XPOHML) that makes use of
Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) machine learning techniques for
efficient XML parsing. The newly developed framework performs analysis and prediction of different
XML parsers using profiling, classification, performance evaluation, and finally generates code for efficient
parsing. The XML profiling phase of the XPOHML framework generates a dataset by evaluating the
performance of PXTG, SAX, StAX, DOM, and JDOM parsing models on separate cores by applying
numerous file sizes. The Classification phase produces the classification model by applying ANN and
SVM techniques to identify the appropriate parsing model. The performance evaluation phase of XPOHML
assesses the performance of both parsing models through classification metrics (accuracy). Additionally,
based on evaluation outcomes, the code generation phase produces an efficient parsing model of XML
files. The newly designed and developed XPOHML framework has shown a meaningful improvement in
the performance of parsing XML files.
INDEX TERMS Artificial intelligence, artificial neural network, eXtensible markup language, framework,
machine learning, model, parsing, support vector machine, XML parsing optimization.
I. INTRODUCTION
Extensible Markup Language, or XML as it is more commonly abbreviated, is a markup language that facilitates
data transfer between platforms, including websites and
databases. This is possible because XML is cross-platform
and allows for incompatibilities between devices and systems. XML is used extensively in online services to store,
carry, and transport data over the Internet. It may be used
in diverse applications including databases, web applications,
e-commerce, multimedia, ERP systems, bioinformatics, and
other scientific applications.
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Yilun Shang.
In XML, the start tag and end tag, which indicate the beginning and finish of the element, separate the data presented
in an XML document. The structure of the document can
be defined with the use of XML Schema (XSD) or Document Type Definition (DTD) [1]. XML can be classified as
either data-centric or document-centric. A highly structured
document is referred to as data-centric and is commonly
used for transferring data from a single platform to another.
Businesses typically include information on sales orders,
stock quotes, travel schedules, and scientific data analysis are
a few examples of data-centric. Document-centric XML is
another category, in addition to data-centric XML. There is a

lot of text in this kind of XML, which has loose structures.
Examples include product catalogs, legal documents, and
news sources like CNN RSS Feeds.
The efficiency of XML parsing depends upon the execution of diverse XML operations including verification of
well-formedness, traversal of tags along with metadata, and
construction of a parse tree. To speed up XML parsing,
a variety of hardware, software, and hybrid techniques are
employed [2]. The hardware-based methods make use of
specialized hardware accelerators like LTMAdder [3] and
FPGA custom circuits [4]. In contrast, the software-based
approaches include methods like pull-based parsing [5], lazy
parsing [6], and schema-specific parsing [7]. In the same way,
both hardware and software parsing techniques are used in
the hybrid XML parsing approaches [8]. To enhance XML
parsing, serial and parallel approaches have been extensively
researched and incorporated into current practices.
The applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in research,
engineering, and industry have grown rapidly in the last
several years [9]. The various machine learning techniques
or algorithms that learn from data and automatically improve
performance for a wide range of applications, including
XML parsing, reverse engineering, fault diagnosis, advanced
modeling, predictive maintenance, quality control, control
strategies, and system or component optimization [10], [11],
[12], [13], [14], [15]. AI generally combines human intelligence and behaviour into computers or systems [16], whereas
machine learning (ML) automates the process of developing
models by training from experience or data [17]. Examples,
such as the data used for learning and evaluation, are utilized as guidelines in the learning stage of machine learning
algorithms. The training set, validation set, and test set comprise the data set. First, the learning algorithm is trained
on the training set. Next, its parameters are adjusted on
the validation set. Lastly, the learning algorithm’s performance is assessed on the test set [18]. Building a model
that learns a function to explain a particular pattern in a
dataset while another unknown pattern exists is the key objective of machine learning. Machine learning algorithms can
be classified into three categories [9], [19], [20] known as
supervised learning, supervised learning, and reinforcement
learning.
In this paper, we propose a framework XML Parsing Optimization using Hybrid Machine Learning (XPOHML) that
incorporates techniques of ANN and SVM to analyze and
predict the performance of different parsers through XML
profiling, classification, performance evaluation, and code
generation for efficient parsing. The XML profiling step
of the XPOHML framework creates a dataset by assessing
the effectiveness of the PXTG, SAX, StAX, DOM, and
JDOM parsing models on various cores using a range of
file sizes. The classification phase produces the prediction
model by applying ANN and SVM techniques to identify
the appropriate algorithm. The XPOHML framework then
evaluates performance to assess these algorithms’ efficacy.
Ultimately, the code generation phase generates the final
code for effectively parsing XML files based on previous
assessment. The remaining document has the following structure. Section II describes the related work, in terms of
XML parsing, ANN, and SVM architectures. The proposed
XPOHML framework used to analyze and predict performance through XML profiling, classification, performance
evaluation, and code generation for efficient parsing is presented in Section III. Section IV presents the experimental
setup and findings achieved by implementing the proposed
framework and the profiling of existing widely known parsing
models. The conclusion and future work are deliberated in the
final Section of this document.
II. RELATED WORK
To enhance the parsing of XML documents, a variety of methods have been widely designed and executed by researchers.
The Document Object Model (DOM) [21] parsers return an
object to control elements after storing a complete hierarchical document in memory after parsing. This leads to an
inefficient parsing for large documents. Another Java-based
parser is Simple API for XML (SAX) [22] parses XML
documents in a top-down manner with no random or direct
access. Similarly, the Streaming API for XML (StAX) uses
a pull-based method for extracting data. On the other hand,
JDOM is a Java-based library that has a small memory
footprint and is used for processing XML files as fast as
SAX but only for small documents. The Parallel XML Tree
Generator (PXTG) algorithm [23] is designed for efficient
parsing. It takes an XML file as input and produces n subtrees.
This approach serially traverses the input file in n parts before
creating parallel subtrees. The traversal is determined by
different number of characters in the XML file. In order to
bring in a proper format for XML traversal, the XML contents
are patched as merged or replaced. The contents of XML
files are tuned by placing duplicate entries for nodes and
edges to achieving the hierarchy and the well-formedness
of each part. Additionally, the well-formed chunks are sent
to individual cores. This process is applied to create parallel pre-parsed subtrees. Lastly, PXTG produces well-formed
subtrees. VTD-XML is a novel non-extracted XML parsing
technique that Zhang introduced [24]. By analyzing the XML
document, VTD-XML generated a one-dimensional array
that could reduce the amount of memory required. Additionally, a variety of formats, such as binary XML [25], have
been suggested in the literature to enhance the performance
of XML parsing.
The requirement for strong predictive models is becoming
more and more demanding, because it is necessary to perform
predictions for many daily life scenarios, such as changes in
stock prices, weather patterns, or the development of features
in complicated industrial processes. Numerous techniques
were employed for this reason, including mathematical/
empirical-based equations, regression, and statistical-based
equations. Recently, various techniques of soft computing,
such as, gene expression programming (GEP), SVM, the
adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), and ANN

algorithm, our proposed framework XPOHML incorporates
SVM with kernel and ANN with a hidden layer.
In this Section, we discuss the extensive usage of ANN
and SVM in the fields of system identification and predictive
control [26], [27]. Even though ANNs produce good results,
there are still significant design challenges. These include
determining how many neurons to include in hidden layers,
the issue of overfitting, and the presence of local minima in
the target function. SVM are considered incredibly effective
regression and classification tools. Among their many benefits are their strong generalization skills and optimization
method, which is based on a convex function without a
local minimum [28]. According to its flexibility to address
challenges in pattern recognition [29], including non-linearity
and multiple dimensions, these models are easy to use and
optimized. SVM finds extensive application in face recognition [30], image processing [31], speech recognition [32],
face detection [33], and related domains.
The most applicable instruments for resolving complex,
contemporary issues are the hybridized classification techniques of optimization algorithms using ANN and SVM.
Sonar targets [34], [35], [36], [37], [38], [39], underwater
acoustical targets [40], [41], medical image categorization [42], [43], and brain [44], [45] or breast tumour
diagnostics [46], [47], [48] are a few examples. In contrast, our approach builds a framework that combines ANN
and SVM methodologies for analyzing and predicting the
performance of various parsers through XML profiling, classification, performance evaluation, and code generation for
effective parsing.
III. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY
This paper proposes an XPOHML framework that analyses the performance of XML parsing, predicts the efficient
parsing model using ANN and SVM techniques, evaluates
performance, and generates code for an optimized XML
parser. The XPOHML framework incorporates classification
models using ANN and SVM while configuring different
parameters. The architecture of the XPOHML framework is
stated in Figure 1. The first phase of the proposed framework
calculates the parsing time of various algorithms including StAX, SAX, DOM, JDOM, PXTG1, PXTG4, PXTG8,
PXTG12, and PXTG16. This phase ends by generating the
dataset by considering the parsing time for these algorithms.
PXTG1 handles XML files as a single chunk, while PXTG4,
PXTG8, PXTG12, and PXTG16 segment XML files into 4, 8,
12, and 16 parts respectively. The XML profiling step utilizes
various XML file sizes to calculate the parsing times of
these algorithms. The next phase of the XPOHML framework
performs classification by applying two machine learning
techniques ANN and SVM. After the configuration of different parameters, ANN and SVM create a classification model
for prediction. The next phase evaluates the performance
of classifiers by applying classification metrics. The final
phase generates code that invokes the most efficient parsing
algorithm in terms of execution time.
FIGURE 1. Proposed framework XPOHML architecture.
Figure 1 describes the four major components that constitute the XPOHML framework. The initial phase of this
framework is XML profiling, which is used to measure the
parsing times of various algorithms to produce a dataset.
The second phase performs classification by applying two
machine learning techniques ANN and SVM to analyze the
performance of parsers and produce classifiers for ANN and
SVM. This step results in the creation of classification models. The third phase of the proposed framework is to find the
best accuracy score by applying classification metrics. The
fourth and final phase parser generator uses user-provided
parameters for size and cores to predict the most effective
algorithm.

XML Profiling is the first phase of the XPOHML framework
that gathers data and produces dataset D. The performance
of several algorithms, such as SAX, StAX, DOM, JDOM,
PXTG, and the PXTG variations, is measured using this
procedure, as shown in Figure 2. XML files are handled as a
single chunk by PXTG1, however, these are divided into 4,

PXTG16, respectively for parallel processing.

profiling phase is to generate the dataset D for the next phase.
The results of XML profiling are given in the result section.
A minor modification is required in a dataset to become
useable for ANN and SVM techniques. The parsing time of
all algorithms is compared and replaced by the name of the
most efficient algorithm in terms of parsing time for each
particular instance. After the modification of the dataset, the
instances of a finalized dataset will be labeled as file size

1) CLASSIFICATION USING ANN
Applications for neural networks (ANN) include data analysis, pattern recognition, and categorization. The primary
structure of ANN consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and one output layer. Many neurons make up each
layer, and the connections between these neurons are assigned
varying weights. In the input layer, each neuron receives a
single data source. The output of every input layer serves
as a source of input for every hidden layer neuron. During
the training phase, each neuron’s weight is determined. Any
novel input vector is fed into the input layer of the neural
network once it has been trained. The value of each node is
determined by adding all the values that enter the node, and
multiplying the value of the input node by the connection
weight. The architecture of ANN used by the XPOHML
framework is given in Figure 3.

low-dimensional, nonlinear regression. A high dimensional
feature is created by nonlinearly mapping the input data,
and a linear regression is then performed in this modified
space. A Support Vector Classifier (SVC) specifically builds
a hyperplane or collection of high-dimensional hyperplanes
that divide training data into several classes and then utilize
the hyperplanes to categorize an image (or set of images)
appropriately. Developed in 1963 by Vapnik and Lerner [49],
the initial SVC algorithm was a linear classifier that yielded
no results if no hyperplane could be located to fully differentiate the training set. More flexibility in training data separation
was proposed by Boser et al. [50] in 1992 by utilizing the
so-called ‘‘Kernels’’ to embed nonlinearity in SVC. The
employment of kernel functions allows SVC to function in
a high-dimensional feature space without converting. All that
is required is the computation of the inner product between
each pair of data in the space [51]. Complete separation of the
training data is not always achievable, even with Kernels. The
most widely used mapping software, such as ENVI [52] and
EnMAP [53], uses the current standard SVM technique for
categorization of remote sensing data (C-SVC), which was
designed in 1995 by Cortes and Vapnik [54]. Even if C-SVC
is unable to fully separate the training data, it can still classify
entities. The terms ‘‘hard margin’’ and ‘‘soft margin’’ classifiers, respectively, refer to SVC and C-SVC. When a classifier
uses a hard margin, it must fully segregate the training set
in order to produce a result. A soft margin classifier, on the
other hand, selects the most effective hyperplanes to divide
the training data while permitting some inaccuracy in the
separation of the training data. In this sense, the soft margin
classifiers always yield a result, but they are highly dependent
on the model’s parameterization and training set.

C. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
The performance evaluation phase of the XPOHML framework is used to compute the performance of ANN and SVM
classifiers by applying accuracy. Accuracy is the most widely
used metrics in machine learning to assess the performance
of classifier [58]. It calculates the percentage of correctly
classified instances (true positives and true negatives) and is
written as:
Accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN)
(48)
False Positive (FP) is, when the model predicted an
algorithm as efficient and actually it was not the case. False
Negative (FN) is, when the model predicted an algorithm as
not efficient and actually it was. True Positive (TP) is, when
the model predicted an algorithm as efficient and actually it
was. True Negative (TN) is, when the model predicted an
algorithm as not efficient and actually it was not the case.
D. PARSER CODE GENERATION
The final module of the XPOHML framework generates the
code of the most efficient parsing model against particular file
size and the number of cores by calling the ParserCodeGenerator module (Algorithm 4), as given below:
ParserCodeGenerator (Algorithm 4) receives an XML file
size and the number of cores. Step 1 calls ANN_Model to
predict an efficient XML parser against a particular file size
and number of cores entered by the user. The next step checks
the accuracy of ANN by applying the classification metrics.
Step 3 calls SVM_Model to predict an efficient XML parser
against a user-entered particular file size and number of cores.
Step 4 applies the classification metrics to check the accuracy
of SVM. Step 5 compares the accuracy of the ANN model and
SVM model. The code of the most effective parsing model
against XML file and core is finally called.
Algorithm 4 ParserCodeGenerator (Size, Core)
1. Efficient_Algo_ANN = ANN_Model(Size, Core)
2. ANN_Score = Accuracy()
3. Efficient_Algo_SVM = SVM_Model(Size,Core)
4. SVM_Score = Accuracy()
5. IF ANN_Score>SVM_Score
Call Efficient_Algo_ANN(Size, Core)
ELSE
Call Efficient_Algo_SVM(Size, Core)
END IF-ELSE

V. CONCLUSION
For efficient XML parsing, the hybrid machine learning
approach proposed in this paper is implemented using the
XPOHML framework that performs analysis and prediction
of different parsers using profiling, classification, performance evaluation, and code generation phases. The XML
profiling phase of the XPOHML framework produces a
dataset by measuring the performance of PXTG, SAX, StAX,
DOM, and JDOM parsing models on different cores by using
multiple file sizes. The classification phase produces the
classifiers by applying ANN and SVM techniques to identify
the appropriate parsing model. The performance evaluation
phase of XPOHML assesses the efficacy of parsing models
by implementing accuracy metrics to compare performance
outcomes. Additionally, based on previous outcomes, the
code generation phase produces an efficient code for parsing
XML files. The parser generated by the XPOHML framework
outperforms other parsing models in terms of parsing time.

Abstract—The posture detection received lots of attention
in the ﬁelds of human sensing and artiﬁcial intelligence.
Posture detection can be used for the monitoring health
status of elderly remotely by identifyingtheir postures such as
standing, sitting and walking. Most of the current studies used
traditional machine learning classiﬁersto identify the posture.
However, these methods do not perform well to detect the
postures accurately. Therefore, in this study, we proposed a
novel hybrid approach based on machine learning classiﬁers
(i. e., support vector machine (SVM), logistic regression
(KNN), decision tree, Naive Bayes, random forest, Linear
discrete analysis and Quadratic discrete analysis) and deep
learning classiﬁers(i. e., 1D-convolutionalneural network (1D-
CNN), 2D-convolutional neural network (2D-CNN), LSTM and bidirectional LSTM) to identify posture detection. The
proposed hybrid approach uses prediction of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) to improve the performance
of ML and DL algorithms. The experimental results on widely benchmark dataset are shown and results achieved an
accuracy of more than 98%.
Index Terms— Posture detection, hybrid approach, deep learning, machine learning.
I. INTRODUCTION
T
HE posture detection is used in different applications
such as healthcare, surveillance, virtual environment,
indoor and outdoor monitoring, the reality for animation and
entertainment. In addition, the posture detection can be used
in framework of home-human interface. With the increased
number of elderly population and limited healthcare resources,
it is important to propose a technology which can support the
remote monitoring of elderly and vulnerable people to live
more independently. Maintain the good posture is signiﬁcant to
lead the healthy life. The posture is about how the people hold
their body and position the limbs. Within the advancement of

Considering the need, the paper reports three major contributions that are outlined below:

II. RELATED WORK
In the literature, extensive research has been carried out to
build different posture models. In this section, we summarize
the related state-of-the-art approaches for detection of human
postures.
In smart city prediction and supervision of human health,
using smart technology and portable system is an important
part. Therefore, posture recognition in this paper is determined
with multisensory and using LoRa (Long Range) technology.
LoRa WAN technology has the advantage of long transmission
distances and low cost. Using these two, multisensory and
loRa technology, wearable clothes are designed which is
comfortable in any given posture. In this paper multiprocessing
is used because LoRa has low transmitting frequency and
data transmission size is small. Hence, multiprocessing is
done by sliding window, feature extraction, data processing
and feature selection is done with Random forest. With
three testers of 500 grouped data set better performance
and accuracy is achieved [6]. Body postures and gestures
are also non-verbal way of communication. In this paper,
Augmented reality is used to determine the static posture
by reducing cost and advanced body tracking technology.
Also unsupervised machine learning on Kinect body posture
sensors are used to detect group cooperation and learning [7].
Posture detection has also play an important role in performing
yoga more accurately. Posture recognition is challenging task
due to real-time bases and less available data set. Therefore,
to overcome this issue large data set has been created with
at least 5500 images of different yoga poses. For posture
detection tf-pose estimation algorithm has been used which
draws skeleton of human body on the real-time bases. Angles
of the joints in the human body are extracted using the tf-pose
skeleton which is used as a feature to implement various
machine learning models (SVM, KNN, Logistic Regression,
DT, NB and random forest). Among all Random forest model
gives best accuracy [8]–[10].
In addition, there is another problem of posture in human
being which occurs due to maximum time in sitting position.
The poor and prolonged sitting effects physical and mental
health. Posture training system is designed for sitting position
and stretch pose data collection. Then for posture recognition,
smart cushion using Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) and pressure
sensing technologies is used. For more than 13 different postures, supervised machine learning models are trained which
give better performances [11]. The sensor chair with pressure
sensor tries to avoid wrong sitting position which may cause
disease. In this posture detection, analysis is compared with
decision tree and random forest. The classiﬁer which gives
better performance is random forest classiﬁer [12]. For the
improvement of sitting posture, sitting posture monitoring
systems (SPMSs) is used. It has mounted sensors on backrest
and seat plate of a chair. For this experiment 6 sitting postures
are considered. Then various machine learning algorithms
(SVM with RBF kernel, SVM linear, random forest, QDA,
LDA, NB and DT) are applied on body weight ratio which
is measured by SPMS. Result from SVM with RBF kernel
gives better accuracy as compare to others [13]. There is
also an intelligent systems design for the posture detection
of sitting person on wheel chair. A network of sensors is
used for data collection using neighbourhood rule (CNN),
then data balancing is done with Kennard-stone algorithm
and reduction in dimensions via principal component analysis.
Finally k-nearest algorithm is applied to pre-processed and
balanced data. In this amount of data is signiﬁcantly reduced
but result is remarkable [14].
A postural habit which has been formed cannot change
easily so it is vital to form a proper postural habit since
childhood. Therefore, machine learning algorithms CNN, NB,
DT, NN, MLR and SVM are used for posture detection. Data
is collected with a sensing cushion which is developed with
(8 ×8) pressure sensor mat inside children chair seat cushion.
Ten children are participated for ﬁve prescribed postures. The
accuracy of CNN is the highest than other algorithms [15].
Dance is also a challenging task for posture recognition. It is
multimedia in nature and its duration is over time as well
as space. For dance analysis few things must be undertaken
like segment of the dance video, recognition of the detected
action element and recognition of the dance sequences. In this
paper focus is on Indian classical dance, Bharatanatyam,
which is driven by music as well as motion for posture
recognition. Then recognition is done by machine and deep
learning techniques which are GMM, SVM and CNN. In the
ﬁnal step Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is applied for data
sequence recognition. The best recognition rate is with CNN
classiﬁer [16].

There are total of six features are used for posture prediction. The features determine the posture are skew, percentile,
square root (SR), standard deviation (SD), mean and kurtosis.
The values for each feature is calculated individually for each
window size. For example, the window size of 90 seconds is
selected and the aforementioned features are calculated. After
the feature extraction, the new dataset is created which consists
of different features. It is to be noted that, after feature extraction, the most important task is to determines the combination

C. Deep Learning (DL) Methods
In next section, we discuss our proposed hybrid model
which integrates the machine learning and DNN methods
including 1D-CNN, 2D-CNN, LSTM and BiLSTM. The deep
learning can be used in different various application such as
cyber-security, sentiment analysis, speech enhancement and
etc. However, in this paper we proposed a novel framework
to detect posture prediction.
Convolutional Neural Network: For comparison, the novel
CNN framework is developed. The implemented CNN consists of input, hidden and output layers. Our proposed CNN
framework contains convolutional, max pooling and fully
connected layers. The 10-layered CNN framework achieved

Long Short Term Memory (LSTM): The long short term
memory (LSTM) proposed architecture contains input layer,
two different stacked LSTM and one output as fully connected
layer. Particularly, the LSTM architecture consists of two
different stacked bidirectional layers (contains 128 cells and
64 cells) with dropout 0.2 and a dense layer with two neurons
and softmax activation.
D. Hybrid Models
The hybrid methods consists of different classiﬁers and
combining their prediction to train meta-learning model. The
hybrid is used to enhance the performance of speciﬁc system. In this study, the prediction of ML classiﬁers (logistic
regression, random forest, KNN, Naïve Bayes, decision tree,
linear discriminant analysis, quadratic discriminant analysis
and SVM) and DL classiﬁers (CNN, LSTM) are used as input
of CNN, LSTM architecture. Fig 2 shows the architecture of
proposed hybrid of ML and DL for posture detection. It is to
be noted that, the parameters of each classiﬁer has been set-up
empirically after several simulation experiments.

A. Discussion
The comparative experimental results show that the hybrid
deep learning method achieved better performance as compared to traditional machine learning and deep learning classi-
ﬁers. The performance achieved on the dataset is to identify the
posture prediction shows that the unique hybrid DL approaches
outperformed the ML and DL technique. In order to train
the DL classiﬁers, the NVIDIA GeForce 940M GPU with
384 Cuda cores and 2 GB DDR3 has been used. The main
advantage of hybrid DL classiﬁers is that their ability to
identify the posture. However, the dataset is only limited to
three posture including standing, sitting and walking. The
main disadvantage of the approach is DL classiﬁers are
computationally expensive. Table XIX shows the comparison
of state-of-the-art approaches with our proposed approach. The
comparison results show that our approach achieved superior
performance in term different evaluation metrics including

accuracy, precision, recall and f-measure as compared to other
approaches.
V. CONCLUSION
The remote health monitoring is important for providing
independent living to elderly and vulnerable. Therefore, in this
paper, we proposed a novel architecture based on deep learning
classiﬁers to identify posture including standing, sitting and
walking. In addition, the novel hybrid approach are developed
based on the DL methods to identify the posture prediction.
The hybrid approach contains different prediction of machine
learning and deep learning to train the meta-learning. The
experimental results show that the proposed hybrid approach
achieved better performance as compared to DL and ML
methods.
