A Machine Learning Approach Using Effective
Connectivity to Predict Response
to Clozapine Treatment
Claudio Ciprian, Student Member, IEEE, Kirill Masychev
, Member, IEEE,
Maryam Ravan
, Senior Member, IEEE, James P. Reilly
, Life Member, IEEE,
and Duncan MacCrimmon
Abstract— Clozapine is an anti-psychotic drug that is
known to be effective in the treatment of patients with
chronic treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS-SCZ), commonly estimated to be around one third of all cases. However, clinicians sometimes delay the initiation of this drug
because of its adverse side-effects. Therefore, identiﬁcation
of predictive biological markers of clozapine response are
extremely valuable to aid on-time initiation of treatment.
In this study, we develop a machine learning (ML) algorithm
based on pre-treatment electroencephalogram (EEG) data
sets to predict response to clozapine treatment in 57 TRS-
SCZs, where the treatment outcome, after at least one-year
follow-up is determined using the positive and negative
syndrome scale (PANSS). The ML algorithm has three steps:
1) a brain source localization (BSL) procedure using the
linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV) beamforming approach is employed on the EEG signals to extract
source waveforms from 30 speciﬁed brain regions. 2) An
effective connectivity measure named symbolic transfer
entropy (STE) is applied to the source waveforms. 3) A
ML algorithm is applied to the STE matrix to determine
whether a set of features can be found to discriminate
most-responder (MR) SCZ patients from least-responder
(LR) ones. The ﬁndings of this study reveal that STE features
can achieve an accuracy of 95.83%. This ﬁnding implies that
analysis of pre-treatment EEG could contribute to our ability
to distinguish MR from LR SCZs, and that the source STE
matrix may prove to be a promising tool for the prediction
of the clinical response to clozapine.
Index Terms— Clozapine treatment, effective connectivity, electroencephalography (EEG), EEG beamforming,
machine learning, odd-ball\paradigm, schizophrenia, symbolic transfer entropy.

I. INTRODUCTION
A
PPROXIMATELY
30%
of
patients
suffering
from
schizophrenia do not beneﬁt from conventional antipsychotic treatment and are classiﬁed as treatment resistant
schizophrenics (TRS-SCZ) [1]. Clozapine is now a wellestablished treatment for TRS patients that can effectively
reduce symptoms in these patients [2]–[5], but it carries the
risk of serious side effects such as seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, or neutropenia and requires regular blood monitoring.
Furthermore, 40% to 70% of TRS-SCZ patients fail to respond
to clozapine. Response currently can only be determined
through a trial of clozapine treatment. For these reasons
TRS-SCZ patients and physicians are often reluctant to use
clozapine and postpone the initiation of treatment. In a study,
Howes et al. (2012) [6] showed that there could be a delay
of around 4 years between diagnosing TRS-SCZ patients and
the initiation of clozapine. Patients are often treated with
alternative medications during this period, that sometimes
can cause adverse effects. Therefore, predicting in advance
whether a given patient is likely to beneﬁt from clozapine
treatment can signiﬁcantly reduce the treatment delay and also
clozapine can selectively be used for the subset of patients in
whom it is more likely to be effective.
An emerging number of studies that have compared TRS to
responsive cases report biological differences between the two
groups, which may suggest that TRS is a distinct subtype of
SCZ [7], and clozapine-resistant SCZ may reveal an additional
biological subtype. This suggests that biological markers may
be able to predict if the symptoms will improve with clozapine
prior to the initiation of treatment [8].
One of the most popular biological markers are neuroimaging markers that are measured by techniques such as structural
imaging, single photon emission computerized tomography
(SPECT), positron emission tomography (PET) of brain perfusion or metabolism, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI),
computerized tomography (CT), and electroencephalography
(EEG). Among these techniques, EEG is an inexpensive and
non-invasive technique that is available even in small hospitals
and private clinics. Therefore, predictive algorithms based on
EEG signals are more practical.
The goal of this study is therefore to develop a machine
learning (ML) algorithm based on pre-treatment EEG data

to automatically predict the response to clozapine treatment.
In so doing, we employ modern state-of-the-art EEG signal
processing methods that demonstrate signiﬁcantly improved
performance over previous approaches for this purpose.
II. RELATED WORKS
Several neuroimaging studies have been proposed in
the literature for predicting response to clozapine therapy based on neuroimaging techniques [8]. Using CT,
Konicki et al. (2001) [9] examined sulcal widening as a predictor of response to clozapine treatment using 26 most responder
(MR) and 10 least responder (LR) patients. They found that the
MR patients have signiﬁcantly lower widening scores in the
prefrontal sulci compared to LR ones, which suggest that poor
response may be associated with a higher degree of frontal
atrophy. Furthermore, Friedman et al. (1991) [10] evaluated
34 patients, 12 of which were classiﬁed as non-responders,
13 as moderate responders and 9 as good responders. They
reported that prefrontal sulcal prominence is inversely related
to clozapine response.
Using MRI, Honer et al. (1995) [11] evaluated 42 patients
(15 MR and 27 LR). They found that large sulci in the
posterior frontal and lateral temporal lobes predict poorer
response. In another study, Lauriello et al. (1998) [12] tested
21 male veterans of the United States armed forces (10 MR
and 11 LR). They found that patients with larger anterior superior temporal lobe cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) volumes showed
greater improvement. Arango et al. (2003) [13] compared
clozapine with Haloperidol, where 22 patients were assigned
to clozapine and 23 patients were assigned to Haloperidol.
They found that larger right prefrontal cortical gray matter
volumes were associated with greater reduction in scale for
the assessment of negative symptoms (SANS) scores after
clozapine treatment. However, they did not ﬁnd any associations with positive symptoms and hippocampal, caudate,
or total intracranial volumes. Molina et al. (2003) [14] investigated associations between different brain region volumes and
response to clozapine treatment using 25 TRS-SCZ patients,
where 12 of them were responders to clozapine treatment.
They showed that temporal cortex volume was directly associated with improvement in positive symptoms, whereas dorsolateral prefrontal cortical (DLPFC) CSF content was inversely
related to the improvement in positive symptoms. Furthermore, DLPFC volume was directly related to improvement
in negative symptom severity, and the intracranial volume was
negatively linked to improvement in disorganization syndrome.
From these studies, greater brain region volumes, mainly in
the frontal regions, are associated with a better response to
clozapine treatment. Moyett et al. (2020) [15] checked the
role of striatal connectivity to predict response using resting
functional MRI (fMRI) of 23 patients (13 MR and 10 LR).
They did not ﬁnd any signiﬁcant difference between striatal
connectivity index (SCI) values of the two groups, which (as
they mentioned) means striatal connectivity may not predict
response to clozapine.
Using brain perfusion, Rodriguez et al. (1997) [16] used
SPECT to investigate whether regional brain perfusion can
be used as a predictor of response to clozapine treatment
for 39 patients (19 MR and 20 LR). MR groups had higher
baseline perfusion in the lower right and upper left DLPFC,
left and right basal ganglia, and thalamus compared to LR
groups. They also could discriminate MR and LR groups with
78.9% accuracy using perfusion in the thalamus and right
DLPFC. Similarly, Ertugrul et al. (2009) [17] reported a link
between increase in the levels of perfusion in the right frontal
cortex and thalamus and better improvement in PANSS score
using clozapine treatment in 22 patients (11 MR and 11 LR).
EEG is one of the most commonly used biological measurements that can effectively capture the abnormalities of different
brain areas due to schizophrenia and the changes due to
clozapine treatment, and thus has been the focus of a number
of clinical studies (e.g. [18]–[23], [25]). Pillay et al. (1996)
[18] investigated whether clozapine response can be predicted
by minor EEG abnormalities such as generalized slowing or
sharp waves, spikes, spike-wave patterns, and focal dysrhythmias using 86 patients. They found greater improvement in
global assessment of functioning score in female participants
with a normal EEG before clozapine treatment. Knott et al.
(2000) [19] reported that clozapine-induced improvements in
positive and negative syndrome scale (PANSS) and global
psychopathology were related to greater pre-treatment quantitative EEG (QEEG) inter and intra-hemispheric spectral power
asymmetry using 13 patients (11 MR and 2 LR). Kang et al.
(2001) [20] used mutual cross-prediction analysis to determine
if activity in one region was driving the dynamics of another
region. Ten TRS chronic SCZ patients (4 MR and 6 LR) were
involved in this study. They observed that the patients without
a frontal lobe driving system and occipital response system had
a higher chance of responding to clozapine. Gross et al. (2004)
[21] examined the changes of theta frequency activity in the
QEEG in 16 SCZ patients (13 MR and 3 LR) during clozapine
treatment. They found changes in QEEG signals with clozapine treatment, mainly in the midline fronto-central area, were
a more sensitive indicator of evaluating clozapine efﬁcacy than
the serum clozapine level. Khodayari-Rostamabad et al. (2010)
[22] for the ﬁrst time applied a machine-learning algorithm to
predict clozapine responders based on their pre-treatment resting EEG measures, using ﬁrst a leave-one-out cross-validation
(LOO-CV) procedure on a group of 23 SCZ patients (12 MR
and 11 LR), and then an independent test dataset with 14 SCZ
patients (7 MR and 7 LR) to test the classiﬁers. Using
statistical features such as coherence, cross-correlation coefﬁ-
cients, and mutual information between EEG electrodes, and
the left-to-right hemisphere and anterior/posterior power ratio
at various frequencies, they could successfully discriminate
MR from LR with more than 85% accuracy. The authors
reported a list of 20 features with highest predictive value,
which mainly were selected from the left temporal and parietal
areas. Ravan et al. (2015) [23] applied a machine-learning
algorithm to Oddball EEG data of 47 SCZ patients before and
after a year of clozapine treatment and 66 healthy controls
(HCs). They ﬁrst applied a source montage approach [24]
to EEG data using BESA software (Megis Software GmbH,
Munich, Germany) with a conventional three-shell spherical
volume conductor head model. The source montage estimates

scalp, without considering deep brain activities, from the
recorded scalp EEG. Then they used the cross-power spectral
density (CPSD) function between these 15 areas as a measure
of connectivity. They found ﬁve discriminating features that
could simultaneously 1) discriminate all pre-treatment SCZ
patients from HCs with the accuracy of 81.4%, 2) discriminate
the pre- vs. post-treatment condition in the MR group with an
accuracy of 85% and 3) discriminate LR-SCZ group from HCs
even after treatment, with an accuracy of 79.6% all using a
LOO-CV procedure, and 4) found no discrimination between
post-treatment MR patients and HCs. The selected features
were mainly from the joint activity between the pre-frontal
and right anterior temporal or right parietal areas at beta
frequency band. Gica et al. (2019) [25] measured the absolute
power change in EEG data after one month post-treatment
for 23 patients to predict long term response. They found
a signiﬁcant correlation between the percentage of change
observed in both the PANSS positive subscale and the general
psychopathology subscale, and the percentage of change in the
theta wave absolute power values in the frontal region in the
ﬁrst month. They also found signiﬁcant correlation between
the percentage of change observed in the global assessment
of functioning (GAF) score, and the change in the theta wave
absolute power values in the central region, and alpha wave
absolute power values in parietal region.
Although there are several such studies identifying and
characterizing deﬁcits of schizophrenia and the efﬁcacy of
clozapine treatment, all these studies employed standard statistical parameters and conventional functional connectivity as
features that are mostly measured based on scalp electrodes,
which may cause false connectivity patterns due to volume
conduction effect [26]. This is partially due to the fact that
EEG data mostly reﬂects the electrical activity of the cortical
areas. The brain activities of deep areas are attenuated and
thus contribute considerably less to the scalp EEG signals.
To address this issue, a number of brain source localization (BSL) techniques have been proposed as an alternative to
channel-related connectivity (e.g. [27]–[29]). BSL techniques
can isolate the signal originating from a particular brain region,
and thereby suppress interference from other nearby regions,
thus increasing the signal to noise ratio (SNR) of the desired
signal. BSL methods can also suppress the volume conduction
effect. Also, because several EEG electrodes can collect the
activity of the same brain source, false connectivity indications
between brain regions may arise.
Non-parametric BSL techniques include minimum norm
estimates
(MNE)
[30]
and
their
generalizations
such
as low-resolution electromagnetic tomography (LORETA)
[31], standard LORETA (sLORETA) [32], exact LORETA
(eLORETA) [33], and the focal underdetermined system solution (FOCUSS) method [34]. However, these approaches are
proven to have poor spatial resolution. In contrast, parametric approaches such as the linearly constrained minimum
variance (LCMV) beamformer [35], the fast fully adaptive
approach [36], the robust minimum variance beamformer
technique [37], and subspace approaches (e.g., MUSIC [38],
RAP-MUSIC [39], and FINES [40] approaches) have been
shown to exhibit better spatial resolution and less localization
error. Among parametric approaches, the LCMV beamformer
is popular because it uses all the adaptive weights or degrees of
freedom (DoFs) and achieves superior spatial resolution with
no localization bias [35].
Effective connectivity across brain regions [41] reveals the
directed information ﬂow through neurons, as opposed to
functional connectivity, which is undirected and only reﬂects
the statistical covariation of signals, as usually shown by
coherency, cross-correlation, or phase lag index measures.
Measures of effective connectivity must meet four requirements, in addition to being directed, to be a useful addition
to already established methods [42]. These include: 1) there
can be no a priori requirement for a deﬁnition or model
of the type of interaction, 2) the method must be able to
detect non-linear interactions, since strong non-linearities are
detected across brain function, 3) must be able to detect
effective connectivity even if there is a wide distribution of
interaction delays between the two signals, as the signals
may move between brain areas through multiple pathways
with different conduction delays, 4) must be robust against
linear cross-talk between signals. Transfer entropy as a nonparametric statistic measuring the degree of directed transfer of
information between two random processes, does indeed fulﬁll
the above requirements, and is therefore a useful approach for
the quantiﬁcation of effective connectivity [42].
Consider two random processes X = (x1, x2, . . . , xN) and
Y = (y1, y2, . . . , yN), where xi and yi are the ith samples
(in this case, originating from two different brain regions).
Transfer entropy, which is related to Granger causality [43],
is deﬁned as the Kullback-Leibler distance between the distributions p(xi+1|xi) and p(xi+1|xi, yi). It is therefore a measure
of the information that yi contributes towards the prediction
of the future sample xi+1. If this quantity is non-zero, then
yi inﬂuences, or causes, xi and there is information ﬂow
from the brain region corresponding to the process Y to
that corresponding to X; i.e. the sources are “connected”.
Note that directionality implies that information ﬂow from
Y to X is not necessarily equivalent to that from X to Y.
Since transfer entropy is based on transition probability
distributions rather than solely on second-order statistics,
(such as e.g., Granger causality [43]) the method includes
dynamical information and is capable of dealing with nonlinear interactions. Thus, transfer entropy has gained growing popularity in several areas, particularly the neurological
sciences.
There are several techniques to estimate transfer entropy
from observed data (e.g. [44]–[46]). However, most of the
techniques require large quantities of data, tuning of parameters, and are highly sensitive to noise, therefore limiting
the use of transfer entropy in many applications. Symbolic
transfer entropy (STE) [47] (which involves estimation of
transfer entropy by adopting a technique referred to as symbolization) has been introduced as a robust, convenient, and
computationally fast measure to quantify information ﬂow in
multidimensional dynamic systems and can be used to infer
the direction of linear and non-linear information exchange
between brain regions over a range of time delays within

EEG data. Therefore, STE has potential for discriminating MR
vs. LR brain activity.
The contribution of this paper is threefold. First, the high
resolution LCMV BSL approach is used
for the ﬁrst
time to extract the activities of different brain regions for
schizophrenic patients. Second, the fast and robust STE
approach is used, again for the ﬁrst time, to measure the
effective connectivity between brain regions. Third, an ML
method is developed based on the features extracted from
these effective connectivity measures to predict response to
clozapine treatment.
The novelty of the present study therefore lies in applying
the combination of advanced signal processing methods, i.e.
LCMV BSL, STE, and ML to predict response. The combination of these more advanced techniques results in a signiﬁcant
improvement in the ability to predict responsiveness, relative
to previous approaches which have not used our proposed
combination of advanced signal processing methods.
III. METHODS
A. Subjects
Auditory oddball evoked potentials were collected from
57 SCZ subjects (age [years]: mean = 36.95, std = 9.22,
min = 17, max = 55, 37 male subjects (64.9%) and 20 female
subjects (35.1%)). All subjects were unpaid volunteer SCZ
subjects for this study. They were recruited from Hamilton
Psychiatric Hospital, Hamilton, Ontario for developing, on an
ongoing basis, analytic methodologies that might reveal QEEG
features differentiating schizophrenia from recruited healthy
volunteers. The study was reviewed and approved by the
Research Ethics Board of the Hospital. All EEG data were collected with the informed consent of the subjects. All SCZ subjects met both the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental
Disorders, fourth edition (DSM-IV) criteria for schizophrenia
and the Kane criteria for treatment resistance [2]. Patients meet
these two criteria typically have chronic schizophrenia and
suffer from severe symptoms. Post treatment EEG data were
collected after a mean treatment duration of 1.4 years (min =
0.4 years, max = 4.6 years). The mean daily dose of clozapine
employed was 347 mg (range 50–800 mg).
To measure the PANNS severity rating scale, ﬁrst all
available clinical information about the symptoms revealed by
the SCZ patients were reviewed by an experienced clinician
prior to starting clozapine treatment. Then the symptoms were
rated by one of the three PANSS rating scales of “present”,
“moderate” or “severe” on a one to six-point scale. The
clinician was instructed to only score the explicitly described
symptoms and avoid scoring the potential symptoms. The
same rating procedure was repeated after clozapine treatment,
at the time when a decision would be made regarding further
on-going long-term maintenance of treatment. Since most
studies report that, on average, only one third of TRS-SCZ
patients respond to clozapine treatment [2], we rank-ordered
all patients by percentage of reduction in severity score from
baseline PANSS and then chose a threshold value of 40% such
that the 57 patients were divided into 33.3% MR and 66.7%
LR patients (19 MR and 38 LR).
B. EEG Recording Procedure
The EEG data were recorded using a QSI-9500 system. Electrodes were referenced to linked ears and were
placed in standardized locations according to the International
10/20 system. The impedances of the electrodes were below
5 k. The system contains 20 EEG electrodes (Fp1, Fp2,
F7, F3, Fz, F4, F8, T7, C3, Cz, C4, T8, P7, P3, Pz, P4,
P8, O1, Oz, O2), as well as 4 additional muscle and eye
movement artifact electrodes. The subjects listened to the
auditory odd-ball paradigm over stereo headphones, where two
different 50 ms, 91.5 dB tone beep stimuli were delivered in
random order. The standard stimulus was a 1000 Hz tone that
presented 80% of the time, while the deviant (also referred
to as an “oddball”) stimulus was a 2000 Hz tone presented
20% of the time. The inter-stimulus interval was randomly
varied between 1.25 and 3 sec. The subjects were seated
comfortably with eyes opened and instructed to show by
ﬁnger lift when they hear a deviant stimulus. The patient’s
performance was monitored continuously for accuracy and
were given a break whenever it was required to maintain the
accuracy in identifying the deviant tones at or beyond the 90%
level. The duration of each epoch was 1024 msec and the
epochs were sampled with a sampling frequency of 250 Hz.
The recording system separately recorded the average of the
standard and deviant epochs at each electrode until the total
of 120 successful deviant epochs were recorded. The signals
were band pass ﬁltered between 0.5 and 80 Hz and notch
ﬁltered at 60 Hz during the recording. The signals were then
digitally band pass ﬁltered between 0.5 Hz and 50 Hz using the
EEGLAB MATLAB toolbox to partially mitigate the effects
of muscle artifacts and eye movements. Only the averages of
the deviant epochs measured by each of the electrodes were
used in subsequent analysis.
C. De-Artifacting
The recording system automatically rejected epochs with a
peak to peak signal amplitude of more than 100 uV on any
electrode. The subjects were given frequent “blink holidays”
to decrease eye blinking during recording. To alleviate muscle
artifacts, the subjects were seated on a comfortable chair.
A trained technician observed the subject continuously during
recording to identify epochs with muscle and eye artifacts.
All such epochs were removed from the recordings. The
recorded signals were then visually inspected off-line to detect
and remove any residual muscle or eye artifacts veriﬁed by
detection of a strong signal on any of the 4 artifact electrodes.
D. EEG Source Connectivity Analysis
This stage was performed using the LCMV beamforming
approach and consists of three steps: 1) The selection of
regions of interest (ROIs) to identify intracerebral electrical sources, 2) application of LCMV beamforming to scalp
EEG data to extract brain activity in the selected ROIs, and
3) application of an STE algorithm to compute the effective
connections between the identiﬁed sources. An ML algorithm
then followed. This method identiﬁes the most relevant of the

E. Machine Learning
In this study the data set consists of the EEG responses
to the odd-ball (or deviant) responses for each of the Mt =
57 subjects, and their corresponding labels, 1 for the 19 MR
patients and 2 for the 38 LR. The ML procedure contains four
steps: feature extraction, feature selection, classiﬁcation, and
evaluation. The objective of the ML procedure is to determine
whether a previously unseen test subject belongs to the MR
or LR class.
The ﬁrst step consists of extracting the candidate features
in the form of Nc = 4350 STE connectivity values from the
EEG data of all SCZ subjects.
After extracting candidate features, the second step is feature selection to reduce the number of features. This step is
critical to avoid overﬁtting, which affects the performance of
the classiﬁer. In this step we identify a set of Nr ≪Nc most
discriminating features to distinguish between the MR and
LR classes. Various feature selection methods are available
that can be separated into three categories: ﬁlter methods,
wrapper methods, and embedded methods [54], [55]. Two
main advantages of the ﬁlter method are computation efﬁ-
ciency and generalizability over different classiﬁers. In this
study, we used the minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) feature selection algorithm, which is a ﬁlter
method, to select the most distinguishable features [56]. The
rationale for choosing the mRMR method is its ability to effectively reduce the number of selected redundant features while
maintaining the most relevant features for the model. It is
known that selecting the N best features individually does not
necessarily lead to the best set of combined features because of
their potential correlation and redundancy [57]. The mRMR
method solves this problem by selecting features that have
maximum statistical dependence (relevance) with the outcome
variable (here the treatment response) and minimum statistical
dependence (redundancy) within the selected features.
In order to avoid choosing features that are dominant in
only a few subjects, we used the newly developed consensus
nested cross validation (CN-CV) procedure [58]. The CN-CV
procedure is an iterative process, where ﬁrst the dataset is split
into k outer folds (here we use stratiﬁed K folds, where each
fold has the same proportion of data for each class). Then at
each iteration, one fold is held out for testing and is omitted
from the training set while the remaining K −1 folds are
merged and split into L inner folds for feature selection. The
iterations repeat until all outer folds have been considered as
a test set once. The CN-CV algorithm structure is similar to
nested CV(N-CV) [59], but unlike N-CV it does not train the
classiﬁers in the inner folds. In contrast, CN-CV only performs
feature selection in the inner folds. The steps of the CN-CV
algorithm are as follows:
1. Divide the dataset into K randomly selected outer
cross-validation folds
2. For each outer fold k = 1, 2, . . . ., K:
2.1 Assign fold k as a test fold.
2.2 Assign the remaining K-1 folds as training dataset.
2.3 Randomly split the training dataset into L inner
folds for feature selection.
2.4 For each inner fold l = 1, 2, …, L, apply the
feature selection approach to the training dataset
for that fold (i.e. the remaining L-1 folds).
2.5 Find consensus (common) features across all the
inner L folds and consider it as the feature set for
outer fold k, Fk.
3. Find the consensus features across all the outer folds k,
k = 1, 2, …, K and consider them as the ﬁnal selected
features, SF
4. For Nr
= 1, 2, . . . , NSF (total number of selected
features)
4.1 Select the ﬁrst Nr consensus features at each outer
fold k, k = 1, 2, …, K.
4.2 Train the classiﬁer based on the Nr selected features on the kth outer fold training dataset and
evaluate its performance on the corresponding test
dataset and save the accuracy metrics for outer fold
k.
4.3 Calculate the average of any accuracy metric over
all K outer folds and report it as the generalization
accuracy metric using Nr features.
5. Select the ﬁrst Nr features with the highest classiﬁcation
performance as the ﬁnal set of selected features, and
the corresponding generalization accuracy metrics as the
ﬁnal performance metrics.
Here we consider k = l = 5 in order to have 80% of
the data for training and 20% for testing in each inner and
outer iteration. At each inner fold, features with mRMR scores
above 10−3 are considered as selected features for that fold.
We use the conservative threshold value of 10−3, because features with smaller scores are likely irrelevant for classiﬁcation.

TABLE II
THE 8 DISCRIMINATING FEATURES BETWEEN MR AND LR GROUPS
The CN-CV algorithm helps us to select most discriminating
features that are in common across inner training folds, while
the use of the inner folds prevents information leakage between
outer folds. Furthermore, selecting features without training
classiﬁers makes CN-CV method more computationally efﬁ-
cient than N-CV and selects fewer irrelevant features than N-
CV [58]. In this study, the lowest number of features that
gave adequate performance was Nr = 8, which is much lower
than the 57 data samples and thus reduces the tendency for
over-ﬁtting (the feature to sample ratio is 8/57 × 100 =
14.03%).
The third step is selecting the classiﬁer for classiﬁcation. In this step, the selected features are employed to
the classiﬁer. The classiﬁer’s function is to provide a class
label for a selected feature set corresponding to a given
data sample. In our study, we compare the performance of
three widely used classiﬁers: support vector machine (SVM),
random forest (RF), and linear discriminate analysis (LDA)
algorithms. A Gaussian radial basis kernel function, which
was determined using the sequential minimal optimization
technique [60], is considered for the SVM algorithm, and
30 trees are considered for the RF algorithm. These methods
were implemented using the Statistics and Machine Learning
Toolbox in MATLAB R2019b.
The ﬁnal step is performance evaluation. Since the size
of our available training set is small, to obtain an effective
estimate of the ML performance, the CN-CV algorithm were
used in this step to evaluate the performance.
IV. RESULTS
A set of 8 features which can discriminate between MR
and LR have been identiﬁed in Table II using the mRMR
feature selection approach. Table III shows the sensitivity,
speciﬁcity, total accuracy, precision, F1 score, and the Kappa
statistic for the widely used SVM, RF, and LDA classiﬁcation
approaches, using the outer 5 folds of the CN-CV method for
performance evaluation. mRMR and the widely-used random
forest (RF) approaches were used for feature selection. With
the RF classiﬁer, the feature selection process is embedded in
the algorithm. The RF feature selection approach is used for
comparison against the mRMR method. For the RF feature
selection method, the features are ranked by the RF classiﬁer
and the best features are selected according to their RF rank.
TABLE III
CLASSIFICATION PERFORMANCE OF DIFFERENT CLASSIFIERS
DISCRIMINATING 19 MR FROM 38 LR SUBJECTS
USING SKF-CV WITH K=5
Fig. 2.
Comparison of ROC curve between SVM, RF, and LDA
approaches.
In this study, sensitivity is the MR prediction rate, which
refers to how well the MR subjects are predicted without being
missed. Speciﬁcity is the LR prediction rate, and total accuracy
is the total test prediction rate considering both the MR and
LR groups. Precision is the fraction of truly predicted MR
cases among all cases that are predicted MR. The F1 score
is a measure of a test’s accuracy that considers both the
precision and the sensitivity of the test data to compute the
score, which is considered to be a better indication of overall
classiﬁcation accuracy. The Kappa statistic [61] corrects the
degree of agreement between the classiﬁer’s predictions and
reality by considering the proportion of predictions that might
occur by chance, and is recommended as an indicator of the
consistency of the accuracy estimate [62].
Furthermore, Fig. 2 compares the performances of all three
classiﬁers in terms of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve [63] and the area under the ROC curve (AUC)
value. ROC is a widely used tool that provides an indication of
the tradeoff between classiﬁcation sensitivity and speciﬁcity as
the classiﬁer conﬁdence threshold increases or decreases. The

AUC provides an aggregate measure of performance across all
possible classiﬁcation thresholds.
From Table III, the SVM classiﬁer can discriminate MR
from LR with the highest averaged total classiﬁcation accuracy
of 95.83% (averaged over the 5 folds) using the mRMR feature
selection method, followed by the RF and LDA classiﬁers with
total accuracies of 93.37% and 91.48%, respectively. The other
ﬁve calculated accuracy metrics are sensitivity, speciﬁcity,
Precision, F1-score, and the kappa statistic. SVM and LDA
have the highest sensitivity of 93.75%, followed by RF with a
sensitivity of 85.42%, while the highest speciﬁcity of 96.87%
belongs to SVM and RF, followed by the LDA with a
speciﬁcity of 90.18%. In terms of precision, RF has the highest
value of 95%, followed by SVM and LDA with precision
values of 93.75% and 85%. Furthermore, SVM has the highest
F1-score (F1=93.75), followed by LDA (F1=88.89%) and RF
(F1=88.65%) and the highest Kappa statistic (κ = 0.91),
followed by RF (κ =0.84) and LDA (κ = 0.82). Finally,
from Fig. 2, SVM has the highest AUC (AUC=0.96) followed
by RF (AUC=0.95) and LDA (AUC=0.94). These high classiﬁcation accuracies across different classiﬁcation algorithms
proves the selected features are highly discriminating between
the two classes. In addition, these results show that SVM
has the highest and most consistent overall classiﬁcation
accuracy. We believe this is due to the fact that SVM can
deal with imbalanced datasets more effectively than RF, since
RF is built on decision trees, which are sensitive to class
imbalance. Also, the radial basis kernel function used by SVM
potentially improves performance by imposing a non-linear
decision boundary that can be adapted to best suit the data,
while LDA can only choose the best linear transformation that
maximizes separability.
In addition, from Table III, the minimum number of features
for the RF algorithm for best performance is Nr
= 12.
Comparing the performance of the three classiﬁers using the
features selected inherently by the RF algorithm, we see
a considerable reduction in classiﬁcation performance for
the SVM and LDA methods, suggesting less generalizability
for the RF feature set. Alternatively, the effect of reducing
feature redundancy afforded by mRMR method leads to a
signiﬁcantly better classiﬁcation performance for all three
classiﬁers. Such distinctive features would also provide better
interpretability, since the model is not overwhelmed with
redundant information.
To demonstrate the clustering behavior of the selected
features, Fig. 3 shows a scatter plot containing 57 points
corresponding to the 19 MR and 38 LR subjects. This ﬁgure is
generated using the kernelized principle component analysis (KPCA) method with a polynomial kernel [64]. Although
the MR and LR clusters are clearly separated in this ﬁgure,
better performance is obtained using all 8 selected features.
Although previous studies (e.g. [9]–[21], [25]) found that
pre-treatment changes in neuroimaging features are correlated with clozapine treatment outcomes, their ﬁndings did
not lead to the development of a quantitative prediction
algorithm. ML was used as a predictive algorithm in [22]
for the ﬁrst time. However, the authors used conventional
functional connectivity that applied to scalp electrodes as
Fig. 3.
Scatter plot of the feature space showing MR (red circles) vs.
LR (black stars) projected onto the ﬁrst two major nonlinear principal
component directions.
features, which may cause false connectivity patterns due
to volume conduction effects in scalp EEG data. BSL is
an alternative to channel-related connectivity to mitigate this
issue.
It is worth noting that some of the selected features using
the proposed feature selection algorithm were from the regions
that are also identiﬁed in previous studies. Most of these
studies showed measures of frontal area as a predictive value to
clozapine treatment [9]–[11], [13], [14], [16], [17], [20], [21]
(features 1, 3, 4, 5, and 8 in Table II). Furthermore, it is
shown there is a link between increase in the levels of
perfusion in thalamus [16], [17] and basal ganglia [16] areas
and response to clozapine treatment. While the thalamus and
basal ganglia areas are not among the ROIs in this study,
Yakovlev et al. (1966) [65] showed the high degree of overlap
of the thalamic projections on the cingulate gyrus, which
is selected in features 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8. Also, the frontal,
premotor and supplementary motor areas, the orbital frontal
cortex, the dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex, and the anterior
cingulate all connect into the basal ganglia [66]. Three more
areas that are included in the selected features are left LTL
(feature 2), left FG (features 6 and 7), and left SPL (feature 1),
where left LTL and left FG are a part of the left temporal
lobe and left SPL is a part of left parietal lobe, where their
measures are shown to be linked to the prediction of clozapine
treatment [22].
V. CONCLUSION
In this study, for the ﬁrst time, we developed an ML
algorithm based on LCMV, BSL and STE effective connectivity techniques to investigate the possibility of predicting response to clozapine treatment using pre-treatment
odd-ball EEG measurements over 19 MR and 38 LR SCZ
patients. We identiﬁed a set of 8 discriminating features
that distinguish MRs from LRs, with the highest and
most consistent accuracy being obtained using the SVM
classiﬁer
(Sensitivity=93.75%,
speciﬁcity=96.87%,
total
accuracy=95.83%, precision=93.75%, F1-score=93.75%, and

source: A Machine Learning Approach Using Effective Connectivity to Predict Response to Clozapine Treatment.pdf
text:
κ = 0.91). This high classiﬁcation accuracy supports the
potential usefulness of ML methods in clinical psychiatry. The
use of the LCMV BSL method is critical in this study to
increase the SNR of the desired signal from a particular ROI
and suppress the volume conduction effect, which may cause
false connectivity estimates between regions.
This study showed that the use of advanced signal processing and ML models improves the prediction accuracy of
responsiveness to clozapine treatment compared to other studies. Furthermore, the sample of 57 subjects in this study is
larger than most of the previous studies and has the advantage
of a lengthy follow-up, which can increase the probability of
detecting clozapine effectiveness [67]. Our ﬁnding suggests
that combining BSL, STE, and ML analytic techniques may
be employed to create a useful psychiatric tool to predict
responsiveness to clozapine treatment. This methodology also
has the potential to be extended to a model that can predict
the response to different treatments available for SCZ patients
or even for other mental disorders. It may be possible to
combine a range of other clinical and laboratory features
such as personal and demographic information, personality
inventory scores, blood tests, and treatment history to EEG
measurements to improve prediction performance even further.
Finally, we note that accuracy values shown in Table III are
signiﬁcantly improved over those of any other similar study
we have seen from the literature. We attribute this improved
performance to the use of the more sophisticated signal
processing techniques adopted in the present study. A major
contribution of this paper is therefore the demonstration that
the use of such advanced signal processing methods results
in signiﬁcantly improved performances over what has been
previously obtained.

Peyman Razmi, Majid Oloomi Buygi, and Mohammad Esmalifalak
Abstract—We aim to provide a tool for independent system
operators to detect the collusion and identify the colluding
firms by using day-ahead data. In this paper, an approach
based on supervised machine learning is presented for collusion
detection in electricity markets. The possible scenarios of the
collusion among generation firms are firstly identified. Then,
for each scenario and possible load demand, market equilibri‐
um is computed. Market equilibrium points under different col‐
lusions and their peripheral points are used to train the collu‐
sion detection machine using supervised learning approaches
such as classification and regression tree (CART) and support
vector machine (SVM) algorithms. By applying the proposed ap‐
proach to a four-firm and ten-generator test system, the accura‐
cy of the proposed approach is evaluated and the efficiency of
SVM and CART algorithms in collusion detection are com‐
pared with other supervised learning and statistical techniques.
Index Terms—Market power, collusion detection, machine
learning, support vector machine (SVM), classification and re‐
gression tree (CART), statistical method.
I. INTRODUCTION
I
N a competitive electricity market, producers cannot af‐
fect the market price. They can only determine the
amount of their own production according to the market
price. Therefore, the optimum production level will be calcu‐
lated by the intersection of the marginal cost curve with mar‐
ket price. The limitations of power systems have pushed the
electricity markets from competitive environment toward oli‐
gopoly market. In an oligopoly market, there is a possibility
for producers to affect the market price. The producers who
are interested in raising the market price may increase their
bids (economic withholding) or reduce the production (physi‐
cal withholding) to influence the market price in their favor‐
able direction. The producers, who can affect the market
with any of the above mentioned methods, have the so
called “market power” [1], [2]. In addition to raising prices
higher than the competitive level, the ability of maintaining
the market price for a long period is important.
After the liberalization of the electricity market, price ma‐
nipulation and market power of individual producers [3]-[5]
can result from the joint decision and the alliance of two or
several producers. In such cases, the collusion is done in the
form of implicit and explicit [6], [7]. A long-term alliance
between several firms to inflate the market price out of its
competitive range is called collusion. Generation firms,
which cannot obtain their desired profit through fair competi‐
tion in oligopoly market, may collude and set their bid and
market prices to a value abnormally higher than what oligop‐
oly competition commands. Explicit collusion is a hidden
agreement for the interaction among electricity power pro‐
ducers who share confidential information in order to control
the market price. The goal of a coalition is to adopt or en‐
force unified strategies to increase the profit of its members.
However, the influence of a coalition does not remain limit‐
ed to the bids of its members and will alter the bids of its
competitors. Stakeholder’s choice of coalition is based on
the projected profit after the formation of the coalition. In
other words, each agent selects the coalition that provides
the maximum profit. Members of an explicit coalition share

With the advent of modern wholesale electricity markets
in developed countries, these markets have become the sub‐
ject of many discussions. These discussions often originate
from the nature of the electricity markets, e.g., they are of‐
ten controlled by a few number of firms, the traded electrici‐
ty cannot be stored, the demand has an inelastic nature, and
technical limitations such as the congestion of transmission
line can lead to the isolation of sub-markets. These character‐
istics provide an enabling environment for coalitions, which
can be regarded as the collusion [10]. The absence of the
competition in a market where prices are set by the collu‐
sion leads to the violation of the consumers’ rights and the
reduction of producer’s efficiency. In light of these adverse
effects, regulatory organizations often prohibit such coali‐
tions to protect the competition [11], [12]. This paper focus‐
es on the explicit collusion and proposes an approach to re‐
veal and detect such collusive behaviors. However, it is not

The basic approach is to use supervised learning, but the
major problem of this approach is the unavailability of data
specifically referring to collusion. The alternative is to use
unsupervised learning techniques for this purpose [13], [14].
The detection mechanism introduced in [13] focuses on cir‐
cular trading, in which a ring of colluder trades a certain
share repeatedly to raise their price. The proposed method is
based on the interpretation of stock flow graph with Markov
clustering algorithm. Reference [14] focuses on the detection
of cross trading and investigates the aptitude of different
clustering algorithms for collusion detection in electricity
markets. Reference [15] detects the collusion using a twostep process in an energy market. Firstly, the behavioral pat‐
tern of the collusion is investigated. Then, by using a
change-point analysis, the behavior of each agent is studied
to reveal the possible structural breakpoints. The existence
of such breakpoints could be a sign for the collusion and has
to be analyzed more in a verification phase. In the verifica‐
tion phase, behavioral similarities of candidates are checked
using statistical methods. The execution of market power
and the inefficiencies of restructured electricity market in Al‐
berta, Canada, are studied in [16]. The hourly wholesale mar‐
ket data set from 2008 to 2014 is used to find that firms con‐
duct considerable power in the highest demand hours with
bounded excess generation capacity. A game-theoretic model
is used in [17] to analyze the behaviours of independent sys‐
tem operator (ISO) and the generator leading to collusive
transactions. Reference [18] demonstrates the relationship be‐
tween market concentration and collusion sustainability and
their dependence to the strength of the network externalities.
In [19], from the regulatory body’s viewpoint, a model pow‐
ered by game theory and agent-based systems is used to in‐
vestigate the behaviours of each market player. The pro‐
posed method looks at the tacit collusive behaviour of gener‐
ation firms as well as the possibility of explicit collusion.
Reference [20] intends to detect the possibility of collusive
behavior in the liberalized retail electricity market by testing
the validity of the Cournot model of imperfect competition.
The monthly data on the Japanese electric power industry
are applied from 2005 to 2010. It indicates that the possibili‐
ty of collusive behavior among the incumbents cannot be ex‐
cluded. Moreover, the test results imply that larger market
size and firm size might reduce the possibility of collusion
among incumbent retail electricity suppliers. Reference [21]
provides an approach to analyze the development of tacit col‐
lusion between a generator company (Genco) and a distribut‐
ed company (Disco) in a simulated electricity market. Behav‐
iors of Gencos and Discos are modeled using state-action-re‐
ward-state-action (SARSA) learning algorithm, and the mod‐
el is used to tune continual exploration and make the tradeoff between the exploration and exploitation. A typical mar‐
ket with three Gencos and two Discos to prove the possibili‐
ty of tacit collusion between a Genco and a Disco is ana‐
lyzed, which shows that the development of this type of col‐
lusion increases their utilities. Reference [22] studies the col‐
lusion during bilateral agreement in the direct electricity pur‐
chase market. Firstly, a multiple-to-multiple (MTM) model
of bilateral negotiation in direct electricity purchase market
is provided based on the traditional Rubinstein negotiation
model. Then, the collusion is divided into two categories.
Specifically, the collusion can be divided into two catego‐
ries. One is based on the pre-specified information and the
other is based on process communication. Then, the bidding
strategies under the above two collusions are studied in de‐
tail. Finally, the impact of the collusion on the market is ana‐
lyzed through simulations, and regulatory proposals are pro‐
posed. Reference [23] investigates the competition on local
electricity markets to avoid the effects of market power and
analyze the impact of tacit collusion on the possibility of ex‐
ercising market power. It shows that more competitions
would diminish the effects of market power, especially when
a high-level competition with market shares of no more than
20%, because each competitor is needed for peak produc‐
tion. They also indicate that the overall effect of tacit collu‐
sion seems to be small in order to manipulate the market
price by the colluder. Furthermore, tacit collusion in the
form of signaling has no impact on base agent markups.
This paper uses supervised learning methods to detect the
collusion in electricity markets. Market equilibrium is firstly
computed for different loads and collusions. Market equilibri‐
um data and their neighboring operation points are used to
train the collusion detection machine by applying support
vector machine (SVM) and decision tree algorithms. The ef‐
ficiencies of these algorithms are compared with other super‐
vised learning and statistical method.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section Ⅱ
describes the process through which Nash equilibrium is
modeled and market equilibrium is computed. Section Ⅲ
overviews the machine learning approach used to detect the
collusion. In Section Ⅳ, the method of finding quasi-actual
system operation points is described. In Section Ⅴ, the devel‐
oped collusion detection method is applied to the model of a
typical electricity market, and then the results are discussed
and analyzed in Section Ⅵ.
II. MODELING OF EQUILIBRIUM POINT
In practice, there is no enough data from different collud‐
ed scenarios to train the collusion detection machine. The
purpose of equilibrium point modeling is to simulate and col‐
lect data for the training process in subsequent steps. Nor‐
mal operation points are usually fluctuating around Nash
equilibrium. Nash equilibrium is the point where no firm is
better by changing its strategy unilaterally [24]. In other
words, the deviation from the Nash equilibrium point by par‐
ticipants will not increase their profits. For the modeling of
equilibrium point, it is necessary to define the assumptions
and conditions of market operation in the restructured power
industry. For this purpose, we assume that the day-ahead

III. MACHINE LEARNING
The concept of machine learning originates from pattern
recognition and computation learning theory in artificial in‐
telligence [26]. The algorithms developed with machine
learning concepts are expected to do their tasks for unspeci‐
fied data [27]. Machine learning has a multitude of tasks,
the most important of which may be the supervised learning
[28]. In the supervised learning, the algorithm with a certain
input, a certain output, and a group of labeled training data
is provided. The algorithm then uses machine inference to
develop a function capable of emulating the process and
mapping the new data.
A. SVM Algorithm
SVM algorithm [29], [30] is one of the most widely used
supervised algorithms in data classification. In fact, SVM al‐
gorithm is a binary classifier that defines the optimal bound‐
ary between two (or more) classes. Mathematically, SVM us‐
es a linear hyper-plane to separate two classes by maximiz‐
ing the distance of each class from this plan. The algorithm
uses a quadratic programming to find data samples that are
in the border of each class, and these samples are known to
support vectors. Then, the algorithm searches for the hyperplane which firstly has the maximum distance from each sup‐
port vector. Secondly, the distances between the hyper-plane
and each support vector are equal. As mentioned above, the
support vector algorithm is used only to separate the two
classes from each other. But for collusion detection and diag‐
nosis of the firms involved in the collusion, the number of
different classes may depend on the type of the collusion,
and the number of firms is more than those of the two class‐
es. Hence, for the category and classification of different
types of the collusion, specific methods of multi-class SVMs
must be used, which include one against one and one
against all methods [31], [32]. If the data are inseparable by
a linear hyper-plane, the data are mapped to a higher dimen‐
sional space which is called feature space by kernel func‐
tion. Through this procedure, the algorithm becomes capable
of fitting the maximum-margin hyper-plane in a transformed
feature space. This transformation could be linear or nonlin‐
ear and the transformed feature space could be of a higher
dimension. Note that in the transformed feature space, the
classifier is a hyper-plane, but in the original input space, it
could be nonlinear [33]. Factors deciding the SVM perfor‐
mance are the chosen kernel function and its parameters as
well as the soft margin parameter C. Gaussian kernel, which
has a single γ, is a typical choice for SVM [34]. The com‐

B. Classification and Regression Tree (CART) Algorithm
As a predictive model, decision tree is one of the super‐
vised learning and non-parametric methods with the hierar‐
chical structure which is used to classify different types of
data, and its results are delivered in a flowchart-like tree
structure. According to the dependent variable type, this algo‐
rithm is divided into two categories: classification trees for
discrete variables and regression trees for continuous vari‐
ables. In this algorithm, the fragmentation of the data is im‐
plemented by using the features as a tree. For better under‐
standing, it is written by using as if-then rules [36]. In each
stage of this method, a feature for the data is selected based
on the training data and the data set is divided into a class
grouping based on the chosen features. This continues until
all the data in a category has a single label. One of the most
famous decision tree algorithms is CART algorithm, which
leads to the creation of a tree with binary division intro‐
duced in [37]. CART algorithm is a non-parametric decision
tree learning technique, which is used to classify any type of
the data. In other words, the CART algorithm produces ei‐
ther the classification or regression trees, depending on
whether the dependent variable is categorical or numerical,
respectively. At each stage, the Gini index is used to select
the best attribute for the data used. One important applica‐
tion of machine learning is to model costumer behaviors in
financial markets, which comes from the fact that finding
mathematical rules to model the behaviors of individual cos‐
tumers is a very complex process, e.g., in credit card fraud
detection. It would be extremely hard to find reasons and
rules for justifying safe versus fraudulent behaviors without
the help of machine learning approaches. This research is an‐
other attempt to model the behavior of market participants
without the detailed knowledge about their incentives. In cre‐
ating synthetic data, it is assumed that we know safe or
fraudulent behaviors, but we let machine learning approach
distinguish those behaviors without access to any of rules
used to create synthetic data.
IV. COLLUSION DETECTION AND CLASSIFICATION
A. Data Generation
The objective of this paper is to provide a tool that would
allow ISO to detect collusion and identify the colluding
firms using the day-ahead data, which is pursued via ma‐
chine learning paradigm. One problem that obstructs the use
of trainable machines in collusion detection and classifica‐
tion is the lack of adequate knowledge about the data associ‐
ated with different collusion among participants. According
to Section Ⅱ, equilibrium points are obtained for different
load demands and different kinds of collusion scenarios. To
achieve a proper collusion detection technique, the modeling
should go beyond the limits of a single period or a certain
class of load demand. An exact match between market opera‐
tion point and computed market equilibrium is rare. But ma‐
ture electricity markets are often close enough to the equilib‐
rium to allow the peripheral points of the equilibrium to be
assumed as quasi-actual operation points [25], [38].
Moreover, due to different changes that occur every day
in power systems, and the fact that power producers do not
know these changes, market players are not faced with a stat‐
ic environment. Hence, electricity markets may not work ex‐
actly on their Nash equilibrium. However, since daily chang‐
es in game environment is small in comparison to the whole
environment, and all producers are rational and smart, it is
reasonable to assume that electricity markets work at a point
close to their Nash equilibrium. Thus we consider peripheral
equilibrium points for creating synthetic data. Nash equilibri‐
um point is located in a ball with the center of Nash equilib‐
rium and a specified radius. To implement this assumption,
the intercept of supply curve of each generation unit is al‐
tered around its value at the equilibrium point. And the re‐

that contains the intercept of bid of all generation units at

operation points for collusion states, we need to model elec‐
tricity market and collusion. To model the collusion, the
firms participating in the collusion are considered as a single
entity, which means that generation firms that participate in
the collusion seek to optimize the sum of profits of all firms
participating in the collusion, instead of optimizing their
profits separately and independently. In other words, in elec‐
tricity markets, the collusion means that two or more power
producers collaborate to increase electricity price for a long
time. The producers’ bid is colluded so that sum of profits
of all colluding firms is maximized. To generate the data
that reflect collusion behavior, equilibrium points for all pos‐
sible collusion scenarios are computed. To simulate the collu‐
sion, in each scenario, all colluding power producers are con‐
sidered as one firm that maximizes the profit of the coali‐
tion. Equilibrium points and their peripherals for different
collusion scenarios at different load levels are considered as
synthetic data for machine learning.
B. Training Machine for Collusion Detection
According to Section Ⅳ-A, the equilibrium points and
quasi-actual operation points are used for training the ma‐
chines. In order to detect the collusion and the firms partici‐
pating in it, some attributes or criteria are required to distin‐
guish the operation points related to the collusion from those
without the collusion, which are used to train the trainable
machines. After training, the data of a real operation point
are given to the trained machine, and the machine detects
the occurrence of the collusion and firms participating in

collusion detection machine are as follows.
1) Marginal cost of generators (MC).
2) Bid price of generators (BP).
3) Lerner index for different generators (LER).
4) Market share of each producer with load demand (MS).
5) Herfindahl Hirschman index of the market with each
load demand (HHI).
Privately-owned generators naturally refuse to publicly re‐
port their marginal cost functions. It is assumed that ISO es‐
timates marginal cost functions of all generators using the
available model in [39], [40]. The Lerner index measures the
extent to which the bid price of a given firm exceeds its real
marginal costs. In other words, the Lerner index measures a
firm’s level of electricity power and describes the relation‐
ship between the elasticity and price margins. The Herfind‐
ahl Hirschman index is accepted as an indicator of market
competition that measures the level of the concentration in a
given market [41], [42]. The market simulation performed in
this paper aims to calculate the above-mentioned criteria at
the quasi-actual operation points under different collusive
conditions. In this paper, for model assessment and error esti‐
mation of classifier, k-fold cross-validation estimator is used
as a randomized method for error estimation [43]. Algorithm
1 shows the procedure of the collusion detection method,
where SC is the collusion scenario.

Table Ⅷshows that SVM outperforms other methods

other words, by choosing appropriate generalization grades,
SVM can be robust even when the training sample has some
biases. Furthermore, SVM is a useful tool for insolvency
analysis when the data are not regularly distributed or have
an unknown distribution as the data of Figs. 3 and 5. In fact,
in many real-world problems such as electricity markets, col‐

Therefore, SVM can work well with higher accuracies. As
shown in Table Ⅷ, CART algorithm also has a good per‐
formance, because it is inherently non-parametric. In other
words, no assumptions are made regarding the distribution
of predictor variables. Thus, CART algorithm can handle nu‐
merical data that are highly skewed or multi-modal as well
as categorical predictors with either ordinal or nonordinal
structure [37].

VI. CONCLUSION
In this paper, an approach for collusion detection in elec‐
tricity market is proposed based on machine learning. First‐
ly, the possible scenarios of collusion among generation
firms are identified. Then, for each load level and possible
collusion scenario, the market equilibrium is computed and
peripheral points of the equilibrium are determined. Collu‐
sion detection criteria are computed for the equilibrium and
their peripheral points. The computed criteria are used to
train the learning machines using SVM and decision tree al‐
gorithms. Simulation results show that the accuracy of the
used machines is acceptable in collusion detection. As the se‐
lected peripheral points deviate from the equilibrium points,
a downward trend in the accuracy of the collusion detection
algorithm is observed. SVM and decision tree algorithms are
compared with other machine learning approaches, and it is
observed that SVM and decision tree algorithms are the
most appropriate techniques to detect the collusion. Finally,
the impact of each criterion on the collusion detection accu‐
racy is evaluated and the MC and LER indices play more
important roles in collusion classification performance than
other criteria. ISO runs the collusion detection program at
any hour. If the results show the collusion of two or more
firms for a long time period, the collusion is valid. However,
if the results show the collusion occurs only in an hour, it
cannot be considered as a collusion.

A Machine Learning Approach for Hierarchical Localization Based on
Multipath MIMO Fingerprints
Jiancun Fan
, Susu Chen, Xinmin Luo, Ying Zhang, and Geoffrey Ye Li
Abstract—Localization based on channel state information
(CSI) ﬁngerprints in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO)
systems is one of the most promising positioning technologies.
In this letter, a machine learning approach is developed for
hierarchical localization exploiting multipath MIMO ﬁngerprints.
By using multipath MIMO CSI in the time domain, instead
in the frequency domain, our hierarchical scheme uses coarseto-ﬁne process and can achieve accurate positioning, which is
demonstrated by simulation results.
Index Terms—Machine learning, hierarchical localization,
multipath MIMO ﬁngerprints, softmax regression classiﬁer.
I. INTRODUCTION
With the remarkable development of intelligent terminals in
the recent years, location-based service (LBS) grows rapidly,
which has dramatically changed our life. Consequently, accurate positioning has became an essential technology and caught
more and more attention. At present, the global positioning
satellite (GPS) is a dominate positioning technique and can
satisfy the localization requirements in the most scenarios
when user equipment (UE) receives strong enough line-ofsight (LOS) signals from satellites [1], [2]. However, GPS
signals may suffer from serious attenuation in some cases,
such as dense urban area or indoor environment. To address
these limitation, various localization technologies are emerging
recently. Among these technologies, ﬁngerprint-based localization is a promising and popular technology and has drawn
wide attention in both academia and industry [3].
The essence of ﬁngerprint-based localization is to establish
the mapping relationship between a location and its corresponding signal features. The mapping relationship is stored
in a database as the ﬁngerprint for positioning. In general,
the exploited signal features mainly include the receive signal
strength (RSS), the angle of arrival (AOA), the angle of
departure (AOD), the amplitude in channel state information
(CSI), the phase in CSI, or their combination [4]. Among these
features, the RSS is the most widely used one due to its simple
hardware and easy implementation. Radar [5] and Horus [6]
are two representative RSS-based localization methods.

Different from RSS, CSI is the ﬁne-grained information of
channels, which contains the path loss, shadowing, orientation,
and delay during the signal transmission. Therefore, CSI
ﬁngerprint has
a
potential to
providing more accurate
localization
[7]–[10].
A
ﬁne-grained
indoor
ﬁngerprint
system (FIFS) exploring the frequency-domain CSI over all
subcarriers has been proposed in [7]. In order to full explore
the channel diversity of multiple subcarriers and multiple
antennas, multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channel
information has been further incorporated into the ﬁngerprintbased positioning system in [8]. Since signal features play
an important role in ﬁngerprint-based positioning, they need
to be manually extracted from the raw data to establish
ﬁngerprint database. Recently, machine learning has been
used in positioning [9], [10]. In [9], a deep learning network
has been designed to train the calibrated CSI phase to obtain
ﬁngerprints. Furthermore, a hierarchical CSI ﬁngerprint-based
classiﬁcation method has been developed in [10] to reduce
the positioning complexity.
Most above works focus on frequency-domain CSI ﬁngerprint localization in order to obtain frequency diversity by
using the average frequency domain CSI, which however may
result in the loss of useful positioning information. Therefore,
the multipath CSI in the time domain should be directly used
for localization since multipath signature of a channel is determined by the user location and the surrounding propagation
environment. Inspired by this fact, we use machine learning
to extract localization features from multi-path MIMO CSI.
II. MULTIPATH MIMO CHANNEL
In this article, a simpliﬁed spatial channel model with a

In this model, we assume that the transmitter and receiver are

III. FINGERPRINT-BASED POSITIONING METHOD
In this section, we will describe our ﬁngerprint-based positioning method in detail. We ﬁrst introduce the network architecture and CSI processing and then discuss ofﬂine training
and online positioning.
A. Network Architecture
Similar to the most of approaches based on supervised
machine learning, the ﬁngerprint-based positioning method
includes ofﬂine training and online positioning. In ofﬂine
stage, the multipath MIMO CSI data is obtained ﬁrst and
then is preprocessed in order to turn it into the required input
data form. After that, two ﬁngerprint databases are established
by training two deep neural networks (DNN) for coarse and
ﬁne positioning. Using the coarse positioning, the training
time will be reduced greatly when the targeted area is large.
In both training, a three-layer back propagation neural network
(BPNN) is adopted as in Fig. 1 which includes an input layer,
a hidden layer, and an output layer. After the output layer,
a softmax regression classiﬁer is followed and will generate
the soft information on the classiﬁed output data. Therefore,
the ﬁnal output in Fig. 1 is actually a probability distribution.
In the online stage, the CSI of the UE at an unknown location is collected and preprocessed ﬁrst. And then, the estimated
location is determined through a coarse-to-ﬁne positioning
algorithm based on the two ﬁngerprint databases. Finally, the K
weighted nearest neighbor (KWNN) method is used to further
improve the positioning accuracy.
B. Preprocessing
As mentioned before, we utilize the distinguished timedomain multipath MIMO CSI for positioning rather than
the frequency-domain CSI. In practical systems, time-domain
multipath CSI is generally estimated from the received signals.
Based the channel estimation result, we can get the equivalent
time-domain channel vector in (2). Since the CSI includes

IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
In this section, we will compare our scheme with the existing schemes by simulation. We ﬁst introduce the experiment
setup and then analyze the simulation results.
A. Experiment Setup
In our experiment, we assume the carrier frequency to be
2.0 GHz and the number of transmit and receive antennas to
be both 4. Assume that the experimental area is 40m × 40m
(1600m2) in an urban microcell environment. According to the
hierarchical positioning, the area is ﬁrst divided into 50 × 50
square blocks, which are labeled i = 1, 2, · · · , 2500. After
that, each block is divided into 16 square sub-blocks, which
are labeled j = 1, 2, · · · , 16. As a result, interval of each
sub-block is 0.2m. The center of each sub-block is used
as training point. Six scatterers are randomly distributed in
the experimental area and three cooperative BSs are used
to improve localization accuracy. It should be noted that the
interval of adjacent blocks and sub-blocks can be set by the
simulation experiment to minimize the localization error.
In addition, the BPNN in our experiment is a three-layer
DNN. The neuron nodes are fully connected between two
adjacent layers and no connection in the same layer. The
number of nodes of input layer depends on the dimension
of input data and the number of hidden nodes is slightly
larger than the number of nodes of input layer. The number
of nodes of output layer is equal to that of classes, which are
2500 and 16 for the coarse positioning and the ﬁne positioning,
respectively. In the learning, we set the learning rate as 0.1 and
the weight decay parameters as 3 × 10−6. As for the KNN
algorithm, we set K = 16 in next paper.

The second one is the method adopted in this article, called

where the amplitudes of CSI corresponding to all antennas are averaged while the phases are retained at different
antennas. The third one is phase-average with amplitude-
MIMO (Ph-ave&AM-MIMO), where the phases are averaged

which only retains the phases. The last one is amplitude and

the phase both are averaged. In both representative methods,
the FIFI one utilizes the CSI amplitudes in different subcarriers

• The AM-ave&Ph-MIMO has almost the same performance as AM-MIMO&Ph-MIMO and has only small
performance difference over AM-MIMO&ph-MIMO.

• The ﬁve proposed positioning schemes based on the
time-domain multi-path MIMO ﬁngerprint are better than
the other existing schemes based on frequency-domain
CSI or RSS.
In summary, using the phases data of the time-domain CSI can
achieve a better localization accuracy than using amplitudes
of the time-domain CSI. Our AM-ave&Ph-MIMO scheme
can effectively balance complexity and positioning accuracy.
Furthermore, from Fig. 3 and Table I, our positioning method
can obtain over 75% MSED below 1m while the other two
schemes are only 41% are 29%, respectively. Meanwhile,
the averaged amplitude information in the AM-ave&Ph-MIMO
scheme can decrease the dimension of the input data so that
the complexity of localization processes is reduced.
V. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we have proposed a hierarchical ﬁngerprintbased localization scheme by using a machine learning
approach to extract the features of time-domain multipath
MIMO CSI. In the processing, the MIMO CSI amplitudes on
different antennas are averaged to reduce the complexity and
retain the phase information to guarantee the localization accuracy. Besides, a softmax regression classiﬁer and a KWNN
network are employed to further improve the localization
accuracy. Finally, various experiments have shown that the
proposed scheme achieves a better performance compared to
the existing ones.

This work involved human subjects or animals in its research. Approval of all ethical and experimental procedures and protocols
was granted by the University of Huddersfield, School of Computing and Engineering Research Ethics Committee.
ABSTRACT Motivation plays a significant role in shaping students’ educational outcomes. Understanding
the factors that influence student motivation is crucial for enhancing academic performance and designing
effective learning environments. This study utilizes Self-Determination Theory to examine various types of
motivation, aiming to develop an integrated framework for analyzing and predicting student motivation.
The proposed framework employs multi-source data and evaluates three machine learning techniques:
Multinomial Regression, Support Vector Machine, and XGBoost. These models are applied to data collected
from a UK-based institution, specifically from the Computer Science department. The findings highlight the
superior performance of the XGBoost model in identifying learning analytics characteristics that influence
each motivation type, achieving precision ranging from 95% to 100%. Additionally, this study explores
the underlying philosophy of using LMS data and its features to classify student motivation, supporting
the effectiveness of XGBoost in this context. While the results are promising within the context of a
single-institution Computer Science setting, further studies are needed to validate the applicability of this
methodology across broader educational frameworks.
INDEX TERMS Self-determination theory, motivation, machine learning, learning analytics, prediction,
XGBoost, explainable AI in education.
I. INTRODUCTION
SStudents Motivation plays a pivotal role in students’
academic success, affecting their learning behaviors, levels
of engagement, and overall performance throughout their
educational journey [1]. This phenomenon places great
responsibility on academic institutions to better understand
the factors that motivate individuals to perform specific
tasks. Several theoretical frameworks have been developed
over the years to explain motivation in educational settings.
One of the most prominent of these frameworks is the
Self-Determination Theory (SDT) proposed by [2], which
creates a three-fold typology for motivational behavior:
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Yiqi Liu
.
intrinsic, extrinsic, and amotivation. Within the context
of education, SDT explains how learning can be either
augmented or impeded depending on the operative type
of motivation. Given its extensive empirical support and
applicability in academic research [3], SDT serves as the
theoretical foundation of this study.
Emerging technologies have been increasingly integrated
into education in recent years. One such innovation is the
use of AI-based techniques, such as Learning Analytics (LA),
Machine Learning (ML), and Data Mining (DM), to enhance
and optimize various educational processes. Many studies
have focused on employing these techniques to predict
student performance [4], [5]. However, relatively few studies
have investigated their potential for analyzing and predicting
academic motivation.

The study by Babić [6] first highlighted this gap
in 2017, noting the limited number of studies that directly
applied LA techniques to model student motivation. Although
more recent studies, such as those by Bulut et al. [7],
Herodotou et al. [8], and González-Yubero et al. [9],
have incorporated motivational constructs within broader
predictive learning frameworks, they typically focus on
performance or engagement rather than motivation as a
primary predictive target. Furthermore, few of these studies
utilize supervised learning techniques grounded in formal psychological frameworks such as Self-Determination
Theory (SDT).
To better explore and understand the learning motivation
of university students, this study proposes utilizing the
predictive capabilities of machine learning (ML) models.
ML has been broadly applied across various industries
to address complex problems [10], [11] [12], and its
role in education is continually expanding [13]. In this
research, ML techniques are intended to detect patterns
in student motivation based on behavioral data extracted
from Learning Management Systems (LMS). By developing
predictive models, the goal is to enable educators and
institutional stakeholders to gain actionable insights into
student motivation, thereby supporting the design of targeted
interventions that foster engagement and improve academic
outcomes.
This study aims to develop an integrated framework for
exploring and predicting student motivation using data from
multiple sources. Grounded in SDT, this study focuses
on key motivation types that influence student behavior,
specifically intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, and
introjected regulation. To achieve this, it proposes to utilize
data from Learning Management Systems (LMS) as input
for the framework. LMS platforms generate vast data through
student interactions, assessments, and engagement activities.
Analyzing these data can provide valuable insights, such
as tracking student progress, evaluating learning activities, identifying at-risk students, and enhancing student
engagement and motivation. To extract meaningful insights,
this research explores the integration of machine learning
techniques for processing large-scale LMS data. A key
contribution of this study lies in the belief that machine
learning can provide deeper insights into student engagement,
highlighting the underlying factors that drive different types
of motivation. This approach serves as a bridge between
AI-driven analytics and educational psychology, fostering
a more data-informed understanding of student learning
behaviors.
Focusing on our contributions, this study begins by

and

framework.
This
