text:
FSVM-CIL: Fuzzy Support Vector Machines
for Class Imbalance Learning
Rukshan Batuwita and Vasile Palade
Abstract—Support vector machines (SVMs) is a popular machine learning technique, which works effectively with balanced
datasets. However, when it comes to imbalanced datasets, SVMs
produce suboptimal classiﬁcation models. On the other hand, the
SVM algorithm is sensitive to outliers and noise present in the
datasets. Therefore, although the existing class imbalance learning
(CIL) methods can make SVMs less sensitive to class imbalance,
they can still suffer from the problem of outliers and noise. Fuzzy
SVMs (FSVMs) is a variant of the SVM algorithm, which has been
proposed to handle the problem of outliers and noise. In FSVMs,
training examples are assigned different fuzzy-membership values
based on their importance, and these membership values are incorporated into the SVM learning algorithm to make it less sensitive
to outliers and noise. However, like the normal SVM algorithm,
FSVMs can also suffer from the problem of class imbalance. In
this paper, we present a method to improve FSVMs for CIL (called
FSVM-CIL), which can be used to handle the class imbalance
problem in the presence of outliers and noise. We thoroughly evaluated the proposed FSVM-CIL method on ten real-world imbalanced datasets and compared its performance with ﬁve existing
CIL methods, which are available for normal SVM training. Based
on the overall results, we can conclude that the proposed FSVM-
CIL method is a very effective method for CIL, especially in the
presence of outliers and noise in datasets.
Index Terms—Class imbalance learning (CIL), fuzzy support
vector machines (FSVMs), outliers, support vector machines
(SVMs).
I. INTRODUCTION
S
UPPORT Vector machines (SVMs) [1]–[3] is a widely used
machine learning technique, which has been successfully
applied to many real-world classiﬁcation problems in various
domains. Due to its solid mathematical background, high generalization capability and ability to ﬁnd global classiﬁcation solutions, SVMs are usually preferred by many researchers over
other available classiﬁcation paradigms.
Although the SVM algorithm works effectively with balanced
datasets, when it comes to imbalanced datasets, it could often
produce suboptimal results [4]–[14], i.e., an SVM classiﬁer,
which is trained with an imbalanced dataset, can produce a
model that is biased toward the majority class and has a low
performance on the minority class. In this paper, we consider
the binary classiﬁcation problem, and the positive class is treated
as the minority class, while the negative class is treated as the

majority class, as in most of the real-world imbalanced datasets.
Generally, a classiﬁer should perform well with respect to both
positive and negative classes for it to be useful in real-world application. There exist techniques to develop better performing
classiﬁers with imbalanced datasets, which are generally called
class imbalance learning (CIL) methods. These methods can be
broadly divided into two categories, namely, external methods
and internal methods. External methods involve preprocessing
of training datasets in order to make them balanced, while internal methods deal with modiﬁcations of the learning algorithms
in order to reduce their sensitiveness to class imbalance. The
available methods for training SVMs with imbalanced datasets
are discussed later in the paper.
On the other hand, since the SVM learning algorithm considers all the training examples uniformly, it is sensitive to outliers
and noise present in datasets [15], [16]. Most of the real-world
datasets usually contain some outliers and noisy examples.
Therefore, although the existing imbalance-learning methods
applied for normal SVMs can solve the problem of class imbalance, they can still suffer from the problem of outliers and
noise. Fuzzy support vector machines (FSVMs) is a variant of
the SVM learning algorithm, which was originally proposed
in [17] in order to handle the problem of outliers and noise.
The FSVM technique ﬁrst assigns different fuzzy-membership
values (weights) for different training examples to reﬂect their
importance and then incorporates these membership values in
the SVM learning algorithm to reduce the effect of outliers/noise
when ﬁnding the separating hyperplane. However, the FSVM
technique, like the normal SVM method, can still be sensitive
to the class imbalance problem. We will show that this, indeed,
is the case with the empirical results obtained in this study.
In this paper, we propose a method to improve FSVMs for
CIL, which can be used to address both the problems of class
imbalance and outliers/noise. In the proposed method, we assign fuzzy-membership values for training examples in order
to reduce the effect of both of these problems under the principle of cost-sensitive learning. We name this method FSVMs
for class imbalance learning (FSVM-CIL). We systematically
evaluated the FSVM-CIL method on ten real-world imbalanced
datasets and compared its performance with ﬁve different existing internal- and external-imbalance-learning methods applied for normal SVMs. We found that the proposed FSVM-CIL
method is a very effective method for CIL in the presence of
outliers/noise in the datasets.
This paper is organized as follows. Section II brieﬂy reviews the SVM learning theory, and Section III discusses the
existing class imbalance solutions that are available for SVM
training. In Section IV, we present the FSVM algorithm, and

III. CLASS IMBALANCE LEARNING METHODS AVAILABLE FOR
SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES
It has been well-studied that the SVM algorithm can be sensitive to class imbalance [4]–[14], i.e., the separating hyperplane of an SVM model, which was developed with an imbalanced dataset, can be skewed toward the minority (positive)
class [5], [6]. This skewness generally causes the generation of
a high number of false-negative predictions, which lower the
model’s performance on the positive class compared with the
performance on the negative (majority) class.
As mentioned earlier, there exist CIL methods that can be
applied to reduce the effect of data imbalance, when developing SVM classiﬁers with imbalanced datasets. Generally, these
methods can be divided into two categories: external methods
and internal methods [14], [18], [19]. A comprehensive review
of different CIL methods can be found in [14]. The following two

text:
sections brieﬂy discuss the external- and internal-imbalancelearning methods that can be applied for SVM training.
A. External Methods
The external methods are independent from the learning algorithm being used, and they involve preprocessing of the training
datasets to balance them before training the classiﬁers. Different
resampling methods, such as random and focused oversampling
and undersampling, fall into to this category. In random undersampling, the majority-class examples are removed randomly,
until a particular class ratio is met [18]. In random oversampling, the minority-class examples are randomly duplicated,
until a particular class ratio is met [14]. Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) [20] is an oversampling method,
where new synthetic examples are generated in the neighborhood of the existing minority-class examples rather than directly
duplicating them. In addition, several informed sampling methods have been introduced in [21]. A clustering-based sampling
method has been proposed in [22], while a genetic algorithmbased sampling method has been proposed in [10].
Ensemble learning has also been applied to handle the problem of class imbalance [23]. SVM-based ensemble systems for
imbalanced dataset learning have been developed in [11]–[13].
Moreover, different boosting methods have also been adopted
for CIL in [24] and [25].
B. Internal Methods
Internal methods deal with modiﬁcations of a learning algorithm to make it less sensitive for the class imbalance. Algorithmic techniques have been developed for the different classiﬁcation algorithms, such as neural networks [26], decision
trees [27], fuzzy systems [28], [29] etc., for imbalanced dataset
learning. For SVMs, several algorithmic solutions have been
proposed in the literature. Veropoulos et al. [4] has proposed
a method called different error costs (DEC), where the SVM
objective function has been modiﬁed to assign two misclassiﬁ-

IV. FUZZY SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES
There has been some signiﬁcant research carried out towards
the combination of fuzzy logic and SVMs in different ways,
and the term ‘‘Fuzzy SVMs’’ has been used to refer to most of
these different approaches. Lin and Wang [17] applies a fuzzymembership value for each training example, which is based on
the importance of that example of its class, and reformulates
the SVM learning algorithm such that different input points can
make different contributions when ﬁnding the separating hyperplane. Wang et al. [30] extended this approach by introducing
two membership values for each training example, which deﬁne
the memberships of both positive and negative classes. This approach has been further extended, which is based on the concept
of “vague sets” in [31]. Another type of fuzzy SVM method,
which uses a special type of kernel function constructed from
fuzzy-basis functions, has been proposed in [32]. A method for
fuzzy support vector regression has been proposed in [33].
In contrast, several other approaches have been developed
to assign fuzzy-membership values for the outputs generated
by SVMs together with the output class. Xie et al. [34] use
the decision value, which is generated by the SVMs, to deﬁne
a membership for the output class, while [35] uses the fuzzyoutput decision values for multiclass classiﬁcation. Mill and
Inoue [36] propose a method that uses the strengths (αi) of

V. FSVM-CIL: FUZZY SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES FOR
CLASS IMBALANCE LEARNING
As stated earlier, the SVM algorithm is sensitive to both
the problems of class imbalance and outliers/noise. Although
the existing CIL methods available for SVMs, which were discussed in Section III, can overcome the problem of class imbalance, they can still be sensitive to the problem of outliers
and noise. On the other hand, although the FSVM method
considered in this paper can overcome the problem of outliers/noise, it can suffer from the problem of class imbalance, since there is no modiﬁcation in the FSVM algorithm
compared with the original SVM algorithm to make it less
sensitive to class imbalance. We show that this is in fact
the case with empirical evidence presented in Section VIII.
In this section, we present an improvement for the FSVM learning method, which is called FSVM-CIL, to overcome the problem of class imbalance.
As we discussed in the previous section, in FSVMs, we can
assign different membership values (or weights) for training
examples to reﬂect their different importance. We also showed
that this is similar to assign different misclassiﬁcation costs
Cmi for different training examples. Therefore, in order to
reduce the effect of class imbalance, we can assign higher
membership values, or higher misclassiﬁcation costs, for the
minority-class examples, while we assign lower membership
values, or lower misclassiﬁcation costs, for the majority-class
examples, as done in the DEC method discussed in Section III,
i.e., if we assign a single membership value, say m+, for all
the minority-class examples and another single membership
value, say m−, for all the majority-class examples such that
m+ > m−, this is exactly equivalent to the DEC method applied for normal SVMs, where C+ = m+C, and C−= m−C.
However, the DEC method applied for normal SVMs can suffer
the problem of outliers/noise, because all the examples in a
separate class are given equal importance.
In the proposed FSVM-CIL method, we assign the membership values for training examples in such a way to satisfy the
following two goals:
1) to suppress the effect of between class imbalance
2) to reﬂect the within-class importance of different training
examples in order to suppress the effect of outliers and
noise.

VII. SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE/FUZZY SUPPORT VECTOR
MACHINE TRAINING AND PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
Before training any classiﬁer, each dataset was scaled into
[−1,+1] interval. As the SVM training environment, we selected the widely used libsvm software package [54]. For
the FSVM program, we used a variant of the libsvm program found in the libsvm tools (http://www.csie.ntu.edu.tw/
∼cjlin/libsvmtools/#14), which can be used to assign different
weights for different training examples. It has been well-studied
that when the training dataset is imbalanced, the commonly
used performance measure accuracy, which is the proportion
of correctly classiﬁed instances, could lead to suboptimal models [5], [18]. Therefore, we used the geometric mean of sensitivity (SE = proportion of the positives correctly recognized)
and speciﬁcity (SP = proportion of the negatives correctly recognized), given by Gm =
√
SE × SP, for the classiﬁer performance evaluation in this study, as commonly used in class
imbalanced-learning research [5], [14], [55].
In
order
to
evaluate
the
performance
of
all
the
SVM/FSVM/FSVM-CIL classiﬁers, which were developed on
each dataset, we carried out an extensive ﬁve-fold crossvalidation method. In this method, a complete dataset was ﬁrst
randomly divided into ﬁve partitions. We used stratiﬁed random
sampling such that each partition contained the same imbalanced
ratio. We used four partitions as the training dataset, and the remaining one as the testing dataset. Using the training dataset partition, we develop an SVM/FSVM/FSVM-CIL classiﬁer either
by applying a CIL method or by not applying one, in the following way. We considered the radial-basis function (RBF) kernel
(K(xi, xj) = e−γ(∥xi −xj ∥2 )) for SVM training and selected the
following ranges for parameters: log2 C = {1, 2, . . . , 15}, and
log2 γ = {−15, −14, . . . , −1}. First, we conducted a coarse
grid-parameter-search to ﬁnd the optimal values for log2 C and
log2 γ over the aforementioned ranges of values. We evaluated the performance of a model trained on each parameter
pair (log2 C, log2 γ) by using ﬁve-fold cross-validation results
on the training dataset. After ﬁnding the optimal values for
the parameters, say ( ¯C,¯γ), again, a narrow grid-parametersearch was conducted over the ranges log2 C = {¯c −0.75, ¯c −
0.5, . . . , ¯c + 0.75}, and log2 γ = {¯γ −0.75, ¯γ −0.5, . . . , ¯γ +
0.75}. Finally, after ﬁnding the optimal values for (log2 C,
log2 γ), a new SVM model was trained by using the complete
training dataset on these parameter values. Then, the performance of that model was tested on the remaining testing partition. This whole training and testing procedure was repeated ﬁve
times with different training and testing partitions in an outer
ﬁve-fold cross-validation loop, and ﬁnally, the results on the testing partitions were averaged and reported. Hereafter, we refer
to this whole cross-validation procedure as the outer–inner–cv
method.

IX. STATISTICAL COMPARISON OF RESULTS
In this section, we present a statistical test used to validate the
signiﬁcance of the results obtained by the proposed FSVM-CIL
methods over the results obtained by the existing CIL methods applied for normal SVMs. Demsar [56] recommends several nonparametric statistical tests that can be used to compare
classiﬁers, which are developed on multiple datasets, when the
conditions to apply the parametric tests are not satisﬁed. Among
these tests, we selected the Friedman test [57], [58] to compare
the proposed FSVM-CIL method with the existing CIL methods
considered. This test ﬁrst ranks the algorithms considered for
each dataset separately, such that the best-performing algorithm

performed better than the Over method (see the actual results
in Tables VII–X and the ranks in Table XI). We believe that
this statistical test is less powerful in ﬁnding the difference between best FSVM-CIL method and the Over method due to
the “granularity” property of the nonparametric tests, i.e., since
the Over method performed better than the other existing CIL
methods (DEC, Under, zSVM, and SMOTE) for most of the
datasets, and therefore, it has obtained the best average rank
among these existing CIL methods, we cannot ﬁnd a signiﬁ-
cant difference between the average ranks of the best FSVM-
CIL method and the Over method, despite how much better
the best FSVM-CIL method performed over the Over method.
However, by considering all these results, we can state that the
best FSVM-CIL method is signiﬁcantly better than the existing
imbalance-learning methods, which are considered in this paper. The reason of FSVM-CIL method to perform better than the
existing CIL methods, which were applied for normal SVMs,
would be the additional capability of the FSVM-CIL method to
handle the problem of outliers and noise, to which the existing
imbalance-learning methods available for normal SVMs are still
sensitive.
Except for the small computational time required to calculate the membership values for the training examples, the proposed FSVM-CIL method does not increase the computational
requirements of the underlying SVM training algorithm at all.
However, as we observed, the best FSVM-CIL setting giving the
highest results was dataset-dependent. Therefore, to explore all
the FSVM-CIL settings in order to ﬁnd the optimal one would
be computationally very demanding. However, we can further

X. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we proposed an improved FSVM method, which
is called FSVM-CIL, for learning from imbalanced datasets in
the presence of outliers and noise. In this method, we assign
fuzzy-membership values for training examples in order to handle both the problems of class imbalance and outliers/noise.
We considered three ways to assign fuzzy-membership values
and six FSVM-CIL settings. We used ten real-world imbalanced datasets to validate the proposed method. We compared
the effectiveness of the FSVM-CIL method with ﬁve other
popular existing imbalance-learning methods that are available
for normal SVM training. We also applied a nonparametric
statistical test to validate the signiﬁcance of the performance
of the proposed method over the existing CIL methods considered. From the overall results obtained, we can conclude
that the proposed FSVM-CIL method could result in signiﬁ-
cantly better classiﬁcation results than the existing imbalancelearning methods applied for normal SVMs, especially in the
presence of outliers/noise in the datasets. Finally, as a rule
of thumb, we can recommend that among the six FSVM-CIL
methods considered, the FSVM −CILhyp
exp setting with the appropriate selection of β value would be an effective choice
for learning from any imbalanced dataset. As future work,
it would be interesting to investigate the effectiveness of using the FSVM method with other existing imbalance-learning
methods, such as resampling techniques, for imbalanced dataset
learning.

text:
Feature Identiﬁcation With a Heuristic Algorithm
and an Unsupervised Machine Learning
Algorithm for Prior Knowledge
of Gait Events
Seth R. Donahue and Michael E. Hahn
Abstract— The purpose of this study was to compare a
heuristic feature identiﬁcation algorithm with output from
the Beta Process Auto Regressive Hidden Markov Model
(BP-AR-HMM) utilizing minimally sampled (≤100 Hz) human
locomotion data for identiﬁcation of gait events prior to
their occurrence. Data were collected from 16 participants
(21-64 years) using a single gyroscopic sensor in an inertial
measurement unit on the dorsum of the foot, across multiple locomotion modes, including level ground walking and
running (across speeds 0.8 m s−1 – 3.0 m s−1), ramps and
stairs. Identiﬁcationof gait events,initial contact(IC) and toe
off (TO) with the heuristic algorithm, was 94% across locomotion modes. The features identiﬁed prior to initial contact
had a lead time of 186.32 ± 86.70 ms, while TO had a
lead time of 63.96 ± 46.30 ms. The BP-AR-HMM identiﬁed
features that indicated an impending IC and TO with 99%
accuracy, with a lead time of 59.41 ± 54.41 ms for IC and
90.79 ± 35.51 ms for TO. These approaches are consistent
in their identiﬁcation of gait events and have the potential
to be utilized for classiﬁcation and prediction of locomotion
mode.
Index Terms— Inertial measurement units, real-world gait
event detection, unsupervised machine learning.
I. INTRODUCTION
H
UMAN locomotion occurs across a range of speeds and
environments that are not easily replicated in the laboratory. Understanding how humans move naturally through
a real-world environment can inform interventions and device
design for individuals with orthopedic or neurologic conditions
limiting full ambulatory function. Proper identiﬁcation of gait
events is crucial for gait analysis in the clinical setting, for
remote monitoring of patient activity levels and the control of
prosthetic devices [1]–[3]. The quantiﬁcation and data driven
extraction of features shared across human locomotion modes
in a real-world environment can provide researchers with
succinct representations of these data. Identiﬁcation of key gait

events, initial contact (IC) and toe off (TO), form the basis of
our understanding of different locomotion modes, commonly
used in the analysis of gait [4]–[6]. Recently, studies have
utilized mobile sensor arrays for the quantiﬁcation of human
locomotion through varied environments [7]. These mobile
sensor arrays have allowed for the development of rules-based
algorithms for the identiﬁcation of gait events. Developments
in algorithmic methods, particularly machine learning, have
improved the potential of mobile sensor technology for analysis of gait in real-world environments [8]–[10]. Of particular
interest, unsupervised machine learning algorithms for the
analysis of multiple time series are being developed and tested
for gait event detection [11], [12]. While these algorithms have
been shown to be accurate for gait event identiﬁcation in the
laboratory, they have not been tested on data collected from
a real-world environment, nor have they been compared to
simple heuristic identiﬁers with minimal sensor data from the
same data set.
The gold standards for identiﬁcation of gait events in a
real-world environment have been force and pressure based
insole systems [6], [13]. These systems can be expensive,
are prone to failure, and are often not feasible for use in
assistive devices or long-term use. Additional options for
mobile sensing are inertial sensors, such as accelerometers
and gyroscopes. These sensors have been utilized extensively
for the identiﬁcation of gait events and locomotion mode,
with varying success [1], [10]–[16]. One of the major limitations of accelerometers regards excess vibrations experienced during initial foot contact which may limit consistency
of accelerometry data when compared to gyroscopic data.
Additionally, the orientation of the gyroscope is unaffected by
gravity [6], therefore gyroscopes may provide more consistent
performance than other inertial quantities for the identiﬁcation
of locomotion and gait events. Previous methodologies have
been primarily focused on level ground walking at the subject’s
preferred speed, or have examined multiple locomotion modes,
including ramps, stairs and running, but not all modalities in
the same study [1], [12], [14], [17]–[20].
There is currently no consensus about the placement of
sensors for gait event detection, though it is common to use
an array of sensors on the lower limb, including the foot,
shank and sacrum [1], [3], [10], [14]–[17], [20]–[22]. Recent
work has employed a single sensor mounted on the shank

text:
DONAHUE AND HAHN: FEATURE IDENTIFICATION

or foot for gait event identiﬁcation using a set of heuristic
rules derived by the expert user, [3], [23], [24], [27], [28],
a combination of user deﬁned phases and supervised machine
learning [17], [22], [25]–[28] or frequency analysis [1], [22]
to detect common gait events. Heuristic algorithms are advantageous because of their computational simplicity. However,
they also require an intimate knowledge of the waveforms,
for a variety of locomotion modes. In contrast, unsupervised
machine learning algorithms have the potential to input the
data with minimal modiﬁcation by the researcher. Indeed, there
have been rare attempts to use unsupervised machine learning
algorithms for identiﬁcation of gait events [11], [12], which
have performed at the same accuracy as the supervised and
heuristic algorithms. These methods have been focused on
determining precisely when a gait event is going to occur.
In this study we look to identify features prior to the occurrence of the gait event.
A key limitation of most gait event detection and locomotion
classiﬁcation algorithms is the reliance on data collected in a
controlled environment, such as a laboratory or clinic. Current
algorithms also typically require a large volume of data (large
sensor arrays with high sampling frequencies) to determine
and differentiate patterns in locomotion. High density data
from multiple inputs, requires computationally intensive methods and feature extraction for the identiﬁcation of gait events.
In real world applications, the identiﬁcation of gait events with
minimal sensor data is ideal as it will reduce the computational
load and preserve the battery life of a device.
In the modern renaissance of machine learning, novel algorithms have been introduced. They have been built speciﬁcally
for analysis of multiple related time series data (e.g. IMU data
collected from the same anatomical location on multiple subjects undergoing the same protocol). One example is switching
linear dynamical systems, developed previously for economic
analysis and the description of dynamical processes [33].
This class of algorithms allows for conditions where not all
possible features are known a priori but can be added when a
new feature is discovered. From this set of novel algorithms,
we propose use of the Beta Process Auto Regressive Hidden
Markov Model (BP-AR-HMM) for the identiﬁcation of gait
events using a single stream of angular velocity data from a
sensor on the foot sampled at 25 Hz. Minimizing the data
input into the algorithm will reduce the number of required
sensors and the computational complexity needed to identify
gait events. This algorithm has been used previously for the
identiﬁcation of unique features in time series from similar
data sources (e.g. position data from motion of different
subjects) [34]. The approach is used to discover dynamics
shared between time series and builds a global set of features
that describe all possible behaviors in the data set. The result
is a feature identiﬁcation algorithm that is not constrained by
user-determined states and is completely unsupervised.
It is currently unknown how well these methods are suited
for locomotion data collected in a real-world environment with
minimal input data. There has yet to be a direct comparison
between a heuristic, peak ﬁnding algorithm and an unsupervised learning algorithm on data collected in a real-world
environment. It is critical to note that the approach used in this
work seeks to identify features that indicate an impending gait
event, as the knowledge prior to the gait event is useful when
designing a controller for application in an assistive device [1].
The purpose of this study was to implement and compare two
different algorithms, a heuristic algorithm and an unsupervised
machine learning algorithm for the detection of gait events
prior to their actual occurrence using minimally sampled
angular velocity data collected in a real-world environment.
II. METHODS
This study was approved by the University of Oregon
Institutional Review Board (protocol #: 08202018.018). All
participants provided written consent prior to involvement
in the study. Data were collected from sixteen participants
(8 male and 8 female; 31.1 ± 14.8 years, 173.4 ± 8.5 cm,
66.7 ± 7.7 kg). All analyses were performed ofﬂine in custom
Matlab programs (Mathworks, Natick, MA). Each subject’s
dominant foot was equipped with an IMU (Vicon, Centennial,
CO) mounted on the dorsal aspect of the foot (Figure 1,
Panel A). Foot ground contact information was recorded
with two different systems. The ﬁrst three participants were
equipped with the Noraxon footswitch Telemyo DTS system
(Noraxon, Scottsdale, AZ), while the other 13 participants
were equipped with Loadsol inserts (Novel Electronics, St.
Paul, MN). The ﬁrst day of the study consisted of multiple
locomotion mode transitions with steady state locomotion
between modes (Figure 1, Panel C). On the second day of
the study, transitions between walking and running were
examined with a protocol based upon the work of Long and
Srinivasan [35] the range of target average speeds ranged
from 1.3 m s−1 to 3.0, m s−1(1.30, 1.51, 1.73, 1.94, 2.15,
2.36, 2.58, 2.79, 3.00 m s−1) encompassing speeds typical
in human locomotion. Participants were asked to cover a
distance of 90 m, during which they received feedback at the
half-way time point and when ﬁve seconds remained in the
trial [35]. The condition order of these trials was randomized
to minimize any learning effects (Figure 1, Panel C).
The IMU data were ﬁrst down sampled to a common
frequency of 100 Hz, then synchronized with the insole force
sensors. Ground reaction force data were converted into an
indicator variable, indicating either no discernable movement
pattern, or consistent pattern such as stance or swing phase.
The data were further labeled with each different locomotion
mode. Input into the rules-based algorithm was the single axis
angular velocity data about the x-axis of the IMU, sampled
at 100 Hz. The data were then ﬁltered with a fourth order zero
lag Butterworth ﬁlter ( f = 6 Hz). Input into the BP-AR-HMM
consisted of the single axis angular velocity data, further down
sampled to 25 Hz (Figure 1, Panel B).
There were four rules utilized for the identiﬁcation of
gait events. Two prominent peaks were identiﬁed as consistent features for the identiﬁcation of gait events. For
the identiﬁcation of an impending IC a minimum must
be < −100 rad s−1. The feature utilized to identify impending TO was a peak > 150 rad s−1. The two other rules to
minimize misclassiﬁcation of peaks were 1) temporal differences between minima or maxima must be ≥0.1 s; 2) if the
difference between IC and TO < 0.1s, ignore the next peak.

This heuristic set results in a peak ﬁnding algorithm, with
minimal constraints, and is computationally simple compared
to the BP-AR-HMM.
The BP-AR-HMM is a machine learning algorithm that
provides a spatial-temporal statistical model and classiﬁcations
for related time series data [34], [36]. Brieﬂy, the Beta Process
provides a sparse subject independent feature set, to be used
by the Auto-Regressive Hidden Markov Model (AR-HMM).
The key element of this algorithm, the beta process, gives the
algorithm the ability to add and remove states. For example,
if two states describe the same feature they will be combined
into a single state. This development of dynamic features is
crucial for use in semi-supervised or unsupervised machine
learning. The HMM assumed that the set of distributions and
transitions between dynamic features follow a Markov process.
This process however was modiﬁed with the presence of the
AR model, which does not assume temporal independence.
The vector auto regression approach provided an estimation of
current state, based upon the previous time steps, the available
states and distributions based on the HMM. A sticky parameter
was used in the BP-AR-HMM to ensure the capture of biomechanically relevant states by encouraging self-transitions [34].
Performance evaluation of the BP-AR-HMM included the
critical timing of states and how consistently the features were
used across all locomotion modes. Each stance and swing
phase were identiﬁed via the force data from force-measuring
insert. The locomotion mode of each step was identiﬁed, and
TABLE I
HEURISTIC ALGORITHM ACCURACY AND LEAD TIME
gait events were identiﬁed using rules generated from the states
output from the BP-AR-HMM. Each gait event was identiﬁed
as the ﬁrst instance of force being higher than 20 N.
Classical machine learning methodologies rely on three
different groupings of the data, a training data set (∼70%),
validation set (∼15%), and test set (∼15%). In this paradigm,
the machine learning algorithms are trained on the training
set, and rules are developed for classiﬁcation or prediction.
During training the validation set is tested with the partially
trained algorithm to ensure the algorithm is not being overﬁt
to the training data. If the training accuracy of the algorithm is
higher than the validation and testing accuracy the algorithm
is considered to be overﬁt. After training, the test data are
used as a measure of accuracy on a novel dataset (i.e. the test
set). These test sets are typically a single novel subject, as in
the Leave One Out Cross Validation (LOOCV) procedure. The
BP-AR-HMM utilized a reversible jump Markov Chain Monte
Carlo method to isolate and extract features, which does not
require the use of LOOCV. More details about this approach
can be found in [37].
III. RESULTS
The output for the identiﬁcation of features that occur
prior to identiﬁed gait events with heuristic rules resulted in
a 94.87% accuracy of all gait events (TO and IC). Accuracy in this study was calculated as the number of features
identiﬁed divided by the number of measured gait events.
Figure 2 demonstrates the consistency with which the state
output indicate impending gait events. The average temporal
difference between measured IC from the insoles and the
peak identiﬁed prior to IC was 186.32 ± 86.70 ms, and
the difference between measured TO and estimated TO was
63.96 ± 46.30 ms (Table I). The only feature that occurred
consistently after the measured gait event was IC for stair
ascent. Figures 3, 4 and 5 (Panel A) show where the estimated
IC and TO events are identiﬁed based upon the aforementioned
rules. The accuracies presented in Tables I and II for IC and
TO are shown out of all of the measured footfalls.
The output from the BP-AR-HMM resulted in 16 states that
described the entirety of the data input. Of these states, 12 were
considered viable features for the description of locomotion in
a real-world environment. From these, the identiﬁcation of IC
and TO was approximately 99.6% across all locomotion modes
(Table II). Nine of the 12 states occurred in >65% of gait
cycles (Table III). Each state described a speciﬁc pattern in the

IV. DISCUSSION
The purpose of this study was to implement and compare
two algorithms, a heuristic algorithm and an unsupervised
machine learning algorithm for identiﬁcation of features and

output from the BP-AR-HMM, indicating that this algorithm
may be useful for classiﬁcation and prediction of locomotion
mode.

ramps, stairs, ascent and descent), with >95% accuracy [3],
[20], [21], [24], [39]. To build real world applications for
this type of gait event detection system, it is important to
anticipate when a gait event is going to occur. One other
study implemented an algorithm with capacity to provide
predictions of gait events using an Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy
Bayesian algorithm from three IMUs on the lower limb of
the subject, collected at 100 Hz over level ground and ramp
walking [21]. That approach was able to predict gait events
based upon the previous gait event but did not provide any
lead time for the calculation of the event and it required up
to 100 ms to make a decision if a gait event was going to
occur [21]. Another study developed an HMM using data from
a foot mounted gyroscope with a detection accuracy of 100%
and an average delay of 43 ms for level ground walking [19],
and another group developed an HMM using data from a
gyroscope with mean detection delay of 60 ms [6]. We have
improved upon these results by identifying features prior to
the occurrence of the gait event. A further improvement is that
the current study utilizes less data than the previous studies.
Other comparable work includes that of Figueiredo et al.
[24], which examined multiple locomotion modes with a
heuristic model based upon data collected from a gyroscope
on the foot of a healthy subject and then input into a ﬁnite
state machine for the detection of gait events. Their approach
was reported to detect IC across multiple locomotion modes
at a rate of > 96.98%, and TO at a rate of > 95.89% [24].
We achieved slightly higher accuracy with > 97.26% using
the BP-AR-HMM across gait events and locomotion modes.
Another study used a heuristic approach with a single IMU
on the shank, identifying gait events with the following
time gaps: level ground IC with 16 ± 9 ms and TO at
–16 ± 15.9 ms, ramp ascent IC at 18.8 ± 11.6 ms and TO
at −17.2 ± 21.3 ms [40]. In the present study, the features
using a heuristic algorithm had a lead time of > 100 ms,
with the exception of stair ascent, for IC and > 60 ms for TO
(Table I). The lead time for the BP-AR-HMM identiﬁcation of
gait events was > 40 ms for both IC and TO (Table II). Other
previous studies utilizing combinations of machine learning
and EMG have identiﬁed gait events approximately when they
occur with high accuracy [8]–[10]. These approaches have
shown the efﬁcacy machine learning and neural networks for
the identiﬁcation of gait events these values are generally
comparable to our level ground walking feature identiﬁcation
from both methods presented in this paper. All aforementioned
studies in this discussion were intended to determine when
a gait event was going to occur. While these have been
immensely valuable, we are looking to adjust the paradigm
slightly, by identifying the known features prior to the actual
gait events. Therefore, our approach the BP-AR-HMM and the
heuristic model identiﬁed the key portions of gait prior to the
actual event with data collected in a real-world environment.
Limitations of this study include but are not limited to
post hoc, ofﬂine data analysis; therefore, we have not yet
demonstrated the ability to detect gait events in real time.
Although the BP-AR-HMM output has a higher accuracy than
the heuristic algorithm, a simpler algorithm might be easier to
include in a control algorithm as it is less computationally
intensive, therefore reducing the temporal delay between the
sensor data input and an identiﬁed gait event. Additionally,
although the data were collected in a real-world environment,
all subjects completed the same course, which is not representative of the natural variation experienced in daily locomotion.
V. CONCLUSION
In this study we have shown the efﬁcacy of both a heuristic
algorithm and an unsupervised machine learning algorithm for
the identiﬁcation of features prior to gait events based on a
single stream of minimally sampled angular velocity data. This
leads us to believe that in practice a near real time system
can be implemented for subject independent identiﬁcation of
gait events across locomotion modes and speeds with either
a heuristic, user deﬁned rule set, or features extracted with
an unsupervised machine learning algorithm. The key to the
BP-AR-HMM used in this study is the Beta Process, allowing
the model to generate and remove states and share them

Fingerprinting IP-Connected Devices Using
Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models
STAMATIS KARNOUSKOS
(Fellow, IEEE)
SAP, 69190 Walldorf, Germany
(e-mail: karnouskos@ieee.org)
ABSTRACT
Device ﬁngerprinting enables various asset management scenarios. This work presents a
comprehensive evaluation of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches for ﬁngerprinting
IP-connected devices using the publicly available network mapper (Nmap) operating system (OS) database.
Focusing on the classiﬁcation of three critical device characteristics, i.e., operating system family, vendor,
and device type, ﬁngerprinting is treated as a multiclass classiﬁcation problem. The performance of eleven
algorithms, including six classical ML models and ﬁve deep neural network (DNN) architectures, is evaluated. The experiments explore the impact of data imbalance, employing synthetic minority oversampling
technique and adaptive synthetic for synthetic data augmentation. The empirical results show that tree-based
ML models, such as decision trees, random forests, and extreme gradient boosting, achieve high accuracy at
signiﬁcantly lower training and inference costs than DNNs. Although DNNs can also yield competitive area
under the curve (AUC) scores, their performance beneﬁts are outweighed by training requirements, making
them less suitable for most practical applications. This study concludes that traditional ML approaches
remain preferable for OS, vendor, and device type classiﬁcation in IP-connected device ﬁngerprinting
scenarios, and it highlights key tradeoffs in performance, complexity, and computational overhead. The
results are of interest to industry stakeholders, including researchers, security practitioners, and system
designers who integrate device identiﬁcation into their asset management, security, and critical infrastructure
systems.
INDEX TERMS Adaptive synthetic (ADASYN), deep learning (DL), device ﬁngerprinting, Internet of
Things (IoT), IP-connected devices, machine learning (ML), nmap, synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE).
I. INTRODUCTION
Billions of Internet of Things (IoT) devices are expected to
be interconnected via various technologies in the years to
come, as also attested by the visions from key industries,
such as Samsung, Intel, ZTE, Huawei, Ericsson, Nokia, NTT
Docomo, and Qualcomm [1]. Some reports estimate 18.8
billion IoT devices, with a forecast of 30 billion by 2030,
while a variety of protocols, languages, and cloud platforms
are used, raising challenges and concerns in developing IoT
applications and services [2], [3]. Internet-connected devices
are prevalent in a multitude of personal, business, and industrial application domains [4], with increasing signiﬁcance
in healthcare, smart cities, and the metaverse. The market
is expected to grow continuously and is forecasted at $991
billion in 2028, which indicates that IoT is transforming the
way devices, systems, people, and businesses interact [5].
There is a wide variety of IoT devices with different communication protocols; however, at some point, these devices
either directly or indirectly (e.g., via gateways) connect to
the Internet and interact with other systems and services. Of
interest are devices that have direct Internet capabilities, e.g.,
via a fully ﬂedged operating system (OS) or an IP stack. IoT
not only offers beneﬁts but also introduces new challenges,
such as heightened security and privacy concerns [3]. This
implies that security concepts, such as intrusion detection
systems (IDSs), need to be extended to cover IoT devices and
their speciﬁc operations in smart environments, leveraging
relevant approaches, including AI [6]. Being able to acquire

speciﬁc information from a device, e.g., its class or OS, can
be important in IoT security, as appropriate actions (patching,
decommissioning, additional protection, etc.) can be taken.
Therefore, IoT device ﬁngerprinting overall is pertinent and
challenging [7].
Device ﬁngerprinting [8] collectively refers to efforts carried out with the aim of collecting information about a device
for the purpose of identifying some of its characteristics.
Typically, these efforts assume a remote device that cannot
be inspected otherwise (e.g., visually) but only via its connectivity angle, e.g., its communication channel. There are
several ﬁngerprint approaches, e.g., active and passive ﬁngerprinting, that utilize different methods, most commonly
though, via the communication protocols used by the device,
e.g., transmission control protocol/Internet protocol (TCP/IP),
Internet control message protocol (ICMP), Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), etc. Effective device ﬁngerprinting is
critical, especially in securing industrial environments and
critical infrastructure [9]. One common requirement is the
identiﬁcation of rogue devices that may be connected to corporate networks, or devices that run obsolete or insecure OS
versions [10]. This holds especially true for IoT devices,
which, due to their constraints, cannot host traditional device management software that enterprises install on their
assets to manage them. Therefore, their identiﬁcation and any
information provision are of interest, as network administrators can begin to manage security and access control for
them [11].
In identifying a device, two device characteristics of interest
are the OS the device runs on and the manufacturer. Being
able to identify the OS of an asset enables, for instance,
security auxiliary services to consider this characteristic in
their authentication processes and tailor their decisions accordingly [12]. OS detection (and sometimes also ﬁrmware
detection [13]) is crucial for security testing, as without this
information, the attacks, probes, and exploits an attacker can
perform on the device are limited. In information security,
gathering information about the target, including its potential
OS, is, therefore, in focus. Once information is available to
network administrators, security, and access control can be
managed. Depending on the class of devices, there are, however, also other beneﬁts, e.g., improving quality of service
(QoS) within the network, simplifying asset monitoring, updating, and its lifecycle management [12], etc., which also
contribute to the build-up of a manageable and trustworthy
environment.
Overall, across the industry, OS device ﬁngerprinting can
yield multiple beneﬁts beyond security, including in enterprise
asset management. Some of them that can beneﬁt from the
results include the following.
1) Risk assessment: The attack space on the device can
be derived from that OS angle, as speciﬁc OS vulnerabilities may be available, e.g., due to outdated security
libraries used by the OS in devices in critical infrastructures. Such info is useful for intrusion detection and
prevention systems, security analysts, etc.
2) Customized security testing: Many of the exploits need
to address OS and even hardware architecture-speciﬁc
information to be successful; otherwise, they might not
be fully effective.
3) Asset management (inventory): Especially in enterprise
systems, there is a need to keep track of all connected
devices and automatically maintain their backend data,
e.g., OS. Management decisions, e.g., maintenance contracts, may rely on such info.
4) Compliance: Enterprises have speciﬁc guidelines on devices that can be connected to their networks, including
the class of devices and their minimum OS version. OS
device ﬁngerprinting can help identify noncompliant or
rogue devices in the network.
5) Camouﬂage/honeypots: In some scenarios, e.g., in critical infrastructures, fake devices can be simulated in
honeypots or even real devices may want to obfuscate
information in order to mislead attackers and enable
their detection by an intrusion detection and prevention
system (IDPS).
6) Strategy: Network cartography with OS device info can
be created, which may help organizations with their
internal strategic decisions and policies on security, operations, support, etc.
As can be seen, there is a need for it and signiﬁcant beneﬁts across several aspects of device identiﬁcation. Being
able to conﬁdently detect a device’s vendor, OS (including
the OS version), or other characteristics can beneﬁt several
stakeholders [14]. Primarily, this information can be utilized
by information security personnel in organizations to make
security and risk-related decisions. The management can consider this to ﬁne-tune an organization’s policies and plan
operational and product development/support strategies. Researchers can also beneﬁt from more thorough investigation of
the applicability of emerging AI technologies in the information security domain, as well as from embedding OS detection
or the estimation of new devices into security tools.
The overarching pursued research question (RQ) can be
formulated as: How can machine learning and deep learning techniques assist in the classiﬁcation of IP-connected
devices? To address this question, we need to identify speciﬁc
aspects of an IP-connected device, i.e.,
1) OS;
2) vendor;
3) device type, all of which are critical information for
identifying key features of a device.
Traditional machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL)
can be utilized to approach the RQ [15]. DL approaches are
of interest to the information security community [16], especially for classiﬁcation, anomaly detection, clustering, etc.
While ML at large has been attempted for OS detection, the
methods utilized are traditional ones, e.g., support vector machine (SVM), C4.5, and Ripper. These have been shown to
have certain limitations, such as difﬁculty with discrimination,
bias in training, a tendency to overﬁt, and an inability to
exploit semantic knowledge of protocols [17]. This work aims

to study exactly this under explored area, i.e., the application
of DL and ML for device OS ﬁngerprinting, compare them,
and provide insights for informed decision-making.
The area of device ﬁngerprinting is vast, and therefore,
some delimitations are necessary to clearly deﬁne the boundaries of this work. The goal is to produce a focused and
realistic outcome that can be seen as the intersection of the
IoT and ML. This work will limit itself to the subarea of
device ﬁngerprinting that deals with Internet-connected devices. While several characteristics can be ﬁngerprinted, this
work will focus exclusively on OS identiﬁcation, vendor, and
device type. In addition, while there are several classiﬁcation
approaches, we will focus on traditional ML algorithms and
DNNs. However, this focus would not aim to provide the best
solutions, nor will it conduct an exhaustive investigation to
ﬁne-tune the algorithms for optimal performance (although
some informed decisions and conﬁgurations will be applied).
II. IOT DEVICE FINGERPRINTING
Tools and research works that offer device identiﬁcation by
analyzing collected ﬁngerprint data use different algorithms
to extrapolate a ﬁt label for the extracted features. Typical
approaches include rule-based and ML-based classiﬁcation,
with neural network-based approaches also available. A short
overview of some relevant approaches is shown in Table 1.
Snacktime [18] and research works that use it utilize its
signature matching algorithm, which awards points for each
match between the probe result and the corresponding feature,
e.g., time to live (TTL), Window Size (WIN) size, etc. The
closer the total points come to the ﬁngerprint, the more conﬁ-
dent the match is. Other approaches use similar point systems
or adopt modiﬁed versions of existing ones, e.g., Leonard
and Loguinov [19] used a modiﬁed approach from [18]. A
passive ﬁngerprinting approach was able to identify OSs with
TCP/IP of 62.3%, which, however, when combined with other
sessions (e.g., HTTP and TLS probing) can reach accuracy
levels of 97.5% [10]. Naive Bayes (argmax) and random forest
are used as techniques for single- and multisession OS classi-
ﬁcation, respectively.
Network mapper (Nmap) also uses a simple point system
for classifying Internet control message internet Protocol Version 4 protocol (IPv4) ﬁngerprints [20]. Probe responses are
compared with those in its OS DB, and if they match, points
are awarded. A conﬁdence factor is calculated by dividing
the acquired points by the maximum obtainable points, re-
ﬂecting the matching probability with the stored ﬁngerprints.
For IPv6, Nmap uses a more sophisticated approach [20] as it
utilizes the liblinear library, which can do large-scale regularized linear classiﬁcation and regression. The map-matching
algorithm computes scores that indicate the similarity between each scan and the ﬁngerprints stored in the Nmap OS
DB. Regularized logistic regression is used for classiﬁcation,
so the computed scores reﬂect the matching probability. For
Nmap, probabilities higher than 0.9 are considered perfect
scores for the respective OS.
General ML techniques are also used for device identiﬁ-
cation, e.g., from device network trafﬁc [29], device behavior [30], or a combination of these [31]. However, such steps
are seen as complementary to the work proposed here and
require context information, which is considered future work.
DL is emerging as a popular approach for device ﬁngerprinting. However, most approaches consider IoT device
behavior or other characteristics, e.g., RF footprint. For example, in ZigBee communication, different DL algorithms based
on DNNs, CNNs, and recurrent neural networks (RNNs)/long
short-term memory networks (LSTMs) are examined [32].
CNNs have been demonstrated on a handful of devices to
create device signatures and identify malicious ones, as they
deviate from the captured ﬁngerprint [33]. However, such
approaches, while similar from an algorithmic perspective
(e.g., using ML/DL), are applied to different aspects of device
ﬁngerprinting and are not further discussed.
A recent analysis of device OS ﬁngerprinting [26] uses several ML methods to compare them. Speciﬁcally, it compares
results from k-nearest neighbors (kNNs), decision tree, and
artiﬁcial neural network (ANN) to those of the traditional
rule-based method and shows that ANN achieves success rates
of 94% [26]. This approach is relevant to the one proposed
in this work; however, there are also signiﬁcant differences,
as the number of data samples and the features considered
are limited. In addition, the approach only classiﬁed into 4
labels, i.e., Windows, AIX, Linux, and Mac, which are seen
as insufﬁcient to characterize the majority of IoT devices. So,
both from the methodology point of view (usage of ML and
DL) as well as from the dataset, enhancements can be made,
which may deliver more generalized results, something that
this work attempts to do by using richer features and labels, as
well as a more sophisticated DL architecture that is capable of
better learning from these rich features.
When it comes to the Nmap DB [20], different techniques
have been applied to extract knowledge from the provided labels. For instance, a self-organizing map, a single-layer ANN,
was used to produce and visualize a Kohonen feature map,
and growing neural gas (GNG) and k-means were applied to
cluster similar OS [34]. SVM was used for OS identiﬁcation,

ANN has been utilized in [25], where a multilayer perceptron with a hidden layer of 42 neurons was used in
conjunction with Nmap signatures and Monte Carlo simulation of generated inputs based on the Nmap DB. This
approach demonstrated the feasibility of using ANNs; however, it did not provide a systematic approach to all Nmap

A recent research work [27] utilizes several ML techniques

been experimented. Results of up to 0.960 were achieved with
the random forest. The dataset used stemmed from Nmap

and transformer architectures, where the tabular transformer
experiments deliver promising results.
III. CORPUS
The dataset used is that of the Nmap project [20], which
is publicly available on GitHub [35], and known as Nmap
DB. This DB has been developed over the last 25 years with
thousands of device ﬁngerprints that reﬂect several classes of
Internet-connected devices from diverse manufacturers running various OSs.
A typical ﬁngerprint stored in the Nmap DB is shown in
Table 2. This ﬁngerprint identiﬁes an IP device from Cisco,
running IOS 15.×, and classiﬁed as a router. The different
ﬁelds are the responses to the probes sent to the TCP devices.
Six TCP probes are sent, and the information acquired from
the responses is used to create an entry with the info shown in
Table 3.
TABLE 4. Nmap Probes: Speciﬁcations Versus Empirical Data
The existence of the Nmap DB is of paramount relevance to
this work, as it enables us to focus on analysis and inference
rather than on data capture, which would not be possible at the
scale and diversity comparable to those in the Nmap DB. This
work uses the DB as of November 2023 [20], with 5780 entries initially. Some slight deviations are observed with respect
to the available documentation, as indicated in Table 4, with
the highlighted values in red color indicating the differences.
Speciﬁcally, some values that are expected according to the
speciﬁcations of the probes [23], e.g., O and W in T1, are not
available in the empirical data captured in the Nmap DB. This
may imply that these have not been observed in the captured
datasets. However, some values are not described in the specs
but do exist in the datasets, e.g., the R values for sequence
number (SEQ), TCP options (OPS), and WIN. For SEQ, OPS,
and WIN, the value R is available only when no reply to
the send probe is captured (R=N). Since the DB format is
evolving, these may not be sufﬁciently depicted in the original
Nmap guide [23]. It also needs to be considered that some of
the results captured in earlier versions of the Nmap DB [23]
have changed over the years, e.g., IP data length for ICMP
responses, ICMP sequence number, IP type of service for
ICMP responses are no longer used in the ICMP echo (IE)
test. In any case, the Nmap DB maintainer is informed via
email about these inconsistencies, hoping that these will be
ﬁxed in future releases of the DB.
The Nmap DB is provided in a rich format, but this information needs to be extracted and properly processed for use with
various ML algorithms. After analyzing the dataset, it was decided to use the entries as classes, i.e., OS family, vendor, and
device type, to which all devices can be classiﬁed. As features,
all the probes and responses are considered as shown in Table 4, e.g., T1–T7, U1, IE, SEQ, OPS, WIN, ECN, but in their
expanded form. For example, from ﬁngerprint test T1, the
features A,DF,F,Q,R,RD,S,T,TG are obtained. Because some
expected values were not observed in the empirical dataset,
and not all probes and responses used the full theoretical
values, several values were missing. It was decided to remove
all columns for which at least 20% of the values were missing.
After this column-level ﬁltering, any row that still contained at
least one missing value was dropped, so that the ﬁnal dataset
contains no missing data and every training instance presents a
complete, internally consistent ﬁngerprint. The 20% columnremoval threshold balances coverage against feature retention
as a stricter threshold would have discarded a substantial

A closer look at the dataset reveals the different device
types (as shown in Fig. 1), vendors (shown in Fig. 2), and
OS families (as shown in Fig. 3). As shown in Fig. 1, which
is on a log scale, the majority of devices can be characterized
as phones. A signiﬁcant portion of devices are wireless access
points (WAPs), various storage devices, printers, and network
devices, such as switches, ﬁrewalls, and routers. Many of
these (e.g., WAPs, phones, printers, embedded storage devices) qualify as IoT devices, while others (e.g., switches,
ﬁrewalls, routers) are traditional IP-connected infrastructure

assets. In this work, no separate IoT-ﬁltering step is applied,
and the full Nmap device-type taxonomy is used as the classi-
ﬁcation target for the device-type experiment.
Regarding the vendors in the dataset, as shown in Fig. 2, the
majority are characterized as Linux devices. It can be assumed
that this stems from their OS and the lack of vendor-speciﬁc
information from other vendors. As an example, the Raspberry Pi device is also listed with vendor characterization as
Linux. Apart from that, most companies known to produce
or market hardware devices, such as Apple, Lexmark, Nokia,
Alcatel, and AVN, are also represented.
Finally, as shown in Fig. 3, OSs are mostly embedded,
while Linux, iOS, ZyNOS, SonicOS, IOS, Android, and other
OSs follow. The embedded characterization is generic and
includes devices that may run Linux or be agnostic to the
device’s OS. As an example, the LogiLink Gigabit NAS device, which is a storage device, is given as an OS for the
characterization embedded in the DB, in the absence of the
concrete OS it runs on.
Overall, the Nmap DB analysis provides valuable insights
into the resulting dataset used for classiﬁcation. It should also
be kept in mind that these ﬁngerprints were contributed by
volunteers and, as such, may contain inaccuracies that may
be corrected in the future Nmap DB revisions. In addition,
this DB does not claim to feature an exhaustive list of IoT
devices connected via the Internet protocol, but rather reﬂects
the ﬁngerprints that volunteers have contributed over the last
25 years.
IV. EXPERIMENT SETUP
Having constructed the corpus and clearly selected features
and labels, the next step is to address the core of the RQ.
To do so, it was decided to use a mix of traditional ML and
more “modern” DL techniques to address the classiﬁcation
problems. Speciﬁcally, three similar experiments were conducted, each using the existing data to predict one of the

available labels: OS family, vendor, and device type. All experiments are multiclass classiﬁcation problems. For all the
same algorithms, the same parameter conﬁguration is used,
with the ﬁlter that each class must have at least 10 samples to
properly support a stratiﬁed 70/10/20 split. While one could
experiment to ﬁne-tune the algorithms for higher performance
on the speciﬁc dataset, this is considered future work.
The steps for each experiment are reﬂected in the workﬂow
in Fig. 4. The dataset is read and split into 70% training,
10% validation, and 20% testing data in a stratiﬁed manner
to preserve the class proportions. However, after the split, a
decision must be made about the imbalanced training dataset.
This would be problematic for training algorithms, as a severe
imbalance could favor the class with the larger number of
samples (the majority class).
It was decided to conduct three experiments to investigate
the impact of imbalanced data and their enrichment with additional synthetic data generated from the original training
dataset. While there are several ways to add synthetic data, we
opted to experiment with two of them: the synthetic minority
oversampling technique (SMOTE) [36], and the oversample
using adaptive synthetic (ADASYN) [37]. ADASYN is similar to SMOTE but differs in that it generates a different
number of samples for each class to be oversampled. Both
ADASYN and SMOTE support multiclass resampling using
the one-versus-rest scheme, which is needed for the multiclass classiﬁcation pursued in this work. The enriched training
datasets that result from utilizing SMOTE or ADASYN are
balanced. It is important to note that SMOTE or ADASYN
is applied only to the training dataset, while the validation
and test datasets are not altered. With this step, all processing
aspects have been concluded, and the experiments in which
the training of the different models can start. Subsequently,
testing is carried out, and the results are reported.
Since this is a multiclass classiﬁcation problem, all selected
algorithms must be suitable for multiclass classiﬁcation. The
following “traditional” ML algorithms were run identically
across all three experiments: decision tree, extra trees, Gaussian naive Bayes, quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA),
random forest, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost).
For XGBoost, as part of the parameter investigation, a grid
search was done, and as a result, it was decided to use 100
boosting rounds with a max tree depth of 5 and a learning
rate of 0.1. For the implementation of these algorithms, the
Scikit-Learn toolkit is used [38]. For XGBoost, the implementation provided by the distributed (deep) ML Community was
used [39].
In addition to the “traditional” ML algorithms, some DNNs
were also realized and run for all three experiments. The
motivation is to see whether they offer any advantages over
traditional ones and to compare them to gain insights. The
following DNNs were used: DNN1 (2 layers: 128, 64), DNN2
(3 layers: 256, 128, 64), DNN3 (2 layers: 512, 256), DNN4
(3 layers: 1024, 512, 256), and DNN5 (6 layers: 128, 256,
512, 256, 128, 64). The speciﬁc DNNs were selected to cover
some basic patterns for DNN design, i.e., DNN1 is relatively
simple, while DNN2 is deeper, DNN3 is wide and shallow,
and DNN4 is deep and wide. Finally, DNN5 is both deep
and wide, and changes in layer width are used to capture
high-level and ﬁne-grained details across a variety of data.
While these were indicative selections, it is not claimed that
any of these designs is the best for the data available. For all
DNNs, the rectiﬁed linear unit activation function was used
after each layer. Adam was chosen as the optimizer, with beta
decay coefﬁcients (0.9, 0.999) and L2 regularization of 1e−5.
The learning rate of 0.01 was used as a starting point, and it
was adjusted via a scheduler with a step size of 10 and gamma
of 0.5. Gradient clipping was used during training to prevent
the gradients from becoming too large. A limit of 200 epochs
was set; however, early stopping was also implemented if the
validation loss did not improve for 10 consecutive epochs.
For all algorithms, a common set of metrics was collected:
F1 (weighted), F1 (macro), and AUC (macro) to compare
performance across models. In addition to these typical ML
metrics, two more aspects were measured: the training and
inference times for each algorithm, which, of course, depend
on the sizes of the training and test datasets. During inference time, the inference-per-sample metric was also derived
to measure how long it takes to classify a single data point.
These metrics are reﬂected in Tables 5–7, and serve as a basis
for the analysis in Sections V-A–V-C, as well as the overall
discussion in Section VI. The highlighted values show the best
one in each category. All experiments were carried out with
Scikit-Learn [38], XGBoost [39], and PyTorch [40] toolkits.

VI. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
The RQs regarding the identiﬁcation of OSs, vendors, and
types of Internet-connected devices have been approached as
a multiclass classiﬁcation problem. The three experiments,
carried out individually, addressed each part of the RQ by
comparing the performance of 11 ML algorithms. From these,
six were selected as traditional ML algorithms, while ﬁve
were different variations of DNNs. The experimental results
have provided several insights.
Selecting the best-performing models, whether based on
traditional ML techniques or on more complex DL approaches, depends on the speciﬁc use case. The training times
are signiﬁcantly lower for traditional ML models, even when
they do not use GPUs (except for XGBoost). However, at
inference time, the gap among them is signiﬁcantly smaller.
In that sense, if there is a need to capture more complex cases,
training could be done centrally for DNNs in resource-rich environments, and inference could be done in more lightweight
devices. However, for the speciﬁc dataset, the traditional ML
models outperform or, in some cases, are at par with DNNs,
and given that they do not require extensive training time and
resources, they are preferred.
Ensemble methods like XGBoost and random forests offer the best tradeoff between performance and computational
resources. These seem to be highly robust and perform well
overall, while decision tree also follows. Overall, tree-based
models mostly outperform other methods on F1 and AUC.
XGBoost shows strong AUC and excellent results across both
F1 scores, but may be sensitive to data augmentation. Simpler models like GaussianNB and QDA are the weakest and
perform poorly, as probabilistic approaches cannot handle the
complexity of the dataset.
The observed dominance of tree-based models is consistent with the structural properties of the data. The Nmap
ﬁngerprint corpus is tabular, where each sample consists
of discrete, heterogeneous probe-response ﬁelds (TCP ﬂags,
window sizes, timing values) that are largely categorical with
no spatial, temporal, or sequential ordering. Tree-based models manage to partition such a feature space via axis-aligned
splits, which align naturally with the categorical and ordinal
Nmap ﬁelds, and they impose no distributional assumptions.
On the contrary, DNNs derive much of their advantage from
structured redundancy, e.g., spatial in images, sequential in
text, and temporal in audio. Because tabular ﬁngerprints lack
such regularities, the representation-learning advantage of
DNNs diminishes relative to the variance-reduction beneﬁts
that bagging (random forest) and boosting (XGBoost) offer
on a corpus with up to 130 classes.
The use of DNNs does not provide sufﬁcient performance
gains to justify their cost. However, the results show that
DNNs often achieve high AUC scores, as shown in Table 7,
making them potential candidates for scenarios where maximizing AUC is critical and computational resources are not
a limitation. While an attempt was made to experiment with
different DNN architectures, including their depth, it cannot
be said that more complex DNNs perform better than simpler
ones on the speciﬁc dataset. In some tests, DNN4 and DNN5
achieved high AUC, which tends to correlate with the view
that deeper, wider networks with more complex architectures
better distinguish among classes. However, in other cases,
DNN3 also performed well despite having fewer layers, suggesting that increasing the number of layers beyond a certain
point may not be beneﬁcial, as it hampers training and requires
more time.
Augmenting data to address imbalances may have positive
effects in speciﬁc cases. While it seemed to beneﬁt some
models, the overall beneﬁts were marginal, and there was also
a case where a model’s performance unexpectedly declined,
as evidenced by XGBoost’s performance in Table 6. Hence,
XGBoost can be used, but only without augmented data from
SMOTE or ADASYN. DNNs may partially beneﬁt from it;
however, the impact on training time is signiﬁcant and not
justiﬁable. Considering also the impact such augmentation has
on the dataset, i.e., the increase of samples and as a result,
of the training time, the augmentation strategy needs to be
well thought out and guided by the requirements the speciﬁc
use case has while balancing resource consumption and model
performance.
The high performance of traditional ML models on this
dataset also opens the way for their integration into lowresource devices at the edge or in the fog computing layer
within a computer network. Inference can also be accelerated on edge or fog systems with specialized GPU and NPU
accelerators, thereby reducing inference time and making it
practical to deploy such complex algorithms at these parts
of the network. Typical examples include the NVIDIA Jetson Orin/Thor family, AMD Versal AI Edge, NXP i.MX 9
with on-die NPU, Arm Ethos NPUs, the Hailo series, and

Texas Instruments Sitara System-on-Chips (TI Sitara SoCs).
As such, ﬁrewalls or security information and event management (SIEM) systems could leverage accelerated inference to
detect unauthorized devices or ﬂag inconsistencies in their
registries in real time.
We have experimented with a speciﬁc hardware platform,
and this inﬂuences the algorithm training and testing, especially the reported training/inference times. As such, potential
future work might involve experimenting with different hardware platforms and reporting on differences. This would be
especially of interest, given modern embedded platforms and
IoT devices, which could serve as local agents assisting larger
IDSs or even asset management systems in more complex
environments, with direct monitoring and ﬁngerprinting of
local network devices.
While in these experiments, traditional ML algorithms are
preferred because they perform better overall, DNNs could
offer an advantage when combined with other, more complex
tasks, such as device behavior, to enhance device ﬁngerprinting capabilities. OS ﬁngerprinting remains important and
challenging, and recent trends indicate that it can be assisted
by combining it with other behavioral information [31]. DNNs
could be used for such complex approaches; however, this is
seen as a potential future direction of work.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting
these results. First, the Nmap DB is a volunteer-contributed
corpus, which biases the device population toward equipment
that security practitioners and enthusiasts commonly scan and
report to the Nmap DB. Therefore, niche or proprietary IP
devices, especially those deployed in industrial settings, are
likely under represented. Second, class and vendor labels are
assigned at submission time and may contain noise, as evidenced by the spec-vs-empirical discrepancies highlighted in
Table 4. Third, the snapshot used (November 2023) reﬂects
the device landscape at one point in time, and classiﬁers
trained on it may degrade without periodic retraining as new
OS variants, chipsets, and vendors emerge. Fourth, Nmap
ﬁngerprints rely on active probing via TCP/UDP/ICMP, which
assumes the target device responds. However, the presence of
ﬁrewalls, NAT, and device hardening may suppress or alter responses in real-world deployments. Consequently, the results
should be interpreted as characterizing ML/DL performance
on this speciﬁc database and its distribution rather than as absolute estimates for arbitrary IoT environments. A deployment
in a speciﬁc industrial or enterprise network would require
validation against a representative sample of that network’s
device population.
We have investigated only some of the capabilities of the
algorithms and DNNs, without, however, claiming that these
are the best achievable results. For XGBoost, a grid search
was performed to ﬁnd better parameters. However, this search
could have been more extensive. The same holds true for
the DNNs, where indicative architectures and layers were
used, but without a more in-depth analysis of their con-
ﬁguration or further ﬁne-tuning. Recently, table transformer
architectures have delivered promising results in device
ﬁngerprinting [28]. As such, developments in DL should be
closely monitored, and the application of new architectures, or
even large language models (LLMs), should be investigated.
One has to consider, though, that since the Nmap DB is
publicly available, its data are likely already seen by LLMs,
and as such, obtaining a reliable unseen test dataset might be
challenging.
VII. CONCLUSION
Device ﬁngerprinting is a critical area in security, and being
able to identify key characteristics of an IP-connected device,
such as the following:
1) the OS family;
2) the vendor;
3) the device type, can provide competitive information
when assessing a device.
Traditional ML and DL algorithms were investigated, and
their performance was analyzed based on the information
captured in the Nmap DB. The results show that tree-based
(decision tree) and ensemble algorithms, such as random forest, extra trees, and XGBoost perform excellently while also
having low training and inference times. DNN algorithms can
also perform at high levels, sometimes at par with more traditional algorithms; however, their high training times do not
make them preferred candidates, at least when these device
aspects are investigated in isolation. DNNs can handle complexity well and, as such, could be considered an extension
of existing tools that already use them or as tools with more
complex features.
Overall, the following algorithms are proposed to be used.
1) OS family identiﬁcation: Decision tree, random forest,
and XGBoost.
2) Vendor identiﬁcation: Decision tree, random forest, and
XGBoost (if no augmentation is applied to the data
during training).
3) Device type identiﬁcation: Random forest, extra trees,
and XGBoost.
The ﬁndings are highly relevant to security researchers,
network administrators, system administrators, and asset managers. These stakeholders can beneﬁt from this research to
create more reliable and secure infrastructures that rely on
device ﬁngerprinting. Several future directions have been
proposed for further advancing this research. These range
from comparative analysis of implementation across different
hardware platforms, especially in the domain of embedded
and low-resource devices, to a more systematic investigation of DNN design and, overall, the conﬁguration of ML
algorithms. For industrial and critical-infrastructure settings,
the lightweight tree-based classiﬁers identiﬁed in this work,
combined with edge accelerators, such as the NVIDIA Jetson Orin/Thor family, AMD Versal AI Edge, NXP i.MX 9
with on-die NPU, Arm Ethos NPUs, the Hailo series, and TI
Sitara SoCs, are particularly attractive for continuous asset
discovery, SIEM integration, and real-time ﬁngerprinting at
the network edge.

, Senior Member, IEEE, Jianhui Wang
, Senior Member, IEEE, and Bo Chen
, Member, IEEE
Abstract—This letter develops a ﬂexible machine learning
detection method for cyberattacks in distribution systems considering spatiotemporal patterns. Spatiotemporal patterns are
recognized by the graph Laplacian based on system-wide measurements. A ﬂexible Bayes classiﬁer (BC) is used to train
spatiotemporal patterns which could be violated when cyberattacks occur. Cyberattacks are detected by using ﬂexible BCs
online. The effectiveness of the developed method is demonstrated
through standard IEEE 13- and 123-node test feeders.
Index Terms—Cyberattack detection, distribution systems,
graph Laplacian, machine learning, spatiotemporal patterns.

of spatiotemporal patterns among system measurements by
developing ﬂexible BCs. Essentially, spatiotemporal patterns

detection on distribution systems. (i) Is it possible to quantitatively capture the spatiotemporal patterns between cyberattack

In this letter, we seek to integrate the spatiotemporal patterns
of system measurements into a ﬂexible BC for cyberattack
detection. Speciﬁcally, spatiotemporal patterns are captured by
the generalized graph Laplacian (GGL) matrix for system measurements. For the training process of the proposed ﬂexible
BC, they are taken as its input variables, while the labels of
cyberattack templates are taken as its output variables. For
the testing process, the online spatiotemporal patterns captured by GGL are put into the proposed ﬂexible BC, which
subsequently outputs the cyberattack detection results.
The organization of this letter is as follows. In Section II,
the ﬂexible BC detection method is brieﬂy introduced based
on spatiotemporal patterns using the graph Laplacian. Case
studies and result analysis performed on the public distribution
load data are discussed in Section III. Concluding remarks are
summarized in Section V.

naive BCs are usually handled by discretization and assume

ﬂexible BC is based on the nonparametric kernel estimation
which does not require any normality assumption and outperforms in most domains. Also, the ﬂexible BC can store every
continuous attribute value it sees during the training process.
