III. CASE STUDIES AND RESULTS
The raw load data is obtained from the Pecan Street
Dataport [6]. 80% of the measurement data in a whole year
(292 days) is used for training with 28,032 samples, while 20%
of those (73 days) is used for testing with 7,008 samples. Four
cyberattack templates are simulated on each node connected
with load, including scaling, ramping, random, and smoothcurve attacks. Detailed information of cyberattack templates
is described in the Appendix. Two distribution systems with
13 and 123 buses are simulated using OpenDSS [7]. Active
and reactive power data in distribution systems is assumed to
be vulnerable under cyberattack scenarios.
A. Robustness of Spatiotemporal Patterns Representation
To verify the robustness of spatiotemporal patterns recognized by GGL, Fig. 2 shows the results with different ambient
noises on system measurements. Figs. 2a and 2b are with
quickly changing false data injection (QCFDI) attacks. Fig. 2a
shows an example of spatial patterns with cyberattacks preset
on Node 675 Phase c. Fig. 2b presents an example of temporal patterns with cyberattacks preset from 8 hour to 14 hour.
As can be seen, the GGL can accurately capture both spatial
and temporal patterns when QCFDI attacks occur. Also, the
results are robust for different ambient noises. Figs. 2c and 2d
are with slowly changing false data injection (SCFDI) attacks.
The slow change amplitude of SCFDI attacks is set as 10% of
that of QCFDI attacks. Similarly, the GGL can accurately capture both spatial and temporal patterns when SCFDI attacks
occur. Also, the results are robust for different ambient noises.

B. Effectiveness Analysis of Flexible BCs
Fig. 3 compares Support Vector Machine (SVM) [8], naive
BCs, and ﬂexible BCs using the visualized performance diagram on the IEEE 13-node test feeder. Four representative
nodes are deployed for comparison. Fig. 4 shows the visualized performance diagram on the IEEE 123-node test feeder.
Eight representative nodes are deployed for comparison. As
can be seen, for different system nodes, the ﬂexible BC method
(rectangles closest to the top right corner) performs better
than SVM and the naive BC method (circles and triangles). In
addition, it can be observed that smooth-curve attacks are relatively challenging to detect for all methods. This is because
they are very secretive while presenting a smooth trending
together with neighboring measurements at both the beginning and the end of one attack. Fig. 5 compares SVM, naive
BC, and ﬂexible BC methods with respect to different scaling
attack parameters (λS = 0.2, 0.5, and 1.0). The TPR metric
is used for validation. As shown in this ﬁgure, for all parameters, ﬂexible BCs perform better than both SVM and naive
BCs with higher TPR values. Also, TPR values are increased
with scaling attack parameters (from 0.2 to 1.0).
To quantitatively evaluate the performance of the developed
method, Table I compares different detection methods for
cyberattacks in the IEEE 123-node test feeder. As can be
seen, the ﬂexible BC shows the largest TPR metric compared
with the naive BC, SVM, and decision tree methods. This
is because the ﬂexible BC does not require any normality
assumption and can store every continuous attribute value it
sees during the training process.
IV. DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS
Spatiotemporal patterns of measurements have been widely
used in the areas of renewable forecasting and plug-in electric
vehicles (PEVs) in recent years. Inspired by this background,
deploying spatiotemporal patterns for cyberattack detection
has a broad prospect by coordinating with machine learning
techniques. Complex distribution networks can be deﬁned as
a graphical model where variables are associated with highly
nonlinear target functions, and complex spatial and temporal
relationships exist among such variables even for cyberattacks.
Since distribution systems are running based on complicated
physical laws and rules, describing the spatiotemporal patterns
by machine learning paves a way for mapping such relationships that could be signiﬁcantly compromised by the injected
cyberattacks. For the future work of this letter, deep learning
techniques will be further involved. That is to say, the spatiotemporal patterns will be mapped to a linear space by using
the Long Short-term Memory (LSTM) network to improve the
potential detection accuracy for cyberattacks.

V. CONCLUSION
In this letter, we develop a ﬂexible machine learning
based cyberattack detection method by using the generalized graph Laplacian (GGL) and ﬂexible Bayes classiﬁers
(BCs). Spatiotemporal patterns are quantitatively characterized by GGL, which could be compromised when cyberattacks
occur. The ﬂexible BCs are used for training spatiotemporal
patterns of system measurements and detecting cyberattacks
online. Numerical results of case studies verify the effectiveness of the developed cyberattack detection method based on
machine learning techniques.
APPENDIX
TEMPLATES OF CYBERATTACKS
In this letter, we are not aiming to develop new adversary models of cyberattack templates. Inspired by existing
adversary models for attacking automatic generation control
(AGC) [9], we assume that attackers with advanced skills
could migrate these adversary models to those on micro-PMU
measurements in distribution systems. The cyberattack templates can be divided into four categories: scaling, ramping,
random, and smooth-curve, which are elaborately described
in [4]. Note that this letter does not aim to develop new
templates for cyberattacks.

Gerardo Ibarra-Vazquez

Abstract—This article aims to study the performance of machine
learning models in forecasting gender based on the students’ open
education competency perception. Data were collected from a convenience sample of 326 students from 26 countries using the eOpen
instrument. The analysis comprises 1) a study of the students’ perceptions of knowledge, skills, and attitudes or values related to open
education and its subcompetencies from a 30-item questionnaire
using machine learning models to forecast participants’ gender,
2) validation of performance through cross-validation methods,
3) statistical analysis to ﬁnd signiﬁcant differences between machine learning models, and 4) an analysis from explainable machine
learning models to ﬁnd relevant features to forecast gender. The
results conﬁrm our hypothesis that the performance of machine
learning models can effectively forecast gender based on the student’s perceptions of knowledge, skills, and attitudes or values
related to open education competency.
Index Terms—Educational innovation, explainable, forecasting,
gender, higher education, machine learning (ML), open education,
student perception.

establishes international scientiﬁc communication to guarantee

free-access educational resources and technology without discrimination as a strategic measure. Their potential is recognized

and through education [2]. More recently, UNESCO reafﬁrmed
its commitment to these goals and strategies by helping all

need to transfer the political orientations of international organizations as sources of innovation is frequently demanded

There is an essential heterogeneity of open education practices. They have mainly focused on the production, use, and mobilization of various OER [5], [6], [7], the analysis of the support

This article makes a valuable and novel contribution to the

By exploring this intersection of ML and gender prediction, this

In this research, we focus on studying the application of ML
models to forecast gender based on students’ perceptions of
open education competency. We delve into the following main
contributions of this research.
1) The study gathered data from 326 students in 26 countries
using the eOpen instrument, which provided a diverse
sample, allowing for more generalizable ﬁndings and
insights into variations in gender perceptions and open
education competency across different contexts.
2) The research utilizes explainable ML models to predict
gender from a 30-item questionnaire, employing crossvalidation to ensure model robustness and conducting a
comparative analysis of different models while enhancing interpretability by identifying relevant features contributing to gender forecasting based on open education
competency perceptions.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II
provides the background and outlines related studies on open

II. RELATED WORKS
A. Open Education
Open education is democratized through facilitators that promote the social appropriation of knowledge. According to the
literature review of Ramirez-Montoya [22], open education is
an educational model comprising the design, development, and
evaluation of learning opportunities freely and with open access to improve students’ quality of learning throughout life.
Different frameworks have been created for the development of
open education in educational institutions: the OpenEd quality
framework [23], the open educators factory framework [24],
the 6E evaluation framework [25], the opening up education: A
support framework for higher education institutions [26], and the
framework for selecting OER based on ﬁtness-for-purpose [27].
At the same time, instruments have been designed for its evaluation, among which the following stand out: the scale of digital
competenceanduseof openeducational resources [28], thescale
of accreditation standards of open and distance education [29],
and the scale of perspectives and opinions on OER and other
online educational resources [30]. The connection between the
institutional framework for academic research and those who
transfer it to practice supposes an added value of the scientiﬁc
communities, which contribute to societal cultural and social development. As depicted in Table I, as part of the implementation
of UNESCO’s Recommendation on OER, Ramirez-Montoya
and Tenorio-Sepulveda [31] propose competence indicators corresponding to each objective.
Furthermore, it has become increasingly evident that fostering changes to advance the development of open education
practices is crucial, as highlighted by the perceptions of students and education professionals regarding various sociodemographic characteristics, including gender [32]. Traditional
research approaches in education have already shed light on the
advancements and limitations of open education practices when
examined through a gender lens. Notably, in a critical analysis
conducted in [17], the texts of OER were scrutinized from a
gender perspective, revealing the imperative to incorporate a
more equitable and inclusive vision. Gender has also been a
signiﬁcant factor in analyzing participation rates in open education programs, motivations for engagement, time allocation to
training, and students’ use of computers and the Internet [33].
Throughthesestudies,adeeperunderstandingoftheintersection
between gender and open education practices has emerged,
emphasizing the need for continued examination and action to
foster more signiﬁcant equity and inclusion in education.
B. ML in Education
ML is substantially changing the conventional research methods in education. ML is a subﬁeld of artiﬁcial intelligence
focused on developing models to enable computers to learn
and make predictions without being explicitly programmed [34].
Leading international organizations, such as UNESCO and Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development have
recommended the integration of artiﬁcial intelligence in educational research to improve the quality of educational systems [20], [35]. ML sets itself apart from traditional linear
regression through its ability to offer robust nonparametric
components that enable greater adaptability and versatility in
its practical applications as a predictive model [36]. These techniques allow researchers and educational experts to design more
personalized curricula tailored to the needs of speciﬁc groups,
optimizing teaching strategies and learning progress to improve

Understanding existing gender differences in skill development is becoming increasingly important to gain valuable information on how to close the gender gap. The analysis of speciﬁc
sociodemographic characteristics in ML studies in education
is still in its infancy [48], [49]. Gender prediction using ML
models mainly focused on gender prediction of educational

and gender stereotyping in academic dropout [54]. These studies
shed light on the potential of ML to provide valuable insights
and guide efforts toward closing the gender gap in education.
Studying students’ perceptions, gender, and the integration
of ML is essential to gaining valuable insights into educational
practices and developing more inclusive and effective learning
environments. Gooria et al. [55] focused on studying students’
perceptions of self-directed learning and performance in open
education processes and found no signiﬁcant differences in

impact open education practices.

limited attention given to studying students’ perceptions in the
context of ML and gender. Thus, studying the perception of open
education competency through ML models while considering

and valuable contribution of ML to education. Advancing techniques for analyzing open education competency, particularly
considering gender as a signiﬁcant sociodemographic variable,

III. METHODOLOGY
In this article, we propose to study the performance of ML
models in forecasting gender based on the students’ perceptions
of their knowledge, skills, and attitudes or values related to open
education. We used eOpen data to perform the experiments to
forecast the participant’s gender using four of the most widely
used ML classiﬁcation models in the following.
1) Decision trees (DTs);
2) LGBM;
3) RF;
4) 1D-CNN.

A DT is a tree-like model composed of a root node, branches,
and leaf nodes. A root node represents each test of an item
response, the output from the root node is a branch, and a leaf
represents each class label [57]. LGBM are based on gradient
boosting DTs with an optimization method that can effectively
reduce the number of features without hurting the accuracy of
split-point determination [58]. RF algorithms are popular ML
algorithms in classiﬁcation and regression tasks [59]. These
algorithms construct a series of DTs on different samples and
use majority voting to assign a class. Convolutional neural network (CNN) is the most popular ML model for most computer
vision tasks. Recently, CNNs have been rapidly used in many
one-dimension applications, becoming state of the art [60].
In our experimentation, data preprocessing was considered to
diminish bias acquired by ML models in the learning process
from categories and questions with high numerical contribution [61], [62]. Then, we followed two steps: 1) oversampling the
class with lower occurrences to level its size to the class with major occurrences using duplicate instances and 2) normalization,
which was applied as the standard procedure over all items in the
eOpen data. We performed initial experimentation by dividing
data into training and testing phases to evaluate the models’
behavior with the most widely used metric: accuracy. Then, we
performed two cross-validation methods to validate the initial
performance of the ML models using the average cross-validated
accuracy and statistical hypothesis test to observe differences
between the ML models.
In ML, two distinct approaches inﬂuence the interpretability of models: explainable and nonexplainable ML [63].
Explainable ML refers to algorithms and techniques that allow
humans to comprehend the rationale behind model predictions.
This approach emphasizes transparency and aims to provide
explanations for the decision-making process [64]. On the other
hand, nonexplainable ML is considered a black-box model,
which focuses on achieving high predictive accuracy without
prioritizing interpretability [65]. These models often rely on
complex architectures, such as deep neural networks, which can
be challenging to interpret due to their intricate inner workings.
Three ML models are explainable from our experimentation due to their DT structure (DT, RF, and LGBM). With
this understanding, we thoroughly analyzed the decision rules
employed by these models. The main objective was to ﬁnd the
most relevant features inﬂuencing the models’ ability to forecast
gender accurately.
A. Cross-Validation
Cross-validation is a statistical method for evaluating and
validating ML models using different parts of the data to train
and validate the model in several operations [66]. Typically,
the cross-validation process resides in subsequent stages of
training and validation sets so that each instance in data has an
opportunity to be validated. The most common cross-validation
method is k-fold cross-validation, where data are separated into
k approximately equally folds. Then, a cycle of k iterations is
executed to train and validate the model using a different data
fold for validation and k −1 folds for training. Therefore, the

Kohavi [67] recommended stratiﬁed tenfold cross-validation as
the best model selection method from a study of several approaches, where he included different cross-validation methods
(regular cross-validation, leave-one-out cross-validation, and
stratiﬁed cross-validation) and bootstrap to estimate the accuracy. Stratiﬁed tenfold cross-validation yielded less tendency
performance estimation.

The data collected in [68] were from a convenience sample
of m = 326 students, of which 226 were females and 100

different academic degrees: 1) Doctoral degree, 2) master’s
degree, and 3) bachelor’s degree and below. Fig. 3 illustrates the

detailed breakdown of the participants by gender and academic
degree. The data collection process involved a voluntary selfassessment questionnaire administered through Google Forms
with the approval of the ethics committees at the participating institutions, and informed consent was obtained from all
individual participants.

C. Instrument
The eOpen instrument is intended to be of value to academic,
scientiﬁc, and social communities interested in open education,
educational innovation, research evaluation, and complex environments. The instrument designed in [68] measures students’
perceptions of knowledge, skills, and attitudes or values related
to open education and its subcompetencies from a 30-item
questionnaire in the following.
1) Capacity building (items 1–8);
2) Development of support policies (items 9–15);
3) Promotion of effective, inclusive, and equitable access
(items 16–21);
4) Creation of sustainability models (items 22–25);
5) Promotion of international cooperation (items 26–30);
The eOpen instrument uses a four-point Likert scale (1:
Strongly disagree, 2: Disagree, 3: Agree, and 4: Strongly agree)
to measure the students’ level of self-assessment.

V. DISCUSSION
The study of open education competency data through ML
models expands data analysis capabilities to extract characteristics from participants’ perceptions to predict gender. In Table VI,
we observed that ML models could predict the participants’
gender from the student’s perception of knowledge, skills, and
attitudes or values related to open education using the eOpen
instrument. This ﬁnding agrees with [69], which employed a
discriminant characteristic to predict student performance using ML algorithms. Thus, ML models enhanced data analysis
from survey researchers by extracting features from students’

Explainable ML models, such as DT, RF, and LGBM, employ
decision rules to determine the most important features to predict
the student’s gender based on their perception of open education

are visually presented in Figs. 6–8, providing a comprehensive overview of the explainable ML models’ ﬁndings. It is
noteworthy that all of these models converge on the promotion of international cooperation subcompetency as a crucial
factor in gender prediction. This convergence highlights the
consistent importance of this particular subcompetency across
the various models and underscores its signiﬁcant inﬂuence on

thedevelopmentofimprovededucationalpoliciesandstrategies.

it a reliable tool for understanding students’ open education
competency perceptions and their connection to gender.
VI. CONCLUSION
Over the past few years, an increasing focus has been on
open education to make learning accessible to all and foster
equality among learners. Effective measuring and evaluating
open education competencies remains challenging despite its
potential beneﬁts. This article aims to study the performance
of ML models in forecasting gender based on the students’
open education competency perception. Our ﬁndings indicate
that ML models can effectively predict participants’ gender
from students’ perceptions of knowledge, skills, and attitudes
or values related to open education and its subcompetencies.
This discovery holds great signiﬁcance as it demonstrates the
potential of ML to offer valuable insights into learners’ competencies perceptions, thereby informing educational practices.
In this study, we considered the following data analyses.
1) Study the students’ perceptions of knowledge, skills, and
attitudes or values related to open education and its subcompetencies with a 30-item questionnaire, using ML
models to forecast participants’ gender
2) Validation performance through cross-validation methods.

3) Statistical analysis to ﬁnd signiﬁcant differences between
ML models.
4) An analysis from DTs to ﬁnd relevant features to forecast
gender.
ML demonstrated the capability to build models that can
predict the gender of unknown participants’ perceptions of
open education with up to 84% mean accuracy. Therefore,
the mathematical models built with ML extracted features
from eOpen data and found differences in the perceptions
by gender. In addition, the higher accuracy exhibited by RF
in gender prediction highlighted its reliability as a valuable
tool for understanding students’ open education competency
perceptions and their relationship to gender. Using explainable
ML models, such as DT, RF, and LGBM, allowed to identify
signiﬁcant features in predicting students’ gender based on their
perceptions of open education competency, providing valuable
insights for educational strategies. In addition, we could contrast
functionalities and performance between explainable and
nonexplainable models.
While this study effectively showcases the potential of ML
models in analyzing perception data and predicting competency
levels,itisessentialtoacknowledgethestudy’slimitations.Even
though the study involved a series of cross-validation methods in
verifying the ML models’ performance, it is crucial to recognize
that further research is needed to establish the generalizability of
the ﬁndings with larger populations. Another limitation is that
DTs only provide insights into the features selected by the model
for constructing decision rules, which necessitates interpretation
and explanation by researchers.
This work has practical and research implications, demonstrating the utility of ML models in predicting participants’
gender based on students’ perceptions of their knowledge,
skills, and attitudes/values related to open education. This has
practical value for educators, enabling them to identify areas
where students may require additional support or resources.
The study also emphasizes the signiﬁcance of utilizing perception data and ML techniques’ efﬁciency in accurately analyzing this data. Our contributions expand the body of literature
on ML applications in education. Our ﬁndings indicate that
ML models can effectively analyze perception data to make
accurate predictions regarding gender. In addition, the study
underscores the importance of comprehending the decisionmaking process of explainable ML models. This work establishes a foundation for future research endeavors exploring the
utilization of ML in education perception data and emphasizes its potential for advancing our understanding of students’
competencies.

Fuzzy Enhanced Kidney Tumor Detection:
Integrating Machine Learning Operations for a
Fusion of Twin Transferable Network and
Weighted Ensemble Machine Learning Classifier
ANANYA GHOSH
AND JYOTISMITA CHAKI
, (Senior Member, IEEE)
School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology, Vellore 632014, India
Corresponding author: Jyotismita Chaki (jyotismita@vit.ac.in)
This work was supported by the Vellore Institute of Technology (VIT), Vellore, India.
ABSTRACT Kidney tumors, often asymptomatic, can lead to serious health problems if left undiagnosed.
This study tackles the crucial issue of kidney tumor detection using CT scans. The proposed approach
leverages the power of image enhancement using fuzzy systems, deep learning, and machine learning for
automated kidney tumor detection in CT images. The study proposes a fuzzy inference system to enhance
kidney CT image contrast. This system analyzes image data and uses fuzzy logic to adjust pixel intensities,
aiming to improve the distinction between features in the image without creating over-enhancement. Two
pre-trained deep convolutional neural networks (PT-DCNNs), DenseNet121 and ResNet101, are used to
extract features from the enhanced CT images. These features capture essential characteristics that differentiate between normal and tumor-containing scans. Combining features from twin PT-DCNNs (ensemble
approach) creates a richer representation of the image content. The informative features are fed into a
combined classifier where Support Vector Machines and Random Forests are combined using a weighted
average to achieve the final and potentially more robust classification of kidney tumors. To improve training,
we amplified the original dataset by creating variations with added noise and artificial modifications to
simulate real-world image imperfections. The integration of Machine Learning Operations practices ensures
the scalability, reproducibility, and clinical deployment of the system. The model achieved an impressive
accuracy of 99.2% on high-quality images and 98.5% on noisy images, surpassing traditional methods. This
automated approach can assist urologists in confirming the presence of kidney tumors, minimizing human
error during physical inspection and potentially leading to improved patient outcomes.
INDEX TERMS Deep neural network, ensemble learning, kidney tumor, machine learning, transfer learning.
I. INTRODUCTION
The human kidneys remove waste products and contaminants
from the blood [1]. Tumors (cancers) result from aberrant
cell proliferation, which affects various persons and creates
diverse symptoms. As a result, early diagnosis of kidney
tumors is critical for reducing the risk of disease development. As a result, this saves the patient’s life [2]. Although
around one-third of kidney tumor instances are detected after

diseases cause no symptoms. They are frequently discovered when individuals are being treated for other conditions.
Kidney tumors can be mistakenly identified on radiography
and present as masses, kidney cysts, or abdominal discomfort

the kidneys [3]. However, some of the most modest signs
or infections caused by kidney tumors include weakness,
low hemoglobin, stomach discomfort, vomiting, high blood
sugar, and blood urine. Anemia develops in around 30% of
kidney tumor patients [4]. Unfortunately, solid masses and

text:
A. Ghosh, J. Chaki: Fuzzy Enhanced Kidney Tumor Detection: Integrating Machine Learning Operations
tumors that form inside the kidneys are generally malignant.
The importance of detecting the presence of the tumor is to
select the proper form of therapy; hence, the rate of recovery
from the disease may be dependent on early diagnosis of
the tumor. One of the required tests to detect kidney tumors
is a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and
pelvis. By analyzing the features of these CT images, healthcare professionals can determine whether a tumor is present.
Kidney tumors pose a serious threat to human life, and various
techniques are being developed to improve tumor diagnosis
and treatment. [5].
Kidney tumors can have various forms, and there may
not be enough visible characteristics in the CT image. However, human interpretation of complicated CT scans is a
time-consuming and arduous process that may be prone to
mistakes that might result in a patient’s death. The development of new technologies, notably artificial intelligence and
machine learning, has a substantial impact on the clinical
profession, allowing for error-free diagnosis. In CT image
processing, many machine-learning approaches are used to
segment and classify image data [6]. Deep learning is a type
of machine learning that uses layered algorithmic architecture
to examine data. Deep learning involves filtering model data
over several levels. Each succeeding layer leverages the prior
layer’s results to create correlations and linkages, increasing
the model’s accuracy. Deep learning can enhance medical
research by enabling better data processing and increased
reliability [6]. Deep learning is gaining popularity in the
medical research business due to its ability to analyze large
amounts of data, including research and patient outcomes,
quickly and accurately. Detecting kidney tumors is crucial for
providing effective therapy for kidney cancer patients. Deep
learning and machine learning are capable of correctly identifying tumors, allowing specialists to quickly make treatment
decisions and provide the best care to patients.
This study proposes a novel system called STREAM-
LINERS (fuSion of twin TransfeR nEurAl network and
enseMbLe machINe lEaRning clasSifier) for kidney tumor
detection. STREAMLINERS developed an automated kidney tumor detection system with a big dataset that contains
both quality and noisy kidney CT images to assure high
performance and accuracy in both quality and noisy environments. This study combines Machine Learning (ML) and
Deep Learning (DL) to create a novel kidney tumor detection model. The model follows a clear framework. Transfer
learning-based pre-trained twin convolution neural networks
(PT-DCNNs) extract unique features from CT scan images,
reducing time and space complexity significantly. Before
extracting the features by using PT-DCNNs, the image contrast is enhanced by using the proposed fuzzy inference
system. The retrieved features are then concatenated to create the ensemble deep feature and this is used in machine
learning models to detect kidney tumor images. Finally,
an ensemble of ML classifiers that uses the weighted average
algorithm provides a superior result than any single ML
classifier. The motivations for using ensemble techniques
for both DL-based feature extraction and ML-based classification stages are as follows. Ensemble learning [7] is a
supervised machine learning approach that combines multiple models to improve predictive performance. By training
and combining these individual models, an ensemble can
often produce more accurate and robust predictions than
a single model alone. This technique can access a wider
range of hypotheses, potentially leading to better results.
Ensemble learning has flexible representative capabilities.
Ensembles typically perform better with high inter-model
variance. Ensemble learning approaches encourage model
diversity. Robust ensemble learning approaches improve
classification efficiency [8]. We assessed the proposed
model (STREAMLINERS) for kidney CT analysis using
recall, F1 score, accuracy, specificity, Matthews Correlation
Coefficient (MCC), precision, kappa score, Classification
Success Index (CSI), and Good Detection rate (GDR) on
high-quality and noisy images from 4 datasets. This confirms
the model’s effectiveness in real-world scenarios. To ensure
the scalability and reproducibility of the STREAMLINERS
system, we have incorporated MLOps principles. We utilize tools like MLflow to track experiments, hyperparameters, and metrics, facilitating efficient model development
and optimization. The model is deployed on a scalable
cloud platform, enabling real-time predictions and continuous monitoring of its performance. Automated pipelines
are implemented to streamline the model development and
deployment process, reducing manual effort and accelerating
time-to-market.
The primary contributions to this study are as follows:
A. PROPOSED FUZZY LOGIC TO ENHANCE KIDNEY CT
IMAGE CONTRAST
This research proposes a new Fuzzy Inference System (FIS)
to improve the contrast of kidney CT scan images. Traditional
methods have limitations, so FIS aims to address these. FIS
works by fuzzifying pixel intensities using input functions
and then applying IF-THEN rules to transform them. Finally,
calculations based on output functions provide a defuzzified
value. This study proposes a specific system with triangular
input and Gaussian output functions, along with 3 rules,
to enhance kidney CT image contrast.
B. ORIGINAL KIDNEY CT DATASET (D) AUGMENTATION
INTO 3 NEW DATASETS (D1, D2, D3)
Data augmentation increases the size and variety of a
dataset [9]. This improves the accuracy and effectiveness of
the STREAMLINERS model for kidney CT analysis. Here,
image flipping and noise are used to augment the dataset,
making the model resistant to such variations. Three kidney
CT datasets (D1, D2, D3) are created from the original dataset
(D) with these augmentations to evaluate the model’s performance under various image qualities.

text:
A. Ghosh, J. Chaki: Fuzzy Enhanced Kidney Tumor Detection: Integrating Machine Learning Operations
C. PROPOSED ENSEMBLE DEEP FEATURES USING TWIN
PT-DCNNs
This study proposed a new ensemble deep feature using
twin PT-DCNNs i.e., ResNet101 and DenseNet121 for the
detection of kidney tumors from CT images. ResNet101 [10]
can be readily trained without increasing the training error
rate. The inclusion of skip connections in ResNet101 has
the advantage of allowing regularization to bypass any layers
that reduce architectural performance. As a result, training
a very deep neural network is achievable without having to
deal with expanding or vanishing gradients. DenseNet121
[11] stands out for its dense connections. This allows features
to be reused throughout the network, reducing reliance on
individual layers. Shortcut connections of various lengths
provide a wider range of informative features. This design
helps combat the vanishing gradient problem, a major hurdle
in deep learning. DenseNets121 may have a smoother training process because of continuous feature propagation across
the network. ResNet101 implements identity mappings via
skip connections, which allows gradients to flow through
the network without attenuation. DenseNet121, on the other
hand, makes dense connections by concatenating feature
maps from previous layers. These are the motivations for
using ResNet101 and DenseNet121 to extract deep features
from kidney CT images in this study. Lastly, these deep
features are concatenated to create the ensemble deep feature
map which is used for the detection of kidney tumor CT
images.
D. PROPOSED ENSEMBLE ML CLASSIFIER
A weighted average ensemble technique is introduced for
the classification of kidney CT images using five different machine learning classifiers: Support Vector Machine
(SVM), Random Forest (RF), Naïve Bayes (NB), K-Nearest
Neighbors (KNN), and Logistic Regression (LR). The motivations for using the weighted average ensemble technique
are as follows. Weighted average ensembles address a limitation of basic voting ensembles. While all votes in a
voting ensemble count equally, a weighted average ensemble
acknowledges that some models might be more reliable than
others. It assigns higher weights (importance) to models with
better past performance, effectively letting their predictions
contribute more to the outcome. This approach aims to use
the strengths of each model and potentially improve the overall accuracy and robustness of the ensemble compared to a
simple voting system.
E. INTEGRATING MLOPs FOR EFFICIENT KIDNEY TUMOR
DETECTION PIPELINES
MLOps (Machine Learning Operations) is a set of practices
that aims to deploy and maintain machine learning models
in production environments. By incorporating MLOps into
our proposed kidney tumor detection method, we can significantly enhance the model’s lifecycle and its impact on clinical
practice.

III. PROPOSED METHODS FROM IMAGE ENHANCEMENT
TO CLASSIFICATION: THE STREAMLINERS PIPELINE
The proposed STREAMLINERS approach addresses challenges in kidney tumor detection from CT scans. Firstly,
a fuzzy logic technique enhances image contrast. Next, image
augmentation creates three diverse datasets (D1, D2, D3)
from the original dataset (D) to improve model robustness.
Pre-trained deep convolutional neural networks (PT-DCNNs)
then extract features from the images. These features are
combined to create a comprehensive feature vector. Finally,
an ensemble machine learning classifier leverages this rich
data for classification. This approach is built on PT-DCNNs,
avoiding the need for massive amounts of labeled training data, which can be scarce in medical imaging. Image
augmentation further strengthens the model’s ability to handle variations in real-world data. Figure 1 illustrates the
STREAMLINERS model’s architecture.

C. ENSEMBLE DEEP FEATURE VECTOR
CNNs are deep neural networks (DCNNs) that employ convolutional layers to filter inputs and extract meaningful
information. Deep CNN’s (DCNN) convolutional layers use
convolutional filters to generate output from neurons linked
to specific parts of the input. It aids in determining the spatial
and temporal aspects of an image. DCNN’s convolutional
layers employ a weight-sharing mechanism to minimize the
number of parameters.
In general, DCNN performs better on bigger datasets than
on smaller ones. Transfer learning can be utilized when it
is not possible to produce a big training dataset. Figure 4
illustrates transfer learning, where a DCNN model trained
on large benchmark datasets (e.g., ImageNet [27]) may be
utilized to extract features from smaller datasets, such as a
CT scan dataset.
In recent years, the transfer learning-based PT-DCNN
approach
has
been
used
effectively
in
a
variety
of
applications, including medical image classification and segmentation [28]. This decreases the length of time necessary
to train DL models from scratch, as well as the need for a big
dataset for the training model.
This work employs a PT-DCNN-based model for deep
learning feature extraction, which captures significant characteristics without human supervision. Our feature extractor
is built using a transfer learning-based PT-DCNN technique
due to the small size of our CT scan dataset, making it difficult
to train and optimize PT-DCNNs like DenseNet121 from
scratch. We employ PT-DCNN models with preset weights
on a large ImageNet dataset to extract deep features from
kidney CT images. The proposed method for automatically
detecting CT kidney tumor images uses two PT-DCNNs i.e.,
ResNet101 [10] and DenseNet121 [11].
Multiple PT-DCNNs are evaluated on all four datasets
(D, D1, D2, D3). While the original D dataset has 8,260
images (unevenly balanced between normal and tumor), the
augmented datasets (D1, D2, D3) all contain 12,000 balanced
images (6,000 normal, 6,000 tumor). These PT-DCNNs,
trained on large image datasets like ImageNet, can effectively extract relevant features from kidney CT scans.
Since STREAMLINERS utilizes multiple PT-DCNNs, their
extracted feature vectors are combined to create a comprehensive ‘deep ensemble feature vector’ for improved
performance.
Focusing on high-quality, balanced data (D1), the top
two performing PT-DCNNs are chosen for further analysis
(Figure 5). Their extracted features are then combined to
create a lightweight ‘ensemble deep feature vector’ for classification. This approach aims to achieve accurate results while
minimizing computational costs.
D. ENSEMBLE ML CLASSIFIER
Weighted Average Ensemble is a sophisticated strategy that
integrates predictions from several models based on their
capabilities and expertise. When merging models, weights are
assigned based on their ability to appropriately identify the
problem. Better-performing models are given more weight
and can influence decision-making.
To optimize performance, hyperparameters of each ML
classifier are fine-tuned using the Grid Search algorithm.
These classifiers are then combined into an ensemble, where
each acts as an estimator. Instead of assuming equal effectiveness, the proposed STREAMLINERS model assigns weights
based on each classifier’s accuracy. These weights prioritize
the influence of high-performing models during the final
prediction, which is a combination of weighted individual

E. INTEGRATING MLOPs FOR EFFICIENT KIDNEY TUMOR
DETECTION PIPELINES
The MLOps framework implemented for the STREAMLIN-
ERS kidney tumor detection model is designed to facilitate
efficient model deployment, continuous monitoring, and
seamless scalability. Each of these components is essential to
ensure that the model remains operational, delivers accurate
results, and can scale as needed in real-world clinical settings.
Below is a breakdown of how this framework is implemented.
The first step is to expose the model’s functionality via
a REST API using the Django Rest Framework (DRF).
This framework allows the model to interact with external
applications efficiently and is robust enough to handle the
complexities of machine learning workflows in a production
environment. The API is built using Django Rest Framework,
which allows the creation of RESTful endpoints to serve the
deep learning model. The core functionality provided by the
API includes accepting CT scan images as input through
POST requests, processing them through the model’s pipeline
(which involves image preprocessing, feature extraction, and
classification), and returning the classification result (tumor
or normal). Each of these steps is encapsulated in a welldefined endpoint. To ensure that the API can securely handle
sensitive medical data, token-based authentication was implemented. This ensures that only authorized users or systems
can access the API and submit requests for tumor detection.
This setup ensures that only requests from authenticated users
with a valid token can access the tumor detection endpoint,
keeping sensitive medical data secure. To ensure the model
can be easily deployed in any environment, Docker was used

Once the model is deployed, monitoring its performance

A dedicated endpoint is set up to automatically evaluate

associated image is logged. This enables quick identification
of problematic areas (e.g., specific areas of tumors that the
model may have trouble detecting). These misclassifications
are reviewed and, where necessary, used as additional training
data for retraining the model, forming a continuous feedback
loop for improvement.
As the demand for processing more CT scan images
grows, scalability becomes an important consideration. The
STREAMLINERS framework was built to handle increasing load while ensuring computational resources are used
efficiently. The model is deployed on the Google Cloud Platform (GCP), utilizing GPU and TPU resources to accelerate
the deep learning inferences. GPUs are utilized for standard
inference tasks, while TPUs are used for more intensive,

This ensures that we can run predictions on CT scan images

V. DISCUSSION
Medical images, like CT scans of kidneys, can be quite large.
However, the region of interest, where the disease might be
present, often occupies only a small portion of the image.
Analyzing the entire image can be inefficient and lead to overlooking important details. Accurately identifying diseases in
medical images often presents a challenge. Disease locations
can be subtle and confined to a small area within the image.
Traditional methods might struggle to capture these crucial
details. This is where the STREAMLINERS model, a novel
approach, comes into play. The proposed STREAMLIN-
ERS model addresses this by focusing on extracting features
specifically from these localized areas. These features are
essentially characteristics extracted from the image that can
be used to identify the presence of a disease. By focusing
on these local regions, the STREAMLINERS model aims
to achieve higher accuracy in disease detection. STREAM-
LINERS model employs an ‘‘ensemble deep feature creator’’.
This fancy term essentially means it uses the power of multiple PT-DCNNs to extract features. Each PT-DCNN might be
adept at identifying different aspects of the image. By combining the features extracted by these individual models, the
STREAMLINERS model aims to create a more comprehensive representation of the localized area. This approach also
taps into the benefits of ‘‘transfer learning’’. Transfer learning
involves taking a DCNN pre-trained on a large dataset for a
similar task and using it as a starting point for a new task.
STREAMLINERS model utilizes twin pre-trained models
like DenseNet121 and ResNet101. These pre-trained models

VI. CONCLUSION
This paper proposes the STREAMLINERS model, a novel
approach for detecting kidney tumors in CT scans. It leverages the strengths of deep learning and machine learning
to achieve accurate and efficient classification. STREAM-
LINERS model addresses the challenge of kidney tumor
detection by extracting ‘‘deep features’’ from CT images.
These features capture essential characteristics that can be
used to differentiate between normal and kidney tumor scans.
The key innovation lies in using an ensemble approach:
(1) Multiple PT-DCNNs: STREAMLINERS model utilizes
twin PT-DCNNs, such as DenseNet121 and ResNet101.
These pre-trained models have already learned valuable
image recognition skills, saving time and resources compared
to training CNNs from scratch. (2) Extracting Deep Features:
Each PT-DCNN extracts deep features from the CT images.
These features represent high-level information about the
image content relevant to kidney tumor detection. (3) Ensemble of Deep Features: The deep features extracted from twin
PT-DCNNs are combined. This ensemble approach aims to
capture a richer and more comprehensive representation of
the CT scans compared to relying on a single DCNN.
The analysis suggests that a weighted average ensemble
combining Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and random
forests delivers superior performance compared to individual
classifiers. This approach leverages the strengths of both
algorithms, resulting in a more robust and accurate classification system. The following can be the reasons for that:
(1) Diversity of Approaches: SVMs and random forests tackle
classification problems differently. SVMs find the optimal
hyperplane that separates data points with the largest margin, while random forests build multiple decision trees and
aggregate their predictions. This diversity can help capture
complex patterns in the data that a single classifier might
miss. (2) Reduced Overfitting: Individual models can sometimes overfit the training data, leading to poor performance
on unseen examples. Combining models through weighted
averages can help mitigate this by averaging out errors.
(3) Robustness to Noise: Both SVMs and random forests
have inherent strengths in dealing with noisy data. Ensemble
learning can further enhance this robustness, leading to more
reliable predictions even in the presence of noise.
The implementation of the MLOps framework for the
STREAMLINERS kidney tumor detection model ensures a
scalable, secure, and continuously improving system. The
integration of Docker, Django Rest Framework, Kubernetes,
and GCP provides a robust infrastructure for deploying
and monitoring the model in real-world clinical environments. Continuous performance monitoring, error analysis,
and auto-scaling ensure that the system remains efficient,
even with growing demand. The use of cloud functions and
containerization guarantees that resources are utilized efficiently, minimizing operational costs.
We conducted a thorough evaluation of the STREAM-
LINERS model using four distinct datasets (D, D1, D2, and
D3). These datasets likely encompass variations in image
quality, potentially including both high-quality and noisy
scans. STREAMLINERS model performed well on both
high-quality and noisy images, suggesting its robustness
in real-world scenarios where image quality might not be
perfect.
While the proposed STREAMLINERS model demonstrates promising results, several limitations and potential
areas for future research are identified: (1) Limited Dataset
Size and Generalizability: The study relied on a dataset
of 6454 CT scans, which may not fully capture the diverse
range of kidney tumor presentations. Expanding the dataset
with more varied and representative data could enhance
the model’s generalizability and robustness. (2) Lack of
Spatial Information: The current model does not provide
spatial information about the location of kidney tumors within
the CT images. Future work could incorporate techniques
like image segmentation to precisely identify and localize
tumor regions. (3) Potential for Broader Applications: The
STREAMLINERS model’s architecture and methodology
have the potential to be applied to other medical imaging
tasks beyond kidney tumor detection. Exploring its applicability to diagnosing other conditions using CT scans or

ABSTRACT AutoML offers significant benefits in solving real-life problems because it accelerates the
development of machine learning models. In contexts involving real scenarios like analyzing companies’
environmental, social and governance (ESG), where the dataset presents some challenges, AutoML is anticipated as a promising solution to address these complexities. Although researchers have shown significant
interest in exploring Genetic Programming (GP) in AutoML for handling complex datasets, a critical issue
that remains unresolved is the comprehensive understanding of GP hyper-parameters that influence machine
learning performance. While GP-based AutoML excels in automating many aspects of the modelling, there
has been a scarcity of research that provides insight into the significance of individual features and GP
population size within the models of GP-based AutoML. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the
models’ performance evaluation from multiple facets, including feature selection, GP population sizes, and
different machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, this study provides insights into the association between
Pearson correlations, machine learning performance, and the importance of machine learning features. The
findings demonstrate that incorporating all the determinants as features in GP-based AutoML or relying
solely on firm characteristics led to superior performance with an excellent trade-off between True Positive
Rate and False Positive Rate. Thus, higher accuracy results exceeding 0.9 of Area Under the Curve (AUC)
are presented by the proposed models. The novelty of this study lies in its empirical evaluation of different
approaches to GP-based AutoML implementation. These findings provide alternative solutions for business
investors to identify companies with strong sustainability practices.
INDEX TERMS Evolutionary computing, genetic programming, machine learning, business intelligence,
classification.
I. INTRODUCTION
Machine learning is a subset of the artificial intelligence
field [1] and has gained considerable recognition as an effective technique for addressing multiple business challenges.
However, despite the vast potential of machine learning, organizations often face resource restrictions and expertise gaps
when attempting to exploit its benefits. Insufficient expertise

All of these challenges are the main reasons why automated
machine learning (AutoML) was invented.
Recently,
researchers
have
increasingly
focused
on
evolutionary-based AutoML. Notably, tools such as Genetic
Programming (GP) for AutoML have shown remarkable
results for various problem domains, particularly in the field
of health diseases [2], [3], [4]; hence, they should be further
explored by researchers. In the current research landscape
of GP-based AutoML over the past three years, the primary
focus has been on evaluating the overall performance of
machine learning models on various problem domains, while
there has been relatively little exploration of the importance
of individual features. A few studies, specifically mentioned
in [5], and [6], have included an analysis of individual
features. Research [5] elaborates the influences of input
variables in the performances of evolutionary algorithm combined with Decision Tree in predicting acute schemic stroke.
In contrast, the research noted in [6] explores how various
features that classified under CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal
failure, anemia, lytic bone lesions) and SLiM (sixty, light
chain ratio, MIR) categories contribute to the development
of malignant plasma cell disease.
In addition, GP involves several crucial hyper-parameters
that warrant careful observation. As an evolutionary computing paradigm, the GP population size has implications
for algorithm performance. However, it is worth noting
that reports on the impact of the GP population size
on machine learning performance are exceedingly rare.
GP-based AutoML has predominantly been applied and evaluated in genomic and medical research, with limited literature
available regarding its use in business and management
domains, especially in the context of sustainability and ESG
(Environmental, Social, and Governance) strategies.
The primary objective of this study is to address the
research gap in GP-based AutoML performance and feature
important analysis related to two crucial aspects of ESG
performance: firm characteristics and industry types. The
contributions of this study are two-fold: First, it presents
the applicability of GP-based AutoML for addressing ESG
challenges with small indicators, particularly in the context
of the Malaysian industrial landscape. Although with minimal factors, the findings demonstrate practicality, flexibility,
and experimental replicability by demonstrating several
approaches for implementing GP-based AutoML. Second,
this paper presents new empirical evaluations of GP-based
AutoML that consider various aspects of feature selection,
GP population size as a GP hyper-parameter, and comparison with other tree-based conventional machine learning
algorithms.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section two presents the theoretical concepts of machine
learning and AutoML. Furthermore, existing conceptual
models of ESG performance are presented in this section.
Section three describes the research methodology while
section four presents the results and discussion. Section five
summarizes the key contributions, concludes the paper, and
discusses the study’s limitations.
II. THEORETICAL BACKGROUND
A. AUTOML
AutoML refers to the process of automating various tasks of
machine learning model development, making the technique
more accessible to non-experts and more useful to expert data
scientists in streamlining the entire workflow in a rapid manner. By automating modelling tasks, such as hyper-parameter
tuning and machine learning algorithm selection, AutoML
reduces the risk of human error, ensuring that the model
development is consistent and reproducible.
Several research studies on AutoML have utilized GP
as a powerful tool for automating and optimizing machine
learning pipelines. GP, owing to its evolutionary nature,
offers a unique approach for solving complex optimization
problems in AutoML. In light of their significant capabilities, researchers have increasingly explored genetic-based
machine learning (GBML) methods, leading to insightful
reviews and studies in the field. An interesting survey finding on GBML and its potential applications in multi-label
classification problems was reported in [7]. It discusses
the use of techniques such as GP in optimizing machine
learning models and the proposed fuzzy rules for generalizing the multi-label classification problem. Additionally, the
researchers in [7] provided insights from their extensive literature review on GBML. While this study primarily focuses
on Genetic Algorithms (GA), a promising evolutionary
algorithm highly relevant to GP, it provides an understanding
of the historical development and prospects. In [7] and [8], the
impact of GP-based AutoML on genomics research and precision medicine has been interesting explained. Researchers
in [9] explored machine learning techniques, specifically
regression and GP, to predict soccer match attendance by
analyzing five years of attendance data in Southern Brazil.
They used Symbolic Regression to determine the best-fitting
function relating to the independent and dependent variables, which evolved through the GP optimization process.
In the realm of business operations and supply chain management, the need for a sophisticated decision support system
capable of handling multicriteria classification problems has
become paramount. Consequently, the integration of Genetic
Programming (GP) and machine learning, particularly Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), has demonstrated its utility
in enhancing both the agility and quality of a company’s
decision-making process, especially in the context of inventory management. All these studies collectively demonstrate
the versatility and effectiveness of GP in machine learning,
particularly in its role as AutoML, across various domains.
A notable tool that supports GP-based AutoML is Treebased Pipeline Optimization Tool (TPOT) [10], [11] which
uses GP as its underlying mechanism. Conventional machine
learning algorithms based on tree data representation are

TPOT has received attention from researchers in various
domains. Recent applications that have utilized TPOT include
medicine [10], [15], [16], engineering [17], and environment [18] domains.
The prevalent adoption of TPOT can be attributed to its
extensive support for over a hundred machine learning algorithms. The main attractive feature of the TPOT is its ability
to suggest hybrid machine learning algorithms based on GP
optimization processes. For example, hybrid algorithms that
combine LassoLrsCV and GradientBoostingRegression, suggested by TPOT, in predicting medical insurance charges
have yielded remarkable results [19]. Additionally, the TPOT
has a valuable capability of optimizing the hyper-parameter
values for each algorithm. Therefore, the TPOT is known to
be a powerful tool, resulting in efficient and effective model
optimization. Figure 1 illustrates the GP operations in the
TPOT.
Because GP is an evolutionary-based algorithm, the initial
step after ingesting the training dataset involves creating
a random population of individuals. Population size is a
parameter that can be specified in TPOT Python code. If no
population size is explicitly set, the TPOT defaults to create
100 individuals. The larger the population size, the more
time-consuming are the prediction tasks. Although a larger
population theoretically offers more solution options for GP,
it is important to note that a smaller value may still yield
good results [20]. If the parameters are not appropriately
configured for the dataset, GP may converge prematurely.
Therefore, it is essential to comprehensively assess how this
parameter affects TPOT’s performance of the TPOT when
applied to specific datasets.

FIGURE 2. Operations of TPOT in each generation.
FIGURE 3. Tree representation of pipeline.
An individual in GP for TPOT is a single machine learning
pipeline, represented as a tree structure. Figure 2 depicts two
examples of the tracing output from the GP fitness evaluation
process, encompassing the creation of pipelines and executing operations for mutation, crossover, and cross-validation
(CV). After evaluating the fitness of all pipelines in a generation, TPOT selects the best-performing pipelines based
on their fitness scores. These top-performing pipelines or
individuals are then used to create the next generation through
genetic operators, such as mutation, crossover, and selection.
This process continues for multiple generations (i), allowing
the TPOT to search for the best machine learning pipelines
that optimize performance on the given dataset.
Users can set the mutation and crossover rates within the
range of 0 to 1, where the difference between the two values
is 1. These parameters allow users to control the exploration and exploitation trade-offs during the search process of
individuals. A higher mutation rate encourages more diversity in the population, whereas crossover roles promote the
exploitation of promising solutions [21]. In the absence of
explicitly specified mutation rates in the parameter settings,
TPOT defaults to use 0.1 of mutation rate (90% of individuals
in the population) to generate new individuals. The TPOT
utilizes a one-point crossover operator, randomly selecting
two individuals from the current population of generation i
for pipeline component exchange. By default, it selects the
top 20 pipelines for crossover, which represents 5% of the
offspring. Figure 3 is an example of a tree representation of
the GP pipeline composition from internal nodes (black line
circle) and leave nodes (blue dot circle).
The internal nodes represent operations applied to data,
feature engineering, and feature construction, as well as a
suitable machine learning algorithm, whereas the leaf nodes
are the hyper-parameters of the algorithm. All the operation
techniques, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA),
t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding(t-SNE), logarithmic transformations, feature scaling, and hyper-parameter
settings, are initially randomly selected to be included
as an individual machine learning pipeline for the GP
population.

1) RETURN ON ASSETS (ROA)
The stand for Return on Assets is defined as a financial ratio
that evaluates a company’s profitability in relation to its total
assets. It measures how effectively a company utilizes its
assets to generate profits.
2) RETURN ON EQUITY (ROE)
The stand for Return on Equity is defined as a financial
metric that measures a company’s profitability in relation
to shareholders’ equity. This indicates how efficiently a
company generates profit from the investment made by its
shareholders.
3) MARKET VALUE (MV)
The stand for Market Value is defined as the share price
multiplied by the number of ordinary shares in issue.
4) SIZE
In this study, firm size is represented by the natural logarithm
of total assets at the end of the period.
5) LEVERAGE
Firm leverage, also known as the total debt-to-equity ratio, is a
financial metric that measures a company’s amount of debt
relative to its equity. This provides insights into a company’s
capital structure and financial risk.
6) GROWTH
Firm growth is measured by calculating the market-to-bookvalue ratio. This financial metric compares the market value
of a company’s outstanding shares with its book value, also
known as shareholder equity or net asset value.
7) FAMILY-OWNED
In the dataset, family owned (FamilyOwn) firms are represented by binary 1, whereas non-family-owned firms are
assigned a value of 0.
8) GOVERNMENT-OWNED

C. FEATURES IMPORTANCE ANALYSIS
This section is presented to address research question three
(RQ3) and achieve research objective three (RO3). As seen
in Table 4 and Figure 14, a notable trend can be observed:
when the number of features is reduced, there is a tendency
that some attributes in TPOT with FC feature selection are
increased in the coefficients.
TABLE 4. Feature importance.
According to Occam’s Razor principle [41], simple models
(with fewer features) are preferred when they perform equally
well. This preference for simplicity leads to higher coefficients for the remaining features, resulting in them being
relatively more important because they have a larger impact
on the prediction of the model. Reducing the number of
features can help alleviate multicollinearity issues, leading to
more stable and interpretable coefficient values.
Responding to the performance results, no substantial
distinction exists that can discern the effectiveness of
TPOT-ALL from TPOT-FC that only utilizing attributes from
firm characteristics. The outcomes were relatively satisfactory for ESG performance prediction models developed using
only TPOT-FC with fewer features.
In addition to the obtained outcomes, it is important to
emphasize that Pearson correlation values alone do not provide a definitive verdict on the influence of attributes. For
instance, consider the attributes ESG-rated year and telecommunications, both of which exhibit contributions exceeding
20% to the ESG performance from the Pearson test. Surprisingly, in many GP-based AutoML models generated with
TPOT as seen in Figure 14, these attributes do not emerge
as the most crucial in terms of feature importance. Leverage
refers to the degree to which a company relies on borrowed
funds such as loans or debt to finance its operations or investments. Surprisingly, leverage has become important in many
machine learning models, mainly in TPOT-FC. Leverage is
relatively having correlation coefficient at 9% contribution
based on the Pearson correlation test. Machine learning can
capture non-linear relationships between variables. Leverage
in comparison to ESG-rated year may have complex and
better non-linear effects with other variables, including ROE,
which showed the strongest correlations (0.44) among other
variables’ relationships.
Furthermore, it is worth noting that company ownership
appears to have a limited contribution to all models, either
from government ownership or from family ownership. This
observation aligns with the initial inference from the Pearson
test, indicating that these factors have a minimal impact
on model performance. This finding suggests that further
in-depth investigation is warranted to gain a deeper understanding of why company ownership factors do not have a
significant influence in Malaysia.
In an exceptional scenario, it was noted that in TPOT-ALL
with a population size of 100 (TPOT-ALL-100), ROE
emerged as the predominant contributor to the prediction
model. This atypical occurrence signifies an extraordinary
nature of this case. Further exploration into the factors that
make it stand out is potential research to be explored in the
future.
V. CONCLUSION AND LIMITATION
This study focused on the prediction of ESG performance
using various GP-based AutoML approaches that have
been investigated with different facets, comprising groups
of feature selection, GP population size as the centered
hyper-parameter, and different conventional tree-based algorithms. The fundamental design and implementation of
GP-based AutoML have been thoroughly described in this
paper, suggesting its effectiveness, flexibility, and potential for reproducibility in diverse research domains. The

GP-based AutoML framework introduced in this paper offers
a user-friendly and intuitive approach, is accessible to novice
data scientists, and is a valuable tool for experts in providing
rapid model development and analysis.
By probing the relationship between feature importance
and GP-based AutoML performance, this study extended its
insights to a broader audience. These findings serve as a valuable resource for researchers seeking to harness the power of
AutoML not only in the context of ESG and sustainability, but
also in other domains of scientific investigation. The versatility and robustness of GP-based AutoML, as demonstrated in
this study, holds promise for advancing predictive modeling
and data-driven research endeavors across diverse disciplines.
Additionally, the outcome from this study underlines the
importance of not relying solely on correlation analysis to
draw conclusions about the determinants’ influences when
implementing machine learning, mainly GP-based AutoML.
This emphasizes the necessity for further investigation, such
as feature importance and performance evaluations, to gain a
comprehensive understanding of the impact of these factors
on the prediction models, specifically for ESG performance
prediction.
Although GP-based AutoML offers the advantage of
automating the feature selection process, it is crucial to
recognize that manual human design remains essential.
GP optimization implements a degree of randomization in
the selection of solutions for feature selection. This property
increases the possibility of utilizing the maximum input of
attributes, particularly for a dataset with a small number
of variables. Subsequent studies could focus on exploring
a complex set of inputs that hold more than hundreds of
attributes and examining how GP manages the feature selection process in such sophisticated scenarios.
Moreover, it is worth noting that the earlier design of this
study, which reduced the number of industry types, may have
played a role in this outcome. The expectation was that a
smaller number of records might lead to issues related to
model stability, which would affect the overall performance
of the modeling process. Accordingly, it is necessary that
future studies focus on gathering more extensive datasets and
exploring the inclusion of a more diverse dataset of industry
categories to enhance predictive modelling capabilities.
The findings of this study have crucial business and management implications for companies and investors. By leveraging GP-based AutoML techniques to incorporate various
ESG factors, businesses can gain deeper insight into the
impact of firm characteristics on their performance. This
understanding can help companies align their strategies
and operations with ESG principles, thereby leading to
improved long-term financial performance and risk management. On the other hand, investors can utilize the predictive
power of machine learning models to make more informed
and sustainable investment decisions.
This study has certain limitations. First, it utilized a specific dataset and sample, particularly on industry types,
which may limit the generalizability of the findings to a
broader population of companies or industries. The dataset’s
scope and timeframe may not entirely capture the complexity
and dynamics of ESG performance across different regions
and time periods. Applying the findings of this study to
real-world scenarios with larger volumes and wider perspectives of variables can lead to more informed and sustainable
decision-making in many industries. Second, the study utilized secondary data sources that could present potential data
quality and accuracy issues. The accuracy of ESG data may
vary among different providers, potentially influencing the
outcomes of predictive models. Third, the research focused
on the selection of machine learning algorithms to benchmark
the GP-based AutoML. There might be other algorithms that
could be compared for performance benchmarking.
Finally, it is important to mention that this study limited
the GP population size to 200 individuals or pipelines. Based
on the study, there was a trend of decreasing accuracy when
the population size increased to 200. Since running more
than 200 population sizes would demand significantly more
computing resources, the extensive variations of population
sizes were not explored in this study.
However, there is potential for future research to explore
a wider range of population sizes, such as between 5,000
and 15,000, but careful experiment design is crucial. Using
the TTC and population size data from this study, the estimated parameter values for a and b in the power-law model
(Refer Equation 2) were determined to be 2.408 and 1.0127,
respectively. Consequently, the estimated time required to
complete the ESG prediction for a GP population size of
5,000 is approximately 13,415.35 seconds, which is equivalent to more than 3 hours.

GuardianML: Anatomy of Privacy-Preserving
Machine Learning Techniques and Frameworks
NGES BRIAN NJUNGLE
1, ERIC JAHNS

LUIGI MASTROMAURO

2Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, 21000 Novi Sad, Serbia
Corresponding author: Nges Brian Njungle (nnjungle@asu.edu)
ABSTRACT Machine learning has become integral to our lives, finding applications in nearly every aspect of
our daily routines. However, using personal information in machine learning applications has raised concerns
about user data privacy and security. As concerns about data privacy grow, algorithms and techniques for
achieving robust privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) have become a pressing technical challenge.
PPML aims to safeguard the confidentiality of both data and models and ensure that sensitive information
remains protected during training and inference processes. Various techniques, protocols, libraries, and
frameworks have been proposed for PPML, but choosing the right combination along with the appropriate
algorithmic or system parameters for a specific deployment instance can be very difficult. In this work,
we introduce GuardianML, an open-source recommendation system for selecting the correct parameters and
suitable framework for specific use cases of PPML. GuardianML allows users to search through a wide range
of PPML frameworks, techniques, protocols, libraries, and more based on a set of objectives. GuardianML
filters potential frameworks based on user-defined criteria, such as the number of parties involved in multiparty computation or the need to minimize communication costs in homomorphic encryption scenarios. The
system’s recommendations and optimizations are formulated as a maximization problem using linear integer
programming to identify the most suitable solution for various use cases. Moreover, this work thoroughly
analyzes and presents seventy relevant frameworks in the system’s database. Additionally, we offer an opensource repository containing practical examples and documentation for some of the frameworks.
INDEX TERMS Differential privacy, federated learning, homomorphic encryption, multi-party computation, privacy preserving machine learning, trusted execution environment.
I. INTRODUCTION
Machine Learning (ML) has intense applications across every
industry, from healthcare, finance, education, government
and public services, transport and logistics, retail and ecommerce, and even cybersecurity [1]. In healthcare, ML is
used pervasively for disease diagnosis and prognosis, drug
discovery and development, treatment recommendation,
health monitoring, wearable devices, and genetic studies [2].
With this prevalent use of ML, data privacy and preservation
have become a major concern as ML models generally require
large amounts of data to train. Sometimes, this data even
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Sangsoon Lim
.
comes from multiple data sources. While the data providers
are interested in protecting their data, the model providers are
also interested in protecting their models. The area concerned
with protecting and preserving data privacy in ML is
generally referred to as Privacy Preserving Machine Learning
(PPML) [3]. PPML is a set of rules, techniques, and protocols
used to preserve and protect the privacy and confidentiality of
customers’ information and machine learning models while
enabling collaboration and productivity scenarios. It allows
organizations to leverage the power of ML while keeping
sensitive information safe, preserving confidentiality, encouraging data sharing and collaboration, and complying with the
law in some cases. Five main techniques are used for PPML,
which include Federated Learning, Multi-party Computation,
