B. Parameter Server Framework
We integrate the idea of data and parameter partition to the
parameter server framework [4]. The parameter server framework consists of servers, workers, and a scheduler. Servers are
in charge of maintaining globally shared parameters of
machine learning models. Workers use subsets of data to solve
sub-problems and update parameters. Each actual machine
contains a server and a worker. All data samples and parameters of the learning model would be divided without duplication into workers and servers, respectively. The assignment is
done by the scheduler before the actual training starts and it is
known to all machines. Besides, the assignment is ﬁxed during
the training process.
The communication is usually the bottleneck of the parameter server. Let k denote the number of machines. Let Di and Pi
denote the data allocated to the worker and server in the i-th
machine, respectively. Before training, the scheduler allocates
data and parameters among available machines. Procedures of
a training round are illustrated in Fig. 2. Workers would fetch
their data, pull the globally shared parameters from servers
(solid lines), calculate the update of parameters, and push the
updated parameters back to servers (dashed lines). The allocation of data samples and parameters assigned by the scheduler
is ﬁxed during training. The worker and server located in the
same machine communicate via memory buses, which is the
inner-machine communication. Workers and servers in different machines communicate via network infrastructures, such
as Ethernet, which is the inter-machine communication. Compared with the inter-machine communication, the time cost of
inner-machine communication is usually negligible. Therefore, we focus on the inter-machine communication volume in
further analysis.

C. Data Sparsity in Inference Problems
Inference problems beneﬁt from data sparsity when they are
solved in a distributed manner. Speciﬁcally, when updating
parameter values with data di, only non-zero attributes in the
data change the parameter value [18], since zero elements bring
no information for the interface. For example, in spam prediction, if a word does not exist in a spam e-mail, we cannot determine whether this word is more frequent in spam or non-spam
e-mails, and cannot update the prediction model accordingly. If
a worker ﬁnds that some attributes of its di are zero, then there
is no need to pull parameters corresponding to these attributes
from servers. The communication volume of this worker is
reduced correspondingly. Therefore, if major attributes in input
data samples are zero, the communication volume of training
inference learning models could be signiﬁcantly reduced. In
practice, the parameter server framework supports to push or
pull part of the parameters during training [5]. Workers can
skip parameters that correspond to zero data attributes during
training. The allocation of data samples and parameters is critical for balancing the communication volume among machines,
and signiﬁcantly affects the training time.

E. Problem Formulation
In this paper, we propose to minimize the training time on
the parameter server by taking advantage of data sparsity. We
consider that the parameter update is synchronous among all
machines, given that some learning algorithms may diverge in
the asynchronous way [12].
We quantify the training time based on the number of
rounds of synchronization and the inter-machine communication volume. Our formulation does not contain the computational time in each round since it is hardly changed by data
partitions. We assume the time consumption of each round is
proportional to the largest communication volume among
machines. As for the number of rounds, typical machine learning algorithms would terminate when the loss function is sufﬁ-
ciently small, i.e. less than a given threshold, or when all the
training data is used. For the worst case analysis, we assume
that each worker terminates when all of the data assigned to it
is used. Then, the number of rounds is determined by the
worker who has the largest amount of data samples. Formally,
it is maxijDij. An unbalanced data partition would slow down
the training process. Solely optimizing inter-machine communication or the number of rounds cannot guarantee the minimal training time. For example, if all data samples and

optimal since all other machines are idle. Therefore, our

both data and parameters at the same time. The multilevel
approach is designed to partition general graphs and we adapt
the algorithm for bipartite graph partition.
The multilevel approach contains three stages: coarsening,
partitioning and reﬁnement. An illustration is shown in Fig. 6.
Unlike the two-step heuristic approach, there is no priority for
data partition or parameter partition. In the coarsening stage,
the graph nodes are iteratively merged and a coarse graph that
has a small number of nodes is generated. In the partitioning
stage, the coarse graph is partitioned. In the reﬁnement stage,
the algorithm would reﬁne the partition and recover the coarse
graph to the original graph.
In the coarsening stage, unlike the multilevel approach for
general graph, we merge data set D and parameter set P
respectively. The merging procedure for D is explained as follows. 1) Mark all d 2 D as available. 2) Randomly choose an
available di 2 D; if there is no available di, then the coarse is
ﬁnished. 3) Find an available dj 2 D such that dj and di have
at least one same neighbor. Formally, there exists a p 2 P
such that p 2 NðfdigÞ and p 2 NðfdjgÞ. If there is no such a
dj, then di is marked as unavailable. 4) Merge di and dj, and
label both as unavailable. Then repeat steps 2-4 until there are
no more available nodes. The merging procedure for P is similar. Finally, the coarse graph with a small number of vertices
is generated.
On the coarse graph, any partition method can be applied.
However, since the coarse graph has a small number of vertices, we use a random partition method to save partition time.
Then the reﬁnement stage starts. Our reﬁnement algorithm is
based on the FM-algorithm [39] whose main idea is local
search. The FM-algorithm is designed for bisection partition
in general graphs. We adapt the algorithm to k-way partition
for bipartite graphs. The idea is to sweep over data and parameters and record the gain of moving each to other machines.
The gain refers to the decrease in the inter-machine communication volume. We move data/parameter to the machine that
brings the largest gain,, as long as the moving would not break
the memory constraint in Eq. (2). The data or parameter node
with larger gain has higher priority for moving, i.e. would be
moved ﬁrst. The gain is updated after each movement. Each
data/parameter is moved at most once to reduce time complexity. The algorithm stops when either there is no improvement
or each data and parameter node have been moved once.
Theorem 4: The worst-case time complexity of the reﬁnement algorithm is Oððm þ nÞjEjÞ.
Proof: To calculate the gain of moving data d 2 Di to Dj,
we need to go through its neighbor set NðdÞ and ﬁnd out the
value of jNðdÞ n Pij jNðdÞ n Pjj. Consequently, calculating
gains for all d 2 D needs to go through all edges in the graph
for ﬁnding neighbor sets of all d 2 D, and costs OðjEjÞ. It is
similar for gain calculation of parameter nodes. Therefore,
ﬁnding the max gain of moving the d among k machines needs
OðkjEjÞ time. Moving a data or parameter node costs Oð1Þ
times. Hence, moving nodes and updating gains costs at most
OðjEjÞ. The moving would repeat for at most ðm þ nÞ rounds.
Therefore, the worst case time complexity is Oððm þ nÞjEjÞ.
VI. EXPERIMENT
A. Dataset
The dataset we use is summarized in Table IV. The ﬁrst
four are real-world datasets. Speciﬁcally, The news20 and
rcv1.binary are text datasets. The CTRa is a click-through
dataset from anonymous Internet companies. These datasets
are stored in libsvm format [40]. The number of data corresponds to the size of set D in our model and the number of features corresponds to the size of P. The soc-liveJournal is a
social network dataset. The social network dataset is a general
graph G0 ¼ ðV;0 E0Þ instead of a bipartite graph, but it can be
easily converted. Speciﬁcally, we treat the nodes in the dataset
as both set D and P, i.e. D ¼ P ¼ V 0. If there is an edge
between two nodes in G0, we connect the corresponding nodes
in D and P. In this way, the original graph could be converted
to a bipartite graph.
Besides the real-world dataset, we also build three sets of
synthetic data with different data sparsity. Speciﬁcally, the
number of correlations between data and parameters is represented by a matrix in the synthetic dataset, where rows represent data and columns represent parameters. The value of each
element in the matrix could be either 0 or 1, showing whether
there is a correlation between the corresponding data and
parameter. The sparsity is controlled by a sparsity coefﬁcient
g, which is deﬁned as the percentage of zero elements in the
matrix. The sparsities of sparse, medium, and dense synthetic
datasets are 0.999, 0.995 and 0.991, respectively. The synthetic dataset may have no meaning from the machine learning
point of view. It is because the data does not contain any realworld meanings. The purpose the of synthetic dataset is used
to test the partition algorithm. During experiments, we ignore
the result of the machine learning algorithms. Instead, we set a
threshold on the the maximum number of iterations of training
models, and want to compare the time used for training under
different data or parameter partitions.
In both real-world and synthetic datasets, the scheduler of
the parameter server would build the dependency graph by
one round of traversal over data samples. The dependency
graph represents the correlation between data and parameters.
It starts from a bipartite graph with no edges. Two sets of vertices in the bipartite graph represent sets of data samples and
parameters. During traversal, for each data sample, if there is
a non-zero attribute, it adds one corresponding edge to the
bipartite graph. After the traversal, the graph partition

B. Experiment Setup
In our experiment, we implement the graph partition on a
local machine and then the learning algorithms on a cluster
which is deployed in Amazon EC2. Our local machine has a
6-core i7-8700 CPU running at 3.2 GHz with 32 GB RAM.
The cluster on EC2 contains 16 t2.large instances. Each t2.
large instance contains 8 GB RAM and runs on Ubuntu 18.04.
The parallel computing environment is set up in all instances.
Speciﬁcally, each instance is installed with the OpenMPI
library and its dependent packages. We deploy PS-lite, an
open-source parameter server framework that is available at
https://github.com/dmlc/ps-lite, on the cluster as the platform
to train machine learning algorithms. The instance where the
partition algorithm is deployed is labeled as the scheduler.
Each instance contains server and worker nodes.
On the local machine, we compare the performance of
graph partition. The baseline is the random partition scheme.
In this scheme, data and parameters are uniformly and randomly allocated to each machine. We implement the two-step
heuristic and investigate the trade-off between its time complexity and performance. Speciﬁcally, in the data partition, we
compare the difference between adding one vertex to a
machine in each iteration (denoted as TSH-1) and adding two
vertices (denoted as TSH-2). The multilevel bipartite partition
approach is denoted as MBP. We also test a popular graph partition algorithm, PaToH [41], which is a well-optimized
hypergraph partitioner and supports taking a bipartite graph as
the input.
The inter-machine communication volume and the training
time are impacted by the partition algorithm and the number
of partitions. To clearly show the improvement caused by
graph partition algorithms under different numbers of partitions, we use relative improvement over the random partition

We ﬁrst test the impact of data sparsity based on our synthetic datasets. The experiment results are shown in Fig. 8. In

In the synthetic-sparse dataset with g ¼ 0:999, the performance gap between TSH-2 and TSH-1 is obvious. When k ¼

could make better use of the data sparsity than TSH-1. However, when the number of partitions becomes larger than 4, the

In addition, we investigate whether the ratio between the
number of data and parameters impacts the performance of partition algorithms in terms of the inter-machine communication
volume. We extract a part of data from the synthetic datasets.
The number of extracted data varies from 50% to 200% of the
parameter amount. Fig. 9 shows the simulation results in communication volume. With larger n=m ratio, the algorithms’
performances decrease. But the decrease rate is smaller when
the ratio of n=m increases. It shows that when the number of
data is smaller, the partition algorithm plays a more important
role. This is because the jNðDiÞj is smaller when the number of
data is smaller. A good partition could avoid the overlap
between NðDiÞ for i ¼ 1; . . . ; k. Their performance seems to

Then we evaluate the impact of k on real-world datasets.
We choose to use the CTRa and the soc-LiveJournal
datasets. Note that the soc-LiveJournal is originally a general graph. Experiment results are shown in Fig. 10. We ﬁnd
that these algorithms have better performance on the CTRa
dataset. The reason for this is that the social network inherently contains many small densely connected clusters. When
the number of partitions becomes larger, the performance of
the MBP and the PaToH drops. The impact of k is stronger
to the PaToH, whose performance begins to drop when k >
4. This shows the weakness of the PaToH’s recursive
approach that uses the bisection partition multiple times to

Besides the communication volume, we also compare the
training and partition time. Fig. 11(a) shows the improvement
on training time. The variation of training time is similar to
that of communication volume. This is because the communication is the bottleneck and takes more time than computation.
When the inter-machine communication volume is reduced,

Fig. 11(b) shows the time consumption of partition algorithms.
The time consumption of TSH-1 or TSH-2 is less than 100 s

Nevertheless, the training usually takes hours in our setting.
Running our TSH algorithms with small overhead (in minutes)
could signiﬁcantly reduce the training time. It is worthy to run
our graph partition algorithms before training.
VII. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we investigate the potential speed-up of
parameter server frameworks brought by the data sparsity,
especially when training inference models. By partitioning the
data among workers and parameters among servers, the intermachine communication volume could be reduced. We formulate a graph partition problem based on this observation. The
partition problem is modeled by a bipartite graph. We investigate two approaches to solve the problem. In the two-step heuristic approach, we ﬁrst solve the data partition by using the
submodular property of the neighbor set cardinality function,
and then partition the parameters among machines. In addition, we adapt the multilevel graph partition approach for general graphs to ﬁt the optimization over the bipartite graph.
Both approaches are tested with synthetic and real-world datasets. Experiment results show that the two-step heuristic
approach provides a trade-off between computational complexity and algorithm performance, which helps the algorithm
adapt to different datasets. The multilevel partition approach
has better performance except in a social network dataset.
Our scheme cannot be applied to all machine learning
models. For deep learning models with millions or billions
of parameters, the data-parameter correlation is complex.
Build the correlation graph is not feasible. Instead, using

Model Reuse in Machine Learning for Author
Name Disambiguation: An Exploration
of Transfer Learning
JINSEOK KIM
1,2 AND JASON OWEN-SMITH
1,2,3
1Institute for Research on Innovation and Science, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48104, USA
2Survey Research Center, Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48104, USA
3Department of Sociology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48104, USA
Corresponding author: Jinseok Kim (jinseokk@umich.edu)
This work was supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant 1917663, Grant 1760609, and Grant 1561687.
ABSTRACT Machine learning for author name disambiguation is usually conducted on the training and
test subsets of labeled data created for a speciﬁc task. As a result, disambiguation models learned on
heterogeneous labeled data are often inapplicable for other purposes that either do not use the same labeled
data or do not make use of any labeled data at all. This article explores the idea of transfer learning in a
new context, author name disambiguation. We focus on cases where a disambiguation task lacking labeled
training data uses models trained on labeled data generated for other tasks. For this purpose, two labeled
source datasets are used for training of disambiguation models to be applied to three test target datasets that
are deﬁcient of labeled training data. Our results show that transfer learning can produce disambiguation
performances similar to those achievable by traditional machine learning in which training and test datasets
come from the same labeled data source. The good performance through transfer learning are possible when
training source datasets have similar feature distributions as test target datasets. This study suggests that
through transfer learning, rich disambiguation models in previous studies can be retained and reused across
ambiguous bibliographic data from different ﬁelds and data sources, motivating further research on how
to correct feature distribution differences between source and target datasets to expand the application of
transfer learning in author name disambiguation beyond the model sharing explored in this research.
INDEX TERMS Data handling, data preprocessing, author name disambiguation, machine learning, transfer
learning, authority control.
I. INTRODUCTION
Digital libraries are widely used for searching trends, references, and developments in science. In using digital libraries,
author name is the most frequent query [1]. One of the
biggest challenges for digital libraries in providing accurate author query results to users is that author names are
ambiguous. The same author can be represented by different name strings (synonyms). For example, a renowned
economist at the University of Michigan, Charlie Brown,
is represented by several names in publication records:
Charlie Brown, Charlie Charles Brown, Charlie C. Brown,
C.C. Brown, and C. Brown.1 In contrast, different authors can
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Ilaria Boscolo Galazzo
.
1 https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=9Fk-UoYAAAAJ&hl=en
have the same name (homonyms). For examples, there are
more than 200 researchers named ‘Wei Wang’ in computer
and information science according to the computing digital
library DBLP.2 This name ambiguity can merge and/or split
author identities in bibliographic data, possibly leading to
ﬂawed research ﬁndings if not properly controlled [2]. So,
scholars in information retrieval and information systems
have proposed a variety of methods to distinguish ambiguous
author names in digital libraries, which has formed a research
area called ‘author name disambiguation.’
Among many methods for author name disambiguation (AND), machine-learning-based approaches have been
reported to produce better disambiguation results than
rule-based algorithms or heuristics [3]–[5]. This might be

J. Kim, J. Owen-Smith: Model Reuse in Machine Learning for AND: An Exploration of Transfer Learning
because machine learning generates models adapted to each
of diverse name ambiguity settings and scenarios by detecting
sophisticated disambiguation patterns through training and
validation on labeled data [6]. Although crucial in machine
learning for AND, creating labeled data is time-consuming
and costly. Also, it does not guarantee accuracy and representativeness [7], [8].
To address the issue of labeled data in machine learning
for AND, this article proposes that disambiguation models
learned on training data for one disambiguation task can be
reused for others. If this transfer learning works in AND,
researchers can focus more on reusing previous labeled data
than creating new training, or ground truth, datasets for every
task. This also means that rich AND models that supported
previous studies can be retained and reused across ambiguous
bibliographic data from different ﬁelds and data sources.
As such, exploring the transfer learning in AND can motivate
researchers to develop AND methods from a novel perspective, which will be a unique contribution of this article to
this topic. Even more importantly, robust transfer learning
approaches could help make work in the ﬁeld more cumulative by enabling strong replication and extension of existing
work.
II. BACKGROUND
When ‘author name disambiguation’ is searched on Google
Scholar, about 60% of the 200 papers that have received at
least one citation rely on machine learning techniques. AND
machine learning approaches can be divided into two general
groups – classiﬁcation studies and clustering studies - based
on the types of learning output they produce [3], [6], [9].
The ﬁrst is focused on producing disambiguation results at
a pair level. Such studies generate disambiguation models
trained on labeled data in which author name instances are
compared in a pairwise fashion over various dataset features
(e.g., coauthor names). Classiﬁcation algorithms assign any
given pair of name instances (for instance, ‘‘C.C. Brown’’ and
‘‘Charles C. Brown’’) an indicator that distinguishes between
pairs that match and thus represent the same author (i.e., positive set) and pairs that do not, indicating that they refer to
different people (i.e., negative set). Then, the learned models
are applied to test data to predict whether a pair of author
name instances that was not included in training data refer to
the same author (match) or not (non-match) [7], [10]–[12].
The latter group of studies disambiguates names at a cluster
level. They train and test models to generate clusters that
contain all (exhaustive; perfect recall) and only (pure; perfect precision) author name instances belonging to the same
authors [13]–[19]. Here, every variant of ‘‘Charles Brown’’
would be clustered by an effective algorithm. Like classiﬁ-
cation studies, clustering studies also train models on labeled
data for pairwise comparison of author name instances over
other dataset features. They, however, differ from the classiﬁcation studies in that models produce similarity scores -
instead of binary classiﬁcations - for instance pairs in test
data. In short, rather than asking whether or not two different
name strings are the same, clustering algorithms ask how
similar they are. Then, clustering algorithms decide which
instances in test data will be grouped into the same cluster
using the similarity scores as distances among instances.
A few studies use pre-deﬁned criteria (e.g., number of clusters) to guide the clustering process, but many others search
for optimal thresholds that produce best clustering results
using part of labeled data (development data).
Machine learning techniques – whether they emphasize
classiﬁcation or clustering – typically perform better than
heuristic- and rule-based methods in AND [3]–[5]. Such good
performances would be due to the fact that machine learning
detects distinct disambiguation patterns in labeled, ground
truth, training data. The learned patterns are then used to
generate disambiguation models that classify cases in test
data (supervised classiﬁcation) or that tune hyper-parameters
to produce the best clustering results (semi-supervised clustering). This contrasts to other AND approaches using heuristics (e.g., two author names with the same full surname and
initialized forename are assumed to refer to the same author)
or a set of pre-deﬁned rules based on disambiguation patterns
found in previous studies or empirical observations (e.g., two
author names that share coauthors are likely to refer to the
same author).
As such, labeled data is indispensable for generating high-performing classiﬁcation or clustering models in
machine learning for AND. A common practice in AND
using machine learning is to create labeled data for each
AND task. This is reasonable because each task deals with
different types and levels of name ambiguity [20]. Creating
labeled data for each task is, however, not an easy job. It is
often a labor-intensive, manual process that requires hiring
human coders for quite a long time even to produce even
relatively small labeled datasets. Despite the costs in time
and resources, recent studies have demonstrated that manual
labeling for AND can produce biased (especially toward
homonyms of East Asian names) and erroneously labeled
data [21], [22].
Alternative labeling methods have been proposed to overcome such problems. Two promising approaches involve
linking author names to external authority data [23], [24]
and automatic labeling by matching author names based on
a strong indicator of author identity (e.g., email address)
or triangulation of such indicators [13], [21], [25]. But the
alternative labeling approaches require advanced techniques
for large-scale, computationally intensive data processing and
record linking. They are also vulnerable to biased sampling
and labeling errors [21].
This article examines a new alternative, transfer learning,
which has been studied actively for use in text mining and
image processing applications [26], [27]. The basic idea
behind transfer learning is that tasks for which labeled data
are too costly or simply impossible to produce can reuse
(or transfer) models trained on labeled data developed for
other tasks. If transfer learning works in AND, researchers
can reduce resources spent on costly data labeling and focus

more on developing and validating models. Most importantly,
rich disambiguation models in prior AND studies can be
reused across diverse disambiguation scenarios and datasets.
Despite their promise for addressing known challenges in
AND, transfer learning approaches have rarely been tested
in this context.
In the following sections, the usefulness of transfer learning in AND is demonstrated by disambiguating author names
in three test or ‘‘target’’ datasets using models learned from
two widely used labeled training datasets developed for AND
research.
III. METHOD
A. OVERVIEW OF TRANSFER LEARNING
This article shows that an algorithmic model for a name
disambiguation task can be reused to disambiguate a different
set of name data for another purpose. Fig.1 compares the different workﬂows of traditional machine learning and transfer
learning in AND. Standard machine learning is conducted
separately for Task A and B using bespoke training and test
datasets. In contrast, the transfer learning approach that is our
focus in this study applies the model learned in Task B to test
data developed for Task A.
FIGURE 1.
A visualized concept of transfer learning in author name
disambiguation. A traditional machine learning (left) generates
algorithmic models for each task using different training data, whereas a
transfer learning (right) applies a model trained for one task (Task B) to
the other task (Task A) for which training data are unavailable.
One common scenario where transfer learning could beneﬁt AND research involves situations where it is necessary
to conduct supervised machine learning in the absence of
labeled data. More formally, we deﬁne transfer learning in
AND as a process in which given a training source data (Ds),
a source task (Ts), a test target data (Dt), and a target task
(Tt), the learning of a disambiguation model for Tt is conducted using the disambiguation model obtained from Ds
for Ts, where Ds̸ = Dt,Ts = Tt, and only Ds is labeled.
Here, ‘Ts = Tt’ means that both tasks aim to disambiguate
author names using the same feature set. In computer and
information science, many different types of transfer learning
have been studied outside AND [26], [27]. As this article is
the ﬁrst attempt to explore the application of transfer learning
to AND, the proposed deﬁnition would serve as a starting
point for further elaboration in future research.
B. SOURCE DATA AND TARGET DATA
We treat three datasets (DBLP, MEDLINE, and APS –
American Physical Society) representing three different
science domains (computer science, biomedicine, and
physics each) as target data for testing, and use two labeled
datasets from computer science (KISTI and AMINER) as
source data for training. Fig. 2 summarizes the process of
transfer learning using the training source data and test target
data. Note that author name instances in target data are linked
to author ids in ORCID – an open-source researcher pro-
ﬁle3 [28] - to label data for benchmark learning (i.e., baseline
learning using standard methods that can be used to contextualize the performance of our transfer learning approach) and
evaluation of test results (details are explained in Evaluation).
FIGURE 2.
An overview of transfer learning in this article. Machine
learning algorithms are trained on two training source data (KISTI and
AMINER recording publications in CS) to learn disambiguation models for
TASK D. The learned models are used on test data for Task A (DBLP
recording publications in CS), Task B (MEDLINE; Biomedicine), and Task C
(APS; Physics) that cannot generate their own models because training
data are unavailable.
1) DBLP (COMPUTER SCIENCE)
Author names in computer science publications have been
the main target of disambiguation studies [3]. DBLP is a
digital library that provides authorship information of computer and information science publications worldwide [29].4
Author names in DBLP are already disambiguated with high
accuracy through machine learning algorithms and manual
correction [30]. For this article, about 700K author name
instances that are linked to ORCID author ids are obtained
from [31]. After deleting author identiﬁers,5 all names are
converted into lowercased, ASCII strings and 10% of their
forenames are stripped into their ﬁrst initials to increase name
ambiguity in the data. Then, name instances are ﬁltered for
disambiguation if they refer to two or more unique authors
when their strings are simpliﬁed into the format of full surname plus their ﬁrst forename initial. For example, three

the same full surname and ﬁrst forename initials, are called
‘blocks.’ This ﬁltering of instances (‘blocking’) is a commonplace pre-processing step conducted by AND researchers to
collate name instances to be disambiguated together. Among
the ﬁltered instances from the ORCID-linked DBLP data,
13,635 instances belonging to 600 blocks were randomly
selected for analysis.
2) MEDLINE (BIOMEDICINE)
Biomedical researcher names have also received much attention from disambiguation scholars. The public MEDLINE
database has been one of the most frequent target datasets for
AND [6]. Maintained by the National Library of Medicine
(NLM), MEDLINE contains the largest collection of publication records in biomedicine.6 We matched author names
in MEDLINE (December 2015 version) to ORCID ids following the steps outlined in [21]. That process resulted in
approximately 2M ORCID ids-linked instances in papers
published between 1991∼2014. As was the case with DBLP,
author names are ﬁltered only if they belong to two or more
unique authors when their ﬁrst forenames are initialized. The
ﬁnal, ﬁltered dataset we analyze uses 36,948 name instances
in 600 randomly chosen blocks as target data.
3) APS (PHYSICS)
This dataset is a collection of papers published in Physical
Review journals managed by the American Physical Society
(APS).7 Many studies have used it for modeling complex
networks [32]. For this study, 198K author name instances
in the raw APS data (2017 version) are linked to ORCID
ids. Among them, 26,217 instances were selected to serve
as target data because they belong to two or more unique
authors when ﬁrst forenames are initialized. Unlike DBLP
and MEDLINE, we use all name instances rather than a
sample for disambiguation because the ORCID-linked APS
dataset is relatively small.
These three target datasets are disambiguated by algorithms trained on two different source datasets – KISTI
and AMINER – which are both commonly used in
AND [20], [21], [33], [34].
4) KISTI (COMPUTER SCIENCE)

5) AMINER (COMPUTER SCIENCE)
This dataset is labeled by an international research team [36]

C. MACHINE LEARNING SET-UP
This article demonstrates the applicability of transfer learning
in AND using both classiﬁcation and clustering techniques.
1) INPUT FEATURES
For both classiﬁcation and clustering, we conduct pairwise comparisons of author name instances in KISTI and
AMINER over four dataset features – author name, coauthor
name, title words, and venue (journal or conference) name –
to generate similarity proﬁles (i.e., vectors of per-feature
similarity scores) for each pair [5], [11], [14], [21], [39].
This is the most commonly used feature set for AND because
they constitute the basic information of a publication record
and they are rarely missing [4], [7]. Strings in all the features are converted into ASCII format and lower-cased after
non-alphanumerical strings are removed. Title words are
stopword-listed using the dictionary in the Stanford Natural Language Processing (NLP) package8 and stemmed
by Porter’s Stemmer.9 After pre-processing, two vectors
of 2∼4 grams of pre-processed strings are compared to calculate their similarity scores. For example, two name author
name strings – ‘Newman, M. E.’ and ‘Newman, M.’ – are
converted into two 2∼4 gram vectors: ‘ne-ew-wm-ma-annm-me-new-ewm-wma-man-anm-nme-newm-ewma-wmanmanm-anme’ and ‘ne-ew-wm-ma-an-nm-new-ewm-wmaman-anm-newm-ewma-wman-manm,’ respectively. Then,

2) ALGORITHMS
Pairwise, feature speciﬁc similarity scores for blocked name
instances are fed into three algorithms – Logistic Regression (LR), Naïve Bayes (NB), and Random Forest (RF) –
that represent the baseline and/or best performing algorithms
reported in multiple AND studies [11], [13], [15], [40], [41].
For classiﬁcation, ﬁrst, each algorithm is tasked to learn
disambiguation patterns on training source data (KISTI and
AMINER). Here, the learning target is to predict whether a
pair of instances refer to the same author (match) or not (nonmatch), given a set of similarity scores. So, when the learned
models are applied to test target data (DBLP, MEDLINE,
and APS), they produce binary decisions of whether instance
pairs in each test data refer to the same author or not. In this
study, Scikit-Learn packages in Python are used to implement
classiﬁers. L2 Regularization with class weight = 1 is used
for Logistic Regression. For Naïve Bayes, Gaussian Naïve
Bayes with maximum likelihood estimator is chosen. For
Random Forest, split quality is measured by Gini Impurity
and 500 trees are used after grid search.
Second, machine learning for clustering also uses the same
features, pre-processing, and algorithms (LR, NB, and RF) as
those for classiﬁcation in blocking and pairwise comparison
of instances. Unlike the classiﬁcation tasks in which models
are used for predicting binary classes, however, the learning target of clustering tasks is to produce groups of name
instances that refer to the same authors. For this, speciﬁcally,
the aforementioned classiﬁcation algorithms learn disambiguation patterns on training source data and assign a probability score to each pair of instances in test data quantifying
how much the pair is likely to represent the same author based
on their feature similarities.
The probability scores among instances in test data are
then used by a Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC)
algorithm which collates into a cluster including all the
name instance pairs that have probability scores beyond a
certain threshold. To decide the best threshold for test data,
the trained models are applied (before test data) to development data (50% of source data) to ﬁnd the average probability
thresholds that produce the best-ﬁtting clustering results per
block [14], [15], [21]. This average score is used to guide
clustering decisions by the HAC algorithm on test target
data. To accomplish this, entire source datasets (KISTI and
AMINER respectively) are randomly split into 50% (training
data) and 50% (development data) subsets. The training data
are used for both classiﬁcation (2-step procedure: train →
test) and clustering, whereas the development data are only
used for clustering (3-step procedure: train →development
→test). The HAC algorithm is implemented by the code
in [14] using its average linkage function.

for target data to be unavailable. To properly assess the

B. CLUSTERING PERFORMANCE
Unlike classiﬁcation results in which positive and negative
pairs are evaluated separately, clustering results are assessed
by quantifying the extent to which predicted clusters contain
only (perfect precision) and all (perfect recall) instances that
should belong to the same authors. For clustering evaluation,
especially, a baseline is added to gauge the performance gains
obtained by transfer learning compared to blocking. The
blocking (all name instances that match on full surnames and
ﬁrst forename initials refer to the same author) has been used
as a disambiguation heuristic in several studies [44]–[46] as
well as the standard author search format by many digital
libraries.

In other words, transfer learning tends to split name instances

C. FEATURE SIMILARITY SCORE DISTRIBUTION
Performance gaps between KISTI- and AMINER-trained
models indicate that the two training source data may have
different feature characteristics for pairwise comparisons.
To check this intuition, we compare distributions of featurespeciﬁc similarity scores for each data source.
As described in III. B. MACHINE LEARNING SET-UP,
name instances in training and test data are compared for
similarity over four features – author name, coauthor name(s),
title words, and venue (conference or journal) names. For this,
ﬁrst, an alphabetical string of a feature is dissected into an
array of 2∼4 grams (e.g., ‘Smith’ →‘sm-mi-it-th-smi-mitith-smit-mith’). Next, two arrays for a pair of instances are
compared to quantify how they are similar by calculating the
cosine similarity of n-gram’s Term Frequency. This cosine
similarity score is calculated for each of four features per
instance pair. Table 2 illustrates this similarity calculation
conducted on a few instances selected from the KISTI dataset.
TABLE 2. An example of per-feature similarity score calculation.

performance we describe above.

How are such different distributions of feature similarity
scores in the training source data related to those in the test

Considering that previous studies have shown that author
name and coauthorship play the most important roles in
distinguishing authors [5], [18], [19], [47], disambiguation
models learned on AMINER may have incorrectly assigned
author name instances with similar author name strings and
coauthor names to belong to different people, producing a
greater number of false negatives and leading to the lower
observed recall scores for transfer learning from AMINER
descried in our discussion of Fig. 4∼7 above. Put more simply, AMINER’s focus on highly similar names led to different
distributions of similarities on key matching features, which
seems to describe the systematic differences in AMINER and
KISTI based transfer learning we ﬁnd.

As such, comparing the feature similarity score distributions between training and test data illustrates that transfer
learning can perform well if pairs in training source data have
feature similarity patterns similar to those of pairs in test target data. In other words, models trained on AMINER would
produce better disambiguation results than KISITI-trained
models for tasks in which homonyms are prevalent. This
suggests that successful transfer learning in the AND context
requires close attention to the design features of training
datasets and the particular patterns of feature similarity distributions across training and target data.
VI. DISCUSSION
This article provides an initial demonstration that transfer
learning works well in the context of AND, a ﬁnding of
potential value to help researchers who may face challenges
in creating bespoke labeled data for their particular machine
learning tasks. However, the issue of labeling still needs
to be addressed, though in a different way, for the sake of

transfer learning. First, the proposed transfer learning does
not eliminate the need of labeling for target data. To test
the performances of transfer-learning-induced models, for
example, part of test data needs to be labeled. It would be
an interesting topic to develop methods for labeling part of
test data that are small but representative to properly evaluate
learning performances.
Second, the systematic performance differences we identify for transfer learning from AMINER and KISTI suggest that labeling some representative part of test data is
also required to identify appropriate labeled source data for
transfer learning. As shown by the comparison of feature
similarity score distributions (Fig. 8∼10), transfer learning
performances in this article appear to be related to the match
of feature similarity score distributions between training
source data and test target data. For high-performing transfer
learning, part of target data may be labeled to generate feature
similarity distributions to be compared with those of candidate source data to ﬁnd the best match. Another direction to
address this issue would focus on correcting differences of
feature distributions between source and target data, which
has been actively researched for transfer learning in text
classiﬁcation [27].
Despite these problems, the transfer learning explored in
this article has important implications for AND. The ﬁrst and
most important advantage of transfer learning would be that
researchers can focus more on disambiguation model building and application development and less on time-consuming,
expensive data labeling.
Second, appropriately speciﬁed transfer learning procedures can facilitate the application of disambiguation models
across different studies increasing both the replicability and
the extensibility of AND research as a whole. Many machine
learning methods for AND have been validated on labeled
data created from publication records in one speciﬁc ﬁeld,
computer science [3], [20]. So, those methods can be assumed
to perform well, if reported so, on data representing authorship characteristics of the computer science ﬁeld. What has
been less clearly demonstrated is how disambiguation methods validated on CS-oriented labeled data can be applied to
disambiguating author names in other ﬁelds like biomedicine,
physics, engineering, and social sciences, where institutional
and other differences may yield different patterns of feature similarity. This study demonstrated that disambiguation
models trained on one CS-oriented labeled dataset, KISTI,
can be used to effectively resolve name ambiguity in authorship data from biomedicine (MEDLINE) and physics (APS)
as well as computer science (DBLP). This suggests that
rich, high-performing methods in previous CS-ﬁeld-focused
studies can be validated and reused for application to other
ﬁelds through transfer learning.
Third, the transfer learning results in this article can
motivate disambiguation scholars to attend more closely to
transfer learning. As shown in V.C.FEATURE SIMILARITY
DISTRIBUTION, three test target data showed very similar distributions across features, despite representing widely
disparate ﬁelds. As a result, enabling effective transfer learning through algorithms trained on KISTI but applied to other
datasets with similar feature score distributions may prove
useful as a means to speed and expand machine-learning
based AND research. This might be because although authorship behavior (e.g., average number of coauthors) differs per
ﬁeld [45], patterns characterizing name pairs of matched or
non-matched author identities tend to be similar across ﬁelds
(e.g., non-matched pairs are likely not to share coauthors).
This suggests that through hyper-parameter tuning and model
modiﬁcation, transfer learning for AND may consistently
be able to hit performance benchmarks similar to or higher
than those achieved through the more traditional approaches
represented in our benchmark learning case.
VII. CONCLUSION
In this article, the idea of transfer learning was tested for
AND tasks for which labeled data for training are unavailable.
Results showed that given training source data that closely
represents key features of target datasets, disambiguation
models developed through transfer learning can produce good
results that are similar to those achievable by a traditional
machine learning approach that trains algorithms on specifically labeled subsets of target data. This does not mean
that transfer learning can replace traditional machine learning
approaches relying on labeled data created for speciﬁc disambiguation tasks. Note that transfer learning in this article
barely surpassed benchmark learning on key disambiguation
performance metrics. However, transfer learning can help disambiguation scholars focus more on modeling and application than on arduous, costly labeling. By enabling researchers
to reuse labeled data and disambiguation methods in previous
studies for novel tasks, transfer learning can bring in a new
stream of methodology to the topic. This study is expected
to provide researchers an opportunity to explore this new
potential further.

ABSTRACT Today, predictive analytics applications became an urgent desire in higher educational institutions. Predictive analytics used advanced analytics that encompasses machine learning implementation
to derive high-quality performance and meaningful information for all education levels. Mostly know that
student grade is one of the key performance indicators that can help educators monitor their academic performance. During the past decade, researchers have proposed many variants of machine learning techniques
in education domains. However, there are severe challenges in handling imbalanced datasets for enhancing
the performance of predicting student grades. Therefore, this paper presents a comprehensive analysis of
machine learning techniques to predict the ﬁnal student grades in the ﬁrst semester courses by improving
the performance of predictive accuracy. Two modules will be highlighted in this paper. First, we compare the
accuracy performance of six well-known machine learning techniques namely Decision Tree (J48), Support
Vector Machine (SVM), Naïve Bayes (NB), K-Nearest Neighbor (kNN), Logistic Regression (LR) and
Random Forest (RF) using 1282 real student’s course grade dataset. Second, we proposed a multiclass prediction model to reduce the overﬁtting and misclassiﬁcation results caused by imbalanced multi-classiﬁcation
based on oversampling Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) with two features selection
methods. The obtained results show that the proposed model integrates with RF give signiﬁcant improvement
with the highest f-measure of 99.5%. This proposed model indicates the comparable and promising results
that can enhance the prediction performance model for imbalanced multi-classiﬁcation for student grade
prediction.
INDEX TERMS
Machine learning, predictive model, imbalanced problem, student grade prediction,
multi-class classiﬁcation.

insightful information related to student academic performance. Solomon et al. [1] indicated that determining student academic performance is a crucial challenge in HEI.
Due to this, many previous researchers have well-deﬁned
the inﬂuence factors that can highly affect student academic
performance [2]. However, most common factors are relying on socioeconomic background, demographics [3] and
learning activities [4] compared to ﬁnal student grades in
the ﬁnal examination [5]. As for this reason, we observe
that the trend of predicting student grades can be one of the
solutions that are applicable to improve student academic
performance [6].
Predictive analytics has shown the successful beneﬁt in
the HEI. It can be a potential approach to beneﬁt the competitive educational domain to ﬁnd hidden patterns and make
predictions trends in a vast database [7]. It has been used to
solve several educational areas that include student performance, dropout prediction, academic early warning systems,
and course selection [8]. Moreover, the application of predictive analytics in predicting student academic performance has
increased over the years [9].
The ability to predict student grade is one of the important
area that can help to improve student academic performance.
Many previous research has found variant machine learning techniques performed in predicting student academic
performance. However, the related works on mechanism to
improve imbalanced multi-classiﬁcation problem in predicting students’ grade prediction are difﬁcult to found [10], [11].
Therefore, in this study, a comparative analysis has been done
to ﬁnd the best prediction model for student grade prediction
by addressing the following questions:
RQ1: Which predictive model among the selected machine
learning algorithms performs high accuracy performance to
predict student’s ﬁnal course grades?
RQ2: How imbalanced multi-classiﬁcation dataset can
be addressed with selected machine learning algorithms
using oversampling Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) and feature selection (FS) methods?
To address the above-mentioned questions, we collect the
student ﬁnal course grades from two core courses in the
ﬁrst semester of the ﬁnal examination result. We present
a descriptive analysis of student datasets to visualize student grade trends, which can lead to strategic planning in
decision making for the lecturers to help students more
effectively. Then, we conduct comparative analysis using
six well-known machine learning algorithms, including LR,
NB, J48, SVM, kNN and RF on the real student data of
Diploma in Information Technology (Digital Technology) at
one of Malaysia Polytechnic. As for addressing the imbalanced multi-classiﬁcation, we endeavor to enhance the performance of each predictive model with data-level solutions
using oversampling SMOTE and FS. The novel contribution
of this paper are summarized as follows:
• We proposed combination of modiﬁcation on oversampling SMOTE and two feature selection algorithms
to automatically determine the sampling ratio with
best selected features to improve imbalanced multiclassiﬁcation for student grade prediction.
• Our comparative analysis showed that the ratio between
the minority class in imbalanced dataset does not necessarily to approach same ratio of majority class to obtain
better performance in student grade prediction.
• Our proposed model shows different impact in improving the performance of student grade prediction model
based on the versatility of two feature selection algorithm after implementing SMOTE.
This paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the
related research work that has been conducted for student
grade prediction. Section III illustrates the methodology of
developing predictive models to predict ﬁnal student grades
by phases. Section IV and Section V present the descriptive analysis and prediction results of this study’s ﬁndings,
respectively. Section VI discusses the ﬁndings result. Lastly,
the paper is highlighted with the main conclusions with some
future directions in Section VII.
II. RELATED WORKS
Several studies have been conducted in HEI for predicting
student grades using various machine learning techniques.
It involves analytical process of many attributes and samples
data from variety of sources for student grade prediction in
different outcome. However, the performance of predictive
model for imbalanced dataset in education domains are still
rarely discussed. Related to this issues, a study from [12]
used discretization and oversampling SMOTE methods to
improve the accuracy of students’ ﬁnal grade prediction.
Several classiﬁcation algorithms have been applied such as
NB, DT and Neural Network (NN) for classifying students’
ﬁnal grade into ﬁve categories; A, B, C, D and F. They
showed that NN and NB applied with SMOTE and optimal
equal width binning outperformed other methods with similar
highest accuracy of 75%. However, NB found better compared to NN as the optimal time to utilize the prediction
models are faster than NN. Research conducted by [13],
has developed a method for predicting future course grades
obtained from the Computer Science and Engineering (CSE)
and Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) programs at
the University of Minnesota. Based on the proposed methods, the results indicated that Matrix Factorization (MF)
and Linear Regression (LinReg) performed more accurate
predictions than the existing traditional methods. The author
also found that the use of a course-speciﬁc subset of data
can improve prediction accuracy for predicting future course
grades. Another study in [14], applied MF, Collaborative Filtering (CF) and Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM) techniques on 225 real data of undergraduate students to predict
student grade in different courses. They observe that using
CF does not indicate good performance especially when
there found many sparsity in the dataset compared to MF.
However, their overall ﬁndings show that the proposed RBM
provides efﬁcient learning and better prediction accuracy
compared to CF and MF with minimum Root Mean Squared

A study in [15] has developed a predictive model that can
predict student’s ﬁnal grades in introductory courses at an
early stage of the semester. They have compared eleven
machine learning algorithms in ﬁve different categories consist of Bayes, Function, Lazy (IBK), Rules-Based (RB) and
Decision Tree (DT) using WEKA. To reduce high dimensionality and unbalanced data, they have performed feature
selection correlation-based and information-gain for datapreprocessing. The author also applied SMOTE to balance
the distribution instances of three different classes. Among
the 11 algorithms, they indicated that Decision Tree classiﬁer (J48) have the highest accuracy of 88% compared to
other categories of algorithms. Al-Barrak [16] used DT (J48)
algorithm to discover classiﬁcation rules for predicting students’ ﬁnal Grade Point Average (GPA) based on student
grades in previous courses. They have used 236 students
who graduated from Computer Science College at King
Saud University in 2012. They found that the classiﬁcation
rule produced from J48 can detect early predictors and can
extract useful knowledge for ﬁnal student GPA based on
their grades in all mandatory courses to improve students’
performance. Another study in [17] have predicted the student’s grade performance using three different DT algorithms; Random Tree (RT), RepTree and J48. In this context,
cross-validation is used to measure the performance of the
predictive model. From the ﬁndings, the results indicated
that RT obtained the highest accuracy of 75.188% better
than the other algorithms. The accuracy of the predictive
models can be improved by adding more number of samples
and attributes in the dataset. [18] has proposed a framework
for predicting student academic performance at University
Sultan Zainal Abidin (UniSZA), Malaysia. The study applied
399 student records from the academic department database
in the eight years’ intakes that contained student demographics, previous academic records and family background information. The results indicated that the Rule-Based (PART) is
the best model with 71.3% accuracy compared to DT and NB.
However, using the small sample size has affected accuracy
performance due to incomplete and missing value found in
the dataset. Anderson and Anderson [19] performed an experimental study on 683 students at the Craig School of Business
at California State University from 2006 to 2015 by applying
three machine learning algorithms to predict student grades.
The study found that SVM is the best classiﬁer. Itfo consistently outperforms a simple average approach that obtained
the lowest error rate to optimize each data class. The result
could be different for the large set of data due to signiﬁcant
changes in the historical grade dataset’s structure and format.

The input of our framework contain student’s ﬁnal course

document and student academic repository. We applied two

The dataset we used was collected by the Department of

June 2016 to December 2019 session. Students need to take
some compulsory, specialization and core courses modules
to qualify them for the next academic semester. However,
in this study we selected only two core courses that contained
the percentage of ﬁnal examination and course assessment

different machine learning algorithms to evaluate which
of the algorithms performed the highest performance for
predicting student’s ﬁnal grades. There are three experiments were conducted in four distinct phases based on
the ﬁve different classes. The accuracy is evaluated using
ten-fold cross-validation which our dataset is partitioned
into 90% for training set and 10% for testing set on the same

• Naïve Bayes (NB) is based on Bayesian theorem that

multi-classiﬁcation problems focus on data-level solution for

student grade prediction. For handling the imbalanced problem, we used the real student’s ﬁnal course grades dataset
from JTMK at one of Malaysia Polytechnics to analyze
and compare the results of the proposed model. A similar
study conducted in [7], [32], also mentioned the signiﬁcant
course grades can help in decision making in the educational domains. To answer our research question, we conducted a comprehensive experiment on real student dataset by
comparing the accuracy performance of the prediction model
in a selected machine learning algorithm. Then, we also
applied oversampling SMOTE and two FS methods to compare the effectiveness of the predictive model by using evaluation metrics of accuracy, precision, recall and f-measure to

Overall results indicated that all predictive model derived
from J48, NB, kNN SVM, LR and RF deliver a better performance when we applied SMOTE independently to the
imbalanced dataset. However, after we applied FS method
on imbalanced dataset using wrapper-based, only kNN and
NB shows signiﬁcant improvement whereas SVM remain
same with none changes. This happened due to the tendency
of overﬁtting and bias result caused by imbalanced data
created when selecting the subgroup features. Other than
that, we noticed the SVM not able to work independently
in solving imbalanced multi-classiﬁcation due to limitation
for computing the best hyperplane for high dimensional
imbalanced dataset [33]. As for NB, the used of FS for
predicting student’s grade also supported in [30] where the
author found NB shows the highest accuracy performance
when wrapper-based subset feature selection was undertaken.
However, we identiﬁed that FS independently not able to

Then, we attempted to reduce the overﬁtting and misclassiﬁcation of the minority class by combining SMOTE with
a selection of appropriate features for all predictive models
by introducing the SFS model. Here, the overall performance
indicated the proposed SFS model outperformed with RF
higher than previous study conducted by [12], [15]. The best
accuracy obtained by the RF with 99.5% slightly higher than
kNN and J48 shows that the RF algorithm was the ideal
solution algorithm to predict student ﬁnal grade. Meanwhile,
kNN was the ideal solution that can work with the best
value of k and optimal features [35]. The experiment results
revealed that the proposed SFS model had more signiﬁcant
effect on kNN depending on the selected of FS algorithms.
Certainly, these result also similar to the best performance of
kNN in handling imbalanced data with different case studies
as depicted in [36]. In this context, we also observe that most
of the predictive models considered beneﬁt when performing
oversampling SMOTE but integrating the accurate features
with different FS algorithms can inﬂuence the prediction
effectiveness as well.
Despite these ﬁndings, we have identiﬁed several limitations to this fact; (1) the analysis is based on a deﬁned
dataset, but other dataset should be tested for data generalization that could affect the analysis results; (2) the analysis
is only carried out with the certain well-known algorithms
but can be analyzed with ensemble or advanced machine
learning algorithms to compare the effectiveness for imbalanced multi-classiﬁcation prediction model. (3) we used only
one method of oversampling SMOTE, more method could
be used to analyze whether they can improve the multi-class
imbalanced problem.
Therefore, this study still needs to be improved in predicting students’ ﬁnal grades by improving the sampling techniques for imbalanced multi-class dataset that might affect the
accurate prediction results. In addition, we also be considered
to use SVM ensemble to be as part of the analysis since it
has produced greater accuracy when predicting students’ ﬁnal
grades as mentioned in [37].
VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
Predicting student grades is one of the key performance
indicators that can help educators monitor their academic
performance. Therefore, it is important to have a predictive model that can reduce the level of uncertainty in the
outcome for an imbalanced dataset. This paper proposes
a multiclass prediction model with six predictive models
to predict ﬁnal student’s grades based on the previous student ﬁnal examination result of the ﬁrst-semester course.
Speciﬁcally, we have done a comparative analysis of combining oversampling SMOTE with different FS methods to
evaluate the performance accuracy of student grade prediction. We also have shown that the explored oversampling
SMOTE is overall improved consistently than using FS alone
with all predictive models. However, our proposed multiclass
prediction model performed more effectively than using oversampling SMOTE and FS alone with some parameter settings
that can inﬂuence the performance accuracy of all predictive models. Here, our ﬁndings contribute to be a practical
approach for addressing the imbalanced multi-classiﬁcation
based on the data-level solution for student grade prediction.
In HEI, predictive analytics plays a signiﬁcant role in governance for improving valuable information and developing
trusted decision-making that contributes to data science [38].
Determining the quality of the collected dataset to reduce
the imbalance and missing values difﬁculties is part of the
challenging issues that adhere to select the relevant and valuable predictive models [39]. Therefore, as for future works,
further investigation on the use of appropriate emerging predictive techniques in such advanced machine learning algorithms [40] and more ensemble algorithms are recommended
to optimize the result for predicting student grades. It is also
essential to select several multi-class imbalanced datasets
to be analyzed with appropriate sampling techniques and
different evaluation metrics which suitable for the imbalanced
multi-class domain such as Kappa, Weighted Accuracy and
other measures. Thus, using machine learning in higher learning institutions for student grade prediction will ultimately
enhance the decision support system to improve their student
academic performance in the future.

Multiple-Swarm Ensembles: Improving the
Predictive Power and Robustness of Predictive
Models and Its Use in Computational Biology
Pedro Alves, Shuang Liu, Daifeng Wang
, and Mark Gerstein
Abstract—Machine learning is an integral part of computational biology, and has already shown its use in various applications, such as
prognostic tests. In the last few years in the non-biological machine learning community, ensembling techniques have shown their
power in data mining competitions such as the Netﬂix challenge; however, such methods have not found wide use in computational
biology. In this work, we endeavor to show how ensembling techniques can be applied to practical problems, including problems in the
ﬁeld of bioinformatics, and how they often outperform other machine learning techniques in both predictive power and robustness.
Furthermore, we develop a methodology of ensembling, Multi-Swarm Ensemble (MSWE) by using multiple particle swarm
optimizations and demonstrate its ability to further enhance the performance of ensembles.
Index Terms—Machine learning, ensemble learning, bioinformatics, data mining, computational biology
Ç
1
INTRODUCTION
T
HE exponential growth in data available in the ﬁeld of
computational biology has been well characterized in
the past few years. The ﬁeld has transformed itself, and the
problems therein, accordingly, have been transformed as
well. The main challenges in the ﬁeld are now linked to its
data availability. On one hand is the issue of how to store
and access the trove of information, and on the other hand
is the issue of how to best extract as much information as
possible from the data available.
Machine learning has been used in many sub-ﬁelds of
computational biology, including genomics, proteomics,
microarrays, systems biology, evolution and text mining,
etc. It has been used in aiding gene prediction [1], identifying regulatory elements [2], [3], [4] and non-coding RNAs
[5], predicting protein structures, interpreting proteomics
experiments [6], [7], [8], analyzing next generation sequencing data [9], modeling biological networks [10], and constructing phylogenetic trees [11].
While there is a good amount of machine learning being
utilized in the ﬁeld of computational biology, the level of
techniques being used lags behind what is being developed
in the ﬁeld of machine learning. Simple, older methods are
the most commonly used in computational biology. Often
in bioinformatics studies techniques such as logistic regression are used, a representative example of this can be seen
in the evaluation of gene expression data from microarray
experiments, as in Chuang et al. [12]. There are many possible reasons for this phenomenon: ease of use, extensive publications on such methods, and ease of understanding.
Ensembling methods have been on the leading edge of
machine learning for a while. For example, random forests
came around nearly 20 years ago [13]. More recently, new
ensembling methods are being developed and they continue
to surpass other methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. This can be exempliﬁed in the example of the NetFlix
challenge [14], [15], where the ﬁnal winner an ensemble of
the ﬁrst 3 teams, who were in turn using ensembling techniques themselves. Another example of the use of ensemble
methods is their prevalence in machine learning challenges
sponsored by machine learning conferences [16].
Based on the idea of emsembling, ensemble learning is a
method that combines multiple machine learning models and
algoirthms to create one ﬁnal model for a given learning problem [17]. There are various combination ways [18]. One way
is achieved by manipulating the training data. Some machine
learning algorithms are very unstable based on the training
data available, and changes in the training data can cause
major changes in the models, hence the ensembling of methods, or even a single method (as in random forests), over different portions of the training data will improve on
performance. Changes in the training data can be achieved by
randomly sampling a subset of the training data available,
usually with replacement allowed, and training a model on
this sample of the dataset, as done in the bagging method
[19]. This is performed multiple times to create several

text:
different versions of the same model, which are later combined into one ﬁnal model. A second way for manipulating
the training set is to assign weights to each training sample,
and after training a model with the training data, updating
the weights by increasing the weights of samples that were
incorrectly classiﬁed, and decreasing the weight of samples
that were correctly classiﬁed before training the next model.
This method will create models that are increasingly better at
predicting the more difﬁcult samples, AdaBoost [20]. Changes
in the features can be similarly performed. One example, as in
Cherkauer et al. [21], in which multiple artiﬁcial neural networks were constructed, each with a different subset of the
features available. Random forests [13] for example uses a
combination of manipulating both features and training samples. There are yet other methods of manipulating data to
achieve varying models, such as including randomness in the
data and manipulating output targets [18]. Besides data
manipulations, one can also achieve different models through
parameter tuning and the utilization of different models.
Ensembles that are generated by combining different
machine learning algorithms seem to be a logical choice,
according to [18] “A necessary and sufﬁcient condition for
an ensemble of classiﬁers to be more accurate than any of its
individual members is if the classiﬁers are accurate [deﬁned
as any improvement over random guessing] and diverse.”
While the methods of data manipulation explained above
do create diversity, the individual models might suffer in
performance from the removal of training samples and/or
features. Instead, by utilizing different algorithms, you can
achieve diversity without the cost of potentially reducing
information content for each individual model.
There are various different methods of combining multiple
models from different machine learning algorithms. One
method is grading [22], in this method the multiple models
are trained on the data and the ﬁnal model is simply a
weighted average of the individual predictions. The weights
are assigned based on the performance of each individual
model. This way a model that performed well has more say in
the ﬁnal results than a model that has performed poorly. A
second method of combining different models is voting [23],
[24]. This is a simpliﬁed version of the grading method. In this
method all models have the same weight, and the predictions
from each model can simply be used in a majority vote manner in order to decide how the ﬁnal model should predict a
particular instance. Stacking [25] is yet another method,
though slightly more involved. In stacking, the multiple models are combined by another model that takes in the outputs of
all the models as features. Finally, the method demonstrated
in Rich et al. [17] uses a greedy hillclimbing algorithm in order
to select which models to utilize in the ensemble. This model
is similar to the grading method in a way since they allow for
multiple copies of the same model, in effect, giving it more
weight. This method of greedy hillclimbing works simply by
ﬁrst selecting the very best performing model from the many
models trained on the data. Once this best model is selected, it
becomes part of the ensemble, which, at this point in the algorithm. consists only of the best method. The next step in this
algorithm is to choose which other model can be added to the
ensemble in order to produce the best overall result. The algorithm attempts all possibilities, and evaluates the ensemble by
simply averaging all the outputs from the models in the
ensemble (as in voting). Once the next best addition to the
ensemble is made, the algorithm continues to add models to
the ensemble until it is no longer beneﬁcial.
Each of the methods above has its advantages. The voting algorithm is simple, fast and performs very well; however, its downside is that it could be further optimized,
given the fact that all models have the same weight in this
ensemble. The Stacking method does achieve some of the
optimization; however, choosing which machine learning
algorithm to use to create the ensemble can have a signiﬁ-
cant impact on the ﬁnal results. Grading is a simple way of
optimizing on the voting method with a machine learning
algorithm bias, albeit not the best optimization technique.
The
ensemble
method
with
greedy
hillclimbing
[17]
improves on the grading technique by attempting to ﬁnd
the best combination of models with a greedy algorithm.
While the greedy hillclimbing ensembling method [17]
does obtain excellent results, the fact that a greedy method
is utilized is a potential area for improvement. Greedy algorithms, while very fast, are very simple and are very prone
to local minima [26]. Greedy algorithms are used due to
their incredibly fast speeds and despite the fact that these
algorithms will likely not output the global optimal solution, their solution should be improved from the worst possible solutions. In the ensembling case, it is assumed that a
greedy method will optimize and outperform a simple voting method. Jogen et al. [26] shows that the greedy algorithm will, under some conditions, output the very worst
possible solution in an optimization problem. Without prior
knowledge of when this occurrence will happen, it seems
unadvisable to rely on such a method. With this in mind,
we were compelled to analyze an ensemble algorithm that
relied on a better performing optimization algorithm.
The particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a popular
computational method to iteratively ﬁnd optimal solutions.
Thus, in this study we aim to use an ensemble of PSOs to
improve on the AUC of an ensemble of various machine
learning algorithms. Since PSO is a very good optimizer, it
is expected that the solutions will outperform those
obtained through greedy algorithms. However, in order to
avoid overﬁtting, and to improve robustness, we decided to
use the combined weights of ten PSO ensembles, in essence
creating an ensemble of ensembles. This will also increase
the consistency of the ensemble, given that PSO is an algorithm with a random element and every run has a degree of
variance, thus avoiding overﬁtting the weights for the
machine learning algorithms. Therefore, in this paper, we
propose a method, Multi-Swarm Ensemble (MSWE) that
utilizes multiple particle swarm optimizations to obtain the
weights of the machine learning algorithms, and then
ensembles them to maximize the AUC. We are able to show
the consistent superior performance of ensemble learning
over conventional machine learning algorithms; furthermore, we show the increased performance of ensembles
when using the MSWE methodology.
2
METHODS
2.1
Datasets
The datasets were collected from the UCI machine learning
repository [30], [31] and from a breast cancer metastasis
