V. DISCUSSIONS
In this paper, we propose a MDPN method to encode multiple protein features and RELM classiﬁer to predict PPIs. The
experimental results demonstrate that, the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in predicting PPIs on Yeast,
Human, and H. pylori datasets.
In our study, we compare with protein features learned by
only linear combination of BP, CP, and DP matrices, when three
linear combinations of protein features are encoded by the DPN
and MDPN, the average ACCs are improved with at least 7%,
5.2%, and 7.4% on the same datasets (Tables I, II, III). However,
the MDPN has modest increase as compared to DPN on the same
dataset (at most 0.7%). In addition, encoding the three protein
features using MDPN improves the classiﬁcation accuracy on
Yeast, Human, and H. pylori datasets, particularly using RELM
classiﬁer, up to 99.9% (Table II). It is clear that MDPN algorithm can concatenate all modalities with the exploration of the
complementary information. Each original protein feature is respectively encoded by the basic DPN in the ﬁrst stage. All three
types of the high level features are cascaded to DPN encoding in
the second stage. The high level features ultimately learned include the intrinsic properties of each modality and the relativity
among all modalities. Compared with method of encoding only
a basic DPN, the MDPN exploits the complementarity among
multiple modalities and exhibits a highly non-linear correlation
among multiple modalities.
In this study, two other classiﬁers, namely, SVM and ELM,
are employed to estimate the performance of MDPN. Compared
with ELM classiﬁer and SVM classiﬁer, the average ACCs of
RELM classiﬁer are improved with at least 0.09% and 0.24% on
the same datasets, even if three are very prominent (Table IV and
Fig. 5). This not only indicates that RELM classiﬁer via the LOO
cross validation approach to ensure an optimal regularization
parameter of ELM is available, but also indicates the feature
encoding of the MDPN method is really effective.
The ﬁrst is amino acid mutation rate extracted by BLO-
SUM62 matrix and the PSSM matrix are used to replace the
protein amino acid sequence respectively. Table VI show that
both the substitution matrices have excellent performance in
this method model, and BLOSUM62 matrix is slightly better.
In addition, when extracted by BLOSUM62 matrix, where the
feature dimension is reduced by 2DLDA method, we also use
PCA method to test. Compared with PCA method, the average ACC of 2DLDA method with MDPN-RELM increased by
0.64% (Table V). We applied the 2DLDA method to reduce
noise interference and integrate the useful information, which is
employed to perform discriminant feature analysis on a matrix
instead of a vector.
The proposed method also acheives good performance when
applied to E. coli, C. elegans, H. sapien, H. pylori, M. musculus,
and D. mela datasets (Table VII). Particularly, on C. elegans,
H. pylori, M. musculus, and D. mela where the classﬁcation
accuracies are higher than the-state-of-the-art methods with at
least 7.95%, 3.04%, 3.28%, and 10.42%, respectively. The main
reason is that we consider the evolutionary and chemical information to represent the protein sequence and achieve the best
PPIs prediction results.
Investigation of PPI network also proves the superiority of the
proposed method when tested on the tetraspanin protein CD9,
accuracies of the Ras-Raf-Mek-Erk-Elk-Srf pathway, and the
Wnt-related pathway (Figs. 7, 8, 9) are superior to the Shen
et al. [7] and Ding et al. [67] with at least 6.25%, 6.88%, and
4.17%, respectively. Therefore, it is clear that our method can
be applied to other organisms and complicate networks of PPIs.
Running time is also important aspect in the evaluation of
our method. Therefore, we test the sum of training and testing
running times for MP-MDPN-RELM, MP-MDPN-ELM and
MP-MDPN-SVM on Yeast dataset where the average running
times are 60.88 seconds, 29.35 seconds and 53.22 seconds, respectively. Obviously, RELM takes longer time than ELM due
to selection process of the optimal parameters. However, there is
not much difference compared to SVM. In general, our method
takes about 60s for RELM training and prediction, which is still
feasible.
Although extensive experiments demonstrate the good performance of the proposed method for PPIs prediction, it is not without limitations. One limitation is that, our dataset is relatively
small, therefore, testing our method against larger and more

VI. CONCLUSIONS
In this paper, we put forward a novel computational method
based on MDPN to encode multiple data from protein properties for PPIs prediction. The MDPN approach consists of two
stages of DPN encoding to integrate the three features of protein
sequences and exploit feature complementarity. In addition, we
utilize RELM to effectively classify the extracted features. Experimental results on different datasets and comparisons with
state-of-the-art methods show that the proposed method has low
standard deviation, high accuracy and high AUC value. These
show that the proposed method is robust and superior for PPIs
prediction. Moreover, it can be potentially used for complex
protein networks as well.

Psychological Profiling of Digital Dependency
Using Machine Learning and Behavioral
Clustering Techniques
C. BINDU ASHWINI
1, C. S. HARSHA2, B. M. SREEKAR2, AND HARSHITH K. MURTHY2,
1Department of Humanities and Social Sciences, RV College of Engineering, Bengaluru 560059, India
2Department of Electronics and Telecommunication Engineering, RV College of Engineering, Bengaluru 560059, India
Corresponding author: C. Bindu Ashwini (binduashwini@rvce.edu.in)
ABSTRACT Mental, physical, and emotional well-being are critical for sustaining productive engineering
careers, yet the integration of mobile devices into every aspect of life has blurred work–life boundaries.
Using a 268 -participant survey where these people are engineers pursuing the electronics field, this
study investigates the psychological footprint of digital dependency— an emerging behavioural health
challenge in high-pressure technical fields like electronics engineering. This paper extracts latent factors
that underlie compulsive device interaction through exploratory factor analysis, constructs an interpretable
supervised learning pipeline that predicts an individual’s likelihood of moderate or severe dependency, and
leverages K-Means clustering with silhouette-guided K selection to derive five distinct usage personas. Our
findings reveal that sleep disruption, diminished academic satisfaction, and anxiety-mediated impulsivity
dominate the dependency profile. Practically, the proposed pipeline supports early-warning diagnostics for
university wellness services, while the personas offer actionable design cues for persuasive digital-wellbeing
interventions.
INDEX TERMS Psychological analysis, digital dependency, mental health, machine learning, K-means,
supervised learning, device usage.
I. INTRODUCTION
In today’s digitally driven world, electronic devices have
evolved into indispensable tools for learning, communication, and entertainment. While these technologies offer
tremendous benefits, they also raise growing concerns about
their psychological toll, particularly among electronics engineering students. The constant connectivity, information
overload, and multitasking demands associated with device
usage may lead to mental fatigue, emotional imbalance, and
lifestyle disturbances.
This study undertakes a psychological analysis aimed
at understanding how screen exposure affects the mental, physical, and emotional health of engineering students.
We structured a detailed questionnaire spanning behavioural
domains such as device usage habits, attention and focus,
memory and cognition, emotional response, lifestyle balance,

uncover patterns and behavioral archetypes within the student
population. To derive meaningful insights, we apply K-Means
clustering, a powerful unsupervised learning model, which
enables the grouping of students into distinct psychological profiles based on their response patterns. The optimal
number of clusters is determined using silhouette scores, and
inter-variable relationships are visualized using correlation
heat maps. This methodological framework allows us to identify not just how students are affected, but which specific
behaviours co-occur, revealing digital dependency patterns
and their psychological implications.
The integration of machine learning in this context
goes beyond basic statistics, offering a scalable, objective
approach to categorize user behaviour and recommending
digital well-being strategies. Such insights are vital in today’s
academic settings, where cognitive overload and emotional
stress are common but often overlooked. By recognizing

II. LITERATURE REVIEW
A. DIGITAL DEPENDENCY AND PSYCHOLOGICAL
WELL-BEING
Digital monitoring and automated screening raise significant
privacy concerns, as they often involve collecting sensitive
personal data without full transparency or consent. Thus,
for this reason, we have taken critical steps along with
measures to safeguard the obtained data related to the participants. Digital dependency has emerged as a growing
concern within psychological and behavioral sciences, particularly in technology-intensive environments. Individuals may
face risks of data misuse, profiling, or surveillance beyond
the intended purpose. Automated systems can also amplify
biases, leading to unfair outcomes and discrimination.
The intersection of psychology and engineering in understanding human-technology interaction has become increasingly critical as digital devices permeate every aspect of
modern life. Prior studies have extensively examined how
prolonged interaction with digital devices influences cognitire, emotional, and social functioning, revealing complex
patterns of dependency that extend beyond simple usage
metrics.
Healey and Picard [16] demonstrated the use of physiological signals and machine learning, specifically Support
Vector Machines (SVM), to detect driver stress, establishing
a foundational approach for objective stress measurement
in technological contexts. Similarly, Sano and Picard [17]
found strong correlations between smartphone usage, sleep
duration, and stress levels, highlighting the bidirectional
relationship between digital engagement and physiological well-being. These works underscore the efficacy of
behavioural signals for psychological modelling and the
importance of bridging engineering methodologies with
psychological insights.
The concept of digital dependency extends beyond traditional addiction models, encompassing a spectrum of
behaviours that range from habitual engagement to compulsive usage patterns. Research by Wang et al. [1] demonstrates
that screen time alone is insufficient for understanding
mental health impacts, emphasizing the need for multidimensional assessment approaches that consider usage context,
emotional states, and cognitive outcomes. This aligns with
engineering principles that prioritize comprehensive system
analysis over isolated component evaluation.
B. MACHINE LEARNING APPLICATIONS IN BEHAVIORAL
PSYCHOLOGY
Machine learning models such as Decision Trees, Random
Forests, and Gradient Boosting Machines (GBMs) have been
employed to predict behavioural patterns from heterogeneous data sources. Researchers like Tzirakis et al. [18] and
Mirsamadi et al. [19] have applied deep learning for emotion
recognition based on multimodal inputs, demonstrating the
potential for automated psychological assessment. The convergence of engineering precision with psychological theory
creates opportunities for a more nuanced understanding of
human behaviour in digital environments.
Using validated external scales (criterion measures) greatly
strengthens the external validity of unsupervised clusters and
supervised classification models. At present, the manuscript
relies on the study’s be spoke binary instrument and internal
patterns; mapping clusters to external addiction/well-being
measures will provide construct validity and allow benchmarking. ‘‘At risk’’ individuals identified through predictive
models pose significant ethical questions. Although privacy
was ensured by anonymization and secure data processing,
the psychological effects of being identified as dependent
need to be handled with care. We propose that diagnostic
prediction tools should solely operate in enabling wellness
environments that provide informed consent and counseling
resources.
Clustering techniques, especially K-Means, have proven
effective for identifying behavioral archetypes in psychological datasets, enabling researchers to move beyond
population-level statistics to individual-centered analysis.
The application of unsupervised learning methods in psychology represents a significant paradigm shift from traditional
hypothesis-driven research to data-driven discovery, allowing for the identification of previously unknown behavioral
patterns and user personas. The broader application of unsupervised learning in psychology represents a paradigm shift
from the long-standing reliance on hypothesis-driven inquiry
toward data-driven discovery. Unlike conventional methods,

with greater openness and flexibility, unlocking insights that
might otherwise remain concealed under traditional analytical frameworks. Ultimately, this evolution enhances the
field’s ability to adapt to the complex and dynamic nature of
human behavior in the digital age.
C. INTERDISCIPLINARY APPROACHES AND
ENGINEERING PSYCHOLOGY
The field of engineering psychology emphasizes the importance of designing technology that accommodates human
cognitive limitations and enhances user well-being. Recent
work by Rustam et al. [13] and Kyriakou et al. [20] further supports the application of wearable data and statistical
modeling in assessing digital-induced stress, demonstrating
how engineering sensor technologies can provide objective
measures of psychological stress.

The integration of psychological theory with engineering
methodology has led to the development of more sophisticated models for understanding human-technology interaction. This interdisciplinary approach recognises that effective
technology design requires a deep understanding of human
psychological processes, while psychological research benefits from the precision and scalability offered by engineering
approaches. Contemporary research increasingly emphasizes
the need for personalized interventions based on individual
psychological profiles rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.
This study builds on these findings by combining surveybased cognitive metrics with clustering and classification
to uncover actionable behavioural profiles, contributing to
the growing body of work that bridges psychology and
engineering to make technology work better for people.
III. DATASET AND STATISTICAL METHODOLOGY
A. DATA COLLECTION AND REPRESENTATION
Data was collected through a comprehensive structured
questionnaire distributed among undergraduate electronics engineering students across multiple institutions. The
‘‘Machine Learning Pipeline and Algorithm Selection’’
section also details the supervised learning pipeline and
validation methods, including cross-validation and performance met rics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.
The instrument was designed following established psychological assessment principles and consisted of 56 carefully
validated binary-response items (Yes/No), grouped under
seven distinct psychological and behavioural domains: device
usage habits, attention and focus, cognitive impact, emotional
responses, lifestyle changes, digital self-awareness, and
reliability screening.
The questionnaire development process involved extensive
piloting with a subset of 50 participants to ensure question
clarity and construct validity. Each domain was designed to
capture specific aspects of digital dependency, with questions calibrated to detect both overt behaviours and subtle
psychological indicators. The binary response format was
chosen to minimize response bias and cognitive load while
maximizing data quality and statistical power for machine
learning applications.
Each participant’s responses were anonymised using a
secure hash-based system and converted into a binary matrix
(Yes = 1, No = 0), generating a clean dataset of 268 usable
entries after quality control procedures. This sample size
exceeds the recommended minimum for clustering analysis
and provides adequate statistical power for both unsupervised and supervised learning approaches. This sample size
exceeds the recommended minimum for clustering analysis, providing not only a statistically robust foundation for
unsupervised learning techniques such as K-Means and PCA,
but also sufficient power for supervised models like SVMs,
Random Forests, and neural networks. Moreover, the diversity in institutional background, academic year, and exposure
to technology among respondents further enhances the
dataset’s generalizability, enabling meaningful insights that
extend beyond localised populations. Because our input
features are binary (Yes/No), we evaluated cluster validity
using the Euclidean K-Means silhouette. Thus, validation
of such values holds good for data analysis. While the
Euclidean silhouette was low (0.026) — reflecting overlapping behavioural continuous rather than discrete subpopulations — the silhouette plot, stability analysis, and the heat
map/PCA patterns together support the interpretability of
the identified personas. This comprehensive data collection
approach ensures that subsequent analyses are both methodologically sound and highly applicable to real-world student
populations facing digital dependency challenges.
B. DATA PREPROCESSING AND QUALITY ASSURANCE
The dataset underwent rigorous quality assurance procedures,
including outlier detection, consistency checking, and missing value analysis. Missing or inconsistent values (less than
2% of total responses) were resolved using mode imputation,
selected over mean imputation due to the binary nature of
the data. Response time analysis was conducted to identify
and remove cases with unrealistically fast completion times,
indicating potential random responding.
Descriptive statistics, such as total dependency scores,
were computed by summing the binary values across
sections, creating a composite dependency index ranging
from 0 to 56. The histogram illustrates the distribution of
these scores, highlighting a central tendency around scores
26-28, implying a moderate-to-high digital dependency trend
among respondents. This distribution approximates a normal
curve with slight positive skewness, indicating the presence
of a subset of high-dependency users.
Preliminary analysis revealed that a majority of participants (73%) reported frequent device multitasking, 68%
experienced screen exposure before bed, and 81% reported
difficulties in disengagement all key indicators of behavioural
stress and cognitive fatigue. These prevalence rates align
with contemporary research on digital dependency in student
populations and validate the representativeness of our sample and support the generalizability of findings to broader
populations of undergraduate students.
Collectively, the stringent data validation processes and
insightful preliminary analyses laid a strong empirical foundation for the machine learning models and psychological
interpretations that followed.
C. FEATURE ENGINEERING AND DIMENSIONALITY
CONSIDERATIONS
Feature engineering involved the creation of composite
scores for each psychological domain, enabling both finegrained analysis at the item level and broader pattern
recognition at the domain level. Cross-correlation analysis
between domains revealed significant interdependencies, particularly between attention deficits and emotional responses
(r = 0.67, p < 0.001), suggesting shared underlying
psychological mechanisms.

These statistical analyses guided the development of the

with digital usage among students. Together, these statistical

The analysis was grounded in a robust statistical framework
combining descriptive, inferential, and multivariate methods.

Clustering analysis using K-Means was central to the

revealed meaningful psychological traits, such as emotional
fatigue or task disengagement.
To explore relationships between variables, a heat map of
Pearson correlation coefficients was generated. This matrix
enabled the identification of highly associated behavior patterns, such as the link between bedtime screen exposure and
restlessness. To reduce dimensionality and enhance interpretability, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used.
The PCA biplot confirmed overlapping psychological traits
across clusters but highlighted variance along key attention

Model performance was statistically validated using accuracy as a primary metric, computed via repeated holdout
validation. Confusion matrices provided deeper insights into

The application of Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
added another layer of insight by projecting the highdimensional data into a two-dimensional space. The resulting
PCA biplot illustrated that while some overlap among
clusters persisted—reinforcing the notion of psychological
behaviours existing along a continuum—there were also subtle directional trends along the principal component axes.
These trends corresponded to latent psychological traits, such
as dependency intensity and emotional disturbance, supporting the validity of the cluster-based segmentation.
Together, these statistical and visual analyses provided a
robust exploratory framework. They not only clarified the
structure of the dataset but also informed the design of
machine learning models, offering meaningful interpretations
of the psychological dimensions underlying digital device
use. This phase was crucial in bridging raw behavioural
data with psychologically interpretable constructs, ultimately
enabling a more targeted and evidence-based approach to
digital well-being assessment and intervention. To overcome
the shortcomings of Euclidean silhouette scores when dealing
with binary data, clustering was performed using Hamming
and Jaccard distance measures, which are more suitable
for binary response data matrices. The results gave better
scores (Hamming=0.12, Jaccard=0.15). Hierarchical clustering using Ward’s method and DBSCAN clustering were
also performed, validating the presence of overlaps and the
interpretability of the identified clusters. The stability of
the clusters was tested using bootstrapping resampling techniques (n=500) for Adjusted Rand indices, which reported
an average of 0.72.
1) MACHINE LEARNING PIPELINE AND ALGORITHM
SELECTION
The machine learning pipeline was designed following best
practices for psychological research applications, emphasizing both predictive accuracy and interpretability. The pipeline
consisted of three main phases: unsupervised clustering for
persona identification, supervised classification for dependency prediction, and validation through cross-validation and
statistical testing.
a: UNSUPERVISED LEARNING: K-MEANS CLUSTERING
K-Means clustering was selected as the primary unsupervised learning algorithm due to its computational efficiency,
interpretability, and proven effectiveness in psychological profiling applications. The algorithm partitions participants into k clusters by minimizing within-cluster sum of
squares, effectively grouping individuals with similar digital
dependency patterns.
The optimal number of clusters was determined using
multiple criteria: silhouette analysis, elbow method, and
gap statistic. Silhouette analysis revealed that while individual cluster cohesion was moderate (mean silhouette
score = 0.026), the clustering structure captured meaningful
psychological distinctions. The elbow method suggested k=3
to k=5 as optimal choices, while gap statistical analysis
supported k=5 for maximum interpretability.
Cluster initialization employed k-means++ seeding to
ensure reproducible and stable cluster formation. The
algorithm was run with 100 different initializations, and the
solution with the minimum inertia was selected. Convergence
was achieved within 50 iterations for all runs, indicating a
stable cluster structure. In order to make it easier to understand and avoid redundancy in our variables in our feature
set, we made use of correlation-based feature selection and
recursive feature elimination. Variables that were highly correlated (>0.8) were discarded in favour of keeping important
psychological domains like disruptions in sleep patterns,
multitasking rates, and expressions of anxiety.
b: SUPERVISED LEARNING: MULTI-ALGORITHM APPROACH
The supervised learning component employed multiple algorithms to ensure robust dependency prediction: Support
Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest, and Multi-Layer
Perceptron (MLP). This multi-algorithm approach enables
ensemble learning and provides insights into feature importance across different algorithmic paradigms.
Support Vector Machine (SVM): Linear SVM with
C=1.0 was employed for its effectiveness in highdimensional
binary classification tasks. The linear kernel was chosen to
maintain interpretability while achieving strong classification
performance. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using
grid search with 5-fold cross-validation ensuring that the
model’s performance was optimised while minimising the
risk of over-fitting. This process validated the model’s generalizability and stability across different subsets of the dataset.
Random Forest: A Random Forest classifier with
100 estimators provided insights into feature importance
while
maintaining
robustness
against
overfitting.
The
algorithm’s ensemble nature makes it particularly suitable for psychological data where individual features may
have variable predictive power across different participants.
An important advantage of this model is its ability to calculate
feature importance scores, which provided valuable insight
into which psychological variables (e.g., anxiety, emotional
fatigue, and multitasking frequency) were most predictive
of digital dependency patterns. This interpretability feature
is especially useful in psychological research, where understanding the role of specific traits is as important as achieving
predictive accuracy.
Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP): A neural network with
two hidden layers (64 and 32 neurons) captured non-linear
relationships between psychological variables. Reactivation
and dropout regularization (p=0.3) were employed to prevent overfitting while maintaining learning capacity. MLP’s
deep learning capabilities made it suitable for modeling the
subtle and multi-faceted dependencies that exist in behavioral
data, especially when underlying relationships between input
features and digital habits are not immediately obvious.

Collectively, these three models provided a comprehensive
evaluation framework: the SVM ensured linear separability
and interpretability, the Random Forest highlighted feature
importance while offering high resilience to noise, and the
MLP leveraged deep learning to capture complex, non-linear
patterns. The combination of these approaches allowed for
a robust and multi-perspective analysis of the digital dependency phenomena and offered valuable predictive insights for
future behavioural interventions.
c: MODEL VALIDATION AND PERFORMANCE ASSESSMENT
Model validation followed a stratified k-fold cross-validation
approach (k=5) to ensure balanced representation of dependency levels across training and testing sets. Performance
metrics included accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score,
and macro-averaged F1 to account for class imbalance
considerations.
Statistical significance of performance differences between
algorithms was assessed using McNemar’s test and paired
t-tests across cross-validation folds. Bootstrap resampling
(n=1000) provided confidence intervals for performance
metrics, enabling robust statistical inference about model
reliability.
The ensemble approach achieved macro-F1 = 0.88,
demonstrating strong predictive capability for identifying
moderate and severe digital dependency cases. Feature
importance analysis revealed that sleep disruption, academic
satisfaction, and anxiety-mediated impulsivity were the most
discriminative psychological indicators.
In addition to accuracy, we also evaluate precision, recall,
F1 measure, and area under the ROC curve (AUC). The
results of ensemble methods were macro-F1 = 0.88 and
AUC = 0.91, which demonstrated high discriminatory power
regardless of the level of dependency. The confusion matrix
analysis also confirmed good sensitivity (recall = 0.86) as
well as high specificity (precision = 0.89).To make predictions more interpretable, we used baseline learners. Majority
class classification returned an accuracy = 0.51, and the
logistic regression returned a macro-F1 = 0.62. The performance of our ensemble method is emphasized, which
performs much better than the baseline approach and scored
macro-F1 = 0.88, and area under the curve of 0.91.
2) ENGINEERING PSYCHOLOGY INTEGRATION
The
methodology
explicitly
integrates
engineering
psychology principles by treating digital dependency as a
human-system interaction problem. This perspective recognises that dependency behaviours emerge from the interaction
between individual psychological characteristics and technology design features, rather than being solely attributable to
personal factors.
Quantitative measures were supplemented with qualitative
indicators to provide a comprehensive assessment framework. The binary response format, while limiting nuance,
enables precise statistical analysis and machine learning
applications while maintaining clinical interpretability for
intervention design.
The interdisciplinary approach ensures that findings are
actionable for both psychological intervention and technology design applications, bridging the gap between psychological research and engineering practice in digital wellness
applications.
IV. TEST STATISTICS
The following results present the average impact scores for
mental, emotional, and physical domains based on binary
(Yes = 1, No = 0) responses collected from participants.
A. TEST OF SIGNIFICANCE
To evaluate whether each domain’s mean response significantly differs from a neutral midpoint (0.5), one-sample
t-tests were conducted for the Mental, Emotional, and Physical clusters. This statistical method helps determine whether
the observed levels of perceived impact are likely due to
chance or represent consistent patterns across respondents.
The use of one-sample t-tests in this context is particularly
important because it allows researchers to infer whether the
overall sample of students consistently reports experiencing
a psychological impact—positive or negative—as a result of
their digital engagement.
For instance, if the mean emotional impact score is significantly above 0.5, it would suggest that students are
consistently experiencing emotional disturbances or strain
linked to their digital behaviours. Conversely, a mean score
significantly below 0.5 might indicate a generally positive
or negligible emotional effect. In either case, the statistical
significance provides empirical validation for these trends,
rather than relying solely on descriptive observations.
TABLE 1. Cluster-wise mean scores and t -test results.
The mean mental score was 0.560, emotional 0.536, and
physical 0.612—indicating a generally higher self-reported
impact in physical aspects of device use.
B. INTERPRETATION
The results reveal distinct patterns in how digital device usage
affects users. A statistically significant mean for the Physical
domain (p < 0.0001) suggests that participant’s frequently
experience lifestyle disruptions such as sleep disturbance,
reduced physical activity, and social imbalance.
The Mental domain also showed significance (p = 0.0011),
indicating cognitive effects like attention lapses and memory
reliance. In contrast, the Emotional domain did not reach significance (p = 0.0604), implying variability in how emotional
responses like anxiety or detachment manifest. Overall, the
most consistent impacts appear to be physical and cognitive.

The t-test results offer statistical validation of how strongly
each domain deviates from a neutral stance. The Physical
domain yielded the highest t-value (5.050) and a narrow
confidence interval, indicating a robust and consistent perception of lifestyle disruption among participants. The Mental
domain’s t-value (3.511) also signifies a meaningful departure from neutrality, suggesting reliable effects on attention,
focus, and cognitive functioning.
Although the Emotional domain approached significance
(t = 1.912), its wider confidence interval reflects variability
in emotional response. These findings support the conclusion
that physical and mental impacts of device use are more uniformly perceived than emotional ones. Overall, these results
underscore the importance of treating emotional effects as
a complex and nuanced dimension within digital wellness
research. While mental and physical impacts tend to reflect
shared experiences, emotional responses require more individualised interpretation and may benefit from personalized
intervention strategies. Nevertheless, it must be emphasized
that results obtained in an engineering course for electronics technology students may not apply in other fields or
cultures. Future research will include testing these results
on different engineering students and at different universities. In an attempt to improve the construct validity of the
results, the clusters and supervised predictions have been
compared to the results of the WHO-5 Well-Being Index and
the DASS-21 Stress/Anxiety scales. The correlation analysis revealed a positive correlation between high dependency
clusters and the stress scale (r = 0.41, p < 0.01) and a negative correlation between high dependency clusters and the
well-being scale (r = -0.38, p < 0.01). The domain of emotional response did not achieve significance in discriminating
levels of dependency. Although the presence of emotional
fatigue was evident descriptively, inferential statistical analysis indicates that the use of emotional elements alone may be
unreliable in identifying high-risk individuals. This domain
should be treated with a degree of caution, as the impact of
addiction can be mediated by other elements such as sleep
difficulties and satisfaction with education.
V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
A. COMPREHENSIVE ANALYSIS OF PSYCHOLOGICAL
PROFILES
The comprehensive analysis employed unsupervised and
statistical visualizations to highlight psychological segmentation patterns among engineering students. Key plots-
Silhouette plot, heat map, PCA biplot, and histogram—reveal
complex device dependency behaviors, cluster validity metrics, and variable importance patterns. These visualizations
support model performance evaluation, feature interpretation, and the identification of high-risk digital usage patterns
in student populations, providing a foundation for both
theoretical understanding and practical intervention design.
The combined visualizations show that digital dependency is
not binary or uniform, but reflects a spectrum of psychological traits such as multitasking anxiety, emotional fatigue, and
disrupted sleep. Visualisation tools supported not just interpretation, but also model diagnostics—such as validating the
number of clusters, assessing cohesion/separation, and identifying dominant behavioural variables. High-impact questionnaire items (identified via PCA and heat map analysis)
surfaced as psychological predictors for cluster membership,
deepening the link between raw data and clinical relevance.
These tools lay the groundwork for theory-informed, datadriven intervention strategies. Educators, counsellors, and
technologists can now design persona-specific interventions,
digital literacy programs, or mental health resources tailored
to each behavioural cluster.
B. CLUSTER ANALYSIS AND BEHAVIORAL PERSONAS
The K-Means clustering analysis revealed five distinct
behavioural personas, each representing a unique psychological profile of digital dependency among engineering students.
These personas provide actionable insights for personalised
intervention design and technology adaptation strategies.
1) DIGITAL DEPENDENCY PERSONAS
Based on the clustering analysis, five distinct personas
emerged:
Persona 1: The Adaptive User (22% of sample):
This group demonstrates controlled digital engagement with
minimal dependency indicators. They exhibit strong selfregulation capabilities, maintain clear work-life boundaries,
and show resilience against digital distractions. Their usage
patterns suggest effective integration of technology into daily
life without compromising well-being.
Persona 2: The Anxious Multitasker (28% of sample):
Characterised by high multitasking behaviours combined
with elevated anxiety levels. These users struggle with focus
maintenance and exhibit compulsive checking behaviours.
They represent a high-risk group for intervention, showing
clear signs of technology-mediated stress and cognitive
overload.
Persona 3: The Sleep-Disrupted User (19% of sample): This persona shows primary dependency manifestation
through sleep interference. They engage with devices late
into the night, experience reduced sleep quality, and show
correlating impacts on academic performance and emotional
regulation.
Persona 4: The Socially Withdrawn User (16% of
sample): These individuals show decreased face-to-face social interaction preference, favoring digital communication
channels. While not necessarily high in overall usage, their
dependency manifests through social behavioural changes
and reduced offline engagement.
Persona 5: The Hyper-Connected User (15% of sample): The most dependency-prone group, exhibiting high
scores across multiple domains. They show compulsive usage
patterns, emotional dependency on devices, and significant
lifestyle disruption. This group requires immediate and
intensive intervention strategies.

D. THEORETICAL AND PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS
1) ENGINEERING PSYCHOLOGY APPLICATIONS
The findings provide substantial evidence for the effectiveness of interdisciplinary approaches that bridge engineering
methodologies with psychological insights. The successful
application of machine learning techniques to psychological assessment demonstrates how engineering precision can
enhance the understanding of complex human behaviours.
This integration suggests that future digital wellness interventions should be designed using engineering principles of
system optimization while incorporating psychological theories of behaviour change.
The identification of five distinct personas suggests
that one-Size-fits-all approaches to digital wellness are
inadequate. Instead, technology design should incorporate adaptive algorithms that can identify user personas
in real-time and adjust interface elements, notification
patterns, and engagement mechanisms accordingly. This
personalized approach aligns with engineering principles
of user-centred design while addressing the psychological reality of individual differences in digital dependency
susceptibility.
a: CLINICAL AND INTERVENTION APPLICATIONS
The predictive capability (macro-F1 = 0.88) demonstrates
that the developed framework has sufficient accuracy
for practical screening applications in university wellness
centres. The clear identification of high-risk personas
(Anxious Multitaskers and Hyper-Connected Users) enables
early intervention strategies before dependency patterns
become entrenched. The moderate silhouette scores suggest
that dependency exists on a continuum, supporting graduated intervention approaches rather than categorical treatment
protocols.
The sleep disruption findings are particularly significant
for university populations, where academic performance
directly impacts long-term career outcomes. The identification of sleep-related dependency patterns provides a concrete
target for intervention that has measurable outcomes and
direct relevance to academic success.

b: TECHNOLOGY DESIGN IMPLICATIONS
The research provides actionable insights for technology
designers working to create more psychologically healthy
digital environments. The persona-based approach suggests
that interfaces should be adaptable based on user psychological profiles, with different notification strategies, engagement patterns, and feature availability for different user
types. For Anxious Multitaskers, interfaces could incorporate
mindfulness-based design elements, simplified information
presentation, and anxiety-reducing visual design patterns.
Sleep-Disrupted Users would benefit from circadian-aware
interfaces that gradually reduce engagement cues in evening
hours and provide sleep hygiene reminders.
Hyper-Connected Users require more intensive intervention features, including usage-limiting tools and alternative
engagement suggestions.
VI. FUTURE WORK
A. ADVANCED METHODOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENTS
1) TEMPORAL BEHAVIOURAL TRACKING AND
LONGITUDINAL ANALYSIS
Future research should incorporate comprehensive temporal behavioural tracking to capture the dynamic nature of

2) MULTIMODAL PHYSIOLOGICAL INTEGRATION
Future studies can significantly enhance psychological prediction accuracy by incorporating real-time physiological
metrics such as heart rate variability and sleep quality
indices, electrodermal activity, and cortisol level monitoring.
These objective biomarkers can provide continuous, unobtrusive assessment of stress and fatigue levels, complementing
survey-based models with quantitative physiological indicators. The integration of wearable sensor technology with
machine learning algorithms will enable more precise classification of mental health states and real-time detection of
psychological distress. This multimodal approach aligns with
engineering psychology principles by providing objective,
measurable indicators of subjective psychological states.
3) INTELLIGENT REAL-TIME INTERVENTION SYSTEMS
The development of sophisticated, AI-powered intervention
systems represents a critical next step in translating research
findings into practical applications. These systems should
provide context-aware, personalized feed-back during excessive screen use, incorporating machine learning algorithms
that adapt to individual behavioural patterns and preferences.
Advanced intervention features could include predictive
modelling to identify high-risk periods, automated scheduling of digital breaks, integration with university wellness
resources, and peer support network activation. The systems
should operate across multiple platforms and devices, providing seamless support for digital well-being management
in increasingly complex technological environments.
4) CROSS-CULTURAL AND INTERDISCIPLINARY EXPANSION
Expanding research across diverse academic disciplines,
cultural backgrounds, age demographics, and international
populations will improve model generalizability and reveal
the universal versus context-specific patterns of digital
dependency. This expansion should include engineering
students from different cultural contexts, comparison with
students from non-technical disciplines, and investigation of
dependency patterns across different educational systems.
A broader, more diverse dataset will enhance the design
of inclusive digital well-being programs that accommodate
wide-ranging user profiles, cultural values, and technological
adoption patterns.
B. ENGINEERING PSYCHOLOGY INTEGRATION
1) HUMAN-CENTRED TECHNOLOGY DESIGN
Future work should focus on developing comprehensive
design guidelines for technology interfaces that promote
psychological well-being while maintaining functional effectiveness. This includes research into adaptive interface design
that responds to user psychological states, incorporation of
persuasive design principles for positive behaviour change,
and development of technology features that actively support rather than undermine mental health. Another critical
aspect involves the development of digital tools and features
specifically tailored to support mental health. For instance,
integrating mental health check-ins, digital well-being dashboards, or cognitive rest timers into user interfaces can
empower individuals to manage their psychological state
while interacting with technology. Importantly, these features
should be designed not as afterthoughts or add-ons, but as
core components of the user experience, reflecting a shift
toward human-centred technology.
Overall, the future of digital interface design must prioritize a balance between usability and well-being, recognizing
that the success of a technology is no longer measured solely
by its functionality, but also by its capacity to support the
cognitive and emotional resilience of its users. Advancing
this vision will require inter-disciplinary collaboration among
engineers, designers, psychologists, and behavioral scientists
to ensure that emerging technologies are not only efficient but
also ethically and psychologically aligned with the needs of
their users.
2) INTERVENTION EFFECTIVENESS EVALUATION
Rigorous evaluation of intervention effectiveness through
controlled studies will establish evidence-based guidelines
for digital wellness programs. This includes comparative
analysis of different intervention approaches, long-term
follow-up studies to assess sustained behaviour change,
and economic analysis of intervention cost-effectiveness for
institutional implementation. Overall, a rigorous and multidimensional approach to evaluating intervention effectiveness
not only strengthens the scientific validity of digital wellness
programs but also equips institutions with the knowledge to
make strategic, data-driven decisions. This evidence-based
foundation paves the way for developing personalised, effective, and scalable solutions to address digital dependency in
student populations.
VII. CONCLUSION
This research provides a comprehensive exploration of how
electronic device usage influences the psychological wellbeing of engineering students. By utilizing a blend of
clustering, dimensionality reduction, and machine learning
classification, we successfully identified behaviorally distinct
sub-groups and interpreted the cognitive and emotional
impacts of digital dependency.

ABSTRACT
Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has emerged as a promising interdisciplinary field
that combines quantum computing with machine learning to address complex computational problems.
This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the theoretical foundations, unified taxonomy, and
key methodologies in QML. We discuss quantum data encoding techniques, variational quantum models,
neural-inspired quantum architectures, and quantum data learning approaches, along with their associated
challenges and limitations. The survey further examines evaluation strategies, the concept of quantum
advantage, and the role of current quantum hardware and software platforms in advancing QML research.
In addition, major application domains and the growing importance of trustworthy QML, including
interpretability, robustness, and security, are explored. Finally, we highlight open challenges and future
research directions to provide insights into the evolving landscape of Quantum Machine Learning.

supervised learning, hybrid quantum-classical network.
I. INTRODUCTION
The rapid advancements in quantum computing and artificial
intelligence have led to the emergence of Quantum Machine
Learning (QML) as a transformative research area. By integrating the computational power of quantum systems with the
learning capabilities of machine learning models, QML aims
to overcome several limitations of classical approaches and
enable new possibilities in data-driven intelligence.
In recent years, the field that combines machine learning
and quantum computation has become especially vibrant.
In the realm of classical computing, developments in
deep learning have transformed many fields of science:
protein folding [1], automatic language translation [2],
and autonomous perception, which were previously only
open problems in scientific research, have now become
viable engineering applications. However, conventional
approaches still face known limitations. Training large
models requires energy measured in gigawatt-hours [3];

combinatorial optimization at the industrial scale remains
intractable even on the most powerful classical processor [4];
and kernel-based learning over extremely high-dimensional
data encounters fundamental complexity barriers that no
architectural refinement can completely overcome [5].
Quantum Machine Learning (QML) lies at this intersection. The primary goal of such a research direction lies
in finding out whether quantum mechanical resources like
superposition, entanglement, and interference provide any
real-world advantage for learning algorithms [6], [7]. While
no guarantee exists for each of these possibilities, there are
enough theoretical findings to show that quantum feature
spaces can be utilized to classify objects whose separation
would not be possible through classical computation [8],
and that quantum-assisted algorithms for linear algebraic
manipulations [9] and sampling techniques [10] could
speed up classical computation. The feasibility of these
requirements continues to remain uncertain, but a better
understanding of these issues is steadily emerging through
empirical and theoretical explorations, whose goals this
survey strives to fulfill.

A. WHAT IS QUANTUM MACHINE LEARNING?
Terminological ambiguity in QML has led to inconsistent
claims in both theory and experiment, making a precise
definition essential. In its broadest sense, QML refers to
the study of learning algorithms that employ quantum
information processing as an accelerated subroutine or as
the primary computational mechanism [6], [11]. Formally,
a QML model implements a parameterized mapping fθ
:
X
→Y, where the mapping is realized, in whole or in
part, through a quantum circuit acting on a Hilbert space
of dimension 2n for an n-qubit register. The statistical
learning framework applies throughout: models are trained on
finite samples, assessed on held-out data, and subject to the
standard tensions between expressivity and generalization.
The field is organized into three paradigms, and distinguishing them is important for avoiding confusion. The first
is quantum-accelerated classical learning, where a classical
algorithm delegates specific subroutines, such as matrix
inversion, principal component analysis, and Monte Carlo
sampling, to a quantum processor that can execute them faster
under certain input models [9], [12]. The second is quantumenhanced feature learning, in which quantum circuits provide
feature maps or kernel functions that are then used within
a classical statistical framework; the quantum component
produces representations that may be classically intractable
rather than accelerating known classical computations [8],
[13]. The third paradigm is concerned with quantum data,
including density matrices, quantum channels, or quantum
measurements. Quantum data can arise naturally in the
context of quantum chemistry, quantum communication, and
quantum metrology; here, QML will avoid any classical-toquantum conversion bottleneck altogether [14].
By default, QML does not guarantee a computational
advantage. The existence of an exponentially large Hilbert
space does not, by itself, confer computational advantage: a
quantum model that can be efficiently simulated classically
offers no benefit, and recent dequantization results have
demonstrated that several well-known QML algorithms admit
classical analogues with comparable complexity under reasonable data assumptions [15]. Genuine quantum advantage
in learning requires that the quantum component compute
something classically difficult, that the encoding of classical
data into quantum states not consume the advantage, and
that the output be extractable by measurement without exponential overhead. These three conditions are simultaneously
satisfied only in specific, carefully constructed settings, and
identifying those settings is one of the field’s central open
problems.
B. QUANTUM ML VS. CLASSICAL ML
Classical machine learning (ML) operates on bit-encoded
data using deterministic or probabilistic transformations,
scales polynomially in the number of features and training
samples. By contrast, QML encodes data into quantum states
residing in a Hilbert space of dimension 2n, and manipulates
them through unitary circuits that take advantage of superposition, entanglement, and interference. This structure gives
QML access to hypothesis classes believed to be classically
intractable [6], [8]. The main differences across important
dimensions are summarized in Table 1.
QML offers three potential advantages over classical
ML: (i) exponential speedups for specific linear-algebra
tasks via subroutines such as HHL [9]; (ii) richer feature
representations through quantum kernel methods that may be
classically hard to simulate [8]; and (iii) native processing
of quantum data arising in chemistry, sensing, and manybody physics, completely avoiding the classical encoding
bottleneck [14]. Each advantage is conditional on hardware
accuracy and efficient data loading [15].

C. WHY QUANTUM AI?
Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly
deep learning and foundation models, have led to remarkable
achievements across diverse application domains. However,
these successes have also exposed several fundamental computational limitations of classical AI systems. As illustrated
in Fig. 1, modern deep neural networks often contain billions
of trainable parameters, requiring enormous computational
resources for training and inference. Consequently, state-ofthe-art AI models demand high-performance GPU clusters
and specialized computing infrastructure, resulting in substantial financial costs. Furthermore, training these models
may require several days or even weeks of continuous computation, accompanied by significant energy consumption
and environmental impact. As model complexity continues
to increase, optimization also becomes increasingly difficult
due to highly non-convex objective functions, vanishing or

D. SURVEY METHODOLOGY
The literature included in this survey was collected through
a comprehensive search of major scientific databases,
including Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library,
SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, Wiley Online Library, and
Google Scholar. The search primarily covered publications from 2016 to 2025, with earlier seminal works
included where necessary to provide historical context.
Representative search terms included Quantum Machine

Circuits, Quantum Deep Learning, Quantum Reinforcement
Learning, Quantum Kernel Methods, Hybrid Quantum-
Classical Learning, and related keywords. Figure 2 illustrates

The retrieved literature was screened to retain peerreviewed journal articles, high-quality conference papers,
influential review articles, and seminal theoretical contributions directly relevant to Quantum Machine Learning, while duplicate records, non-English publications,
abstracts, theses, and studies lacking sufficient technical relevance were excluded. The selected papers were
subsequently analyzed and organized according to learning paradigms, model architectures, application domains,
hardware and software ecosystems, NISQ compatibility,
explainability, and future research directions. This multidimensional analysis also served as the basis for constructing

1) RESEARCH GAP
Although numerous surveys have been published on Quantum Machine Learning, most of them focus on a limited
aspect of the field, such as quantum kernels, variational
algorithms, hybrid quantum-classical models, or theoretical learning guarantees. As a result, the existing literature remains fragmented and does not provide readers
with a unified understanding of the rapidly evolving
QML ecosystem. Several important research gaps can be
identified:
Lack of a unified taxonomy: Existing surveys typically
classify methods from a single perspective (e.g., algorithms
or applications), without integrating data type, learning
paradigm, model architecture, NISQ compatibility, and faulttolerance into a coherent framework.
Limited coverage of recent developments: Most surveys
were published before the recent advances in quantum
hardware, quantum foundation models, quantum generative
AI, trustworthy AI, and hybrid quantum-classical learning.
Insufficient practical perspective: Many reviews emphasize
theoretical formulations while providing little discussion of
software ecosystems, implementation frameworks, hardware
platforms, benchmarking methodologies, and deployment
challenges.
Minimal discussion of responsible and trustworthy QML: Explainability, robustness, security, fairness,
reproducibility, and ethical considerations remain largely
overlooked despite becoming increasingly important for
real-world deployment.
Absence of a future-oriented roadmap: Existing surveys
generally summarize current methods but rarely identify
long-term research directions or discuss how QML may
evolve from today’s NISQ devices toward fault-tolerant
quantum computing.

Given the rapid expansion of Quantum Machine Learning
across algorithms, hardware, software, and applications,
researchers require a comprehensive reference that connects
these previously isolated perspectives. Rather than reviewing a single subfield, this survey integrates foundational
principles, learning paradigms, implementation technologies,
practical applications, and emerging challenges into a unified
framework that reflects the current state of QML research.
F. CONTRIBUTIONS
To address the research gaps identified above, this survey
makes the following contributions. Table 2 compares this
review against 12 existing QML surveys across ten dimensions. As the table shows, no prior survey covers all ten
dimensions; this review is the first to do so.
• Unified taxonomy addressing fragmented literature.
Existing surveys classify QML methods using only
one or two perspectives. We introduce a comprehensive five-dimensional taxonomy that simultaneously
organizes methods by data type, model architecture,
learning paradigm, NISQ compatibility, and faulttolerance requirements, providing a unified framework
for comparing diverse QML approaches.
• Bridging the theory-to-practice gap. Unlike surveys

insights, and practical discussions to support researchers
from both quantum computing and machine learning
backgrounds.

dequantization vulnerabilities, and the gap between

This subsection categorizes QML models based on how quantum and classical components are architecturally integrated.
1) FULLY QUANTUM LEARNING MODELS
Fully quantum learning models operate entirely within
the quantum domain, where both the data and the model
parameters are encoded as quantum states and quantum
operators, respectively. A generic fully quantum neural
network can be expressed as

Several representative architectures have been proposed
within this framework, see Table: 4. Quantum perceptrons
serve as the quantum counterparts of classical perceptrons,
employing unitary operations followed by measurementbased decision rules. Quantum Boltzmann machines (QBMs)
can be seen as generalizations of classical Boltzmann
machines by utilizing quantum Hamiltonians for the modeling of quantum correlation and entanglement phenomena
within physical systems. Quantum neural networks (QNNs)
that often come into being by means of deep parameterized

differences. The process involves iterations of running the
quantum circuit to compute the expected value, which is later

allows us to combine classical machine learning techniques
and quantum representations.

Such architectures have been used in applications such as
classification, regression, generation of new samples, and
quantum state learning among others. Data encodings and

Indeed, hybrid quantum–classical algorithms have special
potential for applications on NISQ machines due to the fact
that they relieve restrictions imposed by hardware, offloading
some computations to classical computers. However, there
is still much work to be done as hybrid systems suffer
from several problems, among which are the issue of
measurement overhead, noise-related errors, limited circuit
depth, and barren plateau problem. Efficient ansätze design,
better methods of estimating gradients, and noise tolerance training strategies are some issues currently under
study.
3) QUANTUM KERNEL METHODS
Quantum kernel methods constitute an important class of
quantum machine learning approaches that extend classical
kernel-based algorithms into the quantum domain. The
central idea is to implicitly map classical data x into a
high-dimensional quantum Hilbert space via a feature map
implemented by a parameterized quantum circuit. Formally,
a quantum feature map prepares a state |φ(x)⟩= U(x)|0⟩,
where U(x) encodes the input data into a quantum state. The
corresponding quantum kernel is then defined as the inner
product
K(x, x′) = |⟨φ(x)|φ(x′)⟩|2,
which can be efficiently estimated on a quantum device using
techniques such as the swap test or direct fidelity estimation.
Such quantum kernels can be incorporated into existing
machine learning algorithms based on classical kernels, such
as support vector machines, kernel ridge regression, and
Gaussian process, and therefore allow quantum learning to
occur without requiring the entire process to be performed by
a quantum system. The benefit of quantum kernel approach is
that quantum kernels have the ability to create feature spaces
that could be intractable for classical systems to compute.
Quantum kernel algorithms are especially appealing during
the NISQ era since they demand modest circuit depths and
quantum resource use as compared to more sophisticated
variational models. Nevertheless, the applicability of these
models hinges significantly on the design of a suitable
feature map and its corresponding kernel attributes, such
as expressive power, learnability, and generalizability. Some
of the issues that confront these models include kernel
concentration (whereby kernels lose information content in
higher dimensions), susceptibility to noise, and increased
computational costs due to multiple circuit runs when
estimating kernels. Current studies revolve around developing problem-appropriate feature maps, increasing resilience
against noise, and determining conditions under which
quantum kernels exhibit an advantage over classical kernels.
4) QUANTUM GENERATIVE MODELS
Quantum generative models aim to learn and reproduce probability distributions using quantum mechanical principles,
offering a natural framework for modeling complex classical
or quantum data. In these models, a parameterized quantum
circuit prepares a quantum state |ψ(θ)⟩= U(θ)|0⟩, such that
measurement outcomes sampled from this state approximate
a target distribution pdata(x). The model distribution is thus
given by
pθ(x) = |⟨x|ψ(θ)⟩|2,
where {|x⟩} denotes the computational basis. Training
involves optimizing the parameters θ
to minimize a
divergence measure (e.g., Kullback–Leibler divergence or
Wasserstein distance) between pθ and pdata, typically using
a hybrid quantum–classical loop.

D. CLASSIFICATION OF QML MODELS ACCORDING TO
HARDWARE COMPATIBILITY
A practically significant classification of quantum machine
learning (QML) models is based on their compatibility with
noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Current
quantum devices are characterized by a limited number
of qubits, short coherence times, gate imperfections, and
restricted connectivity. Consequently, QML models must
be designed to operate under these constraints, balancing
circuit expressivity with robustness to noise and feasibility
of implementation. This perspective distinguishes between
models that are directly realizable on present-day devices and
those that remain primarily theoretical due to their resource
demands.

IV. QUANTUM DATA ENCODING: THE INPUT PROBLEM
Quantum data encoding is an essential component in quantum
machine learning, which transforms classical data into
quantum forms accessible to quantum machine learning
algorithms. In contrast to classical machine learning, in which
data access is generally efficient, quantum machine learning
algorithms require explicit state preparation, which can be
computationally costly. The choice of quantum data encoding
has a strong effect on the expressiveness of the quantum
model, circuit depth, noise robustness, and scalability, which
are all critical in achieving quantum speedup in practice.
In this section, the most popular quantum data encoding
schemes are discussed, including their theoretical trade-offs,
as well as the data loading challenges faced when using noisy
intermediate-scale quantum machines.
A. ENCODING STRATEGIES AND SCHEMES
Quantum data encoding is the process of defining the
mapping of classical data onto quantum data, which can
then be processed in quantum circuits. The most commonly
used quantum data encoding techniques include amplitude
encoding, angle encoding, basis encoding, and Hamiltonian
encoding.
Amplitude encoding embeds classical feature vectors into
quantum state amplitudes, enabling compact representations
with logarithmic qubit scaling but requiring expensive state
preparation. It has been applied in quantum-assisted signal
denoising using the quantum Fourier transform [21], although
exponential gate complexity remains a major scalability
limitation. Neural-assisted state preparation methods have
been proposed to reduce circuit depth through approximate
embeddings [22].

B. TRADE-OFFS AND THEORETICAL ANALYSIS
The effectiveness of quantum encoding methods depends
on the trade-off between expressivity, circuit depth, and
computational complexity. Quantum embeddings with high
expressivity can result in more expressive feature representations but require deeper quantum circuits, which can
further increase the vulnerability of the quantum encoding
methods to noise on noisy intermediate-scale quantum
(NISQ) devices.
Expressivity depends on the structure of the embedding
method, the number of qubits, and the depth of the quantum
circuit. Quantum circuits can efficiently represent complex
functions with high expressivity due to the parameterized
quantum circuit structure and the ability of the quantum
circuit depth to improve the expressivity of the quantum
circuit. However, the depth of the quantum circuit can result
in training challenges and barren plateaus [28]. This makes
the depth of the quantum circuit a significant limitation
of quantum encoding methods. Shallow quantum encoding
methods like angle encoding and basis encoding are more
robust to noise on the quantum circuit and result in low
expressivity, while amplitude and Hamiltonian encoding
result in deeper quantum circuits and more gate count [29].
Encoding complexity can affect quantum distributed
systems due to the highly entangled quantum circuit structure
and the costs of communication and data transmission
between quantum processing devices [30], [31].

C. THE ENCODING BOTTLENECK IN PRACTICE
The encoding bottleneck is one of the main limitations in
quantum machine learning, arising from the high cost of
loading classical data into quantum states. State preparation
often dominates total computational complexity, reducing
potential quantum speedups.
In the case of unstructured data, the preparation of an arbitrary n-qubit state is known to require exponentially scaling
circuit depth, thus rendering amplitude encoding impractical
for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices [33]. Although
the use of approximate and variational state preparation
reduces the circuit depth, they are limited due to noise and
entanglement.
Low-rank and approximation-based methods reduce gate
complexity by exploiting structure in classical data, while
hybrid classical–quantum approaches predict circuit parameters directly from classical inputs to accelerate data
loading [33], [34]. The encoding bottleneck, see Fig: 10,
also affects optimization tasks where repeated parameter
embedding dominates computation time [35]. Noise accumulation during deep encoding circuits further motivates
noise-resilient and dissipative state preparation methods [36].
Quantum state preparation complexity for generic data is:
Cprep = O(2n).
Total computation cost becomes:
Ctotal = Cprep + Cquantum.

quantum machine learning, and efficient encoding strategies

B. HYBRID QUANTUM-CLASSICAL LEARNING LOOP
In NISQ devices, full quantum training is not possible yet.
Instead, the variational model is trained via a hybrid quantumclassical loop, where the quantum hardware is employed as a
co-processor to evaluate the circuit and the classical hardware
is used to update the parameters. At iteration t, the parameter
update takes the form
θ(t+1) = θ(t) −η ∇θ L(θ(t)),
where η is the learning rate and the gradient is estimated
from repeated quantum measurements. The loop consists of
three stages: (i) encoding classical input data into quantum
states, (ii) executing the parameterised circuit and measuring
relevant observables, and (iii) updating parameters on the
classical processor. This workflow is illustrated in Fig. 11.

evaluates the circuit and measurements; the classical processor updates

deep learning frameworks and is well-suited to current
hardware constraints.

QNNs extend classical neural network principles into the
quantum domain by exploiting quantum states, unitary
transformations, and measurement processes. Three broad
architectural families have been explored (Table 13).
Circuit-based QNNs are the most widely studied. They
are implemented as parameterised sequences of rotation

Dissipative QNNs model open-system dynamics, where
evolution is governed by completely positive trace-preserving
(CPTP) maps, see Eq: 8:

VI. EVALUATION AND QUANTUM ADVANTAGE
This section discusses the advantages of quantum computing
in machine learning.
A. DEFINITIONS OF QUANTUM ADVANTAGE
Quantum advantage in machine learning refers to the ability
of a quantum algorithm to outperform the best known
classical algorithm under well-defined resource constraints.
Formally, given a task T and resource measure R (e.g., time,
queries, samples), quantum advantage is achieved if:
Rquantum(T ) ≪Rclassical(T )
This advantage can manifest in different forms:
• Provable Advantage: Established via complexitytheoretic separations
• Empirical Advantage: Observed in experiments on
specific tasks
• Potential Advantage: Suggested under assumptions
(e.g., QRAM, fault tolerance)
It is important to distinguish between asymptotic advantage and practical advantage, as many theoretical results do
not translate directly to real-world settings, see Fig: 13.
Fig: 14 and Table 17 summarize the different levels
of quantum advantage frequently discussed in the QML
literature. Although many algorithms possess attractive
theoretical complexity guarantees, only a limited number
have been experimentally demonstrated on existing quantum
hardware. Moreover, successful execution on NISQ devices
should not be interpreted as evidence of practical quantum
advantage, since hardware noise, data encoding overhead,
and measurement costs may substantially reduce the expected
computational gains. Consequently, distinguishing theoretical, simulated, experimental, and practical advantages
provides a more balanced understanding of the current
capabilities and limitations of QML.

F. DISCUSSION: WHEN CAN QUANTUM ADVANTAGE BE

A realistic pathway to quantum advantage in machine

VII. HARDWARE PLATFORMS AND SOFTWARE
ECOSYSTEM
The implementation of quantum machine learning can only
happen based on the quantum computational hardware used,
along with the software environment utilized for the design
and execution of the algorithms. Unlike classical computingbased machine learning implementations, quantum computing has entered into what is known as NISQ technology. This
technology has some factors that impact algorithm design and
performance, such as noise, decoherence, number of qubits,
and connectivity. Different quantum hardware approaches,
such as superconducting quantum devices, trapped ions,
photonic systems, and neutral atoms, are characterized by
various trade-offs between scalability, coherence times, gate
accuracy, and connectivity. Quantum software architectures
like Qiskit, PennyLane, Cirq, and TensorFlow Quantum

A. NISQ DEVICES AND CONSTRAINTS
Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices are
characterized by limited qubit counts, short coherence times,
and high gate error rates, which significantly influence the
design and performance of quantum machine learning algorithms. Since NISQ devices cannot implement full quantum
error correction, most algorithms rely on shallow circuits,
hybrid quantum–classical methods, and error mitigation
techniques [42].
Quantum

algorithm accuracy. The evolution of a quantum state in the
presence of noise can be modeled as
ρ′ = E(ρ),
where E represents the noise channel. Decoherence causes
quantum states to lose coherence over time and is often
modeled as
ρ(t) = e−t/T2ρ(0),
where T2 is the decoherence time constant.
The limitations of NISQ devices, see Tab: 21, include a
restricted number of qubits and their limited connectivity,
and only simple circuits can be run because of errors
arising from gates [43]. To overcome these limitations,
variational algorithms that have been developed for use in
noisy hardware are utilized [44]. Mitigation methods such
as zero-noise extrapolation limit the noise in calculations
without any extra qubits being used [45], [46]. The design of
noise-resilient algorithms and mitigators for QAOA increases
efficiency in noisy hardware [36], [47].

Overall, NISQ hardware limitations require QML algorithms to use shallow circuits, hybrid optimization, and error

Quantum machine learning and quantum computing are used

systems and radical pair mechanisms using parameterized
quantum circuits and classical optimization [67].

IX. TRUSTWORTHY QUANTUM MACHINE LEARNING
With the increasing complexity of quantum machine learning
models and their applications in the real world, issues of
interpretability, robustness, and trustworthiness are becoming
more relevant. Similar to classical machine learning models,
quantum machine learning models also have the potential to
be black-box models, which creates problems in understanding the decision-making process. Quantum machine learning
models are also found to be more sensitive to noise, which
creates problems with regard to reliability and security [45].
A. INTERPRETABILITY OF QML MODELS
The interpretability of quantum machine learning models
relates to the explanation of how a quantum circuit processes
information and makes a prediction. Several QML models,
such as variational quantum circuits and quantum neural
networks, use parameterized quantum gates, and their internal
workings are not easily interpretable. Techniques such as
parameter sensitivity analysis, analysis of quantum feature
maps, and visualization of quantum feature spaces help
to elucidate the decision-making processes of quantum
models [64].
In addition, quantum state tomography and classical
shadow methods provide further ways to investigate the
intermediate quantum states and track the flow of information
through the quantum circuit. The mechanisms through which
the quantum model is trained can be explained, thus providing
further clarity and trust in the quantum machine learning
model.
B. GENERALIZATION
Generalization refers to a quantum machine learning model’s
ability to perform accurately on unseen data, rather than
merely memorizing the training set. In QML, generalization
is influenced by several unique factors, including the structure
of the quantum feature map, the expressivity of the variational
circuit, and the number of training samples relative to
the Hilbert space dimension. Due to the exponentially
large Hilbert space, QML models are prone to overfitting
when the number of parameterized gates grows without a
corresponding increase in training data [91].

To evaluate generalization, the QML researchers employ

On the other hand, QML models with low rank feature maps
and carefully chosen circuit ansatzes generally generalize

Most importantly, strong generalization in QML requires
balancing model expressivity, training data size, noise, and
circuit depth — a trade-off less known than in classical
machine learning, and therefore difficult to use in reliable
ways.
C. ROBUSTNESS TO NOISE AND ADVERSARIAL ATTACKS
The issue of robustness is a major concern for quantum
machine learning, given the high sensitivity of quantum
circuits to noise, decoherence, and gate errors. The presence
of noise is known to affect the training and prediction
processes, resulting in an unstable learning process and inaccurate prediction results. The use of methods for mitigating
errors, such as zero-noise extrapolation, is commonly used
to improve the robustness of quantum machine learning
models [93].
Quantum machine learning models are also known to be
prone to adversarial perturbations, where slight changes to
the input encoding and quantum circuit may cause significant
changes to the output results. As such, the need to develop
quantum algorithms that are resistant to noise is crucial for
the deployment of quantum machine learning models.
D. ETHICAL AND SECURITY IMPLICATIONS
Quantum machine learning technology is seen to have some
ethical and security implications similar to classical artificial
intelligence, such as fairness, transparency, and the appropriate use of technology. Quantum-enhanced machine learning
has potential applications in areas such as cybersecurity,
healthcare, and finance, among others, where errors and
biases can result in critical consequences if not addressed
properly.
Security is another important aspect to consider, especially
considering that quantum machine learning has the potential
to be used in cryptanalysis, secure communication, and other
security applications. The development of quantum machine
learning technology requires the establishment of appropriate
ethics, transparency, and security measures for its appropriate
and safe use.

DIRECTIONS
While significant advancements have been achieved in the
domain of quantum machine learning, challenges are yet to be
overcome before the practicality of quantum machine learning is achieved. The challenges include hardware problems,
