C. Results
The outcomes of the conducted experiments are comprehensively consolidated in Tables III and IV. The details of each
experiment group will be discussed in Sections IV-C1–IV-C3.
1) Baselines: Our study includes three primary network
configurations for both the LUCAS dataset (see Table III)
and the RaCA dataset (see Table IV), denoted as ViT +
Trans., ViT + LSTM, and CNN + Trans. These configurations
represent distinct hybrid architectural approaches we adopted
for our analysis. Specifically, we utilized the ViT and a conventional CNN, here ResNet-101, to process image data. For
the analysis of time-series data, we substitute long short-term
memory (LSTM) networks over Transformers due to LSTM’s
established efficacy in managing sequential information [48].
Irrespective of the selected method (supervised or SSL) and
the type of input features, our findings generally indicate that
the ViT + Trans. configuration outperforms the other two
configurations across most evaluated metrics.

For the LUCAS dataset, approximately 70 000 unlabeled
randomly selected samples were utilized, whereas for the
RaCA dataset, around 30 000 were employed to prepare our
pre-trained model. To guarantee relevance to soil, we evaluated
the land-cover classes within each downloaded image patch.
If the majority of a Landsat-8 image patch was identified
as irrelevant land-cover classes such as built-up areas or
permanent water bodies, that sample was excluded from our
analysis. We have used using ESA land-cover product [49] for
this purpose.
In both datasets, the performance of SSL-SoilNet was
superior to that of supervised SoilNet, demonstrating the

climate-based information geographically. This integration
of information contributed to enhanced prediction accuracy.
A notable observation was made with the RaCA dataset
results, where the improvement in evaluation metrics was
substantial. Specifically, the RMSE decreased by 8.38 Mg/ha,
the R2 increased by 4%, and the MAE was reduced by
8.39 Mg/ha. This marked enhancement may be attributed to
the model’s ability to address severe data imbalance, especially
in the upper quantiles of SOC ranges. Essentially, leveraging
information from random samples allowed the model to better
understand patterns in samples with high SOC levels. It is
important to highlight that the RPIQ metric does not show
improvement, which is attributed to its definition focusing on
the population spread rather than solely on accuracy. A model
exhibiting a low RMSE can still result in a high RPIQ,
suggesting that RMSE and RPIQ metrics should be analyzed
in conjunction.
3) Ablation Study: To evaluate the contribution of input
features in our study, we conducted an ablation study by
categorizing our input features into four groups: Landsat
images and their derived indices, topographic information
(i.e., elevation and slope), and two types of climate information (i.e., primary and secondary variables), as introduced in
Section III-B4. We tested each feature group across different
configurations, including ViT + Transformer, ViT + LSTM,
and CNN + Transformer models in Tables III and IV.
As expected, the exclusion of all climate information resulted
in the lowest performance across all configurations, underscoring the significance of using time-series information. This
is because soil properties are influenced not only by surface information from satellite images but also by climatic
conditions. Incorporating secondary climate variables yields
marginally improved outcomes in terms of RMSE, CCC, and
R2 compared to primary climate variables, indicating a contributory role of this feature group. Topographic information
consistently enhanced prediction accuracy for both datasets.
The omission of primary and secondary climate variables
sometimes led to a reduction in the MAE, for example, in the
supervised training of ViT + LSTM for the LUCAS dataset
and supervised training of ViT + Trans. for the RaCA dataset.
This is possibly due to the complex nature of time-series
data, which may contain noisy information. Removing such
noisy data can, in some instances, improve overall prediction
accuracy.

In the second step, we compared our results with those
from seven commonly used ML models. The first model we
evaluated was Random Forest (RF), a popular ML algorithm
often applied to regression tasks, especially in the field of soil
science (e.g., [50]). The second model, known as Deep Forest,
is an advanced version of RF. It is a decision tree ensemble
method that requires fewer hyperparameters than DL models [51]. Additionally, we explored two variations of gradient
boosting: XGBoost [52] and Gradient Boosting Decision Tree
(GBDT) [53]. XGBoost is an optimized distributed gradient
boosting library known for enhancing efficiency and performance. GBDT is also a powerful technique that improves
prediction accuracy by building decision trees sequentially,
focusing on minimizing errors from previous trees. We also
evaluated extremely randomized trees (ERT) [54], a variation
of random forest that introduces additional randomness into
the model, potentially increasing the diversity among the trees.
The other ML models used for comparison were support vector
regressor (SVR) and Cubist, which is a rule-based model
that combines decision trees and linear regression [55]. The
hyperparameters for all implemented models were determined
using randomized grid search.
Tables V and VI present the analysis of two datasets,
LUCAS and RaCA, providing insightful observations on
the performance of various models. Across both datasets,
SSL-SoilNet, the self-supervised contrastive learning model,
achieved the highest accuracy as measured by RMSE and R2.
This highlights the superiority of our proposed approach,
largely due to the incorporation of additional information
from unlabeled data during training. Additionally, for the
LUCAS dataset, SSL-SoilNet surpassed other models in MAE,
CCC, and RPIQ metrics, indicating that our approach excels
in accuracy, provides more realistic prediction intervals (as
calculated through RPIQ), and ensures greater concordance
between predictions and observations (measured by CCC), all
while maintaining the lowest mean average error. Supervised
SoilNet also showed commendable performance, surpassing
other ML models. It is important to note that the R2 values
are low in certain cases, such as SVR and ERT, because these
models struggled to capture the nonlinearity inherent in the
data, which arises from the complexity of the soil system [56].

E. Discussion
We have illustrated the spatial distribution of observed SOC
for test samples, alongside the predicted SOC from both SSL
and supervised SoilNet, as well as the top-performing ML
methods, RF for RaCA and GBDT for LUCAS datasets, across
our study areas, which encompass the CONUS and Europe in
Figs. 7 and 8. To enhance the visualization of the various
model performances, we plotted the predicted values against
the observed values in Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2. The
map of residuals is also included in Supplementary Fig. S3.
In our analysis of the RaCA dataset, regions such as the
northeastern area, west coastal area, and rocky mountain area

regarding mountainous regions, this variability can be partly

are characterized by their tendency to be shallow, thin, and

are anticipated to have a more significant influence on SOC

We focused on three distinct areas characterized by varying climatic conditions and land-cover classes to assess the
performance of our implemented methodologies. Area A,
located in the midwestern part of the United States, features
land-cover classes predominantly consisting of wetlands and
tree covers [60]. This region’s land cover is indicative of
its ecological diversity and complexity. Area B, situated in
the northeastern United States, is characterized by wetlands
and forests, along with relatively high precipitation and low
average temperatures [61]. Conversely, Area C is distinguished
by its higher temperatures and above-average precipitation levels, with land cover primarily comprising wetlands, croplands,
and developed areas in the southeastern United States.
Despite the inherent differences among these areas, a commonality emerges in their heterogeneity concerning SOC
values. Each area contains samples with both exceptionally
low and high SOC values, presenting challenges for any
ML/DL models in achieving accurate predictions. This variability underscores the complexity of SOC prediction and
the necessity for sophisticated models capable of accommodating such diverse environmental conditions. The outcomes
obtained from the RF model serve as evidence supporting this
claim, as the final map generated by RF failed to accurately
capture the data trends across Areas A–C. This inadequacy
highlights the model’s limitation in reflecting the intricate
spatial variations inherent to each area. In contrast, supervised-
SoilNet demonstrated a marginally improved performance,
particularly for Area A, as depicted on the right side of Fig. 7.
Supervised-SoilNet’s slight improvement was not enough to
accurately represent the correct data trends on a local scale.
However, SSL-SoilNet outperformed the other models in

SSL-SoilNet demonstrates superior performance in dealing
with the spatial complexity and variability of SOC values,
offering a more precise and reliable prediction capability.
In the context of the LUCAS dataset, all models demonstrated the capability to capture data trends at a continental
scale. In Europe, mountains, and specifically the European
Alps, are of great significance. Forest soils within this region
have the highest organic carbon concentrations [62], where
low air temperatures slow down the decomposition of organic
material, leading to significant accumulation of soil organic
matter. Additionally, grassland soils are considered one of
the most specific biological hotspots, abundant in organic
carbon [63]. Due to the limited accessibility and extensive
spatial heterogeneity of these regions [64], they could be
among the most challenging areas. Utilizing a considerable
quantity of unlabeled samples during the self-supervised training in SSL-SoilNet provides the model with an opportunity
to acquire insights into these regions even in the absence of
plentiful ground-truth samples. This facilitates more accurate
predictions.
Detailed examinations were conducted for three distinct
areas within Europe. Area A is situated in the northern
part of Europe, specifically Finland, Norway, and Sweden,
characterized predominantly by wetlands, high precipitation,
and low temperatures. Area B, located in Germany and
the Netherlands, is primarily composed of grassland, cropland,
and wetlands, coupled with below-average temperatures and
relatively high precipitation. Conversely, Area C in Spain
experiences low precipitation and high temperatures, with its
land-cover classes including cropland, grassland, and bareland.
For Area A, none of the implemented models were fully
successful in accurately reflecting the trends observed in the
ground reference samples. This difficulty in prediction for
Area A aligns with previous studies that have identified it
as a region with high uncertainty in SOC predictions [65].
However, the maps generated by SSL-SoilNet showed a closer
resemblance to the reference samples than those produced
by both supervised training and the GBDT model, indicating
a relatively better performance. A similar observation was
made for Area B, where SSL-SoilNet outperformed other
models in matching the reference data trends. In the case of
Area C, which presents a distinct environmental profile from
Areas A and B, the only model that demonstrated proficiency
in identifying samples with high SOC values was SSL-SoilNet.
This finding underscores the effectiveness of SSL-SoilNet in
dealing with the complex variability of SOC across different
landscapes, particularly in areas where environmental conditions significantly differ.
An intriguing finding from both datasets is the association
between challenging areas and the presence of land-cover class
wetlands. Within these regions, soils have been influenced
by decades of cold and anaerobic conditions, resulting in
significant heterogeneity in composition [66]. This diversity,
reflecting a range of soil microbial activities and decelerated
organic matter decomposition rates [67], presents challenges
in accurately assessing SOC and predicting its distribution in
these areas.
Various factors control SOC, highlighting the complexity of its dynamics. Understanding the spatial distribution
of these variables is crucial for predicting how ecosystems
will adapt to changes in climate conditions. Therefore, it is
essential to consider the primary predictive drivers across
different regions, to effectively model SOC dynamics and
ecosystem responses [58]. Wiesmeier et al. [68] suggested
that regional approaches are needed to estimate the SOC
storage capacity according to specific climatic conditions and
vegetation characteristics. Moreover, another study suggested
that SOC dynamics in more than 70% of topsoil in China
were controlled by climate change and its coupled influence
with environmental variation [69]. In light of these findings,
we employed a comprehensive array of input features in
our study, including satellite data with a spatial resolution
of 30 m and climate time-series data with a spatial resolution
of ∼4 km. Given that the quality of input features and the
uncertainty within the data significantly influence prediction
accuracy, further improvements can be achieved by utilizing
high-resolution satellite images and/or climate datasets with
finer resolutions (e.g., 1 km). This refinement could be particularly crucial for the application of our approach on a regional
scale.
F. Future Work
The achieved results demonstrated the better capability
of the developed model, SSL-SoilNet, in predicting SOC
compared to other implemented ML models. Its applicability extends beyond specific properties and enables accurate
estimation of a diverse range of soil characteristics such as
soil textures particularly clay, in different geographic regions,
ranging from national-scale to larger-scale land management
and environmental assessment projects. The flexibility of
the proposed model allows other researchers and practitioners to adapt it to their specific soil analysis requirements.
This model could also be utilized with hyperspectral data,
which offers a large number of spectral bands. This can
provide a wealth of surface information features compared
to multispectral sensors, significantly enhancing the model’s
prediction ability. Another approach could involve explaining
the model’s predictions by utilizing summarization methods
to combine pattern activations and create attribution graphs.
These graphs would highlight the most important spectral
features, enhancing the model’s interpretability and potentially
improving its performance for further analysis. The versatility of our model enables its adaptation to diverse study
areas and soil datasets. To facilitate further exploration and
adoption of our model, we have made it freely available at
https://github.com/moienr/SoilNet.
V. CONCLUSION
Our research demonstrates an in-depth analysis of selfsupervised contrastive learning with a hybrid architecture for
predicting SOC. The process involves a two-step training:
initially utilizing a vast number of random samples through a
hybrid backbone for SSL, followed by supervised fine-tuning
using ground reference samples. Our extensive experiments

STRATA2.0: A Serverless Middleware for Machine
Learning Training
Dimitrios Tomaras
, Member, IEEE, Sebastian Buschjäger
, Vana Kalogeraki
, Member, IEEE,
Katharina Morik
, Member, IEEE, and Dimitrios Gunopulos, Member, IEEE
Abstract—Serverless computing has gained increasing interest
in recent years for enabling large-scale machine learning tasks.
However, training a machine learning model in a serverless setting
is a complex task and several challenges need to be addressed
particularly in data distribution, result aggregation, resource heterogeneity, failures, container ephemerality, network and execution cost. These difﬁculties stem from the inherent complexity
of distributed computation and the coordination demands of the
machine learning algorithms. We propose STRATA2.0, a serverless
middleware for Machine Learning training in serverless environments. STRATA2.0 provides a comprehensive suite of mechanisms
designed to support efﬁcient training of machine learning models
on serverless infrastructures and address key challenges related to
efﬁcient data communication, coordination and synchronization,
scalable and time efﬁcient training of ML models using heterogeneous containers. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that STRATA2.0 achieves the same level of accuracy with
fewer data points, is on average three times faster in training time
compared to centralized approaches, reduces energy consumption
by up to 50%, and remains resilient when up to 60% of training
instances fail.
Index Terms—Machine learning, middleware, serverless.
I. INTRODUCTION
S
ERVERLESS machine learning has emerged as a powerful
way of building machine learning products and services
on top of loosely coupled serverless functions that provide
compute and storage services [1]. The serverless computing
model operates by abstracting away the underlying infrastructure (i.e., servers), allowing developers to concentrate on writing
application code without the need to manage servers. These
characteristics empower practitioners to iterate rapidly, decouple pipeline components, and leverage ﬁne-grained parallelism

without the overhead of managing the underlying infrastructure,
compared to traditional server-based solutions or VM-based
infrastructures (also known as IaaS) that typically rent and
need to conﬁgure dedicated virtual or physical machines for
a speciﬁed amount of time [2], [3], [4]. The serverless model
provides additional beneﬁts including unlimited elasticity, automatic scaling, built-in high availability, no need to know the
internals of the underlying technologies, a pay-per-use model
(to increase agility and optimize costs), and lower start-up and
set-up overhead, and thus has attracted growing interest. Its
event-driven and modular nature enables the construction of
scalable Machine Learning (ML) pipelines where individual
components such as data ingestion, pre-processing or model
training can be independently deployed, triggered by internal
or external events. Its automatic scaling capability in response
to workload demands, makes it well-suited for parallelizing ML
training tasks such as hyperparameter optimization and model
evaluation. Furthermore, the pay-per-use pricing model reduces
resource utilization, making it particularly advantageous for
sporadic or bursty training workloads. During long periods of
inactivity, the ephemeral containers of the serverless computing
model stop running automatically (scale to zero) to keep operational costs low. This feature has been proven beneﬁcial for
the family of deep learning models (i.e. Deep Neural Networks
(DNNs)), both for training and inference, as shown in recent
works [3], [4], [5], [6].
One notable constraint of serverless frameworks is their frequentassumptionofhomogeneityacrossbothincomingrequests
and the underlying hardware infrastructure. Consequently, autoscalers default to coarse metrics (e.g., queries per second, CPU
utilization) and overlook application- and hardware-speciﬁc
signals. In reality, incoming requests often exhibit signiﬁcant
variability in both task type and data volume, and functions
may require diverse resource conﬁgurations. For example, while
Random Forest inference (one of the most powerful and versatile
ensemble learning models in the ﬁeld of machine learning) is
relatively lightweight and broadly supported, its training process
is considerably more resource-intensive. It is dominated by data
movement, memory management, and coordination efforts necessary to construct large and diverse trees, factors that directly
affect model quality and impose distinct resource demands.
When selecting container speciﬁcations and setting concurrency
levels, developers must navigate a trade-off between deploying
smaller containers with low concurrency and large containers
with high concurrency. In homogeneous serverless container

settings, naive task placement often results to resource fragmentation across cluster nodes, thereby impairing the overall
resource utilization [7]. In practice, resource demands within
serverless architectures are highly dynamic, driven by timevarying workloads. This underscores the need for more agile,
heterogeneity-aware and efﬁcient resource allocation strategies.
Moreover, the ephemeral nature of serverless environments
renders accurate ML training particularly fragile. Existing
frameworks such as Apache MLlib [8] and XGBoost [9], which
are built for long-lived executors, are ill-suited to serverless
settings, especially for applications that require high levels
of accuracy. In the serverless computing model, stateless retries and at-least-once semantics may lead to redundant or
dropped gradient updates unless operations are strictly idempotent, thereby biasing optimization processes and impeding
convergence. Additionally, preemptions can terminate containers mid-execution, introducing silent accuracy regressions upon
resumption. Even “embarrassingly parallel” Random Forests
suffer: retries and preemptions can disrupt bootstrap sampling,
feature subset selection, and shard-level statistics, ultimately
altering tree structure and degrading the integrity of the ﬁ-
nal model. While such conditions necessitate robust serverless
execution mechanisms, prioritizing robustness exclusively by
design, as in LambdaML [5], incurs signiﬁcant time overhead,
thereby hindering time-efﬁcient training.
Consequently, enabling robust ML training (e.g., Random
Forests and DNNs) in serverless settings demands a holistic approach that: (i) ensures model accuracy comparable to
monolithic deployments, despite the transient nature of serverless containers, (ii) minimizes resource fragmentation across
worker nodes, particularly under high concurrency, (iii) exploits container heterogeneity to improve resource utilization,
and (iv) satisﬁes developer-deﬁned service-level objectives for
cost-efﬁciency and latency, through appropriate system-level
abstractions and primitives.
Contributions: We summarize our contributions below:
r We present STRATA2.0, a serverless middleware for
machine learning training in serverless environments.
STRATA2.0 comprises a comprehensive suite of mechanisms designed to enable efﬁcient training of machine
learning models in serverless infrastructures. Our mechanisms address key challenges in data communication,
coordination and synchronization and scalable and timeefﬁcient training of ML models using heterogeneous containers. By improving resource efﬁciency while maintaining model performance, our system addresses fundamental
limitations in scaling ML workloads to large datasets and
increasingly sophisticated model architectures.
r We prove both theoretically and conﬁrm experimentally,
that, STRATA2.0 is fault-tolerant with respect to model
accuracy. We employ a Rademacher-complexity analysis
to demonstrate that failures of individual containers result
in only minor deviations in predictive performance, with
the resulting accuracy loss under failures being provably
bounded (e.g. by O(1/M) for M trees in a Random Forest
model).
Fig. 1.
STRATA2.0 middleware.
r We experimentally illustrate with diverse datasets, and
under heterogeneous container deployments, the generality
of STRATA2.0 across different ML models. Furthermore,
we demonstrate STRATA2.0’s key properties: (i) data ef-
ﬁciency for ML training, (ii) reduced training time and
monthly billing cost, (iii) fault tolerance, and (iv) energy and memory efﬁciency under heterogeneous settings.
Moreover, we demonstrate its cost-beneﬁts in comparison with on-premise deployments of state-of-the-art algorithms (XGBoost [9], Apache MLlib [8]) and serverless
frameworks such as LambdaML [5].
II. STRATA2.0 MIDDLEWARE OVERVIEW
STRATA2.0 is a middleware that offers a comprehensive suite
of mechanisms for deﬁning and efﬁciently supporting the training workﬂows of diverse ML tasks in serverless infrastructures.
STRATA2.0 is designed to address the limitations inherent in the
prevailing serverless model, which lacks native support for data
communication and synchronization, constraining ML work-
ﬂow design, and drives up costs. For example, naive Random
Forests implementations in serverless environments often assign
one worker per tree to train an entire decision tree on the full
dataset [8], [9]. Thus, each worker must load both the complete
training data and the resulting tree into memory. This demands
over-provisioned, memory-rich nodes and prevents ﬁne-grained,
cost-effective scaling.
The STRATA2.0 middleware (Fig. 1) features the following
mechanisms: (i) A container instantiation component that determines appropriately sized serverless containers (as worker
nodes) and distributes the training data (step 4a), (ii) two ef-
ﬁcient, novel data communication mechanisms, Gradient Averaging (GARF) and Model Averaging (MARF), that require
a smaller subset of the training data and construct locally a
decision tree that ﬁts the data appropriately in heterogeneous
worker nodes (steps 4b and 4c), iii) coordination and synchronization mechanisms that orchestrate the training process,
coordinate the worker nodes and aggregate intermediate results
(step 4c). These mechanisms facilitate the execution of e.g. a
Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm (steps 5a and 5b),
which either calculates the gradients of a model or generates an

III. A COMPREHENSIVE SUITE OF MECHANISMS FOR
SERVERLESS ML TRAINING TASKS
A. Container Instantiation Mechanism
STRATA2.0 employs containers to serve as the host environment for the ML training process. Heterogeneous serverless
containers are necessary to accommodate diverse ML training
workloads so that resource conﬁgurations match per-workload
demands and performance objectives are satisﬁed. Exposing
multiple container conﬁgurations mitigates resource fragmentation through ﬁner-grained bin-packing [10] and enables tiered
autoscaling, where smaller containers absorb workload burstiness and larger ones sustain steady-state workloads.
In this work, we focus on Random Forest training, which
assumes that training and test samples are independently and
identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to an unknown distribution D over the input space X and labels Y. We are given a

Rd is a d-dimensional feature-vector and yi ∈Y ⊆RC is the
corresponding target vector, where C is the number of classes.
Each decision tree (DT) in the forest is denoted as hi and its
prediction for the observation x is given by hi(x). The forest
is then given by a set of M trees {h1, h2, . . . , hM} and the
RF’s prediction is given by f(x) = M
i=1 hi(x). Further, let
θ = {θ1, . . . , θM} denote the set of all probability estimates
associated with the leaves of all trees in the forest, and let
fθ(x) represent the prediction of the forest with estimates θ.
STRATA2.0 generates samples of speciﬁc sizes (in terms of the
number of data points) and retrieves the corresponding indices
from the original dataset stored in a distributed storage system
(e.g., S3), ensuring that each sample ﬁts within the memory
constraints of its assigned container [5], instead of utilizing the
whole raw dataset.
Observation 1. Memory requirements vary signiﬁcantly and
can lead to substantial memory waste: We investigated the impact of input feature dimensionality and tree depth on per-worker
memory consumption, and how this behavior varies under heterogeneous containers (with different CPU and memory capacities) for ML training tasks. Fig. 2 compares memory wastage
between homogeneous and heterogeneous deployments for the
same dataset and ML training task. Container selection is driven
by the fraction of training samples used for tree construction,
which serves as a threshold for assigning small or large container
types. As the training data fraction increases, heterogeneous
conﬁgurations improve efﬁciency, reducing memory wastage
by up to 60% at 80% of the data. Based on these observations,
we dynamically instantiate containers by jointly considering
training sample size and model characteristics (e.g., tree depth),
selecting the most appropriate heterogeneous container conﬁguration.
B. Data Communication Mechanisms
Serverless computing offers elasticity and simpliﬁed deployment, but it faces signiﬁcant limitations when handling dataintensive workloads such as ML training. We propose two efﬁ-
cient data communication mechanisms, GARF and MARF, that
reduce the volume of data exchanged during training, thereby
lowering communication costs.
Observation 2. Data communication can be a critical straggler: A key constraint of commercial serverless platforms is their
strict payload size limits (e.g. AWS (6 MB), IBM Openwhisk
(1 MB) and Google Cloud Functions (10 MB)). These restrictions severely limit the volume of data that can be transferred
or processed within a single serverless invocation, constraining
traditional ML training approaches that rely on large datasets.
Parameters such as container size, deﬁned by CPU and memory
(e.g. the different tiers provided in commercial platforms, with
up to 10 GB of memory [11]), can signiﬁcantly impact training
performance. Recent studies [12], [13], [14], [15], [16] have
shown that appropriate selection of container conﬁgurations
can accelerate ML tasks convergence with minimal scheduling
overhead. In designing STRATA2.0, we observed that fetching
all training data using a naive communication strategy quickly
became a dominant straggler for STRATA2.0’s training time,
particularly while scaling.
STRATA2.0’s MARF and GARF algorithms are designed to
effectively address these constraints by operating on smaller
subsets of the training data. Rather than using the original RF
algorithm, we adopt a variant, known as leaf reﬁnement [17],
[18]. Given an already trained forest, the leaf reﬁnement technique improves accuracy by minimizing a global loss function.
It does this by reﬁning the probability estimates in the leaf nodes
based on interactions across the ensemble, without modifying
the underlying tree structures. The beneﬁt of leaf reﬁnement is
that it is model-agnostic and, thus, can be applied to any tree
ensemble, making it compatible with a wide variety of initial
training methods. Note here, that, a decision tree cannot grow
larger than the number of data points in its training sample, thus,
DTs trained on n data points have at most n leaf nodes and, in
total, at most 2n −1 nodes.

C. Distributed Training Mechanisms
Parameter Server: In the literature, two alternatives have
been proposed for other machine learning models, such as deep
neural networks: a) using a parameter server (PS) [2], [20] or
b) adopting a decentralized approach [21]. However, current
production serverless infrastructures do not support direct communication between functions, only indirect communication
via a gateway [22]. This limitation increases synchronization
overhead and burdens developers with managing the consistency
of the global model. STRATA2.0 adopts a parameter server
(PS) approach, similar to [2] and [20]. The PS, acting as a
central node, orchestrates the training process across worker
nodes. Each worker node returns its local updates (the result of
TrainDT function) to the PS, which then updates the global
model and propagates these updates back to the worker nodes.
The core intuition is that many ML algorithms allow workers to
maintain and update local copies of a global model in parallel.
Periodically, after a ﬁxed number of iterations, worker nodes
exchange information (e.g., gradients or model parameters) to
ensure global model consistency. The PS serves as a central
coordination point, acting as a storage backend (e.g., a persistent or in-memory key-value store) responsible for aggregating,
updating, and redistributing model parameters. In STRATA2.0,
1) each TrainDT function returns local updates to the PS,
2) the PS uses them to reﬁne the global model, and 3) each
UpdateDT/GradDT function subsequently pulls the latest
model parameters from the PS.
Communication and Synchronization Semantics: While the
PS is a widely adopted mechanism for coordinating distributed
training, it does not sufﬁce to ensure correct and efﬁcient execution. Existing works in the literature have presented a set
of primitives for data communication across worker nodes.
Such state-of-the-art primitives are Broadcast, AllGather,
AllReduce, Scatter, Reduce and ScatterReduce [8], [23],
[24]. These serve as generic building blocks for training various
machine learning models, including Random Forests, Gradient
Boosted Machines (GBMs), and DNNs. By reﬁning the leaf
nodes of the trees we can further enhance predictive performance (for Gradient Boosted Machines) and support horizontal
Federated Learning (FL) using the FedAvg methodology [25]
(for Deep Neutral Networks). Although state-of-the-art libraries
like mpi4py [26] provide partial support for these primitives,
they exhibit several constraints, such as: i) depend on external
orchestration tools for deployment, ii) are not designed to operate over modern communication protocols such as HTTP or
gRPC, and iii) offer limited or no integration with asynchronous
messagingframeworksrestrictingtheirsuitabilityforsuchapplications. We have implemented these primitives in STRATA2.0
and more speciﬁcally, the AllGather and AllReduce are the
most suitable to exploit for training Random Forests. When
using the AllGather primitive for RFs, trained decision trees
are collected from all serverless functions and redistributed for
gradient computation. On the other hand, with AllReduce, the
trees are aggregated from all functions, and the result is returned
to each one of them.
STRATA2.0adopts theAllGather communicationprimitive,
as it enables seamless data exchange between the parameter server and serverless functions during training. However,
synchronizing the trained local models among the different
serverless functions is a critical task. Two common state-of-theart mechanisms are the Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP) and
the Asynchronous Parallel (ASP) protocols [2], [5]. We have
implemented these communication protocols described above,
and further proposed a hybrid synchronization mechanism that
combines elements of the BSP and ASP paradigms. This hybrid mechanism, along with the ASP and BSP paradigms is
implemented through the gateway agent [22], leveraging the
exposed API and runtime mechanisms. The hybrid mechanism
works as follows: When training Random Forests in a serverless

A small container typically provisions a single vCPU core and

D. Fault Tolerance Mechanisms
Robust serverless ML training: In serverless ML training,
individual function executions are susceptible to mid-execution
failures. To ensure system robustness, we need to address two
distinct but complementary concerns: (i) Infrastructure-level
reliability: Issues such as preemptions, retries, and autoscalerinduced churn can disrupt step-level semantics and degrade
performance unless mitigated through mechanisms such as
idempotent operations, atomic state management, and resilient
coordination protocols [4], [6]. In STRATA2.0, containers are
equipped with health checks and automatically restart upon
failure. (ii) Model-level reliability: Failures at this level, e.g.,
duplicated or missed gradients or loss of optimizer state, can
negativelyimpactconvergenceanddegradetheﬁnalmodelaccuracy [4]. To address this, our data communication primitives are
fault-tolerant by design, providing strong correctness guarantees
that preserve model integrity during training. Below, we analyze
model accuracy under failures, demonstrating tolerance to a
bounded number of faults:
Case 1. Complete loss of a tree and its data: We demonstrate that, in serverless training, the failure of a single tree
results in a small, quantiﬁable degradation in the generalization
bound that vanishes as the number of trees M grows. Since
each tree contributes only O(1/M) to the ensemble, and has
comparable complexity, the impact of any individual failure
becomes negligible in large ensembles. To quantify this effect,
we employ Rademacher complexity bounds [28] to estimate
the generalization error of the Random Forest. Generalization
bounds are typically expressed in the form: L ≤L + R(f) + G,
where L is the (unknown) generalization error on unseen data,
L is the training error, R(f) is the Rademacher complexity term
that depends on the model f and G is some constant that goes
towards 0 for N →∞. This analysis provides theoretical assurance that isolated failures do not signiﬁcantly degrade learning
performance, particularly as the ensemble size grows. Decision
trees have a Rademacher complexity of O(n log(n + d)), where
n denotes the total number of nodes in the tree and d is the
number of training features [28]. Notably, the Rademacher
complexity depends on the tree structure rather than the leaf
values. Thus, each tree retains its Rademacher complexity after
leaf reﬁnement. For additive ensembles such as Random Forests,
the total Rademacher complexity equals the weighted sum of the
individual model complexities [29]. For Random Forests, where
each tree contributes equally, the ensemble complexity scales at
a factor 1/M per tree.

Discussion. Cold Starts, Timeouts and Heterogeneous Data.
To enable scalable serverless training, we have made a number of
architectural and platform choices to address cold-start latency,
execution time limits, and data modality constraints. We chose
Marathon [32] as our serverless platform orchestrator, as it
avoids overlay network creation, thereby reducing the cold-start
latency incurred when redeploying an inactive function (i.e.,
the time required to dispatch and start function execution).
Due to platform limitations and consistent with prior work [5],
[33], STRATA2.0 does not support training scenarios where a
single TrainDT function exceeds 15 minutes of execution time,
mirroring constraints found in commercial serverless platforms.
For longer-running training jobs, VM-based solutions are more
suitable. However, in our experiments, we did not observe any
TrainDT executions exceeding this limit, even for our largest
dataset, higgs. Exceeding the 15-minute threshold would require
training a very large model on a substantially large data sample.
To mitigate this limitation, we implement checkpointing: if a
function approaches its timeout, its execution is migrated to
a newly instantiated container one minute before termination,
similar to [5]. Alternatively, users can reduce data sample sizes
and increase the level of parallelism, to ensure each TrainDT
instancecompleteswithinthetimelimit.Furthermore,unlikeexisting works such as [5] that do not account for parameter server
failures, we employ a checkpointing mechanism that preserves
the state of the parameter server process both before and after
the TrainDT calls. This allows the Random Forest training
to resume without losing previously computed leaf and node
values. Finally, STRATA2.0 supports training on unstructured
data (e.g., text and images) by incorporating preprocessing steps
that transform them into structured representations, e.g., using
IMAGEBIND [34] for images or GloVe [35] for text.
IV. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
In our experimental study, we investigate the following key
properties of our middleware: (1) data efﬁciency for ML training tasks,i.e., accuracy performance when fewer examples are
available, (2) training time and monthly billing cost, (3) fault tolerance, (4) generalization across ML models and (5) energy and
memory efﬁciency under heterogeneous settings. We compare
STRATA2.0withstate-of-the-artdistributedlearningalgorithms
and serverless frameworks.
A. Experimental Setup
We compared MARF and GARF algorithms against stateof-the-art techniques such as Random Forests (RF) [40], Extremely Randomized Trees (EF) [41], Gradient Boosted Machines (GB) [42] and Woody [43]. Prior work [44] shows that
RF performance does not improve beyond M = 128 trees of
unconstrained depth trained on all features, which we also veri-
ﬁed in preliminary experiments. Hence, if not stated otherwise,
we use this setting in our experiments. For MARF and GARF
we minimize the MSE loss (see a detailed discussion in [28])
using the ADAM optimizer [45] with a step size of 0.1. The GB
method uses 32 trees, built sequentially, with a maximum depth
of 5, which is recommended to combat overﬁtting. For Woody,
we used the parameters recommended in [43]. We conducted
our experiments in our local cluster comprising 7 nodes with
a total 56 CPUs and 112 GB of RAM available. The nodes
are interconnected with 1GBps Ethernet and run on Ubuntu
20.04 LTS. STRATA2.0 is deployed on the Apache Mesos
1.9 [46] serverless platform, while we use Marathon 1.5 [32]
to deploy Docker containers on Mesos. We use Marathon only
to start/stop the containers. Existing distributed training and
serverless frameworks, such as XGBoost [9], Apache MLlib [8]
and LambdaML [5] use the vanilla Random Forest algorithm
provided by the scikit-learn Python Library by default and assume homogeneous serverless container conﬁgurations. Similar
to [47] and [5] and given our infrastructure limitations, we varied
the number of serverless function instances from 10 to 40. We
used OpenFaas [27] Python templates to create our TrainDT
and UpdateDT functions. Our approach can leverage accelerators like GPUs or TPUs when available. GPU-based training
with LightGBM [48] or via Hummingbird [49] can be integrated
by updating lines 3 and 9 of Algorithm 1, respectively.
Datasets: We used a total of 9 datasets [36], [38], [39] from
diverse domains ranging from 20,000 to 11,000,000 instances
and comprising 16 to 174 features, as depicted in Table I.
We discarded instances with NaN values and applied one-hot
encoding for categorical features. Let N denote the number of

The majority of the algorithms improve their performance when
having access to more training data. For the adult dataset only,

MARF and GARF consistently have the best performance,
particularly under limited amount of data. For instance, on the
avila dataset, they reach near 100% accuracy using ≤1% of
the training data, whereas other methods require over 50%.
Similarly, on covertype, they outperform the other methods at
small fractions (< 0.5) and converge to better solutions with the

more slowly, while Gradient Boosted Machines underperform,

Training under heterogeneous settings: We evaluated the
beneﬁts of STRATA2.0 using heterogeneous container conﬁgurationsalongfourdimensions:energysavings,accuracy,training
time, and memory wastage. The use of heterogeneous container sizes enables ﬁne-grained resource allocation, allowing
the system to accommodate variability in training workloads
while better reﬂecting realistic cloud and edge environments.
Following [7], we trained the decision trees with varying training
data sample sizes, thus we utilized the fraction of the data as the
criterion to select between small (provisioned with 1 vCPU and
1024 MB of memory) and large size (provisioned with 2 vCPUs
and 2048 MB of memory) containers. In each experiment, a
total of 10 containers were used, evenly divided between the two
proﬁles (5 small and 5 large). The baseline conﬁguration uses 10
small containers. In Figs. 12(a)–12(h) we illustrate the energy
savings when using heterogeneous containers. The energy is
calculated as the area of the trapezoid formed by the power used
(in watts) and the training time. We observe energy savings of
up to 50%, since larger, more efﬁcient containers, despite their
higher power draw, are utilized for shorter durations. Furthermore, as shown in Figs. 13(a)–13(h), Random Forest’s accuracy
remains consistent across datasets and threshold settings, even
with heterogeneous containers. Moreover, in Figs. 14(a)–14(h),
we draw the corresponding training time and memory wastage.
Memory wastage is deﬁned as the difference between the
total memory allocated for M = 128 trees (based on container
capacity) and the actual memory used during training. As observed, training time remains largely unaffected by the threshold
across most datasets. However, memory wastage is reduced,
especially for larger datasets, thus demonstrating better resource
utilization and lower fragmentation. At a 60% data fraction,
the heterogeneous conﬁguration reduces resource wastage by
an average of 43.6% across all eight datasets compared to the
homogeneous baseline. While higher fractions further reduce
wastage, 60% represents a practical trade-off between training
time and memory usage. For example, in the adult, bank, and
higgs datasets (Figs. 14(a), 14(c), 14(h)), thresholds above or
below 60% increase training time due to imbalance of complex
training data points across the trees.
V. RELATED WORK
Training Random Forests has been discussed in the literature,
e.g., parallelism with CPUs/GPUs [57] or implementing RF
training using MapReduce [58], [59], with the entire training
data typically available in the main memory. The work presented in [43] targets the DT induction process itself and not
the aggregation or reﬁnement of a RF, thus it is orthogonal
to STRATA2.0. Similarly, the deployment of tree ensembles
has been optimized through memory layout improvements [60],
[61], implementation-level optimizations [60], [62], and modi-
ﬁcations to the underlying tree traversal algorithms [49], [63],

[64], [65]. These approaches are orthogonal to STRATA2.0.
Serverless ML training has received growing interest [2], [3],
[4], [5], [6], [20], [66]. FedMP [2] addresses the communication
challenge for training DNNs, which is completely different to
RF training. Similarly, Ada-FedSemi [20], LambdaML [5] and
SMLT [6] focus on deep learning models rather than Random
Forests. EdgeTune [67] targets hyperparameter tuning of DNNs,
Aergia [68] addresses CNN training with stragglers, and Slice-
Tune [69] focuses on auto-tuning DNNs on GPU clusters, each
operating in settings fundamentally different from ours. Cirrus [3] supports general ML workﬂows, but does not address data
communication or training synchronization. CRUCIAL [66]
allows programming of parallel stateful serverless applications,
without focusing on RFs and porting them to a serverless environment nor using less amount of training data. SIREN [4] is
a system for scheduling ML jobs, but does not provide insights
how these models work as we do in STRATA2.0. While our
prior work [50] highlighted MARF and GARF for serverless
ML training, STRATA2.0 introduces a comprehensive suite of
mechanisms for data communication, container heterogeneity,
and distributed training, supporting ML models beyond Random
Forests.
VI. CONCLUSION
In this paper we presented STRATA2.0, our middleware for
scalable, cost-effective and fault-tolerant training of ML models
in a serverless environment. STRATA2.0 provides a comprehensive suite of mechanisms designed to support efﬁcient training of
ML models on serverless infrastructures and addresses key challenges related to efﬁcient data communication, coordination,
synchronization and scalable and time-efﬁcient training of ML
models using heterogeneous containers. STRATA2.0 achieves at
least 3x faster training times on average compared to centralized
approaches, reaches the same level of accuracy with fewer data
points, requires up to 50% less energy, minimizes per-container
network usage and tolerates up to 60% of tree failures during
training.

STSF: Spiking Time Sparse Feedback Learning for
Spiking Neural Networks
Ping He , Rong Xiao , Chenwei Tang , Shudong Huang , Member, IEEE,
Jiancheng Lv , Senior Member, IEEE, and Huajin Tang , Senior Member, IEEE
Abstract— Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are biologically
plausible models known for their computational efficiency. A significant advantage of SNNs lies in the binary information
transmission through spike trains, eliminating the need for
multiplication operations. However, due to the spatio-temporal
nature of SNNs, direct application of traditional backpropagation
(BP) training still results in significant computational costs.
Meanwhile, learning methods based on unsupervised synaptic
plasticity provide an alternative for training SNNs but often
yield suboptimal results. Thus, efficiently training high-accuracy
SNNs remains a challenge. In this article, we propose a highly
efficient and biologically plausible spiking time sparse feedback (STSF) learning method. This algorithm modifies synaptic
weights by incorporating a neuromodulator for global supervised
learning using sparse direct feedback alignment (DFA) and
local homeostasis learning with vanilla spike-timing-dependent
plasticity (STDP). Such neuromorphic global–local learning
focuses on instantaneous synaptic activity, enabling independent
and simultaneous optimization of each network layer, thereby
improving biological plausibility, enhancing parallelism, and
reducing storage overhead. Incorporating sparse fixed random
feedback connections for global error modulation, which uses
selection operations instead of multiplication operations, further improves computational efficiency. Experimental results
demonstrate that the proposed algorithm markedly reduces the
computational cost with significantly higher accuracy comparable
to current state-of-the-art algorithms across a wide range of
classification tasks. Our implementation codes are available at
https://github.com/hppeace/STSF.
Index Terms— Global–local spiking learning, sparse direct
feedback alignment (DFA), spiking neural networks (SNNs),
vanilla spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP).

1) This article proposes a novel form of nonlocal synaptic

II. RELATED WORK
Numerous efforts have been made to enhance the computational efficiency and biological plausibility of the learning
process in SNNs. These methods can be broadly categorized into three groups: global error-driven learning, local
correlation-driven learning, and hybrid approaches.
A. Global Error-Driven Learning
The learning process is achieved through layer-wise allocation of global supervised errors. Benefiting from the latest
advancements in deep learning, methods originally designed
for optimizing sequential models (such as STBP [8], [9]) have
been successfully applied to SNNs, demonstrating excellent
accuracy in specific tasks. However, it comes with high
computational and memory complexity.
To address the additional temporal dimension in SNNs,
OTTT [10] simplifies gradient propagation along time within
neurons through the detach reset operation. ELL [12] leverages
trace accumulation of temporal information, decoupling the
learning process over the time dimension. Although these
online BP methods reduce resource consumption in the SNNs
learning process, the errors need to be delivered to earlier
layers through the same weights as the feedforward connections. The precise symmetry constraints required in the
process of reversely weight update of the network are not only
difficult for hardware implementation but also not biologically
feasible [13], [14], [25].
At the same time, Lillicrap et al. [15] discovered that precise
symmetric connectivity between neurons is not necessary for
learning algorithms. Samadi et al. [17] and Neftci et al. [18]
demonstrated that a variant of FA-enabled deep learning with
dynamic spiking neurons. Further, FFA [26] uses two FA
algorithms during the forward and backward processes to
train their respective weights, alleviating the weight transport
problems encountered in BP. To train network layers more
independently, Nøkland [16] introduced DFA connections,
eliminating the need for symmetric weights. Xiao et al. [27]
further proposed an asymmetric online learning algorithm,
which was capable of simultaneously learning spatial and
temporal features in real-time, without prior knowledge of the
duration of spatio-temporal data.
Although attempts have been made to utilize techniques
such as FA or DFA in SNNs, the learning process still heavily
depends on floating-point operations and dense connections
during BP [28], [29]. It is essential to develop a learning
algorithm that can reflect the efficiency and biological characteristics of SNNs.
B. Local Correlation-Driven Learning
Correlation-driven learning serves as the foundation for
learning and memory in biological neural systems, offering
inspiration for the creation of biologically plausible intelligent
neural network systems. Hebbian learning theory [30] posited
that neurons that fire together, wire together, and STDP
extended Hebbian theory by elucidating the temporal relationship between presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes and their
impact on learning [31]. These methods employ unsupervised
learning, with some efforts such as R-STDP [6], [32] and
ReSuMe [33] attempting to optimize the learning process

C. Hybrid Approaches
Hybrid methods aim to combine local plasticity mechanisms
with global supervisory signals to construct more efficient
SNN learning algorithms. Such as EICIL [36] combines STDP
and BP by employing different learning methods at various
network layers or different time steps t, thereby achieving a
global–local learning approach. On the other hand, EIHL [37]
optimizes the network using STBP and enhances network
sparsity through STDP. It implements a global–local hybrid
learning mechanism by dynamically switching between these
two methods. However, these methods implement hybrid
learning by directly using two distinct algorithms, resulting
in high computational complexity.
Recently, an increasing amount of research has explored the
three-factor (3F) learning rule, which integrated presynaptic
activity, postsynaptic activity, and a third factor-comprising
neuromodulators and neurotransmitters-to represent top–down
supervisory signals [38], [39].
A feasible implementation uses BP as the third factor
to modulate the magnitude of local weight updates, combined with STDP to consider noncausal relationships in the
learning process, thereby enhancing generalization and task
performance [24]. SDNN [40] applied the STDP rule for
convolutional layer learning and used SVM as a classifier.
BP-STDP [41] attempted to directly utilize the gradient information of STDP and R-STDP [6], [32] and propagated it
layer by layer using BP. These methods have been successfully
applied to classification tasks [23], [40], [41].
Other approaches adopt biologically plausible supervisory
signals. For example, SBP [21] combines short-term plasticity
(STP) and homeostatic adjustment methods [42], utilizing
synaptic potentiation and depression to enhance the accuracy
of SNNs. GLSNN [22] generates target feedback for hidden
layers through direct target feedback and learns using STDP
rules. Despite significant progress in understanding biological
learning, the study on combining DFA connection to each layer
for propagating global plasticity information with the local
plasticity learning rule to train SNNs has been limited. Developing an efficient and biologically plausible hybrid learning
algorithm for SNNs remains a challenging task.

IV. METHOD
In this section, we begin by presenting an overview of the
overarching framework of STSF. Subsequently, we delve into
detailed explanations of its two components: local synaptic
plasticity and global error modulation.
A. Overview
For the multilayer feedforward SNNs, we have developed
a global–local collaborative learning model called STSF. This
model leverages the forward process to obtain the network’s
state. Subsequently, sparse direct feedback is employed to
obtain targets for the hidden layer, allowing local Vanilla
STDP rules to acquire global plasticity information for the
entire network. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the STSF network
architecture comprises two components: local learning with
vanilla STDP and global learning with sparse feedback.
In this model, sparse feedback connections directly link
from the output layer to the hidden layer, signifying that
the neural network can simultaneously update parameters
for all layers. This approach not only effectively reduces
computational and memory requirements for weight updates
throughout the network but also enhances the optimization
process for parallelization. Simultaneously, Vanilla STDP
eliminates the necessity to store individual previous states,
achieving linear computational complexity.

Although Crafton et al. [47] had emphasized the importance

In this study, we impose constraints on matrices that allow

error information from all categories can be fully utilized while
also ensuring that all neurons receive error information. The
properties of a full-rank matrix ensure that there is at least one
weight connection at each corresponding position, which is the
key factor in guaranteeing performance. Furthermore, by using
matrices that meet these two constraints, each neuron only
needs to receive one error signal [see Fig. 3(b)], eliminating
the need for summation error operations and further reducing
computational complexity.

and STSF+ across various datasets, we present the results on
FashionMNIST [50], N-MNIST [51], DVSGesture [52], and
NETtalk [53] datasets. In the ablation experiments, we first
verify the effectiveness of sparse feedback connections and

A. Empirical Analysis on MNIST
In this section, we delve into the empirical exploration
of algorithmic performance using the MNIST dataset. First,
we use Poisson encoding [56] to convert pixel intensity into
spiking information, where the resulting spiking frequency
is directly proportional to the pixel intensity, and follows a
uniform distribution in the range from 0 to 1. The result of
the training and testing accuracy are shown in Fig. 4(a).
Our primary objective is to validate the effectiveness of
the proposed algorithm while unraveling the nuanced impact
of varying hyperparameters. Specifically, we analyze the
effects of the size of the hidden layer and the value of
the time-window length T . In Fig. 4(b), we observe two
distinct phases in the impact of time-window length T on
model performance. Initially, for T < 10, as T increases,
the model’s accuracy on both the training and testing sets
gradually improves. However, when T > 10, despite the model
maintaining a stable accuracy on the training set, there is a
decline in accuracy on the testing set. This phenomenon is
commonly interpreted as overfitting, leading to a decrease
in the generalization ability of the model on unseen data.
At T = 10, the model reaches its peak accuracy of 98.32%,
and this value of T is consistently used in subsequent MNIST
experiments.
Fig. 4(c) shows the impact of the hidden layer size on the
model’s accuracy. As we increase the hidden layer size from
200 to 1800 with each incremental step of 200, the accuracy
demonstrates a consistent improvement but with a diminishing
increase rate. Also, increasing the size of the hidden layer
results in a significant increase in computational complexity.
Compared to a hidden layer size of 1600 and 800, although the
accuracy slightly decreases (0.2%), the computational workload is reduced by half. To strike a balance between accuracy
and computational efficiency, we opt for a hidden layer size of
800. Besides, to show the classification capabilities of STSF,
we utilized the t-SNE method (a powerful dimensionality
reduction technique that helps visualize high-dimensional data
in a 2-D space, making it easier to observe the clustering and
separation of data points corresponding to different classes) to
visually represent the spiking of the input and output layers
[see Fig. 4(d)–(e)].
Table I shows STSF achieves 98.32% classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art results. First, STSF achieves
similar accuracy to the ELL method [12] while using a smaller
time-window length T . Additionally, despite the complex
convolutional neural network (CNN) structures employed by
STBP [8] and STDP + SVM [40] methods, STSF achieves
comparable results with a simpler MLP network. These findings suggest that STSF is capable of maintaining model
performance while reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, the use of a global–local hybrid approach in STSF,
as opposed to the purely local approach of STDP [34], results
in a 4.32% performance improvement with much smaller timewindow length. In the case of hybrid methods (BP-STDP [41],

Finally, in comparison with the GLSNN and NACA [58] methods, STSF achieves similar accuracy with only three layers,
whereas GLSNN requires five layers and NACA uses CNN
structure. When using a neural network with five layers, the
accuracy increases to 98.51%, as shown in the ablation study.

C. Ablation Study
We first compare feedback methods, including BP, FA, DFA,
and sparse DFA, to validate the effectiveness of sparse DFA in
STSF. In the case of BP, the error signal from the output layer
is precisely propagated layer by layer through exact copies
of the feedforward weight, providing precise information for
each layer of upstream neurons. To further eliminate the
impact, FA replaces these nonbiologically plausible feedback
connections with randomly initialized weights. As the learning process progresses, these randomly initialized feedback
connection weights are adjusted simultaneously with the feedforward connection weights and gradually converge toward the
weights obtained through BP [25]. It is worth noting that in
the FA algorithm, information is still propagated layer by layer
in the same manner as in BP. Another type of architecture,
DFA, feedback connections directly transmit information from
the output layer to each hidden layer. This means that the
neural network can simultaneously update the parameters of
all hidden layers. These random feedback connections remain
fixed and do not change with the update of feedforward
connections, thus avoiding additional computational overhead.
Remarkably, as shown in Fig. 6(a), our research indicates
that, while sparse feedback exhibits a marginally slower convergence rate in comparison to alternative methods, it yields
superior accuracy in results. This result may be attributed to
the fact that neurons in STSF use Vanilla STDP for error computation without involving gradient calculations. Precise and
complex feedback connections used in BP do not contribute
significantly to the network performance in this context, as an
excess of feedback implies more noise.
We also have the ablation studies to investigate the impact of
sparsity rate, the proportion of all-zero rows, and the proportion of all-zero columns on network performance. As shown
in Fig. 7, the sparsity rate of the matrix has minimal impact
on network performance. Comparing a 10% sparsity rate to a
90% sparsity rate, there is only a slight difference of 0.37%.
However, the number of all-zero rows and columns has a

Then, we conduct the experiments to figure out the influence
of the synaptic homeostasis method. As it is known, the
membrane potential serves as a crucial temporal dynamical
variable for information integration and abstraction functions.
The objective of the synaptic homeostasis method is to maintain a balance in neuron states, thereby enhancing overall
performance and stability. We conducted experiments to assess
the impact of the synaptic homeostasis method on model
performance. Fig. 6(b) depicts the changes in the average
membrane potential of neurons in the hidden layer with and

posit that the synaptic homeostasis method plays a role akin

generating excessively large activation values that could otherwise impact overall network performance. Fig. 6(c) shows that

In this section, we compare the computational and memory
complexities of the STSF method with other approaches. It is

crucial to note that, in the context of neural networks, the
primary computational load arises from matrix multiplication,
commonly referred to as multiply-and-accumulate operations
(MACs). In algorithms such as STBP, Online BP, STDP,
and GLSNN, the primary computational overhead stems from
floating-point number multiplications. However, in STSF, the
multiplication of binary spike signals with floating-point numbers is considered a selection operation (the result would
always be floating-point numbers itself or zero, and has
much less computational cost compared with floating-point
number multiplication or addition [62]). We categorize the
computational complexity into three types, including addition
(Add), multiplication (Mul), and selection (Sel) operations. For
memory complexity, we consider the number of variables used
in the optimization process. Furthermore, we divide the overall
computational and memory complexity into two components:
neurons and connections (see Table III).
Consider a fully connected SNN with L layers, each layer
having a size of N, and a time-window length of T . For the
computational complexity of neurons, STBP, Online BP, and
Wu et al. [24] primarily involve addition and multiplication
operations when computing the pseudo-gradient [45], while
STDP and GLSNN use addition and multiplication in calculating local correlation. Regarding the computational complexity
of connections, STBP, Online BP, and Wu et al. [24] are manifested in the matrix multiplication during the error BP across
layers, while STDP is reflected in the computation of local
plasticity within the layer, but they all have the same complexity of O(TLN2). Since GLSNN utilizes direct feedback
connections, the complexity of connection information is influenced by the number of classification categories, denoted as
c. In most cases, c is much smaller than N. This significantly
reduces the computational complexity of addition and multiplication within connections from O(TLN2) to O(cTLN).
Furthermore, STSF reduces the computational complexity by
replacing the multiplication with selection operations.
For the memory complexity, STBP and Wu et al. [24]
involve propagating through the temporal dimension, resulting in a memory complexity multiplied by the time-window
length T compared to other methods such as Online BP and
STDP with O(LN2). As a result of using direct feedback in
GLSNN, the memory complexity of GLSNN will be reduced
to O(cLN). Furthermore, due to the introduction of sparsity,
STSF further reduces the memory complexity of network
connections from O(cLN) to O(LN), as presented in Table III.
VI. CONCLUSION
In this article, we introduced the STSF, which presents a
novel and efficient global–local approach for training SNNs.
Specifically, we propose the Vanilla STDP with the synaptic homeostasis method for local plasticity rules, reducing
memory and computational complexity during the learning
process. Additionally, we introduce a biologically plausible
sparse feedback approach, using only a small number of feedback connections to achieve global error modulation. Through
experimental validation on four diverse datasets (MNIST,
N-MNIST, NETtalk, DVSGesture, and FasionMNIST), the
STSF framework not only achieves performance improvements but also demonstrates computational and memory
efficiency. As a promising direction for future research, we aim
to further extend the network’s depth and integrate mixer
structures [63] to effectively tackle more intricate datasets.
Meanwhile, we plan to use algorithms like PSO [64] for
network initialization to improve performance. Additionally,
we aim to implement STSF on neuromorphic chips [65], [66]
for real-time recognition tasks.

text:
Self-Supervised Learning for
Electroencephalography
Mohammad H. Raﬁei
, Lynne V. Gauthier, Hojjat Adeli
, Fellow, IEEE, and Daniel Takabi , Member, IEEE
Abstract—Decades of research have shown machine learning
superiority in discovering highly nonlinear patterns embedded in
electroencephalography (EEG) records compared with conventional statistical techniques. However, even the most advanced
machine learning techniques require relatively large, labeled
EEG repositories. EEG data collection and labeling are costly.
Moreover, combining available datasets to achieve a large data
volume is usually infeasible due to inconsistent experimental
paradigms across trials. Self-supervised learning (SSL) solves
these challenges because it enables learning from EEG records
across trials with variable experimental paradigms, even when
the trials explore different phenomena. It aggregates multiple
EEG repositories to increase accuracy, reduce bias, and mitigate
overﬁtting in machine learning training. In addition, SSL could
be employed in situations where there is limited labeled training
data, and manual labeling is costly. This article: 1) provides
a brief introduction to SSL; 2) describes some SSL techniques
employed in recent studies, including EEG; 3) proposes current
and potential SSL techniques for future investigations in EEG
studies; 4) discusses the cons and pros of different SSL techniques; and 5) proposes holistic implementation tips and potential
future directions for EEG SSL practices.
Index Terms—Electroencephalography (EEG), machine learning, self-supervised learning (SSL).
I. INTRODUCTION
E
LECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY (EEG) is a noninvasive functional imaging method to examine brainbehavior relationships [1]. EEG records are highly complex
and are often contaminated with artifacts due to participant movements, blinks, and imperfect contact between the
electrode and scalp [2]–[4]. Hence, conventional statistical approaches, such as linear or multivariate regression
analysis [5], cannot capture complex nonlinear relationships
between the EEG signal and behavior [6]. EEG researchers
have employed machine learning approaches to explore
complex nonlinear brain-behavior relationships [7]–[9] with
greater accuracy than conventional statistical models, particularly for brain–computer interface applications [10]–[12].
Machine learning techniques, such as deep artiﬁcial neural
networks [13]–[15], mathematically/statistically simulate the
human brain’s ability to learn, recognize, discover, estimate,

2024. (Corresponding author: Mohammad H. Raﬁei.)
Mohammad H. Raﬁei and Daniel Takabi are with the Department of
Computer Science, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA 30303 USA
(e-mail: mraﬁei@gsu.edu).
Lynne V. Gauthier is with the Department of Physical Therapy and Kinesiology, University of Massachusetts Lowell, Lowell, MA 01854 USA.
Hojjat Adeli is with the Department of Biomedical Informatics and
the Department of Neuroscience, The Ohio State University, Columbus,
OH 43210 USA.

and interpret complicated patterns of sensory inputs [16]–[18].
One might describe a machine learning model, particularly an
artiﬁcial neural network, as a complex multilayer interconnected function of input data (e.g., chunks of multichannel
EEG records) for highly complicated pattern recognition (e.g.,
cognitive state estimation) [19]–[21].
A machine learning model needs to be trained using data
that (usually) a human has collected and categorized/labeled,
termed “supervised learning” [22], [23]. For example, when
training a model to identify neural signatures of successful memory encoding, a human labels EEG traces recorded
during the presentation of information (e.g., words within a
list-learning task) as subsequently remembered versus subsequently forgotten. Supervised learning is, thus, a machine
learning task to efﬁciently optimize the parameters of a
machine learning model to accurately map input data to
their corresponding output, referred to as machine learning
training [24]. An early example of supervised machine learning algorithms is the adaptive conjugate gradient learning
algorithm of Adeli and Hung [25]. Examples of recently developed supervised machine learning/classiﬁcation algorithms are
the enhanced probabilistic neural network [26], the neural
dynamic classiﬁcation algorithm [27], the dynamic ensemble
learning algorithm [28], [29], and the ﬁnite element machine
for fast learning [30]. In EEG studies, a supervised learning
task usually requires a relatively large volume of labeled EEG
data to accurately train a machine learning model because
EEG is complex and is usually contaminated with signiﬁcant
artifacts [31]–[33].
However, obtaining large quantities of labeled data is
not always practical or feasible for EEG experiments. For
example, it is impossible to get fully labeled EEG when
participant-reported outcomes can only be intermittently
recorded throughout an experiment, such as self-reported
fatigue or pain. Moreover, a fully labeled dataset is impossible when the EEG signatures generalize outside a lab
setting. For example, an experimenter may want to establish brain-behavior relationships during a controlled in-lab
task (e.g., detecting EEG signatures of deception [34]) that
can be applied to other tasks/settings (e.g., detection of
deception during an interrogation). When an EEG signature
obtained through one task is applied as a behavioral biomarker during a different task (which may involve different
sensory/cognitive processing that could theoretically inﬂuence
the EEG response), data labels used to establish the biomarker
are available only for the ﬁrst dataset, which represents only
a subset of the more extensive and less task-speciﬁc EEG that
is available for each participant. Finally, practical constraints,
such as the cost of human subjects’ research, may limit

the volume of labeled data. For example, an experiment
designed to detect the neural signatures of successful memory
encoding requires manually labeling list-learning EEG traces
with whether or not a participant later remembered the word.
This is tedious work requiring considerable staff time [35],
[36], which practically limits the amount of data that can be
collected and labeled.
Conventionally, training a supervised model (see Fig. 1)
involves randomly generating parameters (e.g., weights, kernels, and biases). An optimization paradigm, dubbed as “learning algorithm,” will iteratively adjust the magnitude of these
parameters to retrieve a perfect input–output map with proper
“feature representations.” In deep supervised models, as shown
in Fig. 1, feature representations mathematically/statistically
describe speciﬁc characteristics/properties of data relevant to
the outputs. For example, they represent seizure activity characterizations [37]–[39]. They are usually retrieved from the
supervised model’s last (or near-ﬁnal) dense layers (see Fig. 1).
Initial parameters play a signiﬁcant role in converging any
optimization technique, especially learning algorithms [40].
Initial parameters closer to the optimum parameters make the
learning task easier/faster. For example, Hinton and Salakhutdinov [40] proposed an unsupervised pretraining method to
discover better-than-random parameters for each deep belief
network layer. The supervised model is then ﬁne-tuned (i.e.,
trained with a few epochs) using pretrained parameters of
each layer as the initial parameters. The pretraining not
only increased the model’s accuracy but also accelerated the
learning because the pretrained parameters were closer to the
optimum parameters of a well-trained deep belief model than
randomly initiated parameters.
Training a supervised model with initial randomly generated parameters and insufﬁcient labeled data, especially data
obtained under speciﬁc and controlled task conditions, can
result in inaccurate, unreliable estimations or take signiﬁcant
time to converge [40]. An insufﬁcient and limited data repository does not represent all possibilities (known as feasible
domain), leading the models to be overﬁtted on the training
data and be unable to generalize [41]. Self-supervised learning
Fig. 2.
Flowchart of the SSL method.
(SSL), also referred to as “representation learning,” generates
better-than-random initial parameters for the supervised model
and ﬁne-tunes the supervised model with a few labeled data.
Implementing SSL for EEG applications, however, is practically challenging given that SSL has been primarily applied
within the image processing domain [15], [36], [42]–[46].
There have been limited studies focusing on the signal processing domain [47], let alone EEG [44], [48], [49]. Accordingly,
the purpose of this review is to provide a general overview
of EEG-friendly SSL methods, essential considerations when
applying SSL to EEG data, and potential SSL implementation
techniques. This article gives the pros and cons of applying the current state-of-the-art SSL practice to EEG studies.
It concludes by proposing future avenues for methodological
research to improve overall SSL performance.
The rest of this article is organized into seven sections.
Section II provides an overview of SSL. Section III describes
contrastive pretext techniques for supervised and unsupervised
augmentation learning in pretext. Section IV explains generative pretext techniques with a focus on both generative and
reconstructive methods. Section V considers how unconventional and hybrid pretext models may produce enriched feature representations. Section VI describes how archival EEG
datasets can be used to enhance pretext training. Section VII
discusses implementation considerations and future directions.
This article ends with a summary conclusion in Section VIII.
II. OVERVIEW OF SELF-SUPERVISED LEARNING
SSL can be summarized in three tasks, as shown in Fig. 2.
Task 1, the pretext task, includes solutions to generate
better-than-random initial parameters and feature representations from all input data points regardless of their labeling status. For example, for a repository of 90k unlabeled
