RAFIEI et al.: SELF-SUPERVISED LEARNING FOR ELECTROENCEPHALOGRAPHY

data points and 10k labeled data points, the pretext task
uses all 100k input data points to generate such parameters
and feature representations. In SSL, feature representations
mathematically/statistically describe more general (as opposed
to speciﬁc) characteristics/properties of data. For example,
they represent general EEG characteristics not distinct seizure
activity characterizations [37]–[39]. In SSL, feature representations are usually retrieved from the pretext model’s last (or
near-ﬁnal) dense layers. Such models can be supervised or
unsupervised and are primarily in the form of a multilayer
autoencoder [40], multiencoder [50], or adversarial [51]–[53]
neural network model. They might include convolutional [9],
[54], [55], LSTM [56]–[59], and recurrent layers [60], [61].
Task 2, the model modiﬁcation task, is to slightly modify
the pretext model to become compatible with the limited
labeled data; the modiﬁed pretext model is called the “downstream model.” For example, an output layer, such as a Soft-
Max layer (for classiﬁcation) or a regression layer, is added
to the feature representation layer of the trained pretext
model.
Task 3, the downstream task, involves ﬁne-tuning the downstream model using the limited labeled data. One slightly
different practice is ﬁrst to ﬁne-tune the newly added last
layer, i.e., SoftMax or regression layer, without updating
the other layers’ parameters, i.e., freezing all layers except
the newly added layer. Next, ﬁne-tune the whole model by
unfreezing all parameters. Note that the downstream model
has the same architecture as if a “fully supervised” machine
learning model (e.g., Fig. 1) was adopted with randomly
generated initial parameters to learn from the limited labeled
data. The difference is that the downstream task inherited its
initial parameters from the learned pretext model, where the
whole repository, labeled or unlabeled, had been observed.
The purpose of this article is to describe various methods for
developing and implementing a pretext task using both labeled
and unlabeled EEG data.
Recent SSL studies in areas such as image recognition [42],
[62], EEG [49], and natural language processing [47] show
that SSL is effective and boosts performance and accuracy
of estimation, particularly in repositories with limited labeled
data. It is, therefore, a practical methodological approach
to reduce analytic bias (e.g., modeling noise as signal) for
EEG experiments in which additional unlabeled EEG data
are collected. It can also be applied to minimize bias when
analyzing smaller datasets by “informing” the model based
on open-sourced data from previous experiments conducted
under different conditions (e.g., different labs and different
experimental paradigms) [44].
The pretext model design and implementation are the essential SSL tasks (task 1 in Fig. 2). There are many techniques
to develop effective pretext models that produce downstream
relevant feature representations. This article categorizes pretext
techniques into three general categories: contrastive, generative, and unconventional/hybrid. Each is presented along with
examples from primarily previous EEG recognition problems
or alongside applications to illustrate their potential use.
Nevertheless, it is presumed that a trial-and-error approach
will still be required to discover the best pretext model
(i.e., that with the highest downstream accuracy) for a particular experiment.
III. CONTRASTIVE PRETEXT TECHNIQUES
Contrastive pretext techniques recognize the “contrasts”
between different augmentations of input data, regardless of
their labeling status. There are various augmentation techniques, such as adding Gaussian noise or masking, i.e.,
switching the magnitude of a predeﬁned number of randomly
selected variables in input data with 0. Input data and its
augmented version form a contrastive pair. Two augmented
versions of input data can also represent a contrastive pair. One
can design a pretext model to recognize the input data (class
negative) from its augmented version (class positive) [43],
[48], [49]. Another pretext model can be designed to recognize
augmented versions of a particular input data from augmented versions of other input data in a batch of inputs [50].
In general, in contrastive techniques, ﬁrst, a repository of
contrastive pairs is created. Second, a machine learning model,
supervised or unsupervised, along with a proper loss function,
is designed to learn the augmentations. [36]. Once learned, the
downstream task beneﬁts from the pretext learned parameters
(e.g., weights, kernels, and biases).
In supervised contrastive pretext, an augmented input is
pseudolabeled, positive, or negative. For example, a chunk
of EEG trace is selected randomly and pseudolabeled −1
(original chunk). Next, Gaussian noise is added to the chunk;
the noisy chunk is pseudolabeled +1. Hence, a pseudolabeled
repository double the initial number of inputs is automatically
generated to train a supervised pretext model with an architecture similar to Fig. 1. This model learns the patterns of
the original (negative) and augmented (positive) data [43],
[48], [49]. The trained pretext model can be ﬁne-tuned in
the downstream task with/without a minor modiﬁcation of its
output layer; the pretext two-class output layer is replaced
with an output layer compatible with the downstream task.
For example, if the problem is a ﬁve-class problem, then
the two-class output layer of the trained pretext model is
replaced with a ﬁve-class layer (usually a SoftMax [63] layer).
This replacement is also known as “transfer learning” in
the machine learning literature [64], [65]. Once the modiﬁed
architecture is retrieved, the parameters of the last replaced
layer are ﬁrst updated using several learning epochs. Next, all
layers’ parameters are ﬁne-tuned using a few more learning
epochs and usually by implementing a relatively low magnitude learning rate [40].
In unsupervised contrastive pretext, no pseudolabeling is
required; their goal is to learn solely from the input data [66].
They are usually used to “reconstruct” input data points. For
example, the original EEG chunk is reconstructed from the
noisy chunk using an autoencoder. An autoencoder comprises
an encoder and a decoder neural network (see Fig. 3). The
encoder encodes the EEG records into a feature representation layer. The decoder decodes the feature representation and reconstructs the EEG [40], [67]. In a pretext task,
one can encode the low-resolution (masked) (noisy) EEG
records and decode, i.e., reconstruct, the high resolution (complete/unmasked) (denoised) EEG records. The encoder can

layer (model modiﬁcation task in Fig. 2), and ﬁne-tuned in the

Training supervised pretext models with a few pseudolabels
is usually computation- and memory-friendlier and less complex (i.e., fewer parameters) than unsupervised models where,
for example, a whole reconstruction is learned. One might
argue that the feature representations in unsupervised models
are more enriched than those resulting from supervised models
because the model needs to perform a whole reconstruction.
However, there are usually no unique feature representations
for, say, an autoencoder; it could result in different sets of
learned parameters (and feature representations) when trained
with different initial parameters. The learning optimization
can have more local or global solutions (representations) in
unsupervised contrastive models than in supervised ones. The
feasible domain is wider in unsupervised models due to more
optimization (i.e., learning) parameters. Assuming at least one
optimum set of parameters for the downstream model, the
ﬁne-tuning might become harder or easier depending on how
close the encoder-learned parameters are to such optimum
parameters. Under reasonably identical circumstances, supervised pretext models are computationally more efﬁcient than
unsupervised ones.
The pretext data augmentation design signiﬁcantly inﬂuences the downstream accuracy, whether the pretext model
is supervised or unsupervised. Ultimately, most studies will
need to rely on trial and error to identify the effective augmentation design (the one with the most accurate downstream
results) for their problem. To the best of our knowledge,
as of today, only supervised contrastive pretext models have
been utilized in EEG studies, and only a few augmentation
techniques have been tried. However, a theoretical use case
for unsupervised methods is also discussed. It should be noted
that both supervised and unsupervised contrastive approaches
employ most augmentation techniques. The following subsections, A. Banville et al. Augmentations and B. Neurologist-
Recommended Augmentations, detail EEG augmentation techniques utilized in the recent literature.
A. Banville et al. Augmentations

In fact, in relative positioning, a “pair” is labeled positive

However, EEG records include general information that can

Relative positioning and temporal shufﬂing are augmentation methods that are applicable for any temporal records; for
example, video shufﬂing has been examined in SSL studies
in the area of computer vision [45], [57]. It will help the
downstream task if the augmentation techniques are such that
they maintain the informativity of the EEG downstream task
and produce feature representations enriched with EEG critical
information. However, it is still unclear why one augmentation
would result in more enriched representations for a particular
downstream task (i.e., supervised problem) in EEG studies;
the current implementations have been primarily focused on
trial and error. Besides, as a pretext model would learn the
augmented repository to develop initial parameters for the
downstream model, modifying the temporal organization of
the EEG in the pretext task may be suboptimal because
it may compromise the EEG’s physiological footprints; the
approach of dividing EEG into chunks breaks the continuity
of the information. Hence, augmentation techniques could be
tuned/designed to maintain the embedded semantic information required in the downstream task.
B. Neurologist-Recommended Augmentations
Mohsenvand et al. [44] surveyed neurologists to discover to
what extent SSL augmentation techniques would maintain the
physiological meaningfulness of the EEG records and would
not remove/contaminate useful EEG information. They illustrated the effectiveness of such augmentations on various EEG
problems, such as emotion detection [22], [70], abnormality
recognition, and sleep-stage scoring [71]. The preliminary

Zero masking [see Fig. 5(d)] is about switching the magnitude

may remove important information from the EEG records,
particularly with shorter EEG traces. High-frequency Gaussian

IV. GENERATIVE PRETEXT TECHNIQUES
Generative models are usually unsupervised models. They
“reconstruct” or “generate” input data points. An example of
“reconstruction” is an autoencoder (see Fig. 3), such as a
deep restricted Boltzmann machine [40], [67] to reconstruct
the original data (no augmentation required). An example of
“generation” is creating synthetic data with similar distribution and characteristics as an available EEG input repository
(labeled or unlabeled) using generative adversarial networks
(GANs) [72], [73] (see Fig. 6). GANs are usually employed
for generating synthetic data [51], such as computer-generated
EEG traces that appear visually indistinguishable from those
obtained from actual human participants.
GAN comprises two components: a generator and a discriminator (see Fig. 6). The generator generates synthetic
data (e.g., artiﬁcial EEG records). Random values enter into
an input layer called “latent space”. Latent space postulates
a “tuner” where slight changes to its random values result
in variations in generated synthetic data. The discriminator
then receives the synthetic data and computes the probability
of how realistic/valid the generated synthetic data is compared with an available repository (a.k.a. “distribution”) of
actual data (e.g., EEG records from a cognitive recognition
study) [74], [75]. See StyleGAN2 [76], [77] as an example of
GAN’s outcome applied to computer vision [78]. Once trained,
the discriminator can be used in downstream estimation tasks.
The advantage of GAN models is that there is no need for
data augmentations; a model is trained to create synthetic
data that are practically indistinguishable from the distribution
of actual EEG records. However, GANs training comes with
higher computation costs than supervised pretext models.
Today, there has been a shortage of studies employing
generative pretext models for EEG analysis. One reason is the
computationally intensive training of models such as GANs.
In addition, GANs require a large input repository. Given
that a supervised pretext model can substantially boost the
performance of the downstream task with a few training

offset by their practical challenges. Therefore, supervised
pretext models would be preferred over unsupervised methods if limited computer resources are available for real-life
applications. If computer intensity is not a problem, GANs
might be preferred over autoencoders because they do not
need any input augmentation. Besides, their discriminator
learns features addressing the data’s authenticity enriched with
feature representation and learned parameters suitable for the
downstream task.
V. UNCONVENTIONAL AND HYBRID PRETEXT MODELS
The pretext task develops a trained model enriched with
learned parameters and feature representation layers for a
downstream task. Hence, solutions beyond conventional contrastive or generative pretext models could be examined. For
example, contrastive supervised models need not be dichotomous. They could involve discriminating between three or
more categories of pretext data. For example, one could
employ a contrastive pretext task to distinguish two simulated Gaussian noise intensities and the original EEG traces
(three categories). In unsupervised autoencoders, the decoding
process could comprise of two decoders where one decodes the
feature representation to reconstruct from, say, masked EEG
[see Fig. 7(a)], and one to reconstruct, say, from downsampled
EEG resolution [see Fig. 7(b)].
The potential tradeoffs for including more or fewer contrastive categories are still unclear and problem-dependent. For
practical reasons, one might instead have as many categories
as the downstream task to skip the model modiﬁcation task
in Fig. 2. For similar pragmatic reasons, one might prefer
supervised pretext models over unsupervised ones where a
model modiﬁcation task is necessary.

A potential future avenue to create an unconventional pretext task would be creating pseudoregression outputs using the
EEG signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). For example, apply noise
to an original EEG chunk, compute its SNR, and set it as
the output. The goal here is to estimate the SNR for EEG
chunks, a regression output. Whether in EEG or computer
vision, SSL studies usually offer several pretext augmentations
and examine them for their particular problem by trial and
error.
Hybrid models may offer a solution to merge the advantages of both supervised and unsupervised pretext models.
They include both complexity of unsupervised pretext and
a more stable feature representation development capability
of supervised models. The feasibility of using hybrid pretext models has been demonstrated for non-EEG applications. For example, an encoder, a clustering technique, and
a discriminator come together to develop pretext models [43],
[46], [79]. The discriminator investigates if encoded representations of contrastive input pairs are from the same
cluster. Clusters can be computed using techniques, such as
K-means [80], density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise [81], or expectation-maximization [82]. The
resultant models still have the disadvantage of computation
intensity. Still, they can skip the model modiﬁcation task in
Fig. 2 and yield more accurate downstream outcomes since
the feature representations are statistically more robust/stable
than the pretext initial parameters.
In temporal data, such as EEG, one can beneﬁt from
deep correlation tracking to develop a pretext cycle consistency loss similar to Yuan et al. [83]. Cycle consistency
in temporal data provides a unifying representation of the
temporal ﬂow [84]. In video and image recognition problems, trackers are often deep CNNs to predict target positions in forwarding and backward frames. Yuan et al. [83]
developed a pretext tracker and corresponding loss function
that includes deep feature extraction and a deep correlation
tracking framework, a potential unconventional SSL method
for pretext cycle consistency of temporal EEG. Spatiotemporal
representation preservation [85] is another potential for EEG
pretext development where complex dependencies between
EEG adjacent channels are explored for inconspicuous human
activity-EEG investigations. Furthermore, weakly supervised
learning techniques could be investigated in pretext, where,
instead of training, model parameters are carefully investigated
and designed for a contrastive task, and since training is almost
not required, unlabeled data can signiﬁcantly be useful in
parameter investigation [86].
VI. EMPLOYING ADDITIONAL EEG DATASETS TO
ENHANCE PRETEXT TRAINING
In EEG studies, some ﬁne-tuned contrastive models showed
higher accuracy than fully supervised models [43], [44], [48],
[49]. However, the SSL pretext task requires a semantically enriched data repository to achieve accurate downstream
results [44]. As the pretext task does not require labeled EEG,
one might suggest aggregating different EEG datasets to enrich
the pretext repository.
There are a variety of reasons that EEG is recorded,
including, but not limited to, abnormality detection [87], [88],
sleep stage/apnea estimation [89], [90], affective state recognition [44], [91], and cognitive recognition [92]. However, generating EEG records for a particular problem is expensive [93],
[94]. Data aggregation and channel production are techniques
to increase and enrich the required data for EEG-based pattern
recognition problems.
A. Channel Production
An EEG electrode records the difference between the electrode’s voltage and a reference electrode. If an EEG dataset
with N channels is available, one can create new channels
by taking each channel as a reference and computing the
remaining channels based on the reference channel. This way,
( N
2 ) = (N(N −1)/2) possible new channels can be produced
for contrastive SSL pretext tasks [44]. Channel production
is beneﬁcial for SSL techniques in two primary ways: 1) it
produces new neurologically meaningful channels representing
different data views (similar to augmentations) and 2) it
increases the amount of data for a more extensive SSL pretext
learning.
B. Data Aggregation
More accurate model parameters can be derived when the
pretext task is trained using a large dataset. However, EEG
data acquisition is relatively expensive; a potential solution to
this challenge is to leverage previously collected EEG data
from open-sourced EEG repositories. Aggregating EEG data
from multiple sources for the pretext training task would
likely enhance the external validity of the computational
approach, as it markedly increases the volume of EEG being
analyzed and could minimize the inﬂuence of setting-speciﬁc
features. Adding more EEG data helps the pretext model to
observe more EEG samples, learning general EEG feature
representations. The pretext task only requires input data [36],
[43]. Thus, the downstream tasks employed during the various
experiments are irrelevant [95]. Hence, raw EEG data from
various studies, irrespective of the experimental paradigm,
can be preprocessed (e.g., resampled and denoised) using
consistent procedures and then aggregated to generate a larger
repository for any pretext task [44].
It can be presumed that there is a tradeoff between the
size of the data repository for the pretext task (i.e., how
many open-source EEG datasets are aggregated to train the
pretext model) and the similarity of the EEG traces in the
pretext repository to that being collected in the downstream
task. For example, aggregating EEG records of a sleep study
and an affective recognition study will boost the size of
the data repository for training the pretext model but also
might affect the internal validity of the pretext task negatively
as sleep EEG records would differ markedly from those of
awake individuals. In this example, one might hypothesize
that, due to these studies’ different nature, the aggregation
of the EEG records would impoverish the pretext model’s
feature representation, resulting in accuracy decay in the
downstream task. However, late evidence suggests otherwise.

Mohsenvand et al. [44] improved the accuracy of the downstream task in three different EEG studies (sleep apnea,
abnormality, and affective recognition) by combining the three
EEG data repositories in the pretext task.
Although data aggregation seems an effective technique to
enrich the pretext data points, the optimal balance between the
amount of data used to train a pretext model and the similarity
to the downstream task remains an open question ripe for
further investigation. Nevertheless, current best practices can
aggregate the available data repositories with other existing
physiologically “similar” EEG data for pretext training. In this
section, several open-source EEG datasets that have been
implemented in recent research are described. In addition,
Table I summarizes valuable facts about these data, such as
their availability, sampling frequency, and the total number of
EEG channels. In this article, EEG data are categorized into
two major categories: 1) affective recognition and cognitive
assessment and 2) medical diagnosis.
1) Affective
Recognition
and
Cognitive
Assessment: Mohsenvand et al. [44] employed the Shanghai Jiao
Tong University (SJTU), Emotion EEG Dataset (SEED)
[98], [137]–[139] for SSL learning. SEED is divided into
three subdatasets: 1) SEED I [138]; 2) SEED-IV [140];
and 3) SEED-VIG [141]. SEED I includes emotion-related
EEG records when each participant was watching emotional
videos. SEED-IV is an expansion of SEED I, where participants watched four types of emotion-related videos, and
in addition to EEG, their eye movements were recorded
as well. SEED-VIG was designed for vigilance estimation,
where the participant’s stimulation was via a virtual driving
system [142]–[146].
Sarkar and Etemad [147] applied SSL for affective recognition. Out of four datasets they used to illustrate their
model, Affect, Personality, and Mood Research on Individuals and Groups, abbreviated as AMIGOS [116], [148],
and Emotion Recognition Through EEG and ECG Signals
from Wireless Low-Cost Off-the-Shelf Devices, abbreviated
as DREAMER [149], were the repositories that include EEG
records. The AMIGOS dataset consists of two subdatasets.
One is called the short video experiment, where 40 participants watch affective-based videos and rate them as valence,
arousal, or dominance. The other one is called the long
video experiment, where 17 participants watch affective-based
videos alone and 20 participants watch the videos in groups
of a few participants. In addition to video rating, participants
were asked about their emotions on the second experiment’s
videos. The DREAMER dataset consists of EEG records for
self-affective state recognition after video stimuli. The records
were collected using the low-cost Emotiv EPOC wireless EEG
headset [45], [142], [150], [151].
Feradov [152] employed a publicly available dataset for
emotion analysis called EEG, physiological, and video signal
(DEAP) [121] to study the relationship between cognitive
brain activity and state of affect. DEAP includes self-assessed
EEG records from participants watching music videos. Each
participant scores his/her emotional levels regarding ﬁve
affective states of arousal, valence, dominance, liking, and
familiarity after each video, where, except the familiarity,
which is scored between 1 and 5, the rest are scored between
1 and 9 [35], [143], [153].
Seal et al. [96] developed an EEG database for emotion
classiﬁcation. Each participant watched three video patterns of
four emotions: natural, happy, sad, and fear (total of 12 videos
and 150 sec each). EEG was recorded while matching each
video pattern with emotion in a list. Since the frontal lobe
and temporal region have been shown to emit emotion-related
EEG information [154], [155], four frontal EEG channels,
referred to as FP2-F4, FP2-F8, FP1-F3, and FP1-F7 based
on the international 10/20 system [156], were employed.
Sengupta et al. [157] developed an EEG dataset for fatigue
and alertness recognition. Each individual was assigned to
timely tasks that required full individual concentrations. The
tasks include letter counting, psychomotor vigilance, and
Stroop tasks. The experiment was stopped either when the
individual performance drops below certain levels due to
fatigue or when the individual complains about extreme discomfort. After the experiment, each individual self-assessed
his/her level of cognitive fatigue.
Saba-Sadiya et al. [158] employed the EEG During Mental
Arithmetic Dataset [159], [160] for the SSL task. The data
include EEG records during a resting state and a mental arithmetic task. Klaproth et al. [161] proposed a pilot’s
adoptive cognitive assistance computational model based on
EEG records and ﬂight-dec interaction. Cognitive assistance
provides on-time helpful feedback by predicting an individual behavior regarding other individuals’ actions and the
environmental (e.g., the ﬂight simulator) factors/constraints.
Cognitive assistant addresses epistemically (due to lack of
knowledge—needs to be reduced) and aleatory (due to event
variability—needs to be managed) uncertainties. Participants
include aircrews with an average experience of 3230 ﬂight
hours. Each participant’s EEG is recorded before an 18-min
program with nine to 14 events (i.e., ﬂight-deck alerts, such
as fuel pump failure and engine ﬁre) followed by air trafﬁc
control auditory messages. The experiment includes both standard and critical alerts; the goal was to study the EEG patterns
related to various alerts.
2) Medical Diagnosis: The Institute of Systems and Robotics (ISRUC) Sleep (ISRUC-Sleep) [162] and CHB-MIT Scalp
EEG dataset [163] is a potential EEG dataset for SSL pretraining. The ISRUC-Sleep is simply a sleep-scoring dataset. The
CHB-MIT Scalp EEG database includes pediatric participants
with intractable seizures [164]–[167].
Banville et al. [48], [49] employed four publicly available
datasets for sleep studies: Physionet Sleep EDF [100], Montreal Archive of Sleep Studies (MASS) [168], Temple University Hospital (TUH), Abnormal (TUHab) [169], and Physionet
Challenge 2018 (PC18) [170], for SSL EEG recognition. The
MASS and PC18 datasets are sleep studies. The TUHab
dataset is for pathological EEG detection [171], [172].
C. Aggregation Challenges
It remains unclear to what extent SSL can beneﬁt from
data aggregation and how the fusion of data from various
EEG resources would improve the SSL pretext task for a particular problem. The SSL models of Mohsenvand et al. [44]

i.e., Sleep EDF [100], SEED [98], and TUHab [169], when

Although all the aggregated data were EEG records, the
contexts of the studies were different, including the level

It remains unclear whether the results of downstream tasks of

excluded the EEG data of the sleep study from Mohsenvand et al.’s model [44] and aggregated only EEG records
from awake individuals, i.e., the ones corresponding to emotion SEED [98], and abnormality recognition TUHab [169].
Herein lies the potential to run EEG recognition experiments
using data aggregation and sensitivity analysis. An improvement in the results, if sleep data is excluded from the pretext
task, would indicate that data would not enrich the feature

suggest that more data will continue to enhance the pretext

VII. IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS
AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
SSL techniques have undoubtedly helped increase the accuracy of supervised EEG recognition problems, as shown in
recent studies [44], [48], [49]. However, many unanswered
or partially addressed questions exist, for example, how
to select the optimal pretext augmentation or employ contrastive, generative, or hybrid EEG pretext. In this section,
these relevant aspects of methodological decision-making are
elucidated.
1) Optimum Augmentation Technique: The physiologically
approved pretext augmentations maintain the informativity
and ﬁdelity of the EEG records, as was highlighted in
Mohsenvand et al. [44]. However, the contrastive, generative,
and unconventional/hybrid pretext tasks may appear arbitrary
or irrelevant to the downstream task. In contrastive models,
the augmented data (and their labels in supervised contrastive
pretext) usually have no similarity/compatibility with the
downstream task. For example, the pretext task may involve
discriminating between whether Gaussian noise was added
to the EEG trace or not. In contrast, the downstream task
may include distinguishing whether a word is likely to be
subsequently remembered or not based on the EEG power
spectrum.
While learned features eventually assist the downstream
task, it would be fruitful to discover the extent to which various
augmentation techniques could be adapted in conjunction with
downstream tasks to boost downstream accuracy/performance.
For example, suppose that the literature/physiology suggests
an association of alpha power with memory performance.
In that case, the relevant augmentation of those bandwidths
may produce pretext augmentations that are more relevant to

source: Self-Supervised Learning for Electroencephalography.pdf
text:
a downstream task investigating memory performance. For
example, if the downstream application seeks to identify
oscillatory signatures of more successful memory encoding,
a pretext augmentation of the frequency spectrum may be
a more downstream-relevant pretext augmentation. Therefore,
it is possible that the choice of pretext task could be enhanced
by relying on the literature or empirically exploring the
inﬂuence of the pretext task on downstream task performance.
One might accomplish using machine learning feature selection or combinatory pattern recognition methods [173]–[175]
on a few labeled data to shed light on how different data
variables affect the downstream outputs (i.e., the original
problem’s output) and, based on the variable “importance,”
design downstream-relevant contrastive augmentation.
The current supervised contrastive pretext augmentations
suggest developing negative and positive labels; hence, the
pretext model usually has a two-class classiﬁcation output
layer. This output layer must be replaced with a brand new
randomly initiated (instead of pretrained) output layer in the
downstream task for ﬁne-tuning (modiﬁcation task in Fig. 2).
For example, if the downstream task is a three-class problem (a regression problem), one would replace the usually
two-class pretext SoftMax output layer with a three-class one
(a regression output layer). Hence, all the pretext pretrained
output layer’s information (i.e., pretrained weights, kernels,
and biases that connect the last pretext hidden layer to the
output layer) is replaced with randomly generated parameters
(i.e., weights, kernels, and biases) for the downstream task.
As such, the SSL would beneﬁt (in terms of downstream
accuracy, ease of implementation, and maintaining learned
pretext parameters) from contrastive augmentation techniques
with identical output architecture and conﬁguration as the
downstream task (i.e., skipping the model modiﬁcation task in
Fig. 2).
2) Contrastive, Generative, or Hybrid EEG Recognition?:
It is still unclear which pretext technique would be optimally
effective for various EEG problems. A supervised contrastive
model with a few pseudolabels would be less computationally
intensive than an unsupervised contrastive model, such as
autoencoder, where a whole “reconstruction” needs to be
learned (rather than a few labels). However, there is some
theoretical rationale for the unsupervised model’s consideration, such as its ability to extract complex EEG features and
deeply encoded characteristics, giving the downstream model a
chance of higher accuracy. For example, an autoencoder reconstructs the signal after augmentation, such as zero masking
[see Fig. 7(a)], adding noise, and using a time shift, similar
to the augmentations proposed by Mohsenvand et al. [44] and
Banville et al. [48], [49]. In particular, zero masking is similar
to image unpainting and reconstruction in image recognition
studies [176]. In image recognition, one hybrid approach
focuses on the closeness of clusters [27] of encoded representations of different views of an image [177]. A similar
approach in EEG recognition is clustering feature representations of well-overlapped chunks of temporal records. Another
approach is reconstructing high-resolution images from low
resolution [178]. In EEG, a similar approach would require
a signal to be reconstructed from its downsampled record or
vice versa [see Fig. 7(b)]. Another approach would reconstruct
the time domain from the frequency domain [see Fig. 7(c)],
where the most important characteristics of a signal are embedded [66], [67]. Reconstructing an EEG channel from other
channels can be another direction to be investigated, similar
to image channel reconstruction [179]. Whether supervised
or unsupervised, all these methods nonetheless ﬁnd feature
representations that work best for the downstream task. One
area of investigation for future methodological research is to
contrast the various supervised and unsupervised approaches
discussed in this article.
Autoencoders are to “reconstruct” only, usually without
any relevancy to the downstream task. Besides, in contrast
to supervised contrastive models where the “learning” could
be guided by pseudolabels that could have been potentially
designed to be in conjunction with the downstream labels,
an autoencoder’s feature representations and loss function
convergence/learning performance very much depend on initial randomly generated parameters. For example, if a pretext contrastive autoencoder (supervised contrastive model)
is trained twice, each time with different randomly selected
initial parameters, i.e., weights, kernels, and biases, the trained
encoder (model) would generate different (similar) feature
representations in each try. To address this problem while
beneﬁting from autoencoders’ profound encoding–decoding
feature extraction advantage, one would recommend hybrid
models [43], [79] where the autoencoders beneﬁt from loss
functions that are not just addressing reconstruction from any
feature representation but representations relevant to downstream tasks. For example, an autoencoder would employ a
loss function (to be minimized for machine learning) that
reconstructs the original EEG from its augmented version.
At the same time, the model would keep the cluster of
augmented EEG encoded feature representations farther from
the cluster of original EEG similar to Raﬁei and Adeli [27].
In contrast with autoencoders, unsupervised generative models, such as GANs, would lead to a trained discriminator
enriched with feature representations sensitive to data authenticity (compared with contaminated/synthetic data). Note that,
in GANs, no augmentation is required, which may produce a signiﬁcant advantage over unsupervised contrastive
models.
Nevertheless, supervised contrastive models surpass any
generative, hybrid, or unsupervised contrastive models regarding computation efﬁciency, memory usage, and quick pretext
convergence. Usually, with a few epochs (one or two), a supervised pretext model would yield near 100% pretext validation
accuracy (similar to pretraining in [40]), mainly when augmentation intensity is relatively high (i.e., augmentations are
easily distinguishable). However, the motivation to investigate
techniques other than supervised contrastive models is for
boosting downstream accuracy and efﬁciency.
3) Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning Tips: In the standard transfer learning and ﬁne-tuning process, an already
trained model, referred to as the base model, is usually
borrowed entirely or partially and modiﬁed to learn the
current problem quickly using transfer learning and ﬁnetuning techniques. A base model usually includes hundreds

of convolutional, recurrent, or dense (i.e., fully connected)
layers. Using mighty/expensive resources, these layers have
been trained (for days) on a different dataset than the current
problem. Such datasets might have thousands of categories or
include millions of data points. The base model is enriched
with learned parameters, weights, ﬁlters, and kernels capable
of identifying feature representation for any problem within
the same data domain as the one base model was trained on.
The base model’s input and output layers are often modiﬁed
to be compatible with the current problem. For example,
nontrainable lower/upper scaling layers are added to the input
layer for input data dimension compatibility. Output layer/s
are substituted with trainable dense/SoftMax layers compatible
with the current datasets output. The base model (or a portion
of the base model) is frozen in transfer learning, meaning
that its parameters are not updated. Instead, the newly added
output layer is trained using a relatively large learning rate
for many epochs. The base model already produced enriched
feature representation from data; the only task is to learn from
this representation to address the current problem using the
newly added output layer. The base model (or a portion of
the base model) is unfrozen in ﬁne-tuning. Its parameters can
now be updated using a relatively small learning rate for a few
epochs to prevent overﬁtting, especially if the current dataset
has few labeled data. Fine-tuning often boosts the accuracy of
the model signiﬁcantly [180], [181].
Despite the data domain, SSL techniques require careful
transfer learning and ﬁne-tuning implementation in the pretext
and downstream stages. Regardless of the SSL type, there
are two possible scenarios in pretext: 1) the pretext model
is designed from scratch with various layers, including convolution, recurrent, and dense (i.e., fully connected) layers,
all with randomly generated parameters and 2) the pretext
model is the whole or a portion of a base model. Reallife industrial-level implementations usually fall in the second
scenario, where a base model would make the pretext training
computationally much more efﬁcient. In that case, transfer
learning does not help; the goal is not to solve the pretext
task (e.g., learning pseudolabels or contrasts) but to enrich
the feature representation layer of the pretext model with
the information in the current data for the downstream task.
As such, the base model (or a portion of it) is unfrozen and
ﬁne-tuned with a small learning rate only. However, in the
downstream task, the procedure is similar to the standard
transfer learning and ﬁne-tuning, where the pretext model acts
as a base model.
VIII. CONCLUSION
SSL enables learning from EEG records across trials with
variable experimental paradigms, even when the trials explore
different phenomena. It allows for aggregating multiple EEG
repositories to increase accuracy, reduce bias, and mitigate
overﬁtting in machine learning training. This article provided a
thorough review of how SSL techniques, previously reviewed
for their utility in image processing [15], [36], [42]–[46],
have been employed in recent EEG studies. In addition,
this article summarized available datasets for potential data
fusion to help cost-efﬁcient SSL pretext learning. Furthermore,
this article proposes solutions that have been examined in
mostly the image processing domain to be considered in EEG
problems, such as generative models with potentially enriched
augmentations (see Fig. 7). Finally, this article proposed future
avenues to overcome challenges in SSL practice to exploit
efﬁcient EEG recognition. Future research should quantify
the impact of tailoring the pretext task to the downstream
application and explore the potential advantages of generative,
hybrid, or unsupervised contrastive models.

Mohammad H. Raﬁei received the Ph.D. degree in
civil engineering with a focus on machine learning
from The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH,
USA, in December 2016, under the supervision of
Prof. Hojjat Adeli.
He continued his machine learning research in
infrastructure engineering, neuroscience, and physical medicine as a Post-Doctoral Researcher at the
Engineering and Medical Schools, The Ohio State
University, from February 2017 to August 2018.
He then joined the Whiting School of Engineering,
Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA, as a Post-Doctoral Fellow,
in August 2018, and an Adjunct Assistant Research Scientist in September
2019, where he has been working on machine learning nanoscale materials
simulations. He was a Machine Learning Course Developer and an Instructor
at the Engineering for Professionals Graduate-Level Program, Whiting School
of Engineering, Johns Hopkins University, in 2020. He joined the Information
Security and Privacy: Interdisciplinary Research and Education (INSPIRE)
Center, Department of Computer Science, Georgia State University, Atlanta,
GA, USA, in January 2021, as a Post-Doctoral Fellow, where he has been
working on the emerging area of privacy-preserving machine learning.
Lynne V. Gauthier received the Ph.D. degree
in medical psychology from The University of
Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, AL, USA,
in 2011, under the supervision of Dr. Edward Taub.
She was an Assistant Professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation with The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA, from 2011 to 2018.
She joined the Department of Physical Therapy
and Kinesiology, University of Massachusetts Lowell, Lowell, MA, USA, as an Associate Professor,
in 2018. Her research utilizes new motion capture
technology, data analytics, and neuroimaging approaches to derive personalized insights into motor recovery.
Dr. Gauthier has been co-chairing the Neuroplasticity Working Group for
the American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine since 2016.
Hojjat Adeli (Fellow, IEEE) received the Ph.D.
degree from Stanford University, Stanford, CA,
USA, in 1976.
He is currently an Emeritus Academy Professor
with The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH,
USA, where he held the Abba G. Lichtenstein Chair
Professorship for ten years.
Dr. Adeli is also a member of the Norwegian
Academy of Technological Sciences and the Academia Europaea, a Corresponding Member of the
Spanish Royal Academy of Engineering, a Foreign
Member of the Lithuanian Academy of Sciences and the Polish Academy of
Science, a Distinguished Member of the American Society of Civil Engineers
(ASCE), and a fellow of American Association for the Advancement of
Science (AAAS), American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering
(AIMBE), and the American Neurological Association. He was a recipient
of over 70 awards and honors, including seven honorary doctorates, and
honorary professorships at several Asian and European universities. He was
proﬁled as an Engineering Legend in the journal Leadership and Management
in Engineering (ASCE) in April 2010 by a noted biographer of legendary
engineers.
Daniel Takabi (Member, IEEE) is currently an
Associate Professor of computer science and a Next
Generation Scholar with Georgia State University,
Atlanta, GA, USA. He is also a Founding Director
of the Information Security and Privacy: Interdisciplinary Research and Education (INSPIRE) Center, designated as the National Center of Academic
Excellence in Cyber Defense Research (CAE-R),
Georgia State University. His research interests
include various aspects of cybersecurity and privacy, including trustworthy AI, privacy-preserving
machine learning, adversarial learning, advanced access control models,
insider threats, and usable security and privacy.

Semi-Supervised Learning Algorithm for
Identifying High-Priority Drug–Drug Interactions
Through Adverse Event Reports
Ning Liu
, Member, IEEE, Cheng-Bang Chen
, Member, IEEE, and Soundar Kumara
Abstract—Identifying drug-drug interactions (DDIs) is
a critical enabler for reducing adverse drug events and
improving patient safety. Generating proper DDI alerts during prescribing workﬂow has the potential to prevent DDIrelated adverse events. However, the implementation of DDI
alerting system remains a challenge as users are experiencing alert overload which causes alert fatigue. One strategy to optimize the current system is to establish a list
of high-priority DDIs for alerting purposes, though it is a
resource-intensive task. In this study, we propose a machine learning framework to extract useful features from the
FDA adverse event reports and then identify potential highpriority DDIs using an autoencoder-based semi-supervised
learning algorithm. The experimental results demonstrate
the effectiveness of using adverse event feature representations in differentiating high- and low-priority DDIs.
Additionally, the proposed algorithm utilizes stacked autoencoders and weighted support vector machine for boosting classiﬁcation performance, which outperforms other
competing methods in terms of F-measure and AUC score.
This framework integrates multiple information sources,
leverages domain knowledge and clinical evidence, and provides a practical approach for pre-screening high-priority
DDI candidates for medication alerts.
Index Terms—Semi-supervised learning, stacked autoencoder, classiﬁcation, drug-drug interactions, clinical decision support, adverse event reports.
I. INTRODUCTION
A
DVERSE drug events caused by drug-drug interactions
(DDIs) pose a major threat to patient safety, leading to
increased morbidity and mortality, prolonged hospitalizations
and higher healthcare costs [1] [2]. In general, DDI-related adverse drug events are largely preventable provided that proper
warnings and interventions are implemented during provider’s
prescribing workﬂow [3]. To mitigate the risks of preventable
DDIs, medication-related clinical decision support (CDS) is integrated into provider’s electronic health record (EHR) system,

aiming to generate DDI alerts and reduce errors during medication order entry. However, evidence [4] shows that CDS systems
have not successfully reduced the risks of DDI exposure due to
high override rates (as many as 98% [5]) caused by alert fatigue. Currently, most DDI alerting systems in the U.S. rely on
the clinical contents from knowledge base vendors; and they
are prone to include all possible DDIs to reduce legal liability
[6]. The overwhelming number of DDI alerts, inaccurate and
dubious information, and improper display during provider’s
workﬂow constitute the major reasons for poor acceptance of
DDI alerts amongst clinicians [7], [8].
Recent studies suggest that tiering DDI alerts by severity and
optimizing DDI notiﬁcation mechanism represents a potential
strategy to mitigate alert fatigue and establish better usability [6], [9], [10]. After reducing the volume of unnecessary
DDI alerts, clinicians are able to pay more attention to the remaining clinically signiﬁcant alerts. In an attempt to address
this issue, early investigations [11] have been carried out by
Phansalkar et al. under the sponsorship of the U.S. Ofﬁce of the
National Coordinator (ONC) for Health Information Technology, with the purpose of establishing a high-priority DDI list
for alerting purposes. Through expert panel review, a list of 15
class-based DDIs were approved to be high-priority and should
warrant interruptive alerting in CDS systems. In a later study
[12], Phansalkar et al. approved a list of 33 class-based lowpriority DDIs that can be made non-interruptive. These lists
serve as an excellent starter for tiering DDIs alerts, although
they represent a small set. To assess additional high-priority
DDIs is a resource-intensive task and requires endeavors from
all healthcare stakeholders. Moreover, there is a substantial variation among various knowledge bases regarding the most severe
DDIs [11], which makes it difﬁcult to reach a consensus. Currently, there is no standardization on how to tier DDI alerts by
severity, nor is there an implementation plan [5].
To facilitate DDI alert tiering processes and improve the list of
established high-priority DDIs, we propose an evidence-based
machine learning framework to pre-screen high-priority DDI
candidates using the clinical evidences discovered from the
FDA’s Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). Inspired by
the DDI evidence evaluation approaches [13], we focus on the
adverse drug events and outcomes associated with the highand low-priority DDIs, aiming to identify useful features that
help distinguish between these two DDI groups. High-priority
DDIs exhibit different patterns in adverse events than that of

Fig. 1 depicts the overview of the proposed machine learning framework. First, we perform a comprehensive analysis of
FDA adverse event reports of the past three years and identify
110,495 unique drug pairs as experimental candidates. Next,
we calculate the conﬁdence measure of each drug pair and the
corresponding adverse events to create a feature vector and subsequently construct a feature matrix of all drug pairs. Then,
we utilize the knowledge bases of ONC High-Priority and
Non-Interruptive Datasets to assign class labels to drug pairs
with “high-priority”, “low-priority”, and “unlabeled”. Last, we
present an autoencoder-based semi-supervised learning algorithm that yields better classiﬁcation performance by taking
advantage of the unlabeled samples. The proposed algorithm
exploits Stacked Autoencoders (SAE) [14] and Weighted Support Vector Machine (wSVM) [15] for performance boosting. In
particular, a pair of stacked autoencoders are trained separately
with the positive and negative labeled samples; the trained autoencoders serve as screening tools to identify reliable samples
from unlabeled drug pairs via reconstruction errors; the reliable
samples and their predicted class labels are added to original
labeled samples to form an augmented training set for wSVM.
Our contributions can be summarized as follows.
r We present a machine learning framework that utilizes
features extracted from adverse event reports to differentiate high-priority and low-priority DDIs. The feature
engineering approach is shown to be effective for discovering clinical evidence from FDA adverse event reports or
other similar case reports.
r We present an autoencoder-based semi-supervised learning algorithm that improves classiﬁcation performance
by utilizing both labeled and unlabeled samples. The proposed algorithm is a useful alternative in performing semisupervised learning tasks.
r The proposed framework integrates multiple data sources,
leverages domain knowledge and clinical evidence, and
serves as a data-driven approach to improving the DDI
alerting systems. To the best of our knowledge, this is
the ﬁrst machine learning framework to pre-screen highpriority DDI candidates.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. After reviewing
the related work in Section II, we introduce the methodology
in Section III. Experimental design, results and discussion are
presented in Section IV, followed by research limitations in
Section V. We conclude the paper and discuss the future work
in Section VI.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Drug-Drug Interactions Discovery
The application of machine learning algorithms and the
availability of multi-dimensional drug features present promising opportunities for discovering drug-drug interactions during
pre- and post-marketing surveillance. Researchers have investigated a variety of information sources and non-conventional
approaches to facilitate DDI discovery. Features used to predict
DDIs can be summarized into two categories: drug property
features and post-marketing surveillance features. The former
feature group consists of the chemical, biological, physiological,
and other features reﬂecting the intrinsic properties of drugs. The
latter feature group represents drug information collected during post-marketing phase, including conventional information
sources such as hospital EHR systems [16] and adverse event
reports [17], and non-conventional information sources such as
social media [18] and search engine log [19]. Previous work
utilizing one or both feature groups to detect DDIs has varied

application from new drug development [20] to post-marketing
surveillance [21].
DDI discovery is viewed as a classiﬁcation problem by most
related literature. Tatonetti et al. [13] developed a signal detection algorithm based on logistic regression to identify novel
DDIs from adverse event reports. Cheng et al. [22] constructed
a DDI network and compared ﬁve supervised learning algorithms in DDI prediction using similarity-based features. An
ensemble of machine learning algorithms [23] demonstrated an
improved prediction performance. Besides, positive-unlabeled
learning [24] can be utilized in making DDI inference provided
that there is no gold standard for non-interacting DDIs. Other
methods such as association rules [17] and network analysis
[25] also demonstrated promising results. Despite a surprising
amount of research efforts in DDI discovery, there has been little
discussion on using machine learning to pre-screen high-priority
DDIs for medication alerts.
B. Semi-Supervised Learning Algorithms
In healthcare and other real-world application of machine
learning, it is always the case that good-quality labeled data are
rare or very expensive to obtain, while there usually exist abundant unlabeled data. Assigning labels to unlabeled data requires
lots of human efforts and domain knowledge. This study encounters the same issue. As mentioned earlier, the labeled highand low-priority DDIs were determined by expert panel review
processes and only reﬂect a small portion (15 and 31 classbased DDIs respectively). As a consequence, semi-supervised
learning algorithms that exploit unlabeled samples to improve
prediction performance have attracted considerable attention.
Following the taxonomy introduced by Zhu et al. [26], most
semi-supervised learning algorithms can be categorized into
four methodological groups: generative models, graph-based
methods, semi-supervised support vector machine and selflabeled methods. Generative models such as Gaussian mixture
models are based on the assumption that labeled and unlabeled
data follows a particular form of mixture distribution. However,
it is difﬁcult to verify the correctness of the distribution assumption [26], especially for the DDI dataset where there exists lots
of noisy and ambiguous samples. The graph-based methods [27]
utilize graph representations where vertices denote labeled and
unlabeled samples and edges reﬂect the similarity between samples, and then enforce label smoothness over the graph. Most
graph-based methods do not produce conﬁdence level for each
label prediction [28], and low-conﬁdence prediction may not
be beneﬁcial for boosting model performance. The same issue
exists with the semi-supervised support vector machine [29],
along with the computational complexity issue caused by vast
amount of unlabeled samples in our study.
Although the above-mentioned methods (i.e. generative models, graph-based methods, and semi-supervised SVM) have successful applications in various domains [30], the direct usage of
them in this study may not be useful and may even be problematic. In view of the nature and sources of the DDI data, there exist
many ambiguous samples in the unlabeled set that do not belong
to either positive class or negative class. Augmenting training
data with ambiguous samples and their inferred labels imposes
noises and errors and is less likely to improve model performance. Self-labeled methods [28] notably self-training [31], cotraining [32] and democratic co-learning [33] are better-suited
tools to handle the DDI data. In general, self-labeled methods
follow iterative procedures to enlarge the training set, through
which the unlabeled samples with the most conﬁdent predictions
are accepted into the training set incrementally. Stopping criteria
are built-in mechanisms for most self-labeled algorithms which
controls the self-labeling process and determines the amount of
unlabeled samples added to the training set. The proposed algorithm is a subclass of self-labeled techniques and represents an
effective alternative for tackling the DDI data of this study.
III. METHODOLOGY
A. Materials
1) The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS):
FAERS [34] is a public database which contains quarterlyreleased adverse event reports submitted to the FDA. The quarterly data ﬁles include seven data tables and the corresponding
descriptions and summaries. Among all seven data tables, four
of them are of our interests: DEMO (demographic and administrative information), DRUG (drug information), REAC (reaction
and adverse events information), OUTC (patient outcome information). All data tables are linked to each other by a primary
key called “primaryid”. The adverse event reports are coded
using “preferred term” (PT) in the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) terminology [35]. However, the
drug names are allowed to be recorded by valid trade names, abbreviations or verbatim names. Therefore, it is necessary to map
all drug names into generic drug concepts. The adverse event
reports provide clinical evidence for identifying high-priority
DDIs.
2) ONC High-Priority and Non-Interruptive Datasets: The
ONC high-priority drug-drug interactions dataset is a short list
of high-severity and clinically signiﬁcant DDIs for generating
medication alerts in EHRs. The dataset contains 15 high-priority
interactions at drug class level. The list was approved by a panel
of experts and published in a JAMIA article [11]. Besides the
high-priority dataset, the expert panel also derived and approved
a list of 33 class-based low-priority DDIs [12] which can be
safely made non-interruptive, namely requiring no immediate
responses from users when alerts are generated. We obtained
both datasets via a publicly accessible source - potential drug–
drug interactions (PDDIs) knowledge bases [36]. Both datasets
are manually curated by experts with domain knowledge, and
provide the ground truth for tiering DDI alerts. Despite the small
size, they are considered the gold standard for differentiating
high- and low-priority DDIs.
3) DrugBank: Drugbank [37] is an online database containing the biochemical and pharmacological information about
drugs, of which the drug interaction information is one of the
largest and most comprehensive DDI knowledge bases. Drug-
Bank contains no severity levels for drug interactions, i.e.,
the severity levels of DDIs are unknown/unlabeled. DrugBank

4) Drugs.com: Drugs.com (https://www.drugs.com/) is another publicly accessible pharmaceutical database. Different
from DrugBank, Drugs.com contains severity levels for its drug

B. Data Preprocessing
A total of 10 quarterly data ﬁles between 2016 Q1 and 2018
Q2 are downloaded from the FAERS database. An overview
of data preprocessing is described in Fig. 2, and the following
sections illustrate the details of each step.
1) Duplicate Reports Removal and Drug Names Standardization: Duplicate reports in the FAERS database introduce bias
on the proportional reporting ratio of drug usages and adverse
events, thus negatively impact data quality. The reports in the
FAERS database follow a case and version mapping relationship where the same case may have multiple versions. The
“primairyid” of each report is generated by concatenating
the “caseid” and “versionid”. Following the suggestion in the
FAERS document [38], we removed the duplicate reports by
only selecting the most up-to-date version of each report. As we
have mentioned earlier, the drug names in the FAERS database
are reported arbitrarily by drug trade names, abbreviations or
verbatim names which do not follow a standardized coding system. To codify the free-text drug names, we utilize RxNorm API
[39] to map each name to a generic drug concept denoted by a
concept unique identiﬁer (RXCUI). After removing the duplicates, a total of 3,282,868 adverse event reports is obtained for
further processing.
2) Adverse Event Reports Selection: We narrowed down
the number of reports to 1,740,770 by only including those
who have at least one serious outcome [38] such as “death”,
“life-threatening”, “hospitalization”, “disability”, “congenital
anomaly” and “required intervention”. This study focuses on
the interactions of drugs, thus the reports with exactly one drug
listed are considered out of scope. A ﬁnal list of 936,865 reports
remains for further analysis.
3) Drugs Selection and Drug Pairs Generation: To ensure a
reasonable drug reporting frequency, drugs with less than 50
reports in the FAERS database are excluded in the study. After
codifying drug names with RxNorm, we obtained a list of 2,891
unique generic drug concepts. Among all pairwise combination
of 2,891 drugs, we focus on the drug pairs that had at least ten
reports. After removing the drug pairs with less than ten reports,
we obtained a ﬁnal list of 110,495 drug pairs.

the reports that contain harmful interacting drugs, the types and

retrospectively. Inspired by association rules learning [40], we
consider the following three-itemset rules to investigate the relationship between drug pairs and adverse events

D. Autoencoder-Based Semi-Supervised Learning
Algorithm
The overview of autoencoder-based semi-supervised learning algorithm is described as follows. First, stacked autoencoders are carried out to perform representation learning using
the original labeled samples. Second, a screening algorithm is
presented to determine the set of inferred reliable samples using autoencoder reconstruction errors. Third, after augmenting
the original labeled samples with the inferred reliable samples,
a classiﬁcation model is constructed using weighted support
vector machine, where the original labeled samples and the inferred reliable samples are weighted differently by a scoring
function.

1) Autoencoder Preliminaries: Autoencoder [42] is a type
of feedforward neural network and can perform representation
learning in an unsupervised manner. It is trained to reconstruct
its own input, through which the hidden layers can capture
the useful feature representations. Traditionally, autoencoder is
well-known for dimension reduction of high-dimensional data
[43]. Recently, it is recognized as an emerging technique for data
denoising [14], anomaly detection [44] and nonlinear feature
fusion [45].
The general structure of an autoencoder includes an input
layer, an output layer, and a hidden layer connecting them, in
which the output layer has the same dimension as the input layer.

techniques [46]. Autoencoder belongs to the feedforward neural
network family. Some of the well-known optimization methods
such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [47] and Adam [48]
can directly come into play to optimize the weights and biases.
Furthermore, backpropagation algorithm [41] can be applied to
make efﬁcient updates.
2) Stacked Architecture: A simple autoencoder is usually
trained with only one hidden layer. If the dimension of the hidden
layer (code) is lower than the input layer, we refer to this type
of autoencoder as undercomplete autoencoder [42], e.g., Fig. 4.
In other words, undercomplete autoencoder uses a bottleneck
layer to compress the input into a lower-dimensional code. By
limiting the amount of information ﬂowing through the network,
autoencoder is trained to learn the knowledge representations of
the data, rather than copying the input to the output.
In this study, we do not limit the autoencoder structure to
be exactly one layer, instead we use a stack of multiple hidden layers to form a stacked autoencoder. As illustrated in
Fig. 5, a stacked autoencoder (SAE) consists of multiple simple
autoencoders in which the resulting representation layer
(“code”) of the ﬁrst level autoencoder is used as the input layer
of the second level autoencoder. Similar to other feedforward
networks, proper depth in autoencoders reduces the amount of
data needed for training internal functions, hence exponentially
reduces the computational cost [42]. A general strategy to train
a stacked autoencoder is to greedily pre-train a sequence of
simple autoencoders starting from the layer of input data, then
use the resulting “code” layer to train the successive layers, and
ﬁnally apply backpropagation algorithm [41] on the stacked
architecture to achieve ﬁne-tuning [43].
3) Building Stacked Autoencoders on the DDI Dataset: Let
P denote the high-priority DDI drug pairs in the training set,
i.e., positive samples; and N denote the low-priority DDI drug
pairs in the training set, i.e., negative samples. For the drug
pairs without a known label, we use U to denote the set of these
unlabeled samples. All samples in P, N, or U have the same dimension (p = 247) - the number of adverse events determined in
Section III-C. We build two separate stacked autoencoders using
the labeled samples P and N. After training, the stacked autoencoder built on P is expected to reconstruct the positive samples
very well, while failing to reconstruct the negative samples;
thereby it generates higher reconstruction errors on the negative
samples than the positives. On the contrary, the stacked autoencoder built on N should have higher reconstruction errors on
the positive samples than the negative samples. Samples with
high reconstruction errors are ﬂagged as anomalies and most
likely belong to a different class. To use reconstruction errors
as measures represents a strategy to determine reliable samples
from set U.

a screening algorithm using autoencoder reconstruction errors
to screen reliable positives (RP) and negatives (RN) from the

A. Data Partition and Evaluation Metrics
We conducted multiple experiments using the DDI samples
obtained in Section III-C. For the training set, we randomly selected 80% of the original labeled DDI samples to form sets P
and N, and used all unlabeled samples to form set U for screening the reliable samples. The remaining 20% of the original
labeled samples serve as a holdout testing set. For performance
metrics, we utilized the F-measure [49] and AUC score [49] to
evaluate model classiﬁcation performance. The F-measure is the
harmonic mean of precision and recall, and AUC is the average
area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve.
An overview of DDI training and testing sets is shown in
Table I. The proposed semi-supervised learning algorithm utilized a subset of the unlabeled samples for performance boosting. Out of 35,988 unlabeled samples, 719 high-conﬁdence
reliable samples were selected by stacked autoencoders, which
thereafter were added to the original labeled samples for training the weighted SVM. The remaining unlabeled samples are
deﬁned as ambiguous samples (i.e., low-conﬁdence samples
which cannot be classiﬁed as either positive or negative class by
autoencoders) and are not utilized by the proposed algorithm.
B. Descriptive Analysis of DDI Features
Features extracted from the adverse event reports contain
useful information for differentiating the two DDI classes. To
visualize the feature distribution of positive and negative samples P and N, we normalized the feature values using percentile
rank and plotted the results in Fig. 6. It can be observed from
the plot that the feature distributions of positive samples are
evidently different from the negative ones, which conﬁrmed the
assumption that high- and low-priority DDIs exhibit different
patterns in adverse event reports. The feature patterns provide
valuable information about DDIs, and thus can be utilized to
build discriminative machine learning models.
C. Autoencoder Training and Reconstruction
Performance
The autoencoder building and parameter tuning processes
were implemented in TensorFlow [50] framework using Keras
API [51]. Constrained by input dimension (p = 247) and undercomplete structure, we tested an array of architectures with
different layer sizes (4, 8, . . . , 128) for both single hidden layer
and stacked layers scenarios. The model of each scenario was
trained using Adam optimizer [48] with normalized (min-max

(ReLU, tanh, sigmoid), the learning rate (from 1e−5 to 0.1),
and the dropout rate (from 10% to 50%). The best conﬁguration
of hyperparameters were selected to yield the best performance
during validation (validation split = 0.2). The stacked autoencoder with three hidden layers of sizes {64, 32, 64} is the ﬁnal

As shown in Fig. 7, both training and validation loss (measured by average squared errors per dimension) converged after 300 epochs. To evaluate the reconstruction performance,
we reconstructed the testing samples with both autoencoders

large (or small) reconstruction errors via (g ◦f)N , which supports the idea that using the gap between two reconstruction
errors (Δi = errorP
i −errorN
i ) can help determine the reliable samples of the two classes.

D. Parameter Tuning for Weighted Support Vector
Machine
The input data for weighted support vector machine (wSVM)
consists of two sources - the original labeled samples and
the inferred reliable samples. Except the minor changes in
sample weights, the training process of wSVM is no different from a traditional SVM. We trained a wSVM model
with radial basis function kernel (RBF kernel), which is formally deﬁned as k(x, x′) = exp(−σ||x −x′||2). For parameter tuning, we constructed a sequence of kernel parameter
σ ∈{0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100} and a sequence of regularization parameter C ∈{0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000} to form the
grid search space. The best parameters (σ = 0.1, C = 10) were
determined by 5-folded cross-validation [41] with AUC as the
evaluation metric.
E. Sensitivity Analysis on Screening Reliable Samples
The lower and upper thresholds c1 and c2 are used to determine the number of reliable positives and negatives accepted to
the training set. As mentioned before, we varied the values of c1
using the mth percentile of Δi for parameter tuning. Once c1 is
determined, c2 is also ﬁxed (i.e., using (100 −m)th percentile
for c2) in order to add the same amount of reliable negatives for
maintaining class balance.
As described in Fig. 9, whenc1 is set at the 2th percentile of Δi
(where c2 is set at the 98th percentile), the proposed algorithm
achieved the best performance in both AUC and F-measure.
After the peak, the model performance decreased gradually.
The performance curve also suggests that adding ambiguous
samples may deteriorate model’s discriminative performance as
they bring noise and mislabeled data to the training set. For the
proposed algorithm, we selected the 2th and 98th percentile of
Δi as the best parameter values for c1 and c2.
Fig. 9.
The selection of lower threshold c1 and the corresponding upper
threshold c2. The x-axis denotes the value of c1 represented as the mth
percentile of Δi; the value of c2 is ﬁxed to be the (100 −m)th percentiles
to maintain the balance between reliable positives and negatives added
to the DDI training set.
F. Performance Comparison of the Proposed Algorithm
With Other Methods on the DDI Dataset
Following the discussion in Related Work (Section II), we utilized several other state-of-the-art self-labeled semi-supervised
learning methods for performance comparison. In the experimental design, we ﬁrst built a fully-supervised SVM as baseline
with the original labeled samples (P and N only), and then
added the unlabeled samples U to the training set for performing semi-supervised learning. Besides the proposed algorithm,
methods used for semi-supervised learning include self-training
[31], co-training [32] and democratic co-learning [33]. In the
experimentation, we used radial SVM as the base classiﬁer for
both self-training and co-training algorithms, and the maximum
iteration is set to 30 for both algorithms. For co-learning, the
three base classiﬁers are radial SVM, k-NN [41] and C5.0 [41].
All model parameters were properly tuned for the best performance. We repeated the data partitioning, training, and testing
processes ten times for evaluating model performance of all
methods.
Table II shows the summarized results (mean ± standard
deviation) of the experiments. All semi-supervised learning
methods including the proposed algorithm outperformed the
fully-supervised SVM in every performance metrics, which
demonstrates that the unlabeled samples, when properly used
in conjunction with the labeled samples, can produce considerable improvement in model’s generalization capability. The proposed method has the best evaluation performance in both AUC
and F-measure metrics, which reﬂects the fact that stacked autoencoders are superior tools to screen the reliable samples from
the high-dimensional DDI dataset. Meanwhile, self-training and
co-training algorithms are computationally expensive due to the
iterative nature of the algorithm; the proposed method is a
reasonable choice provided there is a necessity to analyze an
enormous amount of unlabeled samples. Moreover, co-training
algorithm relies on the abundance of features as well as the
assumption of two split views of features. As is demonstrated
in the evaluation results, the assumption of split-view does not
hold for the DDI dataset.

G. Performance Comparison on a Benchmark Dataset
To show the effectiveness and scalability of our approach, we extended the experiments using a high-dimensional
benchmark dataset - Epilepsy EEG dataset [52] - from the UCI
Machine Learning Repository [53]. The dataset consists of EEG
recording information used for epileptic seizure detection. Each
data point has 178-dimensional input vector representing the
EEG signal values from brain electrical activity. The response
variable has ﬁve classes representing different EEG signal categories. We transformed the dataset into a binary classiﬁcation
format by selecting two out of the ﬁve classes, namely the “eyes
open” and “eyes closed” classes while removing data points of
the other three classes.
The remaining data was then split into an 80% training set
and a 20% testing set. For assessing the performance of semisupervised learning methods, we assume that only a certain
percentage of training samples (e.g. 10%) have class labels;
while the rest do not, and their class labels were removed. After
removing partial class labels, we obtained a mix of labeled and
unlabeled samples for model training. As shown in Table III,
we incrementally adjusted the percentage of the labeled samples from 10% to 90% to evaluate model performance under
different scenarios. Similar to the experiments with the DDI
samples, each scenario was repeated ten times for comparing
the performance of all competing methods.
The benchmark dataset has balanced class labels (50% v.s.
50%); for this reason we evaluated the model performance using the AUC score. The comparison results of all competing
methods are reported in Table III and also visualized in Fig. 10.
In general, the semi-supervised learning methods outperformed
the SVM in terms of the average AUC score. As the percentage
of visible labels increased from 10% to 90%, the performance
improvement became smaller. It is also noted that the proposed
algorithm outshines its competitors when the percentage of visible labels is located between 20% and 50%.
H. Framework Application and Discussion
The experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness
of using post-marketing surveillance features in pre-screening
high-priority DDIs. Under the proposed framework, we trained
a classiﬁer using the original labeled samples and inferred reliable samples to ﬂag potential high-priority DDIs. Depending
on the adverse event feature input, the classiﬁer outputs a numeric value indicating the probability of the unlabeled drug
pair being a high-priority DDI. To further assess the discriminative capability of adverse event features, we utilized an independent knowledge base - Drugs.com to evaluate the inferred
high-priority DDIs. It should be noted that the “major” and
“Moderate” drug interactions listed in Drugs.com are not the
conﬁrmed high-priority DDIs for use in medication alerts, but
can serve as external opinions on evaluating the predictive performance. The inferred high-priority DDIs are highly associated
with the major and moderate drug interactions in Drugs.com.
Among the top 100 potential high-priority DDIs ﬂagged by the
proposed framework, 20% are marked as “Major” interactions
and 64% are marked as “Moderate” by Drugs.com; while only
17% “Major” and 59% “Moderate” can be ﬂagged without using the unlabeled samples. In Table IV, we listed some of the
major DDIs ﬂagged by the framework.
Although the predictive results are satisfactory, the application of data-driven methods in predicting high-priority DDIs
should always be considered as a complementary approach to
supporting knowledge-based expert decisions. The established
results are solely based on the utilization of post-marketing
surveillance features. As we have discussed in Section II, drug
property features are proven effective features in predicting
DDIs and should be incorporated into the framework for producing more accurate and comprehensive results. The utilization of
drug property features is not yet covered in this study and serves
as one direction of future work.
V. LIMITATIONS
Despite the promising results, this study has a few limitations.
First, the method utilizes post-marketing surveillance features
- namely adverse events for model development, which is not
