system, the conﬁdence measures obtained from adverse event
reports may be biased due to the confounding factors such as
drug indications and variations in patient demographics. Third,
this study only considers the adverse events collected from the
FAERS database; other clinical sources like hospital’s EHRs are
not included. Fourth, due to the scarcity of labeled training data
and the limits of data-driven methods, the predictive results may
not be comprehensive; more expert-conﬁrmed labeled samples
are desirable for producing better results.
VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
Identifying high-priority DDIs is a crucial step to optimize
medication alerts in EHRs. Proper tiering and displaying DDI
alerts by severity levels represents a proven approach to reduce
alert fatigue and improve patient safety. In this paper, we introduce a machine learning framework and a semi-supervised
learning algorithm to pre-screen high-priority DDI candidates
utilizing clinical evidence from adverse event reports. The experimental results show that features derived from adverse
events contain effective information about the severity levels
of DDIs; also demonstrate the desirable performance of the
proposed algorithm in predicting high-priority DDIs.
Several lines of research and investigations have been
emerged for future work. Besides the post-marketing surveillance features, there is a need to incorporate the chemical, biological, and other drug property features for improving model
performance. The proposed method employs the weighted SVM
as the ﬁnal classiﬁer, which can be replaced by other classiﬁers
such as random forest [41], gradient boosting method [41], or an
ensemble of different classiﬁers. Furthermore, the list of highpriority DDIs and the mechanism to display DDI alerts can be
continuously improved through analyzing the retrospective data
collected from user responses.

SemiHAR: Improving Semisupervised Human
Activity Recognition via Multitask Learning
Chixuan Wei , Zhihai Wang , Jidong Yuan , Xiaokang Wang ,
Haiyang Liu , Member, IEEE, and Qiyang Zhao
Abstract— Semisupervised human activity recognition (Semi-
HAR) has attracted attention in recent years from various
domains,
such
as
digital
health
and
ambient
intelligence.
Currently,
it
still
faces
two
challenges.
For
one
thing,
discriminative features may exist among multiple sequences
rather than a single sequence since activities are combinations of
motions involving several body parts. For another thing, labeled
data and unlabeled data suffer from distribution discrepancies
due to the different behavior patterns or biological conditions
of users. For that, we propose a novel SemiHAR method
based on multitask learning. First, a dimension-based Markov
transition field (DMTF) technique is designed to generate 2-D
activity data for capturing the interactions among different
dimensions. Second, we jointly consider the user recognition
(UR) task and the activity recognition (AR) task to reduce
the underlying discrepancy. In addition, a task relation learner
(TRL) is introduced to dynamically learn task relations, which
enables the primary AR task to exploit preferred knowledge from
other secondary tasks. We theoretically analyze the proposed
SemiHAR and provide a novel generalization result. Extensive
experiments conducted on four real-world datasets demonstrate
that SemiHAR outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.
Index Terms— Human activity recognition (HAR), multitask
learning, semisupervised classification, time series.

I. INTRODUCTION
H
UMAN activity recognition (HAR) has great potential
for impacting people’s daily lives in many realms,
such as personalized health monitoring, assistive living, and
rehabilitation [1]. Generally, two mainstream scenarios are
encountered: sensor-based systems and video-based systems
[2],
[3].
This
article
focuses
on
sensor-based
activity
recognition (AR) systems that employ sensors to track human
activity. In practice, it is expensive and time-consuming to
collect and annotate sufficient sensory data [4]. Therefore,
researchers have begun to investigate semisupervised human
activity recognition (SemiHAR), which leverages labeled as
well as unlabeled data to build a classifier. Despite the decades
of extensive research conducted on semisupervised learning,
SemiHAR faces the following challenges.
A. Underlying Correlations Among Sequences
The feature extraction process in HAR aims to capture discriminative information to clearly separate different

class.
activities [5]. In practice, distinctive features can not only
be captured from a single signal but also appear among
multiple sequences. This phenomenon originates from the fact
that activities can be considered combinations of motions
involving several body parts. Taking the Opportunity dataset
that contains various body gestures tracked by on-body sensors
as an example [6], the interactions among multiple dimensions
from the lying class and the walking class exhibit noticeable
differences. Specifically, the entity relations in the lying class
present smooth fluctuations, as shown in the green boxes of
Fig. 1(a), whereas the implicit relations in the walking class
include substantial changes, as shown in the blue boxes of
Fig. 1(b). In recent years, various types of deep learning
approaches have been applied to perform feature extraction,
including recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional
neural networks (CNNs), and they achieved great success [7],
[8], [9]. While embodying some advantages, these methods
were not specifically designed for multivariate sensor-based
data and thus may not fully explore the interactions among
multiple signals.
B. Distribution Discrepancy
Most of the existing SemiHAR methods concentrate
on solving annotation scarcity and rely on the covariate
assumption stating that the input data are collected from
similar distributions [10]. Nevertheless, this assumption does
not always hold since people have diverse behavior patterns,
and data from different participants are distributed variously
[5]. Notably, when limited activity labels are present, the
user labels are easily available during the data collection
process and thus one could independently assign the user
labels to the raw samples irrespective of the corresponding
activity labels [11]. As shown in Fig. 1(c) and (d), the
labeled data and unlabeled data are drawn from two different
subjects user-1 and user-2, respectively. The distributions of
the lying activities of labeled user-1 and unlabeled user-2 are
almost identical. However, the walking class exhibits distinct
distributions, as user-1 may walk slowly, while user-2 tends
to walk faster [5]. This triggers the distribution discrepancy
problem between the labeled and unlabeled data derived from
different users. To tackle this problem, some researchers
employ transfer learning to transfer the model trained on
the labeled data collected from user-1 to the unlabeled
data received from user-2 [12], [13], [14]. Although transfer
learning is effective in solving the distribution shift problem,
it cares most about its performance on the target unlabeled
data [15]. In our setting, we aim to achieve high performance
on both labeled and unlabeled data when they are distributed
differently during training.
C. Dynamic Task Relations
The performance of HAR can be improved by learning
knowledge
from
extra
tasks.
Specifically,
the
tasks
of
learning the underlying relations among different dimensions
and reducing the distribution shift can improve a model’s
generalization. However, the accuracy of HAR may degenerate
when the learned tasks are less related [16]. For example,
as shown in Fig. 1(c), the task of discovering the underlying
relations among sequences is more important than the task
of reducing the distribution discrepancy of the lying class,
while both are crucial for the walking class. Therefore,
it is important to dynamically aggregate information through
different types of tasks. Nevertheless, most of the existing
methods treat each related task equally [17], [18], [19]. This
problem can be alleviated by a task relation learner (TRL),
which is designed in our model. As shown in Fig. 1(e), our
model achieves a clear decision boundary for identifying the
lying and walking classes, and the labeled and unlabeled
walking activities from different users are well merged after
training.
To address the above problems, we propose a novel
SemiHAR framework, which trains multiple tasks together and
dynamically learns task relations. Our main contributions are
given as follows.
1) We propose a dimension-based Markov transition field
(DMTF) technique to capture the inherent interactions
among multiple dimensions.
2) To mitigate the distribution discrepancy problem, the
user recognition (UR) task, identifying the current user
for the labeled and unlabeled data, and the AR task,
identifying the current activity for the labeled data, are
simultaneously handled by sharing parameter spaces.
3) We propose a TRL to dynamically learn task relations,
which
aims
to
balance
multiple
tasks
for
better
recognition.
4) A novel generalization bound with a fast convergence
rate is proven for SemiHAR. In addition, comprehensive
experiments and case studies on four real-world datasets
demonstrate the effectiveness of SemiHAR.
The rest of this article is organized as follows. First, the
related work is introduced in Section II. Then, the problem
statement, the details of the SemiHAR algorithm, and the
theoretical analysis are provided in Section III. In Section IV,
we conduct experiments on real-world datasets, analyze the
effects of different parameters, perform ablation experiments,
and provide case studies. Finally, Section V concludes this
article.

II. RELATED WORK
In this section, we briefly describe the recent advances in
HAR research in terms of feature extraction, multitask learning, distribution discrepancy, and semisupervised learning.
A. Feature Extraction
Feature learning methods for HAR can roughly be classified
into two families: traditional methods and deep learning
methods [5]. General traditional methods include spectral
features,
principal
component
analysis,
and
handcrafted
features, such as the mean, variance, and maximum [20],
[21]. In recent years, deep learning has become a dominant
technique in HAR due to the impressive power of automatic
feature
learning
[5].
RNN-based
methods
segment
raw
multivariate sensory data into individual pieces using a sliding
window and capture features by inputting these subsequences
into RNN cells [7]. In addition, CNNs are a widely applied
deep feature extraction approach in HAR. For example, Xu and
Qiu [8], Huang et al. [9], and Wang et al. [22] employed
CNN algorithms in deep learning to automatically extract
features. However, most of these deep learning approaches
often utilize the same repetitive structures, such as convolution
kernels in CNNs and recursive units in RNNs, to learn
interactions and thus cannot discover the global and different
time scale correlations among all axes. To address this
problem, we transform each multivariate signal into 2-D data
to discover different and crucial interactions.
B. Multitask Learning
Multitask learning aims to jointly learn multiple related
tasks so that the similarity information or shared structures
can be captured with the hope of achieving improved model
performance [23]. In the context of deep learning, multitask
learning approaches can be categorized into hard- and softparameter methods [24]. The former shares hidden layers
across all the tasks and keeps a few task-specific output
layers [17]. For example, Saeed et al. [18] employed a
hard-parameter multitask learning framework to recognize
eight transformations for HAR. Jawed et al. [19] proposed
a novel multitask learning method, named MTL, which trains
forecasting and classification tasks simultaneously under hardparameter sharing settings. Unlike hard-parameter methods,
each task of a soft-parameter method has its own model,
and then, these task-specific models are regularized during
training. For instance, Chen et al. [25] introduced a deep
multitask learning method to softly share parameters between
the corresponding convolutional layers. Most existing hardand soft-parameter methods for HAR treat all tasks equally.
Thus, conflicting information across multiple tasks may
degrade the model’s performance. To alleviate this problem,
we propose the TRL based on the hard-parameter scheme,
which can dynamically learn positive sharing according to the
target activity.
C. Distribution Discrepancy
To reduce the distribution discrepancy arising from user
heterogeneity, transfer learning [12], [13], [14] and multitask
learning [5], [25] techniques have been proposed in the
literature. Transfer learning aims to train a learning model
with the source data collected from a number of participants
and then fine-tune it with the target users [15]. For example,
Ragab et al. [13], Ganin et al. [26], and Chen et al.
[27] are committed to tackling the distribution shift by

transferring knowledge. One backward with these transfer
learning methods is that they care most about the target users,
and hence, the target users play a more important role than
the source users [15], [23]. In practical scenarios, the goal
of HAR is to improve the model’s performance on both the
target users and the source users. In contrast with transfer
learning, multitask learning can tackle this problem by learning
the auxiliary task and the main task simultaneously [23]. For
instance, Shen et al. [17] tried to align distribution across
multiple tasks and improve the performance of all individuals.
However, these works are supervised learning approaches,
which require the collection and annotation of user-specific
training data, and the activity labels are difficult to obtain in
many real-world applications. To fill this gap, our method not
only minimizes the distribution discrepancy via a shared block
but also provides enhanced improvements for semisupervised
learning.
D. Semisupervised Learning
According to the way in which unlabeled data are utilized,
the semisupervised approaches in HAR can be classified into
self-training, co-training, and unsupervised feature extraction
methods [28]. Tang et al. [29] proposed SelfHAR, which
combines the self-training and self-supervised learning tasks
to increase the diversity of training data. The co-training
approach extends self-training to two or more supervised
classifiers that are iteratively built on each other’s most
confident predictions. For example, Bi et al. [30] proposed
the ActSemiCNN, which incorporates activity learning and
semisupervised learning into a single framework to improve
the model’s performance. Chen et al. [31] proposed a
pattern-balanced co-training framework for semisupervised
and imbalanced HAR. However, the misclassification of
several unlabeled data is always inevitable in the self-training
and co-training methods. To tackle this problem, unsupervised
feature extraction methods try to capture useful features in an
unsupervised manner [19], [32], [33]. Tang et al. [34] explored
a contrastive learning framework, called SimCLR, and then
illustrated its adoption in HAR. Nevertheless, most of the
existing semisupervised methods focus on data scarcity and
ignore shifted distributions. Furthermore, their generalization
bounds are not discussed.
III. METHODOLOGY
In this section, we present the proposed model in detail.
Fig. 2 shows the general architecture of SemiHAR. It consists
of one unsupervised task and two supervised tasks. The
unsupervised DMTF task reconstructs a series of 2-D data
transformed from the whole set of input signals to capture
the interactions among different dimensions. The UR task
and the AR task (two supervised tasks) are simultaneously
trained to reduce the distribution discrepancy between them
by sharing parameters. The TRL connects these three tasks
and automatically assigns weights for them.

and segmented to produce equal-sized time series. Given

B. Dimension-Based Markov Transition Field
A Markov transition field (MTF) is a technique that converts
a univariate time series into an image [35]. Given a time series
Ti, the corresponding MTF is constructed by considering all
continuous numerical values from ti,1,k to ti,n,k. Each cell
in the Markov transition matrix can be interpreted as the
likelihood of transition in a time-based axis. However, how to
build this matrix to represent the dimension-based transition
probabilities for multivariate sensory data is still a challenge
in HAR.
In this section, we created a novel representation (i.e.,
DMTF image) by considering the dimensional information
from t1 to td. Two dimensions tm = (t1,m, t2,m, . . . , tn,m) ∈Rn
and tv = (t1,v, t2,v, . . . , tn,v) ∈Rn are randomly selected from
T. tm and tv are first discretized into Q quantile bins, and
thus, each signal value is associated with one of the quantiles
q j( j ∈[1, Q]). Then, a Q × Q weighted transition matrix
is constructed by counting the transitions among the quantile
bins from tm to tv according to a first-order Markov chain.
Finally, the dimension-based Markov transition matrix can be
computed by normalizing the weighted transition matrix. The
DMTF data are defined as

C. Reducing Discrepancy Among Users
In order to make the distributions Po and G ˜o similar,
we consider both the heterogeneity and commonality across
the participants by learning the UR task and the AR
task in a multitask learning framework. The heterogeneity
factors contain individual-specific features, i.e., different users’
behavior patterns, and they can be captured by correctly
predicting the domain labels in the UR task. In contrast, the
commonality factors include individual-agnostic features that
involve conducting the same motion across different users,
and these features are learned by correctly predicting activity
labels. In addition, both the individual-specific and individualagnostic features are shared across the AR and UR tasks
via a shared block to achieve improved performance and
generalization. Specifically, for the UR task, given the whole
set of time series Mk2 = {T i}N
i=1 ∈RN×d×n, which contains
the labeled set P and the unlabeled set G, the common
encoder E yields hu = fe(Mk2) ∈RN×e for the UR task
shown in Fig. 2, where fe maps Mk2 to individual-specific
representations hu and k2 indicates the UR task. For the
AR task, as shown in Fig. 2, given the labeled time series
P = {T i}p

that, the parameters of the model E are shared by the UR task
and the AR task in the multitask learning paradigm. Therefore,
our model can take individual-agnostic and individual-specific
features from the AR and UR tasks into account to minimize
the domain divergence.
D. Task Relation Learner
Most of the existing multitask learning studies treat
all tasks equally, ignoring the dynamic relations among
them. An attention mechanism [4], which can automatically
determine the importance levels of features, is a great way
to address this problem. However, such methods are typically
designed for a single task and thus might not adapt to multiple
tasks well. In this section, we extend the traditional attention
mechanism to the multitask setting, aiming to learn different
weights for the three tasks to achieve a better recognition
performance.
As shown in Fig. 2, the representations hr, hu, and hc

hc ∈RN×e. Then, the dot product and softmax operations are
utilized to calculate the attention coefficients for all the tasks.

IV. EXPERIMENTS
In this section, we first describe the experimental settings
and the effects of different parameters and then compare Semi-
HAR with the state-of-the-art approaches, before performing
ablation experiments and case studies.1
A. Datasets
They are listed as follows.
1) Opportunity Dataset [39]: This dataset is composed of
the recordings of four subjects produced by a wide variety
of on-body sensors and ambient sensors while performing
many activities, including locomotion and gestures. For
our experiment, we chose locomotion activities, including
standing, walking, sitting, and lying.
2) PAMAP2
Dataset
[40]:
This
dataset
is
used
to
benchmark HAR methods based on wearable sensor data.
The dataset contains a total of 18 activities, such as running,
cycling, and ascending stairs, performed by nine subjects with
three inertial measurement units and a heart rate monitor.

3) UCI-HAR Dataset [41]:
This dataset was collected
with three-axis accelerometers and gyroscopes in smartphones
mounted by a group of 30 volunteers on their waists. Each
subject performed six activities: walking, walking upstairs,
walking downstairs, sitting, standing, and lying.
4) Mhealth Dataset [42]: This dataset comprises body
motions and vital sign recordings obtained for ten subjects,
while they performed 12 physical activities. Inertial measurement units were placed on each volunteer’s chest, right wrist,
and left ankle to record their acceleration, rate of turning,
and magnetic field orientation. The sensor positioned on the
chest collected two-lead ECG data, which can be used for
monitoring the activity of the heart and checking for various
arrhythmias.
B. Experimental Settings
Following
the
data
splitting
strategy
used
in
[27],
we simulate distribution discrepancy scenarios by drawing
the labeled set P and the unlabeled set G from two distinct
subjects o and ˜o. The data of o are evenly separated into
two subsets: one is the labeled set P and the other is
the test set. Considering that the labels are imbalanced, the
accuracy metric that always evaluates the performance of a
classifier with regard to frequent classes may lead to false
positive results while keeping high accuracy [43]. As stated
in [44], F1-score is an informative evaluation metric that
considers both precision and recall. Therefore, referring to
[25] and [29], we use both accuracy and weighted macro
F1-score (abbreviated as F1-score) as the performance metrics
in our evaluation. We utilize stochastic gradient descent with
Adam to minimize the loss functions at a learning rate of
1e−3. All models are trained at most 2000 epochs with a
batch size of 100 to monitor the validation results and stop
the training process when no improvement is detected. Results
are achieved by fivefold cross validation.
C. Effects of Parameters
This
section
investigates
the
key
parameters
in
the
SemiHAR model. They include the size of the DMTF data
c, the number of bins in the DMTF task, and the effect of
multiple users.
1) Effect of the DMTF: Fig. 3 shows the parameter test
results for the parameters c and bins on four datasets. Two
parameters vary in a range of c ∈{24, 32, 40, 48} and bins ∈
{6, 8, 16, 32}. c = 24 means that the size of the DMTF data
equals 24 × 24, and bins = 6 suggests that the signal is
discretized into six quantile bins for calculation. The results
demonstrate that c and bins can directly impact the quality of
the extracted information. In addition, all the datasets achieve
higher accuracy when the parameters c and bins are set to
relatively small values (as shown in the top-left corner of each
subfigure). This suggests that global information can assist the
DMTF in capturing the crucial interactions among sequences
and thus yield improved learning performance.
2) Effect of Multiple Users: In practice, the labeled data and
the unlabeled data are separately collected from a large number
of users, and thus, they may include different distributions.

V. CONCLUSION
In this article, we propose SemiHAR, a novel semisupervised human activity recognition model that focuses on
capturing discriminative features contained among dimensions and reducing the distribution discrepancy between
labeled and unlabeled data. In addition, we introduce a
simple and effective attention mechanism TRL in the multitask
setting to dynamically learn task relations. Theoretical and
experimental analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of our
SemiHAR.
Our future research will involve enhancing the accuracy of
semisupervised classification by leveraging more related tasks,
such as sensor placement recognition or sensor orientation
recognition, to obtain high-level complex representations.
Another interesting issue worth investigating is to concentrate
on the real-time implementation of the HAR system for
diverse application scenarios using unlabeled data, including
fall detection and eldercare. Moreover, we are planning to
explore human activity datasets based on images or videos and
apply representation learning techniques to extract meaningful
features effectively.

text:
Received December 11, 2020, accepted December 30, 2020, date of publication January 4, 2021, date of current version January 12, 2021.

Service-Aware Two-Level Partitioning
for Machine Learning-Based Network
Intrusion Detection With High
Performance and High Scalability
YEONGJE UHM1 AND WOOGUIL PAK
2
1DS Mentoring Corporation, Seoul 03909, South Korea
2Department of Information and Communication Engineering, Yeungnam University, Gyeongsan 38541, South Korea
Corresponding author: Wooguil Pak (wooguilpak@yu.ac.kr)
This work was supported in part by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) Grant funded by the Korean Government [Ministry
of Science and ICT (MSIT)] under Grant NRF-2019R1F1A1062320, and in part by the 2020 Yeungnam University Research Grant.
ABSTRACT A network intrusion detection system (NIDS) is an important technology for cyber security.
Recently, machine learning based NIDSs are being actively researched as various machine learning techniques are proposed. However, existing NIDSs have limitation in terms of generality because they have
been designed based on speciﬁc characteristics obtained from analyzing some partial datasets. Moreover,
in reality, the NIDS datasets have a signiﬁcantly imbalanced ratio between normal and abnormal data.
It causes the minority class problem, which needs to be addressed for developing robust and reliable
NIDSs working in various environments. This paper proposes a novel technique using service-aware dataset
partitioning, which provides high scalability to handle huge and rapidly growing network data ﬂexibly, and
helps the classiﬁer to improve the classiﬁcation performance in terms of accuracy and speed. We evaluated
our approach with the Kyoto2016 dataset, which is a well-known dataset for highly imbalanced data,
using various classiﬁcation algorithms and parameters for achieving the best performance and compared it
with existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our experimental results indicated that our approach can classify
network trafﬁcs rapidly and accurately with huge imbalanced datasets. We conclude that it can relieve serious
existing issues of imbalanced datasets for modern machine learning based NIDS solutions.
INDEX TERMS Network intrusion detection, service based partitioning, imbalanced data, machine learning,
minority class problem.
I. INTRODUCTION
Network intrusion detection system (NIDS) is a core technology in modern networks that detects anomaly activities on
the network by analyzing trafﬁcs. It is essential for providing
stable services on various networks, ranging from legacy
networks to latest networks such as 5G and Internet of Things
networks. Furthermore, the importance of NIDSs increases
with vehicle-to-everything emerging, which is requires very
strict QoS requirements. Such technology is directly related
to the daily lives of people, so any network attack threatening
networks is seriously threatening their lives.
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Shadi Aljawarneh
.
Misuse detection and anomaly detection are well-known
approaches for implementing an NIDS. Misuse detection
classiﬁes the incoming trafﬁcs by comparing them with
patterns extracted from past anomaly trafﬁcs. Therefore,
it is also called signature- or knowledge-based detection.
Essentially, misuse detection can detect known attacks with
high accuracy and high speed. However, it can barely
detect any unknown attack. In contrast to misuse detection,
anomaly detection can detect both unknown and known
attacks because it exploits statistical characteristics of attack
trafﬁcs. Owing to the high and steady performance of
anomaly detection, it is being mostly used nowadays, and is
becoming more strengthened in combination with machine
learning.

text:
Y. Uhm, W. Pak: Service-Aware Two-Level Partitioning for Machine Learning-Based Network Intrusion Detection
Various machine learning techniques have been used for
implementing an NIDS, such as random forest (RF) and
decision tree (DT), which is simple but has high classiﬁcation
performance, or a deep neural network (DNN), which has
been actively researched recently due to the growth of neural network (NN) technology. However, these methods have
three critical issues to be used in NIDSs as follows.
First, the performance of existing NIDS cannot be guaranteed in real environments because most of these studies are
based on a balanced and shortened dataset with modiﬁcation
rather than a large and unbalanced original dataset [1]–[6].
Thus, many technical issues arise in adopting unmodiﬁed real
datasets, such as high resource requirements for processing
time and memory. They usually fail to catch all issues persisting in only original datasets using such reﬁned samples of
dataset.
Second, the existing studies are vulnerable to minority
class problem, which refers to the issue that most minority
class data are misclassiﬁed as majority ones for the unbalanced dataset with high skewness. A few existing studies have
attempted to resolve the minority class problem, have faced
critical problems of low classiﬁcation accuracy and poor
classiﬁcation speed [9]–[11], [30]. In fact, we can say that
there is no practical solution for the minority class problem
in the ﬁeld of NIDS research so far.
Third, very few NIDS solutions have been able to handle
the issue of increasing network trafﬁc data efﬁciently. The
researchers face the problem of network trafﬁc data increasing at a signiﬁcant speed. Most NIDS solutions inevitably
take a very long time to process such large network trafﬁc.
If an NIDS cannot provide any efﬁcient solution for supporting high scalability in terms of data size, it cannot be adopted
in real networks. However, very few studies have focused on
huge and increasing size of datasets, and processing speed.
This paper proposes a novel anomaly detection-based
NIDS that is robust against these problems. Our contributions
are as follows.
• We propose a service-aware partitioning algorithm to
mitigate the minority class problem.
• We suggest an NIDS classiﬁer that greatly improve the
overall classiﬁcation performance and scalability.
• We also show a new partitioning approach to provide
partitioning in an incremental manner to support the
rapidly increasing dataset.
We develop a service-aware partitioning algorithm to process the growing network data with high efﬁciency. This
unique partitioning algorithm boosts classiﬁcation accuracy
and speed, and can sustain almost the same performance
regardless of the various and dynamic network attacks.
Reﬁning and partitioning of datasets are a common preprocessing method for machine learning in NIDS. However,
our approach is different from existing works. First, our
approach does not use reﬁned and partial dataset but uses the
original dataset without any modiﬁcation. Second, partitioning is done by application service type, not partitioning size.
To implement service-based partitioning, we have developed
sophisticated algorithms for service-based static and dynamic
partitioning.
We should note that many NIDS solutions suffer from
ﬂuctuating performance according to different attack types.
This characteristic is very important in developing a secure
and robust NIDS. Our approach can provide a fundamental
resolution for the low and ﬂuctuated detection rate, and low
scalability.
There are many studies on the issue of minority classes
such as SMOTE [9]. However, the proposed method offers
a different approach from these studies. It utilizes the actual
protocol and session state information to make sub-partitions.
Each sub-partition created in this way contains similar types
of attack classes, and this homogeneousness improves learning efﬁciency and enables accurate detection on machinelearning. The proposed method has a completely different
approach from existing work, so it can be used in conjunction
with other methods and can achieve higher classiﬁcation performance. It has a limit to effectively solve problems in all situations and environments using only one solution. Therefore,
using the proposed methods individually or together with
other methods will be of great help in solving the minority
class problem.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II,
we introduce the related work, and in Section III, we describe
the minority class problem and our motivation behind conducting this study. In Section IV, we speciﬁcally explain
our approach and its design, and in Section V, we show the
experimental results. Finally, in Section VI, we summarize
and conclude our research.
II. EXISTING WORK
As mentioned earlier, misuse detection-based NIDSs have
very powerful features but also have serious technical issues.
So far, various approaches have been proposed to overcome
the limitation of misuse detection-based NIDSs. Of these,
the single machine learning algorithm-based NIDS is the
most common and popular approach. The NN algorithm
has been also introduced for NIDSs because it has achieved
noticeable performance in areas such as image classiﬁcation
and voice recognition.
Recently, some researchers have attempted to combine
multiple machine learning algorithms to further improve
NIDS performance. This approach adopts multiple supervised machine learning algorithms or unsupervised and
supervised algorithms simultaneously. Some researchers
have tried to improve an NIDS by modifying and optimizing
the training data, to achieve better classiﬁcation.
According to the NIDS approach, we classify machine
learning-based NIDS research into the following categories: single machine learning-based NIDS, hybrid machine
learning-based NIDS, and data optimization-based NIDS.
A. SINGLE MACHINE LEARNING-BASED NIDS
Single machine learning-based NIDS is the most basic and
simple approach in the NIDS research area [1]–[6]. It trains

and evaluates a classiﬁer with a given dataset by using a
speciﬁc machine learning algorithm. In the research, usually, the performance between the proposed and other single
machine learning-based NIDSs or conventional NIDSs is
compared to evaluate the machine learning algorithm. The
performance obtained using multiple datasets is also analyzed
as the classiﬁcation results highly depend on machine learning algorithms and datasets.
Ahmad et al. evaluated and analyzed NIDS performance
in terms of precision and recall with the NSL-KDD dataset,
using some selected algorithms such as multilayer perceptron, support vector machine (SVM), RF, and extreme
learning machine [1], [7]. They also conducted experiments to show the effect of data size, i.e., full, half,
and quarter sizes. Sahu et al. evaluated the suitability of
J48 on an NIDS using 130,000 datasets selected from the
Kyoto2006+ dataset [2], [8]. Cheong et al. also evaluated
various algorithms such as SVM, DT, RF, Naive Bayes (NB),
DNN, and k-nearest neighbor (kNN) using the Kyoto2006+
dataset [3], [12] to ﬁnd the best classiﬁer for an NIDS. They
selected 1,800,000 data with 1% anomaly trafﬁcs from the
Kyoto2006+ dataset to simulate real network circumstances.
Furthermore, they conducted an extended experiment using
3,600,000 data extracted from the original dataset to analyze
the effect of data size on the performance [8]. Yin et al. proposed an NIDS based on the recurrent neural network (RNN)
algorithm, which is one of the most well-known DNNs.
They evaluated the NIDS performance according to various combinations of learning rates and total neuron sizes
in each layer with the NSL-KDD dataset. Park et al. proposed an NIDS using six labels expanded from the original
three labels for the Kyoto2006+ dataset [5]. They developed
additional labels using some features tightly coupled with
the class in the dataset, and then, evaluated the classiﬁcation results of the modiﬁed dataset using the RF algorithm.
Lin et al. attempted to develop an NIDS using the convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm, which is frequently used in image classiﬁcation, and as a result,
suggested an NIDS based on LeNet, which is a CNN variation
for an NIDS.
In general, single machine learning-based NIDS shows
high accuracy for most datasets, but cannot overcome the
minority class problem entirely. Some researchers tried to
resolve this problem using class weight, but found only the
trade-off between the accuracies of multiple classes, thus just
achieving a marginal effect on the overall performance.
B. HYBRID MACHINE LEARNING-BASED NIDS
In the latest NIDS research, hybrid approaches using two
or more machine learning algorithms have been proposed
to increase the classiﬁcation performance of an NIDS.
Semi-supervised learning is a well-known hybrid approach,
using both unsupervised and supervised learning algorithms
simultaneously [18]–[21], [29]. Such hybrid approaches
show higher performance than single machine learning-based
approaches.
Yuan et al. proposed a new hybrid approach that splits the
KDD99 dataset into 10 sub-datasets; generates a prediction
model for each subset using C5.0, one of latest DT algorithm;
and determines the ﬁnal class using NB with results obtained
from the prediction models [18].
Li et al. suggested another semi-supervised learning that
constructs as many C4.5-based binary classiﬁers as the total
number of classes in the training dataset. When each binary
classiﬁer estimates the same class for the input data, the estimated class becomes the ﬁnal output. Otherwise, the input
data are treated as uncertain data. The kNN algorithm is
trained with such uncertain data and used to choose the ﬁnal
class [19].
Soheily-Khah et al. proposed a semi-supervised learning
model and evaluated it using the ISCX 2012 dataset [20], [25].
It uses the k-means algorithm, which is an unsupervised
learning algorithm, as the ﬁrst-level classiﬁer. It ﬁnds the
optimal k and makes clusters based on normal data, and
then, removes the p (<k) farthest clusters from the attack
data to decrease the size of the training data. Next, it trains
the second-level classiﬁer using the RF algorithm with the
data. For performance evaluation, the proposed algorithm
is compared and analyzed with various algorithms such as
SVM, NN, NB, DT, and 1-NN through the Wilcoxon test [22].
Wang et al. proposed two hybrid algorithms, called
HAST-I and HAST-II, using CNN and RNN. They use
raw packet dump as a training dataset, instead of a dataset
generated according to a pre-designed feature set [21].
HAST-I uses CNN to extract features from 2D data constructed by the ﬁrst n bytes of the network ﬂow or packet
data. HAST-II adopts RNN to deal with time-series features in addition to CNN. They achieve very high classiﬁ-
cation accuracy from the evaluation using ISCX 2012 and
DARPA 1998 [23], [24].
The main advantage of NIDS based on multi-supervised or
semi-supervised learning is the higher classiﬁcation performance compared to using single machine learning. As each
classiﬁer compensates the weakness of the other classiﬁer,
the classiﬁcation performance can be increased signiﬁcantly.
This approach requires an efﬁcient solution to ﬁnd an optimal
combination of multiple classiﬁers, which is still unknown
and under research.
C. DATA OPTIMIZATION-BASED NIDS
Some techniques for mitigating the minority class problem
have been proposed, such as over-sampling, under-sampling,
or hybrid sampling adopting both of them such as the
synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE) [9].
SMOTE ﬁnds majority class data that are close to minority
class data and generates synthetic data randomly within the
distance between the majority and minority class data. There
has also been research for extending SMOTE for developing
a more improved dataset for classiﬁcation [10], [11]. Some
researchers have attempted to improve NIDS performance
using feature engineering or using feature engineering and
sampling simultaneously [12]–[14].

Yan
et

proposed
region
adaptive-SMOTE
(RA-SMOTE) as an extended SMOTE [10], where the region
around the minority class data is classiﬁed into independence
point region, safety point region, and danger point region,
and a different sampling policy is applied for each region.
They evaluated RA-SMOTE using various classiﬁcation
algorithms such as SVM, RF, and backpropagation neural
network (BPNN), with the NSL-KDD dataset, and compared
it with SMOTE.
Sun also proposed SMOTE-NCL based on SMOTE, which
calculates an imbalance coefﬁcient from the ratio of each
class size to dataset size and continues to apply SMOTE
to the data until the coefﬁcient exceeds the threshold [11].
Then, it removes noisy data using the neighborhood cleaning
rule [15]. For evaluation, the proposed algorithm was applied
to the KDD99 dataset using DT, C4.5, and SVM [16].
Ambusaidi et al. evaluated various feature selection algorithms such as ﬂexible mutual information-based feature
selection, ﬂexible linear correlation coefﬁcient-based feature
selection, and mutual information-based feature selection.
They chose NB and SVM to develop NIDS classiﬁcation
algorithms, and evaluated the performance of each pair of
feature selection and classiﬁcation algorithms to ﬁnd an optimal combination. Shah et al. compared the results with and
without feature selection based on the information obtained
using the KDD99 dataset and BPNN [13], [16]. Qazi et al.
compared the results of various algorithms such as DT, NB,
RF, and radial basis function by combining SMOTE, undersampling, and feature selection [14].
The abovementioned studies indicate that data optimization is very effective for signiﬁcantly improving the classi-
ﬁcation accuracy by directly modifying the training dataset.
However, it still has some open problems, such as how to
determine tuning parameters, i.e., the size of data sampling
and sampling algorithm. If we choose unoptimized algorithms, the classiﬁcation performance can be rather degraded.
Moreover, over-sampling inevitably increases the dataset
size, leading to a long training time. If the sampling data do
not reﬂect the overall characteristics of the original dataset,
the increasing data can behave as noise, so the overall performance can decrease. On the contrary, under-sampling can
lead to loss of characteristics of the original dataset, causing
the training model to be biased and dependent on the sampling data. NIDS using such a model cannot guarantee high
classiﬁcation performance and the performance can ﬂuctuate
according to the trafﬁc.
Most feature selection algorithms remove features with
low importance, but previous studies have shown that even
features with low importance can improve the overall performance [17]. Thus, we still need to develop feature selection
algorithms to ﬁnd the best combination of features.
III. MOTIVATION
In this section, we discuss in depth the limitations of existing
approaches, especially for the minority class problem occurring in large-scale datasets. We often ﬁnd the occurrence
of a serious imbalance between the amounts of attack and
normal trafﬁcs in a real network dataset. In unﬁltered network
trafﬁcs, most trafﬁcs are normal and only a few are attack
trafﬁcs as shown in Figure 1 (a). On the contrary, when
we analyze network trafﬁcs ﬁltered by the network security
equipment, we ﬁnd that the majority trafﬁc is attack trafﬁc
as shown in Fig. 1 (b). In any case, the imbalance problem
exists.
FIGURE 1. The ratio for each class in CIC-IDS2017 and Kyoto2016 datasets.
The Kyoto2016 dataset was built by gathering trafﬁcs from
2006 to 2015 using honeypots, so it is not a synthesized
dataset but a real one, in contrast to the KDD99 or NSL-KDD
datasets. KDD99 and its variants have been widely used
in most existing studies, but they are outdated and provide
insufﬁcient information about the latest attacks. Moreover,
compared to Kyoto2016, they are too small to include the
various malicious data that have occurred [26]. These limitations lead us to select the Kyto2016 dataset for analyzing
the problems of modern NIDS and creating a solution for
them. For an exact analysis, we use a dataset whose duplicate
data are removed. Table 1 shows the feature list composed of
the Kyoto2016 dataset. Because it contains session-speciﬁc
information, we only use some selected features indexed
to 1 to 14, 20, 22, and 24 in Table 1.
First, we analyze the Kyoto2016 dataset collected in
February 2015 for better understanding the issues of the
NIDS dataset. Table 2 depicts the high imbalance in terms of
size between normal and attack trafﬁcs. We use some selected
metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.
Table 3 presents the classiﬁcation result for the dataset
in Table 2 using RF. As seen, most minority class data
are miss-detected. A serious class imbalance causes biased
training of a machine learning model to majority class data,
so most minority class data can be misclassiﬁed as majority
class if the model is used for classiﬁcation. This phenomenon
is called the minority class problem. Even if the minority class
problem occurs and all minority class data are misclassiﬁed,
some classiﬁcation metrics, such as accuracy, may still appear
to be very high because a minority class data with a very
small size has little impact on the metrics. For an accurate
analysis of the minority class problem, we should evaluate
the classiﬁcation results using the confusion matrix or by
calculating the precision, recall, and F1-score for each class,
as shown in Table 3.

IV. PROPOSED APPROACH
In the previous section, we discussed the minority class problem in an NIDS and an effective approach for addressing
it through preliminary experimental results. In this section,
we will propose a new hybrid machine learning based solution for classifying the NIDS dataset with high speed and
high accuracy regardless of class type, using the derived
conclusion from the results. Our main idea is to partition
the large dataset to sub datasets while the total numbers
of service types and related attacks in each sub dataset are
minimized. The overall structure of the classiﬁer proposed

in this study comprises two partitioning parts, i.e., static
agglomerative partitioning and dynamic divisive partitioning
as shown in Fig. 3. In the static partitioning, any duplicate
data are removed from the training dataset. Then, the dataset
is partitioned into small sub-datasets according to service,
destination port, and session ﬂag in static order. This ﬁxed
order of partitioning features helps the NIDS to increase partitioning speed, and above all, enables the NIDS to handle partial incremental partitioning for increasing dataset efﬁciently
without repartitioning from the scratch. This feature allows
us to apply new training data to NIDS classiﬁer in a short
time. As the service feature is used for the ﬁrst partitioning,
each sub-dataset contains only data related to one service or
similar services.
FIGURE 3. Overall structure of two-level partitioning, where Smax is a
control parameter for deciding the partitioned sub-dataset size.
An NIDS always recognizes the service type of incoming
trafﬁcs, so such service-based partitioning can be adopted
in any NIDS without a technical implementation burden.
Each sub-dataset generated from service-based partitioning
contains almost homogeneous service trafﬁc data. We also
note that the type of attack is closely related to a speciﬁc
service. For example, network attacks such as DoS Slowloris
and DoS SlowHTTPtest generally target only a web service. Thus, each partition generated by service-based partitioning has mostly only attack data for the corresponding
service. This characteristic also applies to normal data of
the partition. Such homogeneity can have great advantage
for better training of machine learning algorithms; therefore,
we can increase the classiﬁcation accuracy effectively under
the minority class problem.
Similar attacks show similar session level behaviors. For
example, every port scanning generates a large number of half
open sessions. Thus, it is a good idea to split dataset using
session state, which is analyzed and represented by ‘ﬂag’
in IDS.
Now, we will describe the entire partitioning algorithm
using an example. Let us assume that we have a dataset
including normal and abnormal classes for three services,
i.e., ‘SSH’, ‘HTTP, SSH’, and ‘DNS’, and for four ﬂags, i.e.,
‘S1’, ‘SF’, ‘REJ’, and ‘SHR’.
We can easily partition it into 12 sub-datasets based
on service and ﬂag. If some partitions are too small,
we need to merge them into larger sub-datasets in order to
avoid the minority class problem. We need to merge similar sub-datasets which include common abnormal classes.
we can use destination ports used for each service to ﬁnd the
most similar services. For the example, ‘SSH’ and ‘HTTP,
SSH’ are basically the same SSH, so the most similar ones
in this example. In other prospects, we can choose these two
services since they use the common destination port, 22. If too
small sub-datasets still exist, it will be reasonable to merge
two sub-datasets, S1 with SF, or REJ with SHR because
S1 and SF include normal sessions, but REJ and SHR include
abnormal ones.
If we still have large sub-datasets after static agglomerative partitioning, we perform additional partitioning, called
dynamic divisive partitioning, which selects the partitioning
feature dynamically. Now, we will describe the proposed
algorithm in detail.
A. SERVICE-AWARE PARTITIONING
We design the proposed partitioning algorithm to effectively satisfy the following three goals: First, we generate sub-partitions whose size is determined by a threshold
value, Smax. It is very important to maintain the optimal size
of the sub-partitions. If the size of the dataset included in a
sub-partition is too large, the minority class problem has the
negative affect in the classiﬁcation, while if the size is too
small, then machine learning cannot be trained sufﬁciently
to reach a high classiﬁcation accuracy. As we independently
apply a machine learning algorithm to each sub-partition,
the sub-partition size is also important for decreasing the total
training time signiﬁcantly.
Second, we construct each sub-dataset to only contain
highly similar data. By doing so, we can include only those
attacks with similar characteristics in the sub-dataset and can
effectively decrease the number of attack types in it. This
maximizes the efﬁcacy of training for the applied machine
learning.
Third, the partitioning algorithm should provide partitioning in an incremental manner to support the rapidly increasing
dataset. It should not rebuild all partitions with high time
costs whenever the dataset size increases. Instead, it should

available, the NIDS should train machine learning using the
dataset to defend the new attack. If partitioning takes long,
the NIDS becomes defenseless against the new attack for a
long partitioning time at least.
To achieve such goals, we partition the dataset according
to the predeﬁned order of some selected features. Such a
static partitioning can be deteriorated over the dynamic one
in terms of partitioning quality but static partitioning can
be simple and fast enough to handle the increasing dataset.
However, we may still have a sub-dataset larger than Smax.
As the number of such sub-datasets is small, we can apply
dynamic partitioning to them for achieving high partitioning efﬁciency. We develop an effective divisive partitioning
algorithm using dynamically selected features. Now, we will
explain each partitioning algorithm in detail.
B. STATIC AGGLOMERATIVE PARTITIONING
The original dataset is ﬁrst partitioned by service type, i.e.,
each sub-dataset including one service type. As mentioned
earlier, most attacks are related to speciﬁc services, so partitioning based on service type is most effective for increasing
homogeneity of attacks in each sub-dataset and decreasing
the total number of attack types in the sub-dataset. If any subdataset is larger than ρSmax (ρ > 1), where ρ is a margin
factor, it is additionally partitioned by the destination port
number. In general, one service can use multiple port numbers
owing to some reasons such as network security or network management policies, although some popular services
already have predeﬁned port numbers, called well-known
ports. These multiple port numbers related to a service can be
a serious burden in designing a policy for a ﬁrewall but are
very useful partitioning criteria for partitioning to decrease
the sub-partition size while maintaining the characteristics of
the partition. Table 5 shows the port number(s) used for each
service in the Kyoto2016 dataset.
When any sub-dataset is smaller than Smax after partitioning, it is merged with another sub-dataset if the new merged
sub-dataset is smaller than ρSmax. To choose the most suitable
sub-datasets for merging, we develop a coefﬁcient, called
merging preference for service, which will be explained in
detail later. In case of sub-datasets with larger size than Smax,
despite two times partitioning based on service and destination ports, the third partitioning is performed using a session
state called ﬂag. According to the similarity, the ﬂags are classiﬁed into three categories for normal and abnormal sessions,
which are represented in Tables 6 and 7. After partitioning,
the new sub-dataset contains only one ﬂag. Among them,
any sub-dataset smaller than Smax is merged with another
sub-dataset when the new sub-dataset is smaller than ρSmax.
In this merging procedure, we also need to develop additional
merging preference for ﬂag.

If we have any sub-dataset larger than ρSmax after static

Unlike static partitioning, we dynamically ﬁnd the best feature to be used in the next partitioning. To evaluate the quality

V. EVAULATION
For evaluating the performance of our proposed algorithm,
we compare it with other recent studies through various
experiments. We use the Kyoto2016 dataset for binary classiﬁcation and CIC-IDS2017 dataset for multi classiﬁcation.
We split each dataset into 60:40 for training and testing.
The testing is performed on a workstation equipped with
Intel i9 9900K, 64GB DDR DRAM, and Nvidia GeForce
RTX2060. We also implement all algorithms using Tensor-
Flow and Scikit-Learn in the Jupyter notebook running on
Ubuntu 18.04. We set ρ and Smax to 1.5 and 300,000, respectively. To ﬁnd the best value for Smax, we searched Smax with
the highest F1-score linearly, where Smax is set to 100,000 and
is increased by 100,000 until it ﬁnds the best one.

VI. CONCLUSION
This paper proposes a new two-level partitioning algorithm
combining agglomerative and divisive partitioning to minimize the size of attack type belonging to each partition.
Unlike most existing studies, we used very large unbalanced
datasets, CIC-IDS2017 and Kyoto2016 datasets, to effectively analyze the minority class problem. We successfully
conﬁrmed that the proposed unique partitioning can increase
the classiﬁcation performance signiﬁcantly by using RF classiﬁer. Compared to the existing approaches, it can achieve
higher classiﬁcation results in terms of accuracy, precision,
recall, and F1-score. It maintains a high performance for both
a very large dataset and a small one. The proposed partitioning algorithm can also achieve higher classiﬁcation speed
than other competitive algorithms regardless of the dataset
size. However, it still cannot support in-ﬂow intrusion prevention. In the future, we will extend the proposed algorithm for
real-time intrusion prevention. Our proposed algorithm was
designed to exploit characteristics of network trafﬁcs. However, it can be extended to support any other classiﬁcation
problems which suffer from minority class problems such as
unreliable telecommunication customers and fraud detection
or image classiﬁcation like medical diagnosis. Thus, we will
also try to extend current research results to apply for other
research areas.

Sleep Apnea Detection From Single-Lead ECG:
A Comprehensive Analysis of Machine Learning
and Deep Learning Algorithms
Mahsa Bahrami
and Mohamad Forouzanfar , Senior Member, IEEE
Abstract—Sleep apnea is a common sleep breathing disorder
(SBD) in which patients suffer from stopping or decreasing
airﬂow to the lungs for more than 10 sec. Accurate detection of sleep apnea episodes is an important step in devising appropriate therapies and management strategies. This
article provides a comprehensive analysis of machine learning and deep learning algorithms on 70 recordings of the
PhysioNet ECG Sleep Apnea v1.0.0 dataset. First, electrocardiogram signals were pre-processed and segmented and then
machine learning and deep learning methods were applied for
sleep apnea detection. Among conventional machine learning
algorithms, linear and quadratic discriminate analyses, logistic
regression, Gaussian naïve Bayes, Gaussian process, supportvector machines, k-nearest neighbor, decision tree, extra tree,
random forest, AdaBoost, gradient boosting, multi-layer perceptron, and majority voting were implemented. Among deep
algorithms, convolutional networks (Alex-Net, VGG16, VGG19,
ZF-Net), recurrent networks (LSTM, bidirectional LSTM, gated
recurrent unit), and hybrid convolutional-recurrent networks
were implemented. All networks were similarly modiﬁed to
handle our biosignal processing task. The available data were
divided into a training set to adjust the model parameters,
a validation set to adjust hyperparameters, avoid overﬁtting,
and improve the generalizability of the models, and a test set
to evaluate the generalizability of the models on unseen data.
This procedure was then repeated in a ﬁvefold cross-validation
scheme so that all the recordings were once located in the test
set. It was found that the best detection performance is achieved
by hybrid deep models where the best accuracy, sensitivity, and
speciﬁcity were 88.13%, 84.26%, and 92.27%, respectively. This
study provides valuable information on how different machine
learning and deep learning algorithms perform in the detection
of sleep apnea and can further be extended toward the detection
of other sleep events. Our developed algorithms are publicly
available on GitHub.

of publication February 15, 2022; date of current version March 11, 2022.

(ECG), machine learning, sleep apnea.
I. INTRODUCTION
S
LEEP accounts for about one-third of the human life
span and plays an important role in health and quality of life. Two main stages of sleep are called rapid eye
movement (REM) and non-REM (NREM) [3]. REM sleep
compared with NREM sleep is associated with increased
sympathetic activity, cardiovascular instability, and hemodynamic variations. During NREM, oxygen consumption and
heart rate decrease as well as the blood pressure, while in
the REM stage, blood pressure and heart rate surge. Sleep
apnea may occur during any stage of sleep, but it is most
dominant during the REM. This is mainly because the muscles
in the upper airway are further relaxed during the REM stage
of sleep.
The rate of people suffering from sleep disorders is increasing [6]. In the United States, it is estimated that about
70 million adults have sleep disorders [8]. The rate of morbidity and mortality increases in patients suffering from sleep
disorders [10]. Insomnia, sleep breathing disorders (SBDs),
central disorders of hypersomnolence, circadian rhythm sleepwake disorders, parasomnias, and movement disorders are the
main types of sleep disorders. Among different sleep disorders,
SBDs are more common. SBDs are divided into obstructive
sleep apnea (OSA), central sleep apnea (CSA), hypoventilation
in sleep, and hypoxia disorders. Upper airway obstruction
leads to OSA, whereas CSA occurs when the brain cannot
send proper signals into muscles responsible for breathing.
It is estimated that one billion people in the world are suffering
from OSA [12]. CSA occurs less than other types of apneas.
CSA mostly occurs in the NREM cycle, while OSA occurs in
both REM and NREM cycles but the severity of OSA in the
REM cycle is higher [14].
To prevent and manage cardiovascular, mental, and other
health issues related to sleep apnea, accurate, affordable, and
portable technologies are required that can detect and monitor
sleep events.
There has been considerable research on the development of automatic algorithms for the detection of sleep
apnea from a variety of physiological signals [15]–[22]
among which ECG has shown the most promising results
in terms of both convenience and precision [2], [4], [5],

[7], [9], [11], [13], [23]. Apnea detection based on a singlelead electrocardiogram (ECG) provides the opportunity for the
design and development of wearable technologies based on a
single sensor.
Conventional machine learning algorithms are among the
ﬁrst automatic algorithms used for the detection of apnea
events. Given the complexity of physiological signals and the
limited feature extraction capability of conventional machine
learning algorithms, the research focus has recently been
shifted toward the more complex deep learning models.
Thanks to the advancements in computational power, deep
learning algorithms have surpassed their conventional machine
learning counterparts by having the capability of automatic
extraction of most representative features. Given the variety of
the algorithms designed for the detection of sleep apnea, the
different datasets and physiological signals used for training
them, and the various validation strategies as well as performance metrics used for evaluation of the algorithms, it is hard
to compare the algorithms’ performance.
In this article, we provide a fair and unbiased comparison between different conventional machine learning and
deep learning algorithms in the detection of sleep apnea
occurrence from a single-lead ECG. All the experiments
are performed on the same dataset and under the same
setting to be able to properly evaluate and compare the
performances of different algorithms. Unlike most studies
that tune their model hyperparameters based on the same
data used for ﬁnal evaluation, we used three sets of data:
a training set to train the model parameters, a validation
set to ﬁnd the model optimum hyperparameters, and a test
set to evaluate the generalizability of the developed models
on unseen data. This article is an extended version of our
work presented in the 16th edition of IEEE International
Symposium on Medical Measurements and Applications [1],
where the performance of a few deep learning methods was
analyzed for the detection of sleep apnea. In this article,
we have signiﬁcantly extended our comparisons by studying
the performance of 14 different conventional machine learning
methods and 19 different deep learning methods. A detailed
comparison between different models as well as eight other
state-of-the-art techniques is provided. We also performed a
feature importance analysis and demonstrated which ECG
features are most effective for the detection of apnea episodes.
We have made our algorithms publicly available on GitHub at
https://github.com/mahsaabahrami/sleep-apnea.
II. BACKGROUND
Accurate detection of sleep apnea is an important step for
the management of apnea side effects. Questionnaires, image
processing techniques, and signal analysis methods are the
main approaches for sleep apnea monitoring. Questionnaires
are low-cost methods for the identiﬁcation of patients with
sleep disorders [24]. Medical image analysis is a capable
method for analyzing sleep apnea especially in severe sleep
apnea [25]. Medical image analysis also provides a unique
opportunity for screening anatomical changes during sleep
apnea. Polysomnography (PSG) is a gold standard for sleep
apnea monitoring [26]. PSG consists of various biological
signals, such as ECG, electroencephalogram, airﬂow pulse
oximetry, arterial blood oxygen saturation, and nasal ﬂow.
However, none of these techniques can be performed in nonspecialist settings, such as in home. Wearable and noncontact sleep technologies are required that can unobtrusively
monitor and manage sleep without the need for direct expert
presence [27], [28]. Different physiological signals have been
analyzed for the detection of sleep apnea among which ECG
provides a better possibility for implementation in wearable
monitors.
Conventional machine learning and novel deep learning are
two main automatic approaches for sleep apnea monitoring
from physiological signals. The performance of conventional
machine learning algorithms relies on expert-deﬁned extracted
features. In [15], ECG signals were decomposed to frequency
bands by Fourier transform, and statistical features were
extracted. A support vector machine (SVM) with Gaussian
kernel function was then used to detect sleep apnea. In [2],
the performance of different machine learning methods was
compared. For this purpose, after extracting different timedomain features of heart rate variability (HRV) and ECGderived respiration, artiﬁcial neural network (ANN), SVM,
linear discriminate analysis (LDA), partial least-square regression, and augmented naïve Bayes regression were applied for
the detection of sleep apnea events. The best accuracy and
sensitivity were achieved by ANN; however, the speciﬁcity
of augmented naïve Bayes regression was higher than other
methods.
Recently, deep learning methods have revolutionized sleep
apnea
detection. Despite
conventional machine
learning
approaches, deep learning methods rely on automatic feature
extraction. Deep recurrent neural networks (DRNNs) and
convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are two main types of
deep learning models that have been used for sleep apnea
monitoring. In [4], continuous wavelet transformation and
Alex-Net were used for feature extraction and then different
machine learning methods were used for the classiﬁcation of
sleep apnea episodes from single-lead ECG signals. It was
shown that extracting time-frequency features improves the
performance of sleep apnea detection. In [5], it was shown that
the accuracy of sleep apnea detection can be improved by a
two-layer CNN. In [7], a long short-term memory (LSTM) was
used for OSA detection from single-lead ECG that provided an
accurate and real-time method for sleep apnea detection. In [9],
unsupervised feature learning from ECG signal was done
by a frequential stacked auto-encoder, and a hidden Markov
model was used for classiﬁcation. In [11], a multiscale dilation
attention convolution module was used and was shown that the
combination of a multiscale attention convolutional module
and a weighted-loss time-dependent classiﬁer improves the
performance of sleep apnea detection. In [1], we performed
a comparison between a few deep networks and found that a
hybrid CNN-LSTM achieves superior results.
In [29], a real-time sleep apnea detection method based on
motion detection was proposed by using quadrature microwave
Doppler radar. In [30], a wearable device based on single-lead
ECG was proposed for improving the performance of home

III. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
A. Dataset
In this article, PhysioNet Apnea-ECG Database v1.0.0 [32]
was used to build our models and to compare their performances. The database contains 70 recordings from 32 individuals (seven females, age: 44 ± 11, apnea–hypopnea index,
AHI: 24 ± 25, height: 175 ± 6, weight: 86 ± 22) divided
into four groups: A, B, C, and X. Thirteen individuals in
this dataset have AHI ≤5 and are categorized as normal,
13 individuals have AHI > 30, and are categorized in the
severe sleep apnea class, and six individuals have 5 < AHI <
30 and are categorized in the mild and moderate apnea class.
The length of the 70 recordings is 8.2 ± 0.52 h. ECG signals
are digitized at 100 Hz. The annotation of the presence of
sleep apnea is provided for every 1 min by a sleep expert.
B. Preprocessing
ECG signals were segmented into 1-min intervals. To extract
the R–R Intervals from the ECG signal, the Hamilton Rpeak detection method based on an open-source code was
employed [33]. A median ﬁlter proposed by Chen et al. [34]
was used for removing physiologically uninterpretable points.
The extracted
R–R Intervals were then presented to
the developed machine learning algorithms after appropriate
processing as is discussed in the Section IV.
In addition to the R–R Intervals, the amplitudes of R-peaks
were also extracted and presented to the deep models. Cubic
interpolation at 3 Hz was applied to sample R–R intervals and
R-peak amplitudes at an equal rate. Finally, the interpolated
R–R Intervals and R-peak amplitudes were fed to the deep
models. To capture the time pattern of the input data when
using DRNNs, the input data were segmented into n segments
of 60/n s and n-cell DRNNs were designed to learn from the
input data (here, n was set to 2).
IV. CONVENTIONAL MACHINE LEARNING
Feature extraction, feature selection, and classiﬁcation are
the main steps in conventional machine learning methods. Feature engineering plays a vital role in boosting the performance
of these machine learning algorithms. Here, we developed a
uniﬁed feature engineering framework for the conventional
machine learning algorithms (shown in Fig. 1). First, ECG
signals were pre-processed. Then time, frequency, and nonlinear features of the ECG signal were extracted. In addition
to this, principal component analysis (PCA) was applied for
dimension reduction, coping with the curse of dimensionality,
and extracting the most robust features. Finally, the ECG signal
was classiﬁed into apnea and normal episodes.
A. Feature Extraction
The most important features of ECG for apnea detection
are HRV parameters [35]. In this article, a comprehensive
set of time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear features
of HRV were extracted and presented to different machine
learning models for sleep apnea detection.
1) Time-Domain Features: Time-domain features of HRV
are mainly divided into statistical, long-term, and shortterm features [36]. Minimum, range, median, mean, standard
deviation (SDNN), skewness (third momentum), and kurtosis
(fourth momentum) were the main statistical features extracted
from R–R intervals. The standard deviation of successive
differences between adjacent R–R Intervals (SDSD) was the
main long-term extracted feature of HRV. Short-term features
of HRV consisted of the number of R–R intervals that differ
from each other by more than 50 ms (NN50), the number of
R–R intervals that differ from each other by more than 20 ms
(NN20), percentage of successive R–R differences greater
than 50 ms (pNN50), and the percentage of successive R–R
differences greater than 20 ms (pNN20). In addition, the root
mean square of successive differences between normal heartbeats (rMSSD) was extracted from the HRV signal. In total,
13 features were extracted from each ECG segment in the time
domain.
2) Frequency-Domain Features: HRV has three predominant frequency bands [36]. Very low-frequency (VLF) band,
that is, frequencies between 0.0033 and 0.04 Hz, exhibits the
thermoregulation mechanisms. Low-frequency (LF) band, that
is, frequencies between 0.04 and 0.15 Hz, exhibits mostly the
sympathetic activity, and the high-frequency (HF) band, that is,
frequencies between 0.15 and 0.4 Hz, exhibits parasympathetic
activities.
Total power, VLF power, LF power, HF power, LF to HF
ratio, normalized HF power (HFnu), and normalized LF power
(LFnu) were extracted. In total, seven features were extracted
from each ECG segment in the frequency domain.
3) Nonlinear Features: Nonlinear features are mainly used
for modeling and analyzing ECG patterns before, during,
and after sleep apnea. Poincaré plot features including SD1
and SD2, and their ratio (SD2/SD1) [37], cardiovagal index
(CVI) [38], cardio sympathetic index (CSI) [38], and modiﬁed
CVI [38] were extracted from the ECG signal. Permutation
entropy [39] explaining the complexity of the HRV time series
was also calculated. In total, seven nonlinear HRV features
were extracted.
In total, 27 HRV features were extracted.
B. Dimension Reduction
Many irrelevant features lead to the curse of dimensionality
problem and have a detrimental impact on the performance
of machine learning methods. To cope with these problems,
feature selection techniques are applied before classiﬁcation.

C. Classiﬁcation
Different machine learning algorithms have been applied for
sleep apnea detection. However, the main problem in this ﬁeld
is the lack of a fair and uniﬁed comparison between different
algorithms. In this study, different well-known machine learning algorithms are compared. More information about these
machine learning algorithms is available in [40].
1) Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA): LDA is a simple
classiﬁer that uses a linear decision boundary, generated by
ﬁtting Gaussian densities to each class using Bayes’ rule [16].
The main hyperparameters that need to be predeﬁned before
training LDA are the solver algorithm and a tolerance parameter that deﬁnes the absolute threshold for a singular value
to be considered signiﬁcant.
2) Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA): QDA is similar
to LDA but uses a quadratic boundary decision [17]. The
solver for QDA is usually set to SVD, and therefore tolerance
is the main hyperparameter that needs to be deﬁned before
training.
3) Logistic Regression (LR): LR uses a logistic function for
modeling dependent binary variables [20]. Solver algorithm,
tolerance for stopping criteria, regularization strength (1/C),
and penalty norm are its main hyperparameters.
4) Gaussian Naïve Bayes (GNB): GNB is a probabilistic
method based on applying Bayes’ theorem with naïve independence assumption between features. Its main hyperparameter
is the portion of the largest variance of all features that has to
be added to variances for stability [41].
5) Gaussian Process (GP): GP classiﬁcation is a nonparametric approach that uses a kernel function to assign class
labels. Kernel, optimizer algorithm, and the maximum number
of iterations for approximation posterior in Newton’s method
are its main hyperparameters.
6) SVM: SVM uses a kernel function for mapping data into
a higher dimension. Lagrange equations are used to solve the
problem in higher dimensions [21]. The type of the kernel and
the kernel parameters are its main hyperparameters.
7) K-Nearest Neighborhood (KNN): KNN classiﬁes data
samples based on their nearest neighbors. There are different
criteria for the distance metric in the KNN method, including
Euclidean distance and Mahalanobis distance [22]. Distance
metric, the metric parameters, number of nearest neighbors,
and leaf size are its main hyperparameters.
8) Decision Tree (DT): DT is a nonparametric classiﬁer
that predicts the class labels by learning simple decision rules

inferred from the extracted features [18]. Interpretability is
the main advantage of this method. Max depth of trees, the
strategy used to choose the split, and the criterion measuring
the quality of splits are the main hyperparameters of DT.
9) Random Forest (RF): RF is an extended version of DT.
RF uses several DTs for combinational learning by subsampling the input data with replacement (bootstrapping) [20].
This method largely prevents over-ﬁtting during training,
although improving performance in this method and reducing
over-ﬁtting depends on the type of dataset. Maximum depth,
the minimum number of samples required to split an internal
node, split criterion, and the number of estimators (trees) are
the main hyperparameters to be set.
10) Extra Tree (ET): ET is another evolved model based on
DTs that is similar to RF but unlike RF that uses bootstrapping methods, uses the whole original sample. In addition,
unlike RF which chooses the optimum cut points to split
nodes, ET chooses them randomly. In terms of computational
complexity and time required to implement the algorithms,
ET is faster and more efﬁcient than RF. Maximum depth, the
minimum number of samples required to split an internal node,
split criterion, and the number of estimators (trees) are the
main hyperparameters to be set.
11) AdaBoost (AB): AB combines several weak learners
(decision stumps, trees with one node and two leaves) to
build a stronger classiﬁer. Unlike RF that samples the training
data based on the bagging technique, AB, at each iteration,
upweights the misclassiﬁed samples so that they appear in
the training subset of the next learner with higher probability.
After each learner is trained, a weight is assigned to it based
on its performance. Number of estimators (trees), boosting
algorithm, and learning rate are its main hyperparameters.
12) Gradient Boosting (GB): GB is a generalization of AB
that casts boosting as an optimization problem by using a
gradient descent like procedure to minimize the loss of the
model when adding new weak learners (here, DTs). Loss
function, number of estimators, maximum depth, learning rate,
the fraction of samples to be used for ﬁtting the individual base
learners, and split criterion are its main hyperparameters.
13) Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP): MLP is a feed-forward
neural network consisting of multiple layers of nonlinear nodes
capable of modeling complex and nonlinear relationships [20].
Its main hyperparameters are the number of layers, number of
nodes, learning rate, type of activation functions used in the
nodes, optimization method, and the loss tolerance to stop
training. The number of hidden layers was set to 1.
14) Majority Vote (MV): MV is an ensemble method for
classiﬁcation by combining several classiﬁers using a majority voting scenario. Here, we used MV to combine all the
conventional machine learning algorithms.
V. DEEP LEARNING
Different CNNs and DRNNs [42] were employed to build
standalone and hybrid deep models for the detection of sleep
apnea. The ﬂowchart of the proposed approach for sleep apnea
detection using deep learning is shown in Fig. 2.
CNN provides a unique opportunity for automatic feature
extraction and classiﬁcation of images, signals, and other
