Kamarov and Susvoc [23] describe Autonomous Photovoltaic Systems with great applicability at different scales,
from small photovoltaic systems that power lamps to networks capable of supplying electricity to entire populations.
They usually have an energy storage system that allows them
to function when there is no solar resource, at which time
there is usually a greater demand for energy [24].
Ma, Hu, and Cheng [25] investigated a new data-driven
method that can estimate SOC and SOE simultaneously based
on a deep short-term memory (LSTM) neural network. The
proposed algorithm is validated with two dynamic, driven
cycles under various working conditions, such as different
temperatures, different battery materials, and noise interference. Furthermore, the performance of the proposed method
is compared with other popular algorithms, including support vector regression (SVR), random forest (RF), and simple recurrent neural network (Simple RNN). The results
show that the proposed method obtains greater precision and
robustness.
Tian et al. [26] indicate that recent development in deep
learning provided an emerging solution for SOC estimation
and proposed incorporating two types of domain knowledge
in deep learning-based methods. First, the voltage and current
sequences are decoupled into open circuit voltage (OCV),
ohmic response, and bias voltage to augment the input of
deep neural networks (DNN). Second, since conventional
DNNs ignore the time dependency in SOC estimation results,
they proposed a combination framework to adaptively merge
DNN SOC estimation results from the DNN and short-term
Ampere-hour predictions. The results show that the proposed
method can drastically reduce the mean square error of the
SOC estimate and the maximum absolute error.
In another work by Tian et al. [27], they propose a ﬂexible
method that uses only short chunks of load data to estimate
maximum and remaining capacities to address state-of-health
and state-of-charge estimation problems simultaneously. The
proposed method is based on a convolutional neural network
that only requires short-term load data to estimate two states.
The results offer a ﬂexible and easy-to-implement approach
to accurate multi-state estimation over battery life.

V. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
Our results show that the state of charge of batteries in
photovoltaic systems in the mining sector could be predicted
using supervised learning techniques in an acceptable manner, which was validated with the construction of the software
to make the indicated prediction through the passing results
in the tests carried out.
These results coincide with those found by Henri and
Lu [31] when they state that a machine learning approach
can predict and program the operation mode in real time of
an operation interval for residential battery/photovoltaic systems. This is related to what was expressed by Henri, Lu, and
Carreio [32], who state that a machine learning approach for
predicting the optimal operating mode of the battery in realtime in residential photovoltaic applications. Rehman et al.
[33] show that machine learning can investigate monitoring
data and simulate and optimize case studies.
This study represents a signiﬁcant contribution to the prediction of the state of charge of batteries; however, a limitation found in the study was not having had sufﬁcient
resources to have achieved a greater coverage of companies
dedicated to this area, and although it was not the purpose of
the study, it could have generated a baseline on the load status
prediction of photovoltaic batteries.

through the Victron Energy System, which has the function of monitoring the energy variables of the solar panels;

TCLPI: Machine Learning-Driven Framework for
Hybrid Learning Mode Identification
CHAMAN VERMA
1, ZOLTÁN ILLÉS
1, AND DEEPAK KUMAR
2
1Department of Media and Educational Informatics, Eötvös Loránd University, 1053 Budapest, Hungary
2Apex Institute of Technology, Chandigarh University, Sahibzada Ajit Singh Nagar 140413, India
Corresponding author: Chaman Verma (chaman@inf.elte.hu)
The work of Chaman Verma was supported in part by ÚNKP, Ministry of Innovation and Technology (MIT); in part by the National
Research, Development, and Innovation (NRDI) Fund, Hungarian Government; and in part by under Grant ÚNKP-23-4-II-ELTE-97.
ABSTRACT Since the COVID-19 pandemic, teachers and students have started using online and hybrid
learning in education. There might be several obstacles to adopting hybrid learning in theory classes or
lab practice sessions. Based on student opinions, deciding what is appropriate for theoretical class and lab
practice is challenging. We employed machine learning approaches to forecast the hybrid learning mode for
theory classes and lab practices. We introduce a framework that utilizes machine learning to automate the
identification of hybrid learning for Theory Class and Lab practice (TCLPI). Four machine learning models
form the foundation of this framework: Random Forest (RDT), Support Vector Machine (SVN), Logistic
Regression (LGR), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XBT). In the context of Theory Class Identification
(TCI), the SVN achieves a maximum test accuracy of 0.93, whereas the LGR achieves a minimum accuracy
of 0.90. On the other hand, the Lab Practice Identification (LPI), XBT, RDT, and SVN achieved a test
accuracy of 0.80. The outcome of trained algorithms is assessed using the Shapley Additive Explanation
(SHAP), an explainable Artificial intelligence (AI) approach. This research found that student-teacher
interaction decreased during lab practice, which is crucial. Internet disconnections, a lack of support during
technological malfunctions, and the likelihood of cheating in exams without monitoring are also issues.
We also found that students were accepting of hybrid learning for theory classes. Each model’s intrinsic
feature relevance and SHAP values helped prove this. Research shows that hybrid learning works more for
theory classes; it is less needed for lab practice for students.
INDEX TERMS ATL, classification, hybrid learning, LPI, student, SHAP, TCLPI, Prediction.
I. INTRODUCTION AND RELATED WORK
Learning involves procuring memories, skills, knowledge,
and even wisdom through experiences and education. Higher
learning via the technologies of the internet has transformed
modern education, and many universities offer onlinebased courses, while others have switched to fully online
programs. Incorporating information, communication, and
technology is crucial in promoting student participation
and facilitating online learning, which involves ICT, independent, or supplementary learning with other physical
presence classes referred to as hybrids [1]. According to
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and
approving it for publication was Claudio Zunino.
previous research [2], online learning threatens conventional
methods by allowing flexibility and fostering social interaction. During the pandemic, students and UAE residents
were positive about online education. Online resources
are available to remote learners for self-guided study
and collaborative learning. The self-contained web-based
coaching modules included the flexibility necessary for
self-directed study away from conventional teacher-centered
instruction [3]. Online course strategies seek to enhance
content, empower students, and cultivate collaboration. These
strategies encompass suggesting projects, organizing group
assignments, facilitating discussions, and encouraging virtual
interactions [4]. Hybrid learning integrates face-to-face and
online methods to overcome specific limitations. Fixed

Hybrid courses, by combining classroom and online components, enhance teacher-student relationships. This approach
provides improved performance, flexible scheduling, diverse
learning options, community building, and increased interaction [5]. Evaluating the cost-effectiveness and directing
investments in hybrid learning heavily depends on the satisfaction and experience of learners. Cognitive engagement
is closely connected to both satisfaction and experience [6].
Remote access showed enhanced effectiveness and higher
student satisfaction. Assessment results supported this, indicating a 27.69% average increase in grades, and 81.25% of
students favored Web-lab [7]. However, the abrupt switch
to remote learning presents challenges such as connectivity
issues, socioeconomic disparities, and declining student
motivation.
Student feedback is essential for determining its effectiveness, considering factors such as learning styles and
motivations. Adapting learning environments to individual
variances can lead to better long-term learning results [8].
In Jordan, teachers are happy with new restrictions that
require some courses to be taught online, while others use
a hybrid method [9]. Portugal’s educational system proposes
online and hybrid learning pedagogy instruction [10]. Portugal’s educational system proposes online and hybrid learning
pedagogy instruction [10]. A hybrid learning strategy with
gamification has worked well for programming classes at
a Croatian university [11]. Mobile learning was used in
Abu Dhabi to maintain classroom education during the
pandemic [12]. Online learning and courses affected the
satisfaction of Egyptian university students towards hybrid
learning [13].
Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, scholars delved into the
obstacles experienced by English as a Foreign Language
(EFL) students in online education. These hurdles included
a need for more technological proficiency, challenges with
completing assignments, and problems with internet connectivity. For educators and policymakers looking to improve
online education, these findings offer insightful information [14]. A study focused on the pandemic’s impact on education, highlighting the rise of virtual learning and increased
online program enrollment and discussing the advantages and
drawbacks [15]. A few issues with the pandemic-related shift
to virtual learning were examined, along with how it affected
soft skills and the necessity for creative teaching strategies.
They also looked at issues like cheating on online tests, the
long-term impacts on instructional activities and teachers’
stress, and the impact of virtual tools on social skills [16].
Considering essential factors such as resource competition
and student retention, it’s wise to assess how technology
impacts learning thoroughly. Supporters of hybrid learning
advocate for its adoption with thoughtful consideration,
offering valuable perspectives from different angles [17].
Researchers highlighted the crucial need to synchronize
learning objectives between traditional and ICT-based programs, emphasizing collaborative and social learning. They
emphasized the vital role of social affordances in crafting
productive learning settings and endorsed hybrid learning,
stressing the importance of collaboration among students,
educators, and researchers [18]. The authors suggested
using hybrid learning spaces for curriculum enhancement,
highlighting the value of technology in enhancing student
skills, especially for mobile learners. Hybrid learning gained
traction during the COVID-19 pandemic, which led the
University of Sciences and Humanities to introduce strategies
for continuous education. Following the transition from an
entirely virtual setup to a hybrid model, which experienced
a significant 35% dropout rate and inadequate teacher preparation, connectivity issues became apparent [19]. The swift
switch to online instruction during the COVID-19 pandemic
disrupted the educational landscape, posing challenges for
students and educators. This prompted a comprehensive
assessment, highlighting the academic importance of hybrid
methodologies [20]. Namyssova et al. underscored the necessity of thorough teacher training before introducing blended
learning, noting the obstacles stemming from inadequate
infrastructure and restricted technology access. Identified
challenges include policy gaps, insufficient faculty support,
and a shortage of technological resources [21]. Students
have widely acclaimed hybrid learning for its accessibility,
integrating online platforms like Blackboard with face-toface elements. The innovative teaching methods, fostering
connectivity and student engagement, received high praise,
as did the flexibility provided by the online component’s
scheduling. Challenges, including varying levels of student
engagement and the necessity for instructors to adeptly
manage the hybrid format, highlighted the importance of
gradually integrating technology and prioritizing pedagogy
in hybrid course design [22]. Engaged students demonstrated
a well-distributed allocation of time between in-person
and virtual tasks, preferred outdoor activities, and prioritized measures to prevent musculoskeletal problems [23].
The previously developed and validated blended learning
experiment was successful for Bangladeshi students. These
findings revealed positive associations with attitudes toward
online learning and openness to technology and negative
correlations with technology skills, learning flexibility, and
study management [24].
To investigate critical features for precise predictions, this

of the paper. Section II outlines the study’s methodology and

includes sections on dataset descriptions, statistical features
of factor analysis, prepossess, testing of datasets, testing,
training, and tuning of machine learning algorithms. The
experiments conducted using machine learning techniques
present their results in Section IV. Section V delves into the

In Section VI, we offer the study’s discussions, and in
Section VII, we explain its findings as conclusions. Major

II. PROBLEM STATEMENT
A previous study did not provide a fully automated AI-based
framework that predicts hybrid learning for theory classes
and lab practices. Because of this, we showed the first
hybrid framework with Theory Class Identification (TCI)
and Lab Practice Identification (LPI), along with supervised
machine learning algorithms that correctly predicted the
features of hybrid learning. Further, the current research did
not use the explainable artificial intelligence approach SHAP
to investigate the characteristics of hybrid learning. As a
result, we also investigated the benefits of using the SHAP
methodology to apply machine learning algorithms. The
primary performance metrics of each algorithm determine
its effectiveness. After investigating novel key features and
confirming their presence, we identified a hybrid learning
style for theory classes and practical labs.
III. METHODS AND MATERIALS
A. CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK
The suggested work’s visual representation embodies an
archetype of morality. For both theory and lab sessions,
Figure 1 foresees a hybrid learning approach that is
visually identifiable. At the outset, we gather and compile
the primary dataset based on student responses regarding
demographic features, challenges, benefits, and assistance
throughout hybrid learning. In the subsequent preparation
steps, we handled missing values and standardized and
balanced the data. Next, we created essential factors using
a factor analysis approach. Next, we test and train four
supervised machine learning algorithms on the preprocessed
and cleaned samples. Crucial parameters of each algorithm
were identified by grid search cross-validation with a
stratified method, allowing for maximum accuracy. We also
graph, graphically compute, and display learning curves,
confusion matrices, classification reports, recall, precision,
gain, ROC, and learning scores to illustrate the comparison
of algorithms. Coefficient computation and significance
estimation show how each method uses intrinsic features.
Finally, we implemented the SHAP model using trained
algorithms to provide a detailed description of the features.
B. DATASET DESCRIPTION, PREPROCESS AND FACTOR
ANALYSIS
We used primary data samples and conducted all tests in
Python 3.9 using the necessary libraries [29]. After removing
outliers, the current study used 99 out of 103 students’
primary data samples. ELTE University enrolled the students
in its informatics program. Every year, ELTE University
enrolls roughly 30,000 students, of whom 2,500 study
informatics with faculty members on average. Consequently,
the samples obtained were adequate for analysis for both
populations and factor analysis was used to confirm this [28].

We used a random sampling strategy with Google Forms’
assistance to gather samples [29]. The dataset has 58 students
older than 21 and 41 younger than 20. There were 76 boys and
23 girls who participated. The master’s program had thirtyone students, while the bachelor’s course had sixty-eight.
We selected the Google Forms questions after consulting
with students and academic experts. We used the Likert scale
(1-10) as the measurement tool, with 10 representing the
highest level of agreement and 1 representing the lowest level
of response to the questions. The dataset had no missing
values. Added demographics are age, gender, and course.
We divide the age group into those under 20 and those
over 21. There are master’s and bachelor’s courses under the
course feature. Eight binary features and one ternary feature
were present. We split a ternary feature into three dummy
features using one hot encoder.
We conducted an exploratory factor analysis to identify important factors warrant further investigation. The
factor analysis utilizes the following parameters: Principal
Component Analysis (PCA), Varimax Method, Anti-Image,
convergence iterations set to 25, KMO (Kaiser-Meyer-
Olkin), and Bartlett’s test of sphericity. Table 1 displays the
comprehensive sufficiency of the obtained samples for each
variable, estimated at a value of 0.942. Therefore, the partial
correlations among variables are minimal. The absence of
an identifiable correlation matrix demonstrated a significant
(p < 0.05) value of Bartlett’s sphericity. The entire cumulative
variation accounted for 72% of the participant’s scores.
The dataset has 45 features. Out of 45, 19 were exempted
from the factor analysis (see in Table 2), 23 were used to

VI. DISCUSSION
This study uses machine learning and explainable AI to
predict informatics students’ hybrid learning for theoretical
class and lab practice. All the algorithms achieved training
scores of 0.90 and cross-validation scores higher than 0.82,
while the sample size was approaching 100—the process of
identifying the theory class accomplished this. For the lab
identification task, 90 samples are sufficient to train 0.95 to
0.80 accuracy scores. Hence, more samples can reduce this
gap between test and train scores. All models estimated more
than 0.90 AUC values to identify the theoretical class while
retaining 0.81-0.84 AUC ratings to identify lab practice.
In theory class identification, XBT and SVN did better than
others, explaining 80% of samples and having a cumulative
actual positive rate of 87%. In lab practice identification,
XBT and RDT were 100% accurate, with a cumulative true
positive rate of 50%. For theory class prediction, SVN,
XBT, and RDT had the same most excellent mean accuracy,
f1-score, and recall of 0.94; for lab practice prediction,
it was 0.80. In theory class prediction, LGR, RD, XBT,
and SVN algorithms correctly identified 156, 157, 160, and
163, respectively. However, these algorithms misinterpret
records 18, 17, 14, and 11, respectively. The algorithms
LGR, RD, XBT, and SVN accurately determined the total
number of records as 77, 80, 80, and 80, respectively, for lab
identification. However, these algorithms wrongly identified
records as 23, 20, 20, and 20, respectively.
When making predictions in theory class, factors such as
gender, course, future hybrid learning mode, and long-term
solutions are essential. Additionally, my parents’ valuable
perspective also plays a significant role. It is crucial to
consider factors such as reduced quality of interaction with
teachers, hurdles encountered, isolation from a natural study
environment, lower stress levels, ease of communication, and
university assistance when predicting laboratory outcomes.
Significant features emerge from these factors. The SVN
model’s SHAP scores in theoretical class prediction, teacher
interaction quality, and absence reduction were substantial.
Other noteworthy aspects included time management, the
convenience of attending two classes at once, the ability
to turn on mic video camera interrupts, the encouragement
of website learning, and the isolation of a natural study
environment. The XBT, RDT, and SVN model SHAP values
forecast lab practice, which isolates university initiatives
and support within a genuine study environment. Lower
teacher interaction quality, less stress, and more accessible
communication were all essential features.

VII. CONCLUSION
In this study, we employed machine learning techniques to
identify the possibilities of incorporating hybrid learning into
the education of informatics students, whether in lab practice
or theory classes. Furthermore, we evaluate the explanatory
power of the proposed models using an explainable AI
approach (SHAP). We also presented a combined framework
that identifies the applicability of hybrid learning with
significant accuracy. The factor analysis technique created
novel and essential factors for the experiments. The SVN
algorithms achieved a test accuracy of 0.93% in predicting
hybrid learning for theoretical classes, while XBT achieved
the second-greatest accuracy of 92%. RDT and LGR achieved
an identical accuracy rate of 90%. We demonstrated that
students and parents eagerly accept hybrid learning for theory
classes. Each model’s intrinsic feature importance and SHAP
values proved this. While a viable solution for theory classes,
hybrid learning lacks significance for lab practice. Using
hybrid learning makes students less stressed and makes it
easy to join two different classes simultaneously. They also
believed the hybrid learning mode separated them from the
natural study environments. To predict the hybrid learning
for lab practice, RDT, XBT, and SVN scored a homogeneous
accuracy of 80%, and LGR scored the lowest accuracy of
0.77%. During the lab practice, there was a decrease in the
quality of interaction between the students and the teachers,
which is an important aspect. Furthermore, students face
challenges, including intermittent Internet access, inadequate
assistance in the event of technical difficulties, and the risk
of exam cheating as a result of insufficient monitoring. They
experience a decrease in their ability to concentrate and
engage with people.
VIII. FUTURE STUDY
The present research has identified the features of hybrid
learning that played a vital role in predicting its applicability in informatics students’ lab practice and theory
classes. Future experiments could involve students from
other domains like medicine, economics, social science,
or physiology. We can also implement other algorithms
like artificial neural networks and discriminant analysis.
Future hybrid learning mode features allow for the extraction
of additional features. Furthermore, we can apply more
feature selection algorithms, like gain ratio and infogain, to the samples. Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic
Explanations (LIME) is a new machine-learning explanation method that can provide more dataset insights.
After increasing accuracy, we must deploy the models as
Python-based applications to put this research into actual
use.

ABSTRACT More and more, edge devices embark Artificial Neuron Networks. In this context, a trend is to
simultaneously decentralize their training as much as possible while shrinking their resource requirements,
both for inference and training—tasks that are typically intensive in terms of data, memory, and computation.
At the edge’s extremity, a specific challenge arises concerning the inclusion of microcontroller-based
devices typically deployed in the IoT. So far, no general framework has been provided for that. Such
devices not only have extremely challenging resource constraints (weak CPUs, slow network connections,
memory budgets measured in kilobytes) but also exhibit high polymorphism, leading to large variability in
computational performance among these devices. In this paper, we design and implement TDMiL, a versatile
framework for distributed training, and transfer learning. TDMiL interconnects and combines logical
components including CoAPerator (a central aggregator) and various tiny embedded software runtimes
that are specifically tailored for networks comprising heterogeneous, resource-constrained devices built
on diverse types of microcontrollers. We report on experiments conducted with the TDMiL framework,
which we use to comparatively evaluate several schemes devised to address computational variability among
distributed learning microcontroller-based devices, i.e., stragglers. Additionally, we release the code of our
implementation of TDMiL as an open-source project, which is compatible with common commercial offthe-shelf IoT hardware and a well-known open-access IoT testbed.
INDEX TERMS Distributed learning, federated learning (FL), Internet of Things (IoT), machine learning,
microcontrollers, TinyML-as-a-Service (TMLaaS).

neural networks (DNNs), has undergone a significant
transformation over the last decade, making an indelible
impact across various sectors. The standard deployment
of ML involves a data pipeline that utilizes a model —
a sophisticated framework of algorithms that process and
interpret data to make informed decisions. Such models are
initially subjected to an intensive training phase, equipping

Federated Learning (FL) emerges as a decentralized ML
technique that trains models across numerous collaborating
devices without centralized training, thereby safeguarding
privacy and enabling local customization. By leveraging such
decentralized strategies, the ML landscape is witnessing a
transformative shift, enabling global model training without
any exposing, transmitting (centralizing) of raw data. This
influential approach initially introduced in a seminal paper
on Federated Averaging [7], with subsequent research such
as [8] focusing on communication efficiency and enhanced
privacy via strategies such as sub-sampling and quantization.
The typical FL workflow involves selecting participating
devices, distributing a global model, training locally, sending
updates to a central server, aggregating for a new global
model, and iterating until convergence. This collaborative
learning process ensures that the resulting model is refined
and suitable for inference across all participating devices.
Throughout the FL process, communication protocols play
a pivotal role.
In addition to the general challenges encountered in FL,
such as heterogeneity stemming from differences in client
systems, including hardware resources and network availability (system heterogeneity), as well as variations in data
distributions across these devices (statistical heterogeneity),
tiny distributed ML must confront the overarching problem
of resource constraints. Moreover, solutions like FedProx
[9], aimed at mitigating heterogeneity under less constrained
conditions, raise questions. They necessitate the tracking of
both global and local models during a client’s update, posing
challenges in terms of its direct applicability.
A. CHALLENGES IN DISTRIBUTED LEARNING WITH
INTERCONNECTED MICROCONTROLLERS
Current research into FL for edge devices often glosses
over a critical aspect—the in-depth analysis of computational
and communication costs—imperative for devices with
limited resources. Additionally, EdgeML’s [10] work on
multi-hop wireless network-based learning underscores the
need for a robust communication stack for collaborative
learning, emphasizing that much of the existing research
primarily focuses on optimizing computational performance,
neglecting the importance of the communication layer.
More loosely related work on Gossip Learning (GL)
aims to further decentralize model aggregation, in a peer-topeer fashion. However, studies such as [11] point towards
the limitations of the GL framework, notably in terms of
delayed convergence, especially when dealing with diverse
data distributions. Further work on GossipFL [12] focused on
improving the convergence rate and accuracy in constrained
IoT environments.
Considering the diverse nature of wireless networks,
differences in hardware specifications among edge devices,
and varying data distributions across these devices, we can
make two key observations:
• The presence of computational variability entails the
occurrence of slow-performing workers, commonly
termed ‘‘stragglers’’. If not dealt with effectively, these
stragglers have the potential to significantly impact the
overall convergence of the training process, as indicated
in FedProx [9].
• Communication protocols need to be optimized not
only for resource constraints but also to be adaptable
across a diverse range of link layers. This includes
typical wireless technologies like Bluetooth Low Energy
(BLE), IEEE 802.15.4, and LoRa, as well as various
network technologies, including wired options such
as BACnet, PLC as specified in [13], and local bus
communications (USB, Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C),
etc.). Ensuring the use of secure protocols is crucial,
especially when handling the exchange of (privacy)
sensitive information among tiny devices reliably.
It’s important to note that existing studies in the domain
of low-resource distributed machine learning have not been
specifically designed to tackle these particular challenges.
Additionally, certain methodologies are limited by wired
setups [14], which poses scalability challenges and diminishes the overall effectiveness and the applicability of the
implementation.
Conversely, current approaches that handle heterogeneous networks, like FedProx [9], [15], have not been
explored within the context of resource-constrained devices.
Commonly employed communication stacks for federated
learning, such as Google’s Remote Procedure Call (gRPC)
[16], Websockets [17], etc., lack adaptability for highly constrained microcontroller-based IoT devices. These devices,
operating under stringent resource limitations, require specialized and lightweight communication frameworks. The
challenges arise from unique constraints such as limited
processing power, communication bandwidth, memory, and
energy resources. Addressing these challenges necessitates

In light of the challenges outlined above, there arises
a compelling need for a dedicated communication stack
tailored to meet the constraints of IoT devices, thus enabling
on-device learning. The remainder of this paper is organized
as follows. First, section II delves into existing research
on distributed learning with interconnected microcontrollers,
then section III explores available IoT communication
protocols. A selection thereof is presented, which is tailored

Then, a foundational scenario is presented to illustrate the

II. RELATED WORK
The typical machine learning pipeline feeds data into a model
(an artificial neural network), which generates classification
or regression outputs that drive further decision-making
processes. Machine learning is divided into two sequential
phases: the inference phase (using the model) and the
learning phase (training the model before use). While the
learning phase is more relevant to our present work, key
aspects of the inference phase also play a significant role.
Additionally, federating the training phase across distinct
machines introduces complexities related to networking and
distributed systems. Resource constraints on microcontrollers
necessitate specific optimizations throughout the process.
A. INFERENCE & MODEL OPTIMIZATION FOR
MICROCONTROLLERS
Inference optimization strategies can be coarsely categorized
in two levels: the algorithm level and the system scheduling
level [18]. At the algorithm level, the main focus is typically
model compression techniques, including pruning [4], [19],
low-rank decomposition of weights [20], [21], efficient
model architecture [4], [19], and quantization [20], [22]
in order to decrease resource consumption of models and
inference on-board microcontroller-based devices. On the
other hand, at system scheduling level, emphasis is put on the
allocation of computation and memory resources [4], [23],
or on scheduling between model operators, in prior work such
as [24]. In particular, intermediate results required for the
training stage (e.g., activations) can be cached in the memory
for subsequent gradient calculation. Another domain of prior
work such as [25] aims at integrating model optimization and
transpilers for diverse model architectures (such as TVM)
with common low-power embedded software platforms (such
as RIOT [26]) to support a wide range of Microcontroller
Units (MCUs).
B. MODEL TRAINING ON MICROCONTROLLERS
On-device training primitives pose an additional optimization
and integration challenges on microcontroller-based devices.
Prior work on frameworks such as (TinyTrain [27], TTE
[28], MCUNet [4], TinyOL [29], POET [30], etc.) have
explored model training on microcontroller-based devices,
proposing specialized model architectures [4], [29], optimized operators [28], [30], and sparse update algorithms [27],
[28] for efficient on-device training. However, these efforts
primarily focused on refining local models with local
datasets, lacking consideration for FL. In contrast, this work
introduces a general, model-agnostic FL framework, which
can seamlessly integrate as a plug-and-play extension for
existing on-device training frameworks.
C. DISTRIBUTED LEARNING ON MICROCONTROLLERS
Early work in the area of resource-constrained FL training
was presented in [31], using Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense1
boards. In a subsequent study [32], a cost-effective transfer
learning method was proposed for resource-constrained
devices within the FL framework. This method effectively
addresses storage challenges during on-device training. The
paper emphasizes the need to reduce the number of weight
parameters and promote sparsity for improved latency.
Additionally, it advocates for the development of a resilient
and cost-effective communication protocol to enhance overall
system efficiency.

Meta-learning, akin to transfer learning, facilitates fast
adaptation to new but similar tasks using limited data samples. It promotes collaborative learning by adjusting neural
network initialization. TinyReptile pioneers meta-learning
on resource-constrained devices, introduces a novel audio
classification dataset, and reduces resource consumption,
offering practical insights.
Similarly, TinyMetaFed [34] streamlines collaborative
neural network initialization training. It optimizes communication, safeguards privacy, enhances computational efficiency, and ensures robustness through selective transmission
of weight parameters. These advancements significantly
enhance TinyML, making it more adept for resourceconstrained IoT environments.
One observes that much of the aforementioned prior
research has primarily focused on computational aspects, [31]
brought attention to a bandwidth limitation in communication
between MCUs and the server, resulting from the use of a
serial port. This limitation leads to increased latency when
transferring from the server to the client compared to the
client-to-server direction. Likewise, [32] emphasized the
critical necessity of enhancing communication costs. The
TinyFL approach [14] proposes an alternative network protocol using a hybrid primary-subordinate I2C configuration
to address these challenges. However, this wired approach
raises significant scalability concerns and cannot effectively
leverage cross-device FL with a substantial number of
connected tiny devices. Other prior work such as [35]
propose efficient model serialization to aiming to decrease
network load due to model transfers over the network. On the
other hand, TinyMetaFed [34], takes a different approach to
alleviate communication costs in FL. Specifically, it suggests
transmitting a selective portion of model weights significant
for the overall training objective.
We observe that none such prior work addresses the
inherent issue of distributed learning asynchronicity, which
stems from slow-performing clients i.e. stragglers. This
observation highlights a notable gap in the existing literature,
which motivates our work.
D. OUR CONTRIBUTIONS
The work we present provides a principled approach to
distributed learning in the context of microcontroller-based
resource-constrained IoT environments, tackling its fundamental challenges, including constraints stemming from typical wireless communication and the issue of stragglers. Our
approach can complement aforementioned meta-learning
solutions, such as TinyReptile [33] and TinyMetaFed [34].
More in detail, our contributions are the following:
• Generic Resource-Constrained Communication for
Model & Parameter Transfer: We introduce a framework utilizing Concise Binary Object Representation
(CBOR) and Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
for efficient exchange of model updates (weights and
gradients) from arbitrary model architectures, facilitating various distributed learning approaches such as
synchronous and asynchronous FL.
• Handling
Asynchronous
Resource-Constrained
Stragglers: We introduce strategies for managing
asynchronous stragglers with varying workloads in
distributed networks, ensuring their effective integration
into the learning process.
• On-Board Training & Transfer Learning: We design
an embedded software platform enabling on-board
training and transfer learning on several families of
models: simple neural network Multi-Layer Perceptron
(MLP) architectures and for deeper networks like
LeNet-5, MobileNetV3-M, etc.
• Comparative Performance Evaluation: We evaluate
the straggler strategies using various standard FL benchmark datasets from the TinyML domain. We experimentally analyze computation, communication costs,
latency, and memory footprint on microcontroller-based
IoT devices.
• Open Source Implementation: We released our code,
which builds upon a popular microcontroller-based
embedded software platform (RIOT [36]) thus providing
a practical basis for future experimental research in this
domain.
III. BACKGROUND ON IoT DEVICES & PROTOCOLS
Microcontrollers
in
smart
appliances
operate
within
extremely limited processing capabilities. For instance,
as analyzed in [37], low CPU clock frequencies from 10 MHz
to 100 MHz and total memory budgets as small as 32 KiB
to 512 KiB are not uncommon. Additional hurdles must be
faced too: for instance, network links used by these devices
are often inadequate for the low latency and high throughput
required by most communication protocols. The conventional
stack, for instance combining TCP and HTTPS places a
significant burden on these devices, making inadequate for
resource-constrained environments.
Common FL frameworks like TensorFlow Federated [38]
and Flower [39] often rely on Google’s Remote Procedure
Call (gRPC) [16] as a core element in their communication stack. gRPC, an open-source framework, enables
language-agnostic communication between distributed systems using Protocol Buffers (protobuf) [40] for efficient data
serialization and transmission. However, deploying gRPC,
which entails using TCP and HTTPS, leads to communication
bottlenecks on typical resource-constrained devices.
Alternative protocols like WebSockets, which enable
lightweight, real-time communication between devices, and
Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT), designed
to minimize network bandwidth and power consumption,
are commonly considered for resource-constrained environments in FL scenarios. WebSockets facilitate bidirectional,
efficient data transfer, while MQTT operates on a publishsubscribe model, particularly suited for scenarios with low
bandwidth and unreliable networks. However, it’s important
to note that even these protocols, while effective, can be

We next survey the landscape of such protocols.
A. IoT COMMUNICATION PROTOCOL LANDSCAPE
Constrained IoT devices require optimizations of all the
components of the system, including communication protocols at different layers of the protocol stack. While the IoT
communication protocol landscape is still very polymorphic
and fragmented, there has been some solidification around IP
protocols standards from the Internet Engineering Task Force
(IETF), depicted in Figure 1. Let’s overview this landscape,
keeping in mind potential applicability to distributed learning
on microcontrollers.
• Convergence Layer: The Convergence Layer begins
with the Internet Protocol (IP), either IPv4 or IPv6,
which serves as a universal protocol. In order to
ensure compatibility with various IoT technologies,
there are adaptations made for constrained link-layer
connections, such as 802.15.4 through 6LoWPAN [41]
which enables to abstract away the variety of MAC
layers (for instance low-power radios such as IEEE
802.15.4, BLE, LoRa, etc.).
• Transport Protocols: Above IP, one finds transport
protocols such as UDP, TCP, and QUIC. DTLS provides
security for UDP, while TLS is an option on top of
TCP and is mandatory in QUIC. At this level, there
are clear tradeoffs between supporting very constrained
devices and providing convenient features. For instance,
TCP automatically manages multiple packets in parallel,
while QUIC (on top of UDP) allows for multiplexing
of streams. These features, however, require buffering
(RAM) and a more complex state machine (CPU).
FIGURE 1. Communication protocol landscape for IoT.
• Web Transfer Protocols: On top and along the transport
protocols, web transfer protocols are used for named
data exchanges. While on the less resource-constrained
machines protocols such as HTTP (secured with TLS)
or MQTT are used, on microcontroller-based IoT
devices more lightweight equivalents are used such
as, respectively, CoAP (secured with OSCORE or
DTLS) and MQTT-SN. Work such as [42] suggests
that in scenarios with highly dynamic clients, especially
during asynchronous events, the recommendation is to
utilize CoAP Pub/Sub rather than Message Queuing
Telemetry Transport-Sensor Networks (MQTT-SN), for
applications handling large payloads in environments
prone to high packet loss, which matches our scenario.
This preference is rooted in CoAP’s inherent support for
application layer fragmentation, effectively preventing
message drops caused by exceeding the allowed number
of retransmissions.
• Management Protocols: Above web transfer protocols,
another layer of protocols may be used to provide
remote management of devices, over the network. While
the less resource-constrained machines use protocols
such as gPRC, Websockets (or NetConf, SNMP, etc),
on microcontroller-based IoT devices more lightweight
alternatives are used such as Light-weight Machineto-Machine (LwM2M). For instance, LwM2M can use
CoAP as a transfer protocol and extend its capabilities
to unify management tasks, offering a standardized,
foundational IoT device management framework.
• Data Representation & Serialization Tools: Actual
application data transferred from one machine to another
(potentially based on different hardware!) must be represented and serialized in a convenient and interoperable
format. While the less resource-constrained machines
use serialization schemes such as JSON and XML,
on microcontroller-based IoT devices more lightweight
alternatives are used to incur fewer bits-over-the air, such
as with Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
binary formats or protobuf.
We now transition towards solution space, considering the
following simple yet generic scenario.
IV. SIMPLE SCENARIO WITH DISTRIBUTED LEARNING
The scenario, we will study for the remainder of the paper
involves a PC server without resource constraints (i.e. with
typical computer with several order of magnitude more
resources compared to a microcontroller), which is connected
via an arbitrary network to N microcontroller-based machine
learning clients, as depicted in Figure 2.
The FL server (the PC) takes on both the roles of orchestrator (registering clients, receiving/sending data to/from clients,
etc.) and aggregator (combining models from multiple
clients into a single aggregated model). Note that the roles
orchestrator and aggregator can either be split across separate

A. ASSUMPTIONS & LIMITS OF THE SCENARIO
In our scenario, we consider that individual network paths
(including their low-power segments) from a client to the
orchestrator are not significantly impacted by external,
internal or cross-interference or side-traffic.
• Basic network & node fault tolerance: We assume
network and node fault tolerance mechanisms typically
at work within the IoT network stack can handle
most cases. Such mechanisms include for e.g., CoAP
confirmable message retransmissions at the application
layer (see [43] section II-A), while complementary
mechanisms are provided in the routing protocol and in
the lower layers of the stack (e.g., IEEE 802.15.4 retransmissions [44]).
Indeed, prior work (see [45] Table 4) confirms that
large network transfers such as firmware updates of size
≈100 kB are transmitted without significant issues over
a comparable low-power link (IEEE 802.15.4 using the
6LoWPAN and CoAP). Other related work (see [25]
Table 3) indicates that models in typical TinyML model
zoos, incur comparable transfer load over the network,
i.e., ≈100 kB. Hence, while significant follow-up work
should be dedicated to develop additional mechanisms
to optimize specifically for FL the handling of network
disruptions and node failures, our work on the above
basic scenario should serve as solid base for such followup work.
• Number of clients: In the scenario we consider, and
in our experiments below, we tackle only a handful
of clients. However, since we assume that clients’
data transmissions do not significantly interfere with
one another, the bottleneck is essentially shifted to
the orchestrator’s (unconstrained) link to the network
and its (unconstrained) processing power. Therefore,
we do not further address this scalability issue in this
paper. Conversely, in cases where significant external
interference or cross-interference are observed for data
transmission from clients to the orchestrator, specific
additional mechanisms would be required to handle
these appropriately. Nevertheless, our work on the
simple scenario we describe should serve as a solid base
for such follow-up work.
V. SYSTEM DESIGN
A. COMMUNICATION STACK FOR DISTRIBUTED
LEARNING ON MICROCONTROLLERS
We design our communication stack on top of CoAP and
CBOR for serialization, which offers specific advantages
in addressing challenges posed by resource-constrained
environments. We leverage CoAP capabilities for reliable
asynchronous communication and blockwise transfer, which
cater both for dynamic settings and large payloads in face
small maximum packet size, and packet loss typical in IoT.
Additionally, we leverage CoAP support for Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS), securing efficiently IoT clientserver communications. We chose CBOR over protobuf for
serialization because prior work such as [35] hints that, for
arbitrary model sizes, best-case CBOR outperforms bestcase protobuf, which makes it favorable for optimal data
representation. The combination of CBOR and CoAP thus
streamlines IoT client-server data exchanges, and caters to
the unique needs of communication of heterogeneous, lowpower network links. The stack further allows seamless
integration with established FL frameworks like Flower [39],
TensorFlow Federated [38], etc. The shift we propose here
stems from our realization that these frameworks, in their
current configurations, primarily cater to unconstrained
server setups. In contrast, our framework takes a progressive
step forward and opens the door towards accommodating
even more diverse configurations, such as (in future work)
hosting the orchestrator/aggregator on constrained devices
too, or designing and implementing model aggregation
without a central agent at all (e.g. Gossip Learning).
B. MODEL SERIALIZATION
As the orchestrator is in full control of the distributed FL
process, it requires multiple types of messages exchanged to
fully control the learning process on the clients. We define
multiple CBOR encoded messages for this purpose. By using
CBOR as message serialization format the message size

As part of the communication stack, we design a number of
messages passed between clients and the central server. A key
part of this is the efficient serialization of the ML models. Part
of the requirements is that the message must allow for partial
updates of the ML model, without the need to transfer the full
ML models over the network.
To achieve this, we split a ML model into a logical set
of operators used within the model. Each operator has one
or more sets of parameters, or weights. Our serialization
contains both the set of parameters and the operators, with
the operators containing a reference to which parameters are
used by the operator. Note that parameters can be shared
between different operators where possible. A full model
update contains the full set of parameters and operators in
the model, while a partial update only transfers the set of
operators and parameters required for the update useful in
case of transfer learning task.
The ML models contain an Universally Unique Identifier
(UUID) as handle, used in the communication messages.
Together with the layer and parameter identifiers, a client is
able to request an individual set of parameters from the server
for the purpose of partial model updates.
C. COMPONENT INTERACTION
The CoAP interaction between the clients and the orchestrator using CoAP leverages a mixed strategy with both the
GET + Observe mechanism and FETCH-type [46] requests
to minimize the data overhead between the clients and the
orchestrator as described in Figure 3.
On start-up, the clients register themselves using the CoAP
resource directory protocol [47] with the orchestrator. This
provides the orchestrator with a full view of which clients are
available for the FL process.
After a client has registered, the orchestrator establishes
a bidirectional message channel with the client based on a
CoAP GET + Observe [48] request and POST requests to
a /ev endpoint on the client. Via this channel, a client can
report an event to the orchestrator as one of the responses
to the GET + Observe request. The orchestrator can send
events to the client using a regular CoAP POST request.
This channel is used as a bidirectional event and RPC
channel, specifically for short commands and events in our
design.
Via the bidirectional message channel, the clients can
for example be instructed to fetch a new model from
the orchestrator. Clients download the model via CoAP
FETCH requests at the /ml endpoint provided by the
orchestrator, with the payload in the initial FETCH request
specifying which model and, when needed, which operators
are requested. The models are transferred via the block-wise
mechanism by CoAP to keep the network packets within the
limitations of the typical constrained network links such as
IEEE 802.15.4 networks.
The orchestrator manages the FL clients on behalf of the
aggregator. The aggregator provides the orchestrator with
new model updates and retrieves the training meta-data
from the orchestrator. While the aggregator is aware of
successive model updates based on rounds, the orchestrator
and clients do not need to be aware of relations between
models provided and operate on models based on their
UUID.
D. DISTRIBUTED LEARNING SCHEMES

their raw local data directly to the server, compromising data privacy, our work emphasizes the exchange
of trained model parameters instead of raw datasets.
We consider the following approaches for distributed
learning:
• Algorithm 1: Synchronous - FedAvg approach [7]).
Clients train local models using their datasets and
send model updates to the central server. The server
aggregates these updates and returns the aggregated
model. However, updates from slow-performing clients
(stragglers) are discarded.

VI. TDMiL IMPLEMENTATION
Our implementation consists of systems aspects on the one
hand, and on the other hand, on data sets and data handling
aspects.
A. SYSTEM
Our implementation consists of multiple components spread
across different systems.
1) MODEL AGGREGATOR
The model aggregator is a central entity responsible for
combining locally trained models from participating clients.
One common aggregation method is weighted averaging
applied in [7], where the updates from each client are
weighted based on the ratio of local data points to the total
data points across all clients.

2) ORCHESTRATOR
Our custom orchestrator, ‘‘CoAPerator’’, is a key actor in our
distributed learning setup. It manages CoAP-enabled client
devices and provides the interface for the Model Aggregator
to facilitate the FL algorithms. Developed with FastAPI [49]
and aiocoap [50], CoAPerator is a Python-based application
that seamlessly integrates robust functionality, providing
streamlined device management within the CoAP ecosystem.
It allows clients to register themselves with the orchestrator, through a CoAP resource directory service. From there
on the orchestrator sets up a bidirectional communication
channel over CoAP to manage the registered clients by
providing RPC-style commands to the clients. Furthermore,
it provides the endpoints for providing ML models to the
clients. As previously mentioned the orchestrator exposes
these services via CoAP.
Interaction with the orchestrator by administrators and by
the model aggregator does not occur via the constrained
network used by the clients. To ease interaction with this
interface, it is provided via a REST-like API using HTTP and
JSON. This interface is used to upload new models to the
orchestrator, for example by the Model Aggregator when a
new round is to be started.
3) FL CLIENTS
The FL clients run on constrained devices with firmware
consisting of: RIOT [36] as an embedded operating system;
An IPv6-enabled network stack; A CoAP stack; and the
necessary primitives for FL and ML.
The clients are pre-provisioned with the location of the
orchestrator and on start-up contact the orchestrator for
registration. After registration, the clients expect a channel to
be established, and initiated by the orchestrator in response
to the completed registration process.
The clients are able to update the parameter and configuration of the FL process on the fly, based on instructions
from the orchestrator. However, updating the structure of
the deployed models is not possible without resorting to a
firmware update.

B. DATA HANDLING
Tabular Dataset – We implemented min-max scaling to
normalize features within the range of 0 to 1. Given the
relatively small size of the original tabular datasets (iris
[51], wine [52], and breast cancer [53]) shown in Table 1,
comprising a few hundred data samples, we employed a data
augmentation technique. This involved applying Gaussian
noise with a mean of zero and a standard deviation ranging
from 0.05 to 0.25, effectively expanding the size of the
original dataset.
The augmented dataset was subsequently utilized for both
training and validation purposes, employing an 80-20% split.
This divided dataset was then further partitioned among five
clients. The data distribution among these clients could either
be independent and identically distributed (IID) or non-IID,
and we will showcase results for both scenarios. The original
dataset remained unchanged and was utilized as the test set
for the final evaluation (presented in Table 6) of the model
trained in a distributed manner.
To analyze the impact of varying levels of diversity across
clients, we employed the widely recognized technique of
Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) [54]. By adjusting the
hyperparameter α, we could control the diversity among
clients, thus creating local datasets that maximally capture
real-world variations. Specifically, we set α to a low value,
10−6, to depict an extreme scenario where diversity across
clients is high. This approach results in clients receiving data
points with imbalanced label classes in the non-IID case,
as opposed to balanced labels in the IID case. This is evident
when examining the class distributions across clients within
our experiments: in the IID case, the height of the bars in
histograms is relatively comparable across classes, while in
the non-IID case, the heights vary significantly, indicating
statistical heterogeneity among clients. This variation is
illustrated in Figure 4,Figure 5, and Figure 6. The data used in
the experiments can be accessed through our code repository.
MNIST Dataset – This dataset is a widely used collection
of handwritten digits (28 × 28 pixel, grayscale) that serves

VII. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
A. HARDWARE SETUP
CoAPerator, our Python-based orchestrator, runs on a basic
laptop running Linux. Our TDMiL clients are tested running
on several commercially available boards such as the

(rpi-pico) and STM32F746 discovery board (stm32f746gdisco). For instance, the nrf52840dk is based on an Arm

STM32F746 board is equipped with a powerful MCU -

Note on generality & reproducibility: as TDMiL is based

B. NETWORK SETUP
We test our implementations interconnected as such: one
CoAPerator instance is connected in hub-and-spoke fashion
(star topology) to five TDMiL clients as shown in Figure 7.
We test our different schemes for (i) distributed learning
and (ii) model aggregation on top of this setup.
Note on generality & reproducibility: our experiments can
be reproduced in two easy ways. The first way is using
five RIOT native instances [56] and tap interfaces together
with ZEP (Zigbee Encapsulation Protocol, used to tunnel
6LowPAN over UDP). This topology can be emulated and
tested on any Linux machine. Another way is to actually
book five nrf52840dk boards co-located on the open-access
testbed IoT-lab [57], [58] and to flash them with TDMiL
client firmware.

We used RIOT version 2023.10, with compiler a toolchain
based on GCC 12.2.

D. METHODOLOGY FOR STRAGGLERS
To simulate stragglers, deliberate delays were introduced
between local epochs, leading the orchestrator to potentially
direct clients to cease local training. In this context,
incomplete work from paused clients undergoes one of two
variants, outlined in subection V-D: either it is discarded
entirely (Algorithm 1), or it is effectively weighed by the
aggregator (Algorithm 2).
1) IMPLEMENTED MODELS & ON-BOARD TRAINING
In order to test our design on relevant models, we picked
the one that had a few ‘‘toy’’ models based on a basic
Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture, and on the other
hand, LeNet5 and MobileNetV3-M models, which are more
complex models used in TinyML literature (e.g., see model
zoo used in [25]).
• MLP models: We have implemented a three-layer
MLP with a variable number of neurons tailored to
different tabular datasets with input, hidden and output
dimensions as [4, 2, 3], [13, 10, 3] and [30, 10, 2] for
the respective iris, wine, and breast cancer datasets.
For the classification tasks with a cross-entropy loss,
the number of trainable parameters for the respective
datasets are as follows: 19, 173, and 332 parameters.
In this straightforward configuration, we have manually
crafted the gradient computation. The model’s weights
and biases are updated using a stochastic gradient
descent (SGD) approach, and the computations are
performed in an Eigen [59] C++ based library. For a
more in-depth understanding of the implementation, the
code can be accessed through the provided link.
• LeNet5 [60]: This representative early model with
about 44.6K parameters specialized in classifying handwritten digits is a simple convolutional neural network
with two convolutional layers and three fully connected
layers. It consumes 28 × 28 grayscale image and
produces likelihoods over 10 digit classes.
• MobileNetV3-M:
This
model
is
based
on
MobileNetV3 [61], an advanced backbone focuses on
optimizing mobile and embedded vision applications
efficiently. It leverages depth-wise separable convolution to achieve significantly higher efficiency compared
to standard convolution (roughly 8 to 9 times less
computation) with only a slight decrease in accuracy.
In this study, we tailored it to mirror the input, output and
classifier structures of LeNet5, yielding approximately
112.8K parameters. The classifier contains 84 and
10 neuron units in the last two fully connected
layers, respectively. This customization of MobileNetV3
decreased drastically the resource consumption of tiny
devices with slightly degradation of model accuracy on
MNIST dataset. For the sake of clarity, we use the name
‘‘MobileNetV3-M’’ for this tailored model in this work.
Transfer learning setup – Both LeNet5 and MobileNetV3-
M were pre-trained on the MNIST dataset, then transpiled
and deployed on constrained devices using U-TOE [25]. For
purpose of experiments, only the weights of the final layer
(classifier) were reinitialized on uniform distribution and
federated fine-tuned on devices. We also used cross-entropy
for loss calculation and SGD optimizer with a learning rate
of 0.01 and a weight decay of 0.01 for model training.
VIII. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
A. RESOURCE CONSUMPTION ON DEVICE
We measured storage (FLASH) and memory (RAM) use,
as well as compute latency for each model in Table 2,
Table 3 and Table 4. Peculiarly, the MLP model consumed
a disproportionate amount of memory and more storage
than expected based on the number of model parameters.
As it turns out, dynamic-sized types from the Eigen library
pre-allocate relatively large vectors and matrices. Further
optimizations are needed here for low-end MCUs.
While the models exhibit similar memory and storage
usage across the three MCUs, the compute latency varies
significantly due to differences in core frequencies and
instruction sets. The stm32f746g-disco board (Cortex-M7),
with its advanced architecture, and highest core frequency,
achieved the best compute performance on all models.
One notable outlier is the RP2040-based (Cortex-M0+)
Raspberry Pi Pico board. Despite having a higher core clock
frequency than the nrf52840dk board (133 MHz vs. 64
MHz), its compute latency is approximately 10× slower on
LeNet5 and MobileNetV3-M. This is due to the RP2040
microcontroller lacking a hardware floating-point unit (FPU),
leading to a significant performance drop when testing
unquantized models using floating points.

C. FL RESULTS WITH STRAGGLERS
We now compare Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 when facing
stragglers as specified in Section VII-D.
1) BITS OVER-THE-AIR
The primary payload, encoded in CBOR, comprises mostly
float-represented model parameters during over-the-air transmission. Control data makes up the remaining portion
(Figure 10), transmitted via CoAP in 64-byte blocks.
FETCH requests are employed to request models, and the
corresponding responses include CBOR encoded payloads,
with the associated costs elaborated in Table 5. We conducted
a controlled experiment involving two stragglers in each
round. Algorithm 1 minimizes communication overhead by
leveraging the orchestrator’s ability to execute fetch requests
exclusively on clients that have completed local training,
as determined by the status of all clients. This results in a
notable reduction in the number of fetch requests, decreasing
from 5 to 3 in comparison to Algorithm 2. The total
number of requests and responses between all clients and
the orchestrator remains constant at 5 for both algorithms.
Notably, Algorithm 1 achieves a lower exchanged bits per
round by strategically excluding stragglers from contributing
their model updates for aggregation.

IX. DISCUSSION & FUTURE WORK
One significant limitation of our system thus far is the single
point of failure presented by the FL server. This centralized
architecture poses risks to system reliability and scalability,
particularly in dynamic IoT environments. To mitigate this
issue, we propose enabling model aggregation without a
central agent, in a peer-to-peer fashion, such as Gossip Learning (GL). This approach would distribute the aggregation
process across multiple nodes, enhancing system resilience
and potentially improving network efficiency. Notably,

while our implementation of CoAPerator on Linux is not
suitable for microcontroller-based devices due to resource
constraints, our implementation of TDMiL clients on RIOT
provides an excellent foundation for further development.
This RIOT-based implementation can be leveraged to design,
implement, and comparatively evaluate fully decentralized,
peer-to-peer model aggregation schemes on various wireless
microcontroller-based IoT devices. Such an evaluation would
offer valuable insights into the performance and scalability of
decentralized learning in resource-constrained environments,
focusing on the challenges specific to microcontroller-based
systems.
Another critical limitation of TDMiL is its potential
vulnerability in terms of privacy. While the most sensitive
information (raw data) is indeed protected by not leaving the
devices on which it is produced and trained, the models themselves and their parameters (e.g., the weights) also constitute
sensitive information that may need to remain confidential.
Compromised model aggregators could potentially leak the
models (or parameters) provided by the clients, leading to
unauthorized access to information about the training data.
Currently, TDMiL does not provide any mechanism to ensure
such confidentiality, which is a significant concern in many
real-world applications, especially those involving sensitive
or proprietary data.
In future work, we plan to focus on privacy-enhancing
techniques for TDMiL and CoAPerator to address these
concerns. Specifically, we aim to augment the framework
with a robust layer for privacy protection based on Differential Privacy (DP) techniques and secure aggregation
strategies using homomorphic encryption. DP would allow
us to add controlled noise to the model updates, providing a
provable privacy guarantee while maintaining useful learning
outcomes. Homomorphic encryption, on the other hand,
would enable computations on encrypted data, ensuring
that the aggregator can combine model updates without
accessing the raw parameters. Both the design and practical
implementation of such a layer present significant challenges
on microcontroller-based devices, given their limited computational resources. Nevertheless, addressing these challenges

Our solution is specifically engineered to operate efficiently within the constraints of low-bandwidth, lossy wireless networks, facilitating seamless interconnection among
resource-limited devices built on diverse microcontroller
architectures.
At the core of our research lies a critical challenge
inherent to fleets of microcontroller-based IoT devices: the
computational disparity among distributed learning nodes,
commonly referred to as the ‘‘straggler’’ problem. Through
rigorous experimentation with TDMiL, we conducted a
comprehensive comparative analysis of multiple novel
schemes devised to mitigate this issue. These experiments
yield valuable insights into optimizing distributed learning
processes within heterogeneous IoT ecosystems, paving
the way for more efficient and robust AI deployments in
resource-constrained environments.
To foster innovation and collaboration in this rapidly evolving domain, we have released our TDMiL implementation
as open-source, portable software. This strategic decision
empowers researchers and practitioners to not only reproduce
our findings but also to extend and adapt our work to diverse
hardware configurations and application scenarios. By leveraging either proprietary setups or established open-access
IoT testbeds, the community can build upon our foundation,
accelerating progress in the field of distributed AI for IoT
systems.
Our work represents a significant stride towards harmonizing the ambitious demands of AI with the inherent
limitations of IoT deployments. As these technological
domains continue to evolve and converge, the framework
we’ve developed serves as a robust platform for future innovations in distributed learning on resource-constrained devices.
By addressing the unique challenges at the intersection of AI
and IoT, we contribute to the broader vision of ubiquitous,
intelligent systems that can operate efficiently at the edge of
networks.

Sensor systems
Texture Perception Using Tactile Sensing Glove Based on PVDF Sensors and
Machine Learning
Yahya Abbass∗
, Christian Gianoglio∗
, Haydar Al Haj Ali
, Moustafa Saleh,
and Maurizio Valle∗∗
Department of Electrical, Electronic, Telecommunications Engineering, and Naval Architecture (DITEN), University of Genoa, 16145
Genova, Italy
∗Member, IEEE
∗∗Senior Member, IEEE
Manuscript received 26 April 2024; revised 31 May 2024; accepted 15 June 2024. Date of publication 24 June 2024; date of current version 2 July 2024.
Abstract—This letter presents a tactile sensing glove based
on piezoelectric sensors, embedded electronics, and a machine learning (ML)-based approach for texture discrimination. Various time and frequency features were extracted
and evaluated through ML algorithms, including support
vector machines (SVM), single-layer feed-forward neural
networks, and 1-D convolution neural networks. Six naturalistic surface textures were explored by simply sliding the index ﬁnger of seven participants on the surfaces with
and without the tactile glove. Results showed that by employing an SVM classiﬁer trained on both time and frequency features, a discrimination accuracy of 87% is achieved while utilizing only two sensors. Furthermore, this
discrimination behavior was found to exceed the participants (76.79%) when attempting to discriminate the textures
using their somatosensory system. This study demonstrated the capability of the tactile sensing glove in extracting
tactile information, opening up interesting perspectives for wearable feedback systems for post-stroke rehabilitation.
Index Terms—Sensor systems, machine learning (ML), tactile sensing glove, textural features, texture discrimination, wearable sensing
systems.
I. INTRODUCTION
Humans can grasp, feel, and explore diverse objects and surfaces,
and simultaneously infer their material properties—a challenging set
of tasks for post-stroke patients characterized by motor injuries associated with sensory deﬁcits. These sensory deﬁcits can affect different
modalities of sensation and control, including pressure and proprioception [1]. Different technologies have been proposed for sensory
restoration and post-stroke rehabilitation [2], [3]. However, it remains
challenging to simulate human tactile perception as the sense of touch
not only reﬂects the tactile response to external physical stimuli (e.g.,
temperature and pressure) but also includes neural processing based
on extraction and analysis of information, such as recognition of
texture and roughness through tactile sensation [4]. It has been proved
that sensory restoration with repetitive detection of various textures
improved proprioceptive, tactile discriminative, and object recognition
senses along with postural control [5], [6], [7]. Exposing patients to
differenttextures,thesensorypathwaysthatprocesstactileinformation
are continuously stimulated, reﬁning the sensory receptors and neural
circuits responsible for detecting and interpreting tactile stimuli. This
is strongly related to the fact that surface texture is an important object
property that signiﬁcantly affects the wear resistance and fatigue life of
components [8]. To this end, texture perception and learning methods
for embodiment intelligence can be designed by developing large-scale
tactile sensing arrays [9] and machine learning (ML) techniques [10].
Corresponding author: Yahya Abbass (e-mail: yahya.abbass@unige.it).
Associate Editor: Sri-Rajasekhar Kothapalli.
Digital Object Identiﬁer 10.1109/LSENS.2024.3418500
Soft sensors improve the performance, reliability, and biocompatibility of human–machine interface with human bodies [11], [12].
In particular, tremendous efforts have been made to recognize the
material’s properties (e.g. Hardness [13]) using intelligent tactile
sensors [4]. For instance, various types of artiﬁcial tactile sensors
combined with ML techniques have been developed to capture the
surface texture [8]. For example, researchers in [14] utilized a ﬁnger
cap equipped with triboelectric sensors and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for the identiﬁcation of artiﬁcial textures and materials.
Similarly, Qu et al. [15] integrated triboelectric sensors into a rigid
ﬁnger and used a linear discriminant analysis algorithm to identify the
textures and material. Piezoelectric sensors exhibit a high-frequency
range similar to that of mechanoreceptors in human skin [16], making
them well-suited for surface texture detection. In [17], it has been
demonstrated that combining piezoelectric sensors and support vector
machines SVMs or k-nearest neighbors is useful for texture exploration. However, most of the works in the literature proposed bulky
texture classiﬁcation systems and methods that are computationally
demanding. Moreover, these approaches were validated in a controlled
manner, in which the sliding velocity and force were controlled and
used to identify artiﬁcial textures and materials. This is important as
the sliding action is crucial for the discrimination of textures [18];
therefore, the touch force and velocity affect the perception of its
roughness since they may alter the intensity and frequency content
of the vibrations it elicits in the skin [19]. For that reason, it is crucial
to consider the sliding velocity and force while developing a tactile
sensing system for texture identiﬁcation. Based on this, this letter
attempts to develop a sensing system capable of restoring texture
